- Cost Takeout Sprint: labor cost reduction options (layoffs, furloughs,
  salary reductions) with legal and severance cost analysis; supplier
  renegotiation playbook for top 20 vendors by spend
- Working Capital Release: AR acceleration (factoring, early payment
  discounts), inventory liquidation plan, AP extension program
- EBITDA Bridge to Stabilization: show the path from current negative
  EBITDA to EBITDA-positive within 90 days — which levers get you there?

Capital Structure Remediation (90 Days – 12 Months):
- Out-of-Court Options: amendment & extend, covenant waiver, debt
  exchange offer, equity injection from existing sponsors or new capital
- In-Court Options: Chapter 11 pre-pack vs. free-fall; estimated timeline,
  cost, and professional fee budget ($M); going-concern viability threshold
- Stakeholder Alignment: map each creditor class to their likely position
  (cooperative vs. adversarial); identify the fulcrum creditor

Format as an AlixPartners CRO Playbook with:
  • 13-Week Cash Flow Forecast (week-by-week table)
  • Liquidity Action Priority Matrix (Impact vs. Speed)
  • EBITDA Stabilization Bridge
  • Capital Structure Options Comparison (Out-of-Court vs. Chapter 11)
  • Stakeholder Alignment Map

My inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INDUSTRY | LTM REVENUE | LTM EBITDA (NEGATIVE OR LOW) |
            TOTAL DEBT | CASH ON HAND | NEXT DEBT MATURITY OR COVENANT TEST DATE |
            PRIMARY CAUSE OF DISTRESS]

title: The FTI Consulting Chapter 11 Restructuring & Plan of Reorganization
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Managing Director at FTI Consulting's Economic & Financial
Consulting practice, serving as financial advisor to a creditors' committee
or debtor-in-possession (DIP) in a complex Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceeding.

I need a comprehensive Chapter 11 restructuring analysis and Plan of
Reorganization (POR) framework.

Structure the analysis:

Pre-Filing Assessment:
- Going-concern value vs. liquidation value analysis: build both scenarios;
  the difference is the "reorganization value" that justifies Chapter 11
  over Chapter 7 liquidation
- DIP Financing sizing: how much new money is required to fund operations
  through the Chapter 11 process? DIP facility terms (superpriority lien,
  roll-up of prepetition debt, milestones, fees)
- First-Day Motions priority: identify the critical orders needed on Day 1
  (cash collateral, DIP financing, critical vendor payments, employee wages)

Valuation & Plan Feasibility:
- Enterprise valuation for POR purposes using 3 methodologies:
  (1) DCF with court-appropriate WACC and terminal assumptions
  (2) Comparable company analysis with distressed peer adjustments
  (3) Precedent transaction analysis for similar Chapter 11 exits
- Reorganization value allocation: EV → secured debt recovery → unsecured
  recovery → equity value (if any); show cents-on-dollar by class
- New capital structure design: post-emergence debt capacity at 4–5x EBITDA;
  new equity distribution among creditor classes
- Feasibility test: can the reorganized company service its post-emergence
  debt and maintain adequate liquidity? Project 3 years post-emergence

Creditor Negotiation Framework:
- Absolute Priority Rule: who is in-the-money and out-of-the-money?
- Intercreditor disputes: identify likely objecting classes and their
  negotiating leverage
- Plan support agreement (PSA) strategy: which creditors to lock up first
  and how to structure the RSA (Restructuring Support Agreement)
- Timeline: filing → first-day orders → 341 meeting → disclosure statement
  approval → plan confirmation → emergence (typical 6–18 months)

Format as an FTI Chapter 11 Advisory Memorandum with:
  • Going-Concern vs. Liquidation Value Table
  • Reorganization Value Waterfall (by creditor class)
  • Post-Emergence Capital Structure & Feasibility Model
  • Creditor Class Recovery Analysis
  • Chapter 11 Process Timeline

My inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INDUSTRY | LTM REVENUE | LTM EBITDA | DEBT STRUCTURE
            BY TRANCHE WITH AMOUNTS | PRIMARY REASON FOR FILING | KNOWN CREDITOR DISPUTES]

title: The McKinsey Corporate Performance Transformation (CPT) Program
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Partner at McKinsey & Company's Transformation Practice who
leads large-scale corporate performance transformations for underperforming
companies that are not in financial distress but have chronically lagged
peers on ROIC, TSR, and organic growth.

I need a comprehensive corporate performance transformation program design
for a company that needs a step-change improvement in financial performance
without the urgency of a liquidity crisis.

Design the transformation:

Performance Diagnostic:
- Value creation gap: quantify the TSR underperformance vs. sector peers
  over 1, 3, and 5 years; decompose into: revenue growth gap, margin gap,
  multiple gap, and capital efficiency gap
- Root cause hypothesis tree: use a MECE issue tree to identify whether
  underperformance is caused by (a) strategy, (b) operations, (c) talent
  and organization, (d) capital allocation, or (e) external factors
- Peer benchmarking: rank the company on 10 key financial metrics vs.
  10 closest peers; identify the 3 metrics with the largest gaps

Transformation Architecture:
- Design the transformation across 4 horizons:
  H1 (0–6 months): Performance Baseline & Quick Wins — initiatives that
    generate EBITDA improvement within 6 months; no capital required
  H2 (6–18 months): Core Business Excellence — operational improvements,
    commercial productivity, and organizational effectiveness
  H3 (18–36 months): Strategic Repositioning — portfolio changes, M&A,
    new business models, digital transformation
  H4 (3–5 years): Sustained Outperformance — culture embedding, talent
    pipeline, continuous improvement operating system
- For each horizon: total EBITDA/TSR impact, investment required, key
  milestones, and required management capabilities

Execution Infrastructure:
- Transformation Office (TMO) design: governance, cadence, reporting
- Change management: the 7 elements of successful transformation
  (McKinsey's "Influence Model" applied)
- Performance management: new KPI framework tied to value creation;
  consequence management for underperforming leaders
- Talent strategy: who needs to be replaced, developed, or recruited
  to execute the transformation?

Format as a McKinsey CPT Program Launch Document with:
  • Value Creation Gap Waterfall (TSR decomposition)
  • Root Cause Hypothesis Tree
  • Transformation Initiative Portfolio (Horizon × EBITDA Impact × Investment)
  • TMO Governance Structure
  • 5-Year Value Creation Roadmap

My inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INDUSTRY | REVENUE | CURRENT EBITDA MARGIN |
            PEER MEDIAN EBITDA MARGIN | TSR VS SECTOR | PRIMARY PERFORMANCE CONCERN]

title: The Macquarie Infrastructure Investment Underwriting Model
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director at Macquarie Asset Management's Infrastructure
division — the world's largest infrastructure asset manager — responsible
for underwriting greenfield and brownfield infrastructure investments in
energy, transportation, utilities, and digital infrastructure.

I need a comprehensive infrastructure investment underwriting analysis and
financial model for a specific infrastructure asset or project.

Underwrite the investment:

Asset Quality & Regulatory Framework:
- Asset type classification: (1) Regulated utility, (2) Long-term contracted,
  (3) Merchant/market-exposed — rate the revenue certainty and inflation
  linkage for each type
- Regulatory framework analysis: rate-of-return regulation, revenue cap
  regulation, or price cap? Key regulatory reset risk and RAB (Regulatory
  Asset Base) methodology
- Concession / contract terms: duration, revenue floor, volume guarantees,
  force majeure provisions, termination compensation

Cash Flow Modeling:
- Revenue model: regulated revenue or contracted revenue; inflation
  escalation (CPI-linked, PPI-linked, or fixed); volume / throughput
  assumptions with downside stress
- Operating cost structure: fixed vs. variable; O&M cost benchmarks;
  lifecycle maintenance capex schedule (major maintenance reserve)
- EBITDA margin: benchmark vs. comparable assets; operating leverage
- Capital structure: target Debt/EBITDA or Debt/RAB; typical infra
  financing: senior secured project finance, EIB/IFI debt, green bonds
- DSCR (Debt Service Coverage Ratio): minimum DSCR covenant; model
  DSCR under base and stress; identify the minimum revenue required
  to maintain DSCR ≥ 1.20x
- Equity return metrics: levered IRR, equity yield (cash yield on cost),
  and MOIC over the hold period (typically 10–25 years for infra)

Risk Assessment:
- Construction risk (for greenfield): contractor credit quality, fixed-price
  EPC contract, performance bonds, delay LDs
- Operating risk: technology risk, counterparty risk (offtaker credit),
  input cost risk (fuel, commodities)
- ESG & physical climate risk: exposure to extreme weather, stranded asset
  risk from energy transition, carbon pricing risk

Format as a Macquarie Infrastructure Investment Committee Paper with:
  • Asset Profile & Regulatory Framework Summary
  • Financial Model Summary (Revenue / EBITDA / DSCR / IRR by year)
  • Risk Matrix (Risk | Probability | Impact | Mitigation)
  • Capital Structure & Financing Plan
  • Investment Recommendation with Return Sensitivity Table

My inputs: [ASSET TYPE | COUNTRY/JURISDICTION | ASSET SIZE (EV) | CONTRACTED VS.
            MERCHANT REVENUE % | CONCESSION DURATION | TARGET EQUITY IRR |
            PRIMARY RISK CONCERN]

title: The Blackstone Real Estate Private Equity (BREP) Acquisition Underwriter
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Vice President at Blackstone Real Estate Partners (BREP) —
the world's largest real estate private equity firm — who underwrites large
commercial real estate acquisitions across office, logistics, residential,
hospitality, and data center sectors.

I need a full real estate private equity underwriting analysis for a
commercial property acquisition.

Underwrite the deal:

Market & Asset Analysis:
- Market fundamentals: supply and demand dynamics in the target submarket;
  vacancy rate trend; rent growth trajectory (nominal and real); new supply
  pipeline as % of stock
- Asset quality assessment: physical condition score, location grade (A/B/C),
  tenant mix quality, WALT (Weighted Average Lease Term), and lease expiry
  profile
- ESG & sustainability positioning: LEED/BREEAM certification, energy
  intensity vs. benchmark, capex required to meet future sustainability
  standards (avoid stranded asset risk)

Financial Underwriting:
- In-Place NOI (Net Operating Income): Gross Revenue − Vacancy −
  OpEx − Management Fees − CapEx Reserve
- Going-In Cap Rate: In-Place NOI ÷ Purchase Price vs. market cap rates
- Value-Add Business Plan: identify the 3–5 initiatives to grow NOI
  (lease-up vacancy, mark-to-market rents, capex improvement program,
  operational efficiency) — with cost and NOI impact for each
- Exit Cap Rate assumption with sensitivity (±50bps) and rationale
- Waterfall Model: LP/GP structure with preferred return hurdle,
  catch-up, and carried interest split; calculate LP and GP returns
  in Base / Bull / Bear

Financing Structure:
- Senior mortgage: LTV (target 55–65%), DSCR, IO vs. amortizing,
  rate (fixed vs. floating + cap), and recourse provisions
- Mezzanine or preferred equity if applicable
- Total return metrics: Levered IRR, Equity Multiple, Cash-on-Cash Yield
  in Year 1, Year 3, and at exit

Scenario Analysis:
- Bear case: NOI 15% below base + exit cap rate 50bps wider → IRR impact
- Bull case: full lease-up achieved 12 months early + compression of exit
  cap rate 25bps → IRR upside
- Stress test: what rent decline % causes the loan to breach DSCR covenant?

Format as a BREP Investment Committee Underwriting Package with:
  • Asset Summary & Market Comparables Table
  • Financial Underwriting Model (Year-by-Year NOI, Debt Service, Cash Flow)
  • Waterfall Distribution Analysis
  • IRR Sensitivity Table (Entry Cap Rate × Exit Cap Rate)
  • Investment Recommendation

My inputs: [PROPERTY TYPE | LOCATION | PURCHASE PRICE | IN-PLACE NOI |
            VACANCY RATE | WALT | TARGET HOLD PERIOD | VALUE-ADD STRATEGY |
            TARGET LEVERED IRR]

title: The GIC / Temasek Sovereign Wealth Fund Infrastructure Allocation Strategy
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Portfolio Manager at GIC (Singapore's sovereign wealth fund)
responsible for the Real Assets portfolio, which allocates to infrastructure,
real estate, and natural resources with a 20-year investment horizon and an
inflation-protection mandate.

I need a comprehensive infrastructure allocation strategy for a sovereign
wealth fund looking to increase its infrastructure weighting.

Design the allocation strategy:

Strategic Asset Allocation for Infrastructure:
- Justify the optimal infrastructure allocation (% of total fund) using:
  (a) Return expectations: historical real returns for infrastructure
      vs. equities, bonds, and PE over 10-year, 20-year periods
  (b) Portfolio construction benefits: low correlation to equities,
      inflation linkage (CPI beta of infrastructure vs. other asset classes),
      and cash yield characteristics (yield vs. duration)
  (c) Liability matching: how infrastructure cash flows match a SWF's
      long-term obligations and spending rules
- Infrastructure sub-asset class allocation: Core / Core-Plus / Value-Add /
  Opportunistic — recommended weighting for a SWF and expected return/risk
  for each bucket

Market Opportunity Assessment:
- Global infrastructure investment gap: quantify the OECD/McKinsey-estimated
  annual infrastructure investment shortfall; where is private capital most
  needed and most welcome?
- Sector allocation: Energy Transition (renewables, grid, storage),
  Digital (data centers, fiber, towers), Transport (airports, ports, toll
  roads), Social (PPP healthcare, schools), Water — rate each for:
  return potential, competition for deals, ESG alignment, and political risk
- Geographic allocation: OECD Core markets vs. Emerging Market
  infrastructure — risk/return trade-off, currency considerations, and
  political risk mitigation (MIGA, bilateral investment treaties)

Portfolio Construction:
- Direct vs. co-investment vs. fund investment: pros, cons, and
  recommended mix for a $50B+ SWF
- Liquidity management: illiquidity premium justification; secondary
  market infrastructure liquidity; GP-led secondaries as an exit tool
- Manager selection criteria: track record, deal sourcing capability,
  value-add expertise, ESG integration, and fee structure

Format as a GIC Infrastructure Strategy Paper with:
  • Strategic Asset Allocation Rationale (Return, Correlation, Inflation Tables)
  • Infrastructure Sub-Asset Class Matrix
  • Sector & Geographic Opportunity Map
  • Portfolio Construction Recommendation
  • Manager Selection Scorecard

My inputs: [FUND SIZE | CURRENT INFRASTRUCTURE ALLOCATION % | TARGET ALLOCATION % |
            INVESTMENT HORIZON | LIQUIDITY REQUIREMENTS | PRIMARY OBJECTIVE:
            RETURN / INCOME / INFLATION PROTECTION / ESG]

title: The MSCI ESG Integration & Portfolio Decarbonization Advisor
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Director at MSCI's ESG & Climate Research team — the global
standard for ESG ratings and climate risk analysis — advising asset managers
and pension funds on integrating ESG factors into investment processes and
meeting net-zero portfolio commitments.

I need a comprehensive ESG integration framework and portfolio decarbonization
roadmap for an institutional investment portfolio.

Design the framework:

ESG Integration Methodology:
- ESG Rating Framework: explain MSCI's ESG Rating methodology (Key Issue
  identification, exposure vs. management scoring, industry-relative rating);
  how does an ESG rating translate into financial risk/return insight?
- Material ESG Factor Identification: using the SASB Materiality Map,
  identify the 3–5 most financially material ESG factors for each sector
  in the portfolio; rank by potential financial impact
- ESG Integration in Valuation: how to adjust DCF models for ESG risk
  (e.g., increase WACC for high-carbon-risk companies, reduce terminal
  growth rate for companies with poor governance, adjust revenue forecasts
  for transition risk)
- Portfolio ESG Scoring: aggregate the portfolio's weighted-average ESG score;
  identify the top 5 ESG laggards that pose the greatest risk

Climate Risk Analysis (TCFD Framework):
- Physical Risk Assessment: identify portfolio companies most exposed to
  chronic physical risks (sea level rise, heat stress, water scarcity) and
  acute physical risks (hurricanes, floods) using RCP 2.6 / 4.5 / 8.5 scenarios
- Transition Risk Assessment: estimate the "carbon cost" of each holding
  under a $50/tonne, $100/tonne, $200/tonne carbon price scenario; which
  holdings become uneconomic?
- Portfolio Carbon Footprint: calculate Scope 1+2 WACI (Weighted Average
  Carbon Intensity, tCO2e/$M revenue) vs. benchmark
- Net-Zero Alignment: PAII / SBTi methodology — is the portfolio aligned
  with a 1.5°C or 2°C pathway? What is the implied temperature score?

Decarbonization Roadmap:
- Year 1: eliminate the top 10 highest-carbon-intensity holdings or engage
  for credible transition plans
- Year 3: portfolio WACI reduction target (e.g., 50% below 2020 baseline)
- Year 5: Green / Transition asset allocation target (% of portfolio in
  SFDR Article 8/9 funds or green bond issuers)
- Engagement vs. divestment framework: when to engage and when to divest

Format as an MSCI ESG & Climate Advisory Report with:
  • ESG Materiality Matrix by Sector
  • Portfolio Carbon Footprint Dashboard
  • Climate Scenario Impact Table (Portfolio P&L under each carbon price)
  • Decarbonization Roadmap (Year 1, 3, 5 targets and actions)
  • ESG Integration Score: how advanced is the current investment process?

My inputs: [PORTFOLIO SECTOR BREAKDOWN | GEOGRAPHIC FOCUS | CURRENT ESG APPROACH |
            NET-ZERO COMMITMENT DATE IF ANY | BIGGEST ESG RISK CONCERN]

title: The Goldman Sachs Sustainable Finance & Green Bond Structuring Advisor
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director in Goldman Sachs' Sustainable Finance Group, which
structures green bonds, sustainability-linked bonds (SLBs), social bonds, and
transition bonds for corporate issuers, sovereigns, and multilateral development
banks.

I need a comprehensive sustainable finance instrument selection and issuance
strategy for a corporate issuer seeking to access sustainable capital markets.

Deliver:

Sustainable Finance Instrument Selection:
- Green Bond (ICMA Green Bond Principles): eligible use of proceeds
  (renewable energy, energy efficiency, clean transport, green buildings,
  water management, circular economy); eligibility assessment for the
  company's capex pipeline; required second-party opinion (SPO) process
- Sustainability-Linked Bond (SLB): how SLBs differ from green bonds
  (general purpose proceeds, KPI-linked coupon step-up); design the 2–3
  KPIs and Sustainability Performance Targets (SPTs) that are ambitious,
  material, and verifiable; coupon step-up mechanism (typically 25–50bps)
- Social Bond: eligible social project categories; suitability for the
  company's social impact investments
- Transition Bond: for high-emission sectors (steel, cement, aviation,
  shipping) — credibility requirements and investor skepticism to address
- Sovereign Green Bond (if applicable): country eligibility framework and
  sovereign green bond market development strategy

Issuance Strategy & Pricing:
- "Greenium" Analysis: quantify the pricing benefit of sustainable labels
  in current market conditions (typically 1–5bps tighter vs. vanilla bonds)
- Investor Base Expansion: ESG-mandated investors that a green/SLB label
  unlocks that a vanilla bond would not attract
- Recommended instrument for this issuer with rationale
- Issuance size, tenor, currency, and timing recommendation
- Disclosure & Reporting requirements post-issuance: annual allocation
  and impact report; external verification

Green Finance Framework Design:
- Draft the Green / Sustainable Finance Framework structure
  (4 pillars: Use of Proceeds, Process for Evaluation & Selection,
  Management of Proceeds, Reporting)
- Identify the top 3 eligible projects with estimated green proceeds
- Select and brief the SPO provider (Sustainalytics, ISS ESG, Vigeo Eiris)

Format as a Goldman Sachs Sustainable Finance Advisory Memo with:
  • Instrument Selection Comparison Matrix
  • SLB KPI Design (KPI | Baseline | SPT 2025 | SPT 2030 | Verification Method)
  • Greenium Pricing Analysis
  • Green Finance Framework Outline
  • Issuance Timeline (Framework → SPO → Roadshow → Pricing → Reporting)

My inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INDUSTRY | ANNUAL CAPEX | GREEN/SUSTAINABLE CAPEX
            PIPELINE | EXISTING DEBT STRUCTURE | ESG COMMITMENTS ALREADY MADE |
            TARGET RAISE AMOUNT AND TENOR]

title: The BCG Climate Strategy & Carbon Pricing Business Impact Analyzer
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Partner at Boston Consulting Group's Climate & Sustainability
practice who advises Fortune 500 companies on building a credible climate
strategy that is both environmentally impactful and financially value-accretive.

I need a comprehensive corporate climate strategy and carbon pricing
business impact analysis.

Deliver:

Carbon Footprint & Transition Risk Assessment:
- Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions inventory: for each scope — current annual
  tCO2e, intensity (tCO2e/$M revenue), trend, and % of total footprint;
  identify the top 3 emission sources within each scope
- Carbon pricing exposure: model the P&L impact of an internal carbon price
  at $50/tonne, $100/tonne, and $200/tonne; which business units are most
  exposed? What is the total annual carbon cost at each price level?
- Transition risk by business segment: how does the transition to a
  low-carbon economy affect each revenue stream? (New regulations,
  customer preference shifts, technology substitution risk)
- Physical climate risk: financial exposure to extreme weather events and
  chronic climate trends (asset damage, supply chain disruption, productivity)

Decarbonization Pathway Design:
- Science-Based Target (SBTi): calculate the required emissions reduction
  to align with 1.5°C; gap between current trajectory and required pathway
- Abatement cost curve: rank all decarbonization levers by:
  (a) Annual emissions reduction (tCO2e)
  (b) Cost per tonne abated ($/tCO2e) — from negative cost (efficiency
      savings) to high cost (breakthrough technology)
  (c) Timeline to deploy at scale
- Priority decarbonization investments: renewable energy procurement (PPAs),
  energy efficiency, electrification of fleet/heat, supply chain engagement,
  nature-based solutions vs. engineered removals
- Carbon credits strategy: role of offsets in the transition pathway;
  quality criteria for high-integrity offsets (Gold Standard, VCS)

Climate Strategy Business Case:
- Revenue opportunities from climate strategy: green products/services,
  sustainable procurement preferences, carbon market revenues
- Cost savings from decarbonization: energy cost reduction, efficiency gains
- Multiple re-rating potential: ESG premium for companies with credible
  net-zero plans — quantify the valuation impact
- Stakeholder benefits: customer retention, talent attraction, regulatory
  goodwill, and investor ESG demand

Format as a BCG Climate Strategy Report with:
  • Carbon Footprint Dashboard (Scope 1, 2, 3)
  • Carbon Pricing P&L Impact Table
  • Abatement Cost Curve (described)
  • Decarbonization Pathway Timeline (2025 / 2030 / 2040 / 2050 milestones)
  • Business Case Summary (Revenue + Cost Savings + Valuation Impact)

My inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INDUSTRY | ANNUAL REVENUE | SCOPE 1+2 EMISSIONS
            (tCO2e) | NET-ZERO COMMITMENT IF ANY | BIGGEST DECARBONIZATION CHALLENGE |
            CARBON PRICING EXPOSURE CONCERN]

title: The UBS Global Wealth Management Ultra-HNW Portfolio Architect
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director at UBS Global Wealth Management responsible for
designing and managing bespoke investment portfolios for ultra-high-net-worth
(UHNW) clients with investable assets of $50M–$500M.

I need a comprehensive UHNW portfolio strategy covering all asset classes,
tax efficiency, liquidity management, and wealth preservation.

Design the portfolio:

Strategic Asset Allocation for UHNW:
- Why UHNW asset allocation differs from retail investors: access to
  private markets, longer time horizons, more complex tax situations,
  multi-generational objectives, concentrated single-stock risk
- Recommended allocation across: (1) Public Equities (global, factor-tilted),
  (2) Fixed Income (munis, TIPS, IG credit), (3) Private Equity (buyout,
  growth, venture), (4) Private Credit (direct lending, mezzanine),
  (5) Real Assets (infrastructure, real estate, commodities), (6) Hedge
  Funds (multi-strat, macro, equity L/S), (7) Cash & Liquidity
  — provide % allocation with rationale for each
- Private market allocation sizing: J-curve effect management; target
  vintage year diversification; commitment pacing model over 5 years to
  achieve target steady-state allocation

Concentrated Stock Risk Management:
- Identify the problem: single-stock concentration > 20% of net worth
  is a significant risk — quantify the VaR and CVaR of a 50% stock decline
- Risk mitigation toolkit: (a) Exchange Fund — defer capital gains while
  diversifying, (b) Variable Prepaid Forward — monetize while retaining
  upside, (c) Protective Put / Costless Collar — insurance strategies,
  (d) Charitable tools: CRT (Charitable Remainder Trust), DAF
  — compare each on tax efficiency, cost, flexibility, and lock-up

Tax & Estate Planning Integration:
- Tax-loss harvesting: systematic methodology and estimated after-tax
  return enhancement (typically 50–150bps/year for UHNW portfolios)
- Asset location strategy: which assets go in taxable accounts vs.
  tax-deferred vs. tax-exempt accounts
- Wealth transfer tools: GRATs, IDGTs, QPRTs, family limited
  partnerships — rank by efficiency for current estate tax environment
- International considerations: domicile optimization, CFC rules, PFIC
  treatment of foreign investments, FBAR/FATCA compliance

Format as a UBS UHNW Investment Policy Statement with:
  • Strategic Asset Allocation Table with Ranges
  • Private Market Commitment Pacing Schedule
  • Concentrated Stock Risk Analysis & Recommendation
  • Tax Efficiency Enhancement Opportunities ($ value estimated)
  • Governance & Reporting Framework (quarterly review cadence)

My inputs: [NET WORTH | INVESTABLE ASSETS | AGE & FAMILY SITUATION |
            LIQUIDITY NEEDS (ANNUAL SPENDING) | CONCENTRATED POSITIONS |
            TIME HORIZON | ESTATE PLANNING OBJECTIVES | TAX SITUATION]

title: The JP Morgan Private Bank Single-Family Office (SFO) Design Blueprint
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Private Banker at JP Morgan Private Bank who advises
entrepreneurs and first-generation billionaires on establishing a Single
Family Office (SFO) after a liquidity event (IPO, acquisition, or secondary sale).

I need a comprehensive Single Family Office design and operating model for a
newly liquid family with $200M–$1B in net worth.

Design the SFO:

Make vs. Buy Decision:
- SFO vs. Multi-Family Office vs. Private Bank: compare on cost, control,
  privacy, customization, and talent for this specific wealth level;
  at what AUM does an SFO become cost-effective?
- Hybrid model option: outsourced CIO model with lean internal team

SFO Operating Model:
- Governance: Family Investment Committee structure, Investment Policy
  Statement (IPS), and family constitution / charter elements
- Staffing: recommended org chart with roles and responsibilities —
  CEO/COO, CIO (in-house vs. outsourced), CFO/Controller, Tax Director,
  Legal/General Counsel, Operations; fully-loaded compensation benchmarks
  for each role
- Technology Stack: portfolio accounting and reporting (Addepar, Archway,
  Black Diamond), tax/legal management, document management, cybersecurity
  — recommended vendors for each with cost estimates
- Annual Operating Budget: staff + technology + professional advisors
  (legal, tax, audit) + fund expenses; benchmark as % of AUM (typically
  0.5%–1.5% of AUM per year for an SFO)

Investment Management Framework:
- Core vs. satellite portfolio architecture: which strategies to manage
  internally (passive, systematic) vs. outsource to external managers
- Manager selection and monitoring: due diligence process for external
  managers; performance measurement vs. benchmarks; manager replacement
  criteria
- Alternative investments access: direct co-investments alongside top PE
  firms; club deals; private credit; secondary market opportunities
- Liquidity management: maintain 12–18 months of family spending in
  highly liquid instruments; liquidity ladder design

Family Governance & Generational Wealth Transfer:
- Next-generation financial education program
- Philanthropic vehicle: Private Foundation vs. Donor-Advised Fund
  vs. Impact Investing — recommend based on the family's objectives

Format as a JP Morgan SFO Design Blueprint with:
  • Make vs. Buy Decision Matrix
  • SFO Org Chart & Staffing Plan
  • Annual Operating Budget Estimate
  • Investment Framework Summary
  • 12-Month SFO Launch Roadmap

My inputs: [FAMILY NET WORTH | LIQUIDITY EVENT TYPE | FAMILY STRUCTURE (AGES,
            MEMBERS) | ANNUAL SPENDING NEEDS | GEOGRAPHIC DOMICILE |
            PRIMARY OBJECTIVES: PRESERVATION / GROWTH / PHILANTHROPY / LEGACY]

title: The Citi Private Bank Multi-Generational Wealth Preservation Strategy
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Private Banker at Citi Private Bank's Global Family Office
practice, advising a second- or third-generation family on preserving
and growing wealth across generations while managing family dynamics.

I need a comprehensive multi-generational wealth preservation strategy
covering investment policy, estate planning, and family governance.

Design the strategy:

Wealth Preservation Philosophy:
- Define "success" for this family: wealth preservation in real terms
  (beat inflation), absolute growth, or transfer of specific assets?
- The "Shirtsleeves to Shirtsleeves" problem: statistics on multigenerational
  wealth erosion; the 3 root causes (investment risk, taxation, family
  conflict); how the strategy addresses each
- Return requirement: calculate the minimum real return needed to preserve
  purchasing power after: (a) inflation, (b) annual family spending, (c)
  estate taxes over 30 years at current wealth level

Investment Strategy for Preservation:
- "Endowment Model" adapted for family wealth: equity-heavy, long-horizon,
  illiquidity premium capture — recommended asset allocation with
  rationale for multigenerational time horizon
- Volatility tolerance calibration: with a 30-year horizon, how much
  short-term volatility can the family psychologically and financially absorb?
- Inflation protection: TIPS, infrastructure, real estate, commodities,
  and private equity — sizing each for inflation-hedging purposes
- Spending policy: sustainable withdrawal rate (endowment-style 5% rule
  vs. total-return approach); annual distribution framework

Estate & Tax Planning:

title: The Palantir / Anaplan Integrated Business Planning (IBP) Architect
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Finance Transformation Director who has implemented Integrated
Business Planning (IBP) programs at 10+ Fortune 500 companies using Anaplan,
SAP IBP, or similar connected planning platforms.

I need a comprehensive Integrated Business Planning design that connects
financial planning, supply chain planning, and commercial planning into
a single, real-time planning ecosystem.

IBP Process Design:
- Define the 5 IBP management cycles and their monthly cadence:

- Escalation protocol: what decisions get made at each level vs.
  escalated to the executive team?
- Rolling forecast process: replace the annual budget with a 12-quarter

Financial-Commercial Integration:
- Connect the commercial revenue forecast to the financial P&L:

- Price-volume-mix bridge: real-time dashboard showing the drivers of

- Territory and quota planning integration: sales capacity model linked

Financial-Supply Chain Integration:

  plan → inventory build → COGS and working capital impact
- Inventory optimization model: safety stock targets linked to COGS and

- Supplier capacity constraints integration: how supply constraints feed

Technology Architecture:

title: The McKinsey Revenue Growth Management (RGM) & Pricing Strategy
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Partner at McKinsey & Company's Revenue Growth Management
practice who has delivered 5–15% revenue and margin uplift programs for
CPG, retail, and B2B industrial companies through disciplined pricing,
trade spend optimization, and portfolio management.

I need a comprehensive Revenue Growth Management strategy to maximize
revenue and gross margin without volume sacrifice.

Design the RGM program:

Pricing Architecture:
- Price-value mapping: plot each SKU/product on a price vs. perceived
  value matrix vs. competitive alternatives; identify under-priced and
  over-priced products
- Price elasticity analysis: segment customers by price sensitivity
  (must have / nice to have / commodity) and design differentiated
  pricing by segment
- Price architecture design: entry / core / premium tier strategy;
  price pack architecture (size and format mix optimization)
- Pricing rules engine: clear guidelines for when to give discounts,
  what approvals are required, and the floor below which sales cannot go

Promotional Effectiveness:
- Trade spend ROI analysis: for each promotion type (price promotion,
  display, feature) — measure revenue lift, baseline shift, and profit
  contribution; eliminate "negative ROI" promotions
- Customer P&L analysis: calculate the true profitability of each
  major customer after trade spend, logistics, and service costs
- Promotional calendar optimization: reduce non-working trade spend;
  redirect budget to highest-ROI activation types

Portfolio & Mix Management:
- SKU profitability analysis: identify the 20% of SKUs generating
  80% of profit; flag tail SKUs for rationalization
- Mix improvement strategy: trade customers up to higher-margin SKUs
  and formats; innovation pipeline focused on premium segment
- Channel mix optimization: compare gross margins by channel (e-commerce,
  mass, specialty, foodservice); recommend channel investment priorities

Revenue Realization & Leakage:
- Gross-to-net revenue waterfall: from list price → invoice price →
  net revenue after all trade, freight, and SG&A allocations
- Identify the top 5 revenue leakage points and the value at stake

Format as a McKinsey RGM Strategy Presentation with:
  • Price-Value Positioning Map (described)
  • Trade Spend ROI Analysis Table
  • Customer Profitability Ranking
  • SKU Rationalization Recommendation
  • RGM Value at Stake Summary (Revenue + Margin Impact by Initiative)

title: The Deloitte M&A Finance Integration & Day-1 Reporting Readiness
prompt_text:
Act as a Director in Deloitte's Finance Integration practice who ensures
that the finance and reporting function of a newly acquired company is
fully integrated and able to report accurately on Day-1 post-close.

I need a comprehensive Finance Integration Program design covering financial
reporting integration, system migration, and internal controls readiness.

Design the program:

Pre-Close Finance Integration Planning:
- Finance integration workstream map: Accounting & Close, Financial
  Reporting, Tax, Treasury, FP&A, Internal Controls (SOX), ERP/Systems
- Chart of Accounts harmonization: mapping the acquired company's CoA
  to the acquirer's CoA; identify gaps and required new accounts
- Accounting policy alignment: identify top 10 accounting policy
  differences (revenue recognition, lease accounting, impairment testing,
  inventory valuation) and the financial impact of harmonization
- Legal entity simplification: target legal entity structure post-close
  and the steps to collapse/merge entities

Day-1 Reporting Readiness:
- Minimum reporting requirements on Day-1: management flash report,

- Opening balance sheet: PPA (Purchase Price Allocation) process;

  impacts of PPA adjustments
- ERP cutover plan: go-live on Day-1 vs. TSA-supported parallel run;

SOX / Internal Controls:
- Controls gap assessment: which controls in the acquired company do
  not meet acquirer's SOX standards?
- Remediation timeline: for each material weakness or significant
  deficiency — remediation owner, target date, and testing plan
- First post-acquisition 10-K or 10-Q: additional disclosures required
  for the acquired business; auditor coordination plan

Post-Close Reporting Integration (Year 1):
- Segment reporting redesign: how to present the acquired business in
  external financial statements
- Management reporting harmonization: align the acquired company's
  management accounts to the acquirer's MRP format within 90 days
- Finance headcount optimization: identify finance FTE redundancies

  • Accounting Policy Gap Analysis Table

title: The Oliver Wyman Financial Services Strategy & Disruption Analyzer
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Partner at Oliver Wyman's Financial Services practice —
the leading strategy consultancy for banks, insurers, asset managers, and
fintechs — who advises Tier-1 financial institutions on competitive
positioning in the face of fintech disruption and regulatory change.

I need a comprehensive competitive strategy and disruption assessment
for a traditional financial institution.

Deliver:

Disruption Landscape Assessment:
- Map the fintech and BigTech disruption threats to each revenue line of
  a traditional bank / insurer / asset manager; quantify the revenue at
  risk over 5 years for each threat
- Technology-driven disruption vectors: AI/ML in credit underwriting,
  blockchain in payments/settlement, embedded finance in distribution,
  and robo-advisory in wealth management
- Regulatory disruption: Open Banking / PSD2 / CDR impact on competitive
  dynamics; regulatory capital changes (Basel IV) and their effects on
  business model viability

Strategic Response Options:
- Defend the Core: investment required to protect existing market share
  through digital customer experience improvement and operational
  efficiency; ROI on defense
- Partner / Embed: white-label or API partnerships with fintechs to
  access new distribution and capabilities without building in-house
- Build New Ventures: internal venture studio or innovation lab — what
  does it take to compete with fintechs on their own terms?
- Acquire: M&A strategy targeting fintech capabilities; evaluation
  criteria for fintech targets; valuation multiples in current market
- Retreat to Fortress: focus on segments where the institution has
  durable advantage and exit commoditized segments

Business Model Transformation:
- Fee vs. spread economics: as net interest income compresses, how
  does the institution build fee-based and advisory revenue?
- Data monetization strategy: how to leverage proprietary customer data
  to create new revenue streams (within regulatory boundaries)
- Platform strategy: can the institution become a financial platform
  that distributes third-party products alongside its own?

Format as an Oliver Wyman Financial Services Strategy Report with:
  • Disruption Revenue-at-Risk Matrix (Business Line × Threat Type)
  • Strategic Response Options Comparison
  • Business Model Transformation Roadmap
  • Investment Priority Matrix

My inputs: [INSTITUTION TYPE (BANK/INSURER/ASSET MANAGER) | GEOGRAPHY |

title: The Roland Berger Industrial Company Strategy & China+1 Supply Chain
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Partner at Roland Berger's Operations Strategy practice who
advises European and North American industrial companies on supply chain
de-risking and the "China+1" manufacturing diversification strategy.

I need a comprehensive supply chain geopolitical risk assessment and
manufacturing footprint redesign strategy.

Deliver:

Geopolitical Supply Chain Risk Assessment:
- Map the company's supply chain by tier: Tier-1 suppliers (direct) →
  Tier-2 (sub-suppliers) → raw material origins; identify the % of spend
  and % of revenue at risk for each geography
- China concentration risk: calculate the company's total China-dependent
  revenue (direct manufacturing + supplier exposure); assess risk across
  5 dimensions: (1) tariff risk, (2) export control/technology transfer
  risk, (3) logistics disruption risk, (4) IP protection risk, (5) FX risk
- Geopolitical scenario modeling: under a US-China decoupling scenario
  and a Taiwan Strait contingency — estimate the revenue and margin impact

China+1 Manufacturing Strategy:
- Candidate country evaluation for alternative manufacturing: Vietnam,
  India, Mexico (nearshoring), Eastern Europe, Indonesia — score each on:
  labor cost, skill availability, infrastructure, political stability,
  FTA access, lead time to US/EU markets, and ramp-up timeline
- Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) analysis: compare China manufacturing cost
  vs. the China+1 candidate including: labor, logistics, tariffs, tooling,
  and inventory carrying costs
- Phased migration plan: which product lines to migrate first (high-
  tariff risk, low-complexity first); timeline and one-time migration costs

Operational Resilience Framework:
- Dual-sourcing strategy: which components to dual-source vs. single-source

- Safety stock and inventory buffer strategy for critical components
- Supply chain mapping technology: real-time visibility tools for Tier-2/3

Format as a Roland Berger Supply Chain Strategy Report with:

  • China Concentration Risk Quantification

title: The Accenture Strategy Corporate Venture Capital (CVC) Program Design
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director at Accenture Strategy who designs and launches
Corporate Venture Capital (CVC) programs for Fortune 500 companies seeking
to accelerate innovation, gain early access to disruptive technologies,
and generate financial returns.

I need a comprehensive CVC program design for a corporate that wants to
invest in startups strategically.

Design the program:

CVC Strategic Rationale & Mandate:
- Strategic vs. Financial CVC: define the primary objective — is the
  CVC designed to: (a) access emerging technologies before competitors,
  (b) create future M&A pipeline, (c) generate financial returns, or
  (d) all three? Rank by priority and explain the trade-offs
- Investment thesis: define the 3–5 technology and market themes the CVC
  will focus on; explain why each is strategically critical to the parent
- "Strategic fit" scoring criteria: how will the investment team score
  a startup's strategic relevance to the parent on a 1–10 scale?

CVC Structure & Governance:
- Fund structure: evergreen corporate balance sheet fund vs. dedicated
  LP fund structure (advantages of each)
- Fund size and deployment strategy: recommended initial fund size
  relative to corporate revenue; investment pace (# deals per year);
  check size range (seed, Series A, B, C)
- Governance: Investment Committee composition (business unit leaders,
  CFO, external VC); decision-making speed (a common CVC failure point
  — how to move as fast as VCs?)
- Carried interest and incentive design for the CVC team: how to retain
  talent who could earn more at a pure-play VC firm?

Portfolio Construction:
- Stage allocation: % in seed/Series A (high risk/high reward) vs.
  Series B/C (lower risk, nearer to strategic use)
- Co-investment strategy: which top-tier VC firms to co-invest alongside
  to improve deal quality and signaling?
- Reserve ratio: how much capital to reserve for follow-on investments
  in portfolio winners?

Value Creation Beyond Capital:
- Strategic value-add playbook: how the parent corporation helps portfolio
  startups (customer introductions, distribution access, technology
  integration, talent) — and how to avoid the "corporate vampire" problem
  (taking without giving)
- Portfolio company engagement model: dedicated relationship manager per
  portfolio company; quarterly business reviews; M&A option framework

Format as an Accenture CVC Program Design Document with:
  • CVC Investment Thesis (3–5 themes)
  • Fund Structure Comparison
  • Governance & Decision-Making Framework

title: The Perella Weinberg Partners Hostile Takeover Defense & Proxy Fight Advisor
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Partner at Perella Weinberg Partners' Shareholder Advisory
and M&A Defense practice, advising a target company's Board on how to
respond to an unsolicited takeover bid and potential proxy contest.

I need a comprehensive hostile takeover defense strategy for a public company
that has received an unsolicited acquisition proposal.

Deliver:

Immediate Response Protocol (48–72 Hours):
- Board fiduciary duty framework: Revlon duties vs. Unocal standard vs.
  business judgment rule — which applies here and what it requires
- The "Just Say No" defense: under what conditions can the Board reject
  a premium bid? What process must be followed to be defensible in court?
- Communication strategy: Board response statement language; employee
  communication; analyst/investor messaging; media holding statement
- Financial advisor engagement: how to convene the Special Committee and
  engage financial advisors for an independent fairness opinion

Defensive Measures Assessment:
- Existing defenses audit: does the company have a poison pill (rights
  plan), staggered board, supermajority voting requirements, or advance
  notice bylaws? Rate the strength of each defense
- New defense implementation: if the pill has expired, should the Board
  adopt a new rights plan? Structure and pricing of a modern "flip-in"
  rights plan; Delaware court scrutiny risk
- White Knight strategy: identify 3–5 potential white knight acquirers
  who would pay more than the hostile bidder; how to approach them
  discreetly while in a deal process
- Crown Jewel defense and Pac-Man defense: explain and evaluate for
  applicability to this situation

Proxy Fight Preparation:
- Proxy advisor engagement: ISS and Glass Lewis preliminary outreach;
  understand their likely recommendation framework
- Shareholder base analysis: identify swing voters (index funds,
  activists, arbitrageurs) and their likely position
- Proxy contest defense playbook: investor outreach plan, enhanced
  disclosure strategy, and director nomination defense

Standalone Value Enhancement:
- Accelerated value creation plan: what can the Board do NOW to
  demonstrate standalone value exceeds the hostile bid? (Buyback
  acceleration, strategic announcement, earnings pull-forward)

Format as a Perella Weinberg Hostile Defense War Room Playbook with:
  • 72-Hour Response Checklist
  • Defensive Measures Strength Assessment
  • White Knight Candidate List (anonymous profiles)
  • Shareholder Base Swing Voter Analysis
  • Standalone Value Enhancement Actions

title: The Duff & Phelps Purchase Price Allocation (PPA) & Intangible Asset Valuation
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director at Duff & Phelps (now Kroll) — the leading independent
valuation firm — who performs Purchase Price Allocation (PPA) analyses for M&A
transactions under ASC 805 (US GAAP) and IFRS 3.

I need a comprehensive Purchase Price Allocation analysis for a completed
acquisition to properly allocate the purchase price to identifiable
intangible assets and determine the residual goodwill.

Deliver:

PPA Framework & Methodology:
- Explain the ASC 805 / IFRS 3 requirements: the acquirer must recognize
  all identifiable assets acquired and liabilities assumed at fair value
  on the acquisition date; goodwill is the residual
- Timeline: typical PPA must be finalized within 12 months of acquisition
  date ("measurement period")
- Required third-party specialists: valuation firm for intangibles, real
  estate appraiser for property, actuarial for pension obligations

Intangible Asset Identification & Valuation:
For each category, identify applicable intangibles and describe the
valuation methodology:

1. Customer-Related Intangibles:
   - Customer relationships: Multi-Period Excess Earnings Method (MPEEM)
   - Order / production backlog: Lost profits method
   - Key inputs: customer attrition rate, revenue per customer, EBIT margin,
     contributory asset charge (CAC)

2. Technology-Based Intangibles:
   - Developed technology / IP: Relief-from-Royalty (RFR) method
   - In-process R&D (IPR&D): Stage-of-completion adjusted MPEEM
   - Key inputs: royalty rate (Knobbe database benchmarks), technology
     life, obsolescence rate

3. Marketing-Related Intangibles:
   - Trade names and trademarks: Relief-from-Royalty method
   - Non-compete agreements: With/Without method

4. Contract-Based Intangibles:
   - Favorable/unfavorable contracts, licenses, franchise rights

Goodwill Analysis:
- Residual goodwill calculation: Purchase Price − Fair Value of Net
  Identifiable Assets = Goodwill
- Goodwill allocation to reporting units for impairment testing (ASC 350)
- Deferred tax impact: book vs. tax basis differences for each intangible
  create a deferred tax liability that increases goodwill

Fair Value of PP&E:
- Real property: sales comparison / income capitalization approach
- Machinery & equipment: replacement cost new less depreciation (RCNLD)

Format as a Duff & Phelps PPA Valuation Report Outline with:
  • Purchase Price Reconciliation Table
  • Intangible Asset Identification & Fair Value Summary
  • Goodwill Calculation Bridge
  • Key Assumptions and Sensitivity Analysis per Intangible
  • Deferred Tax Impact Summary

My inputs: [ACQUIRER | TARGET | PURCHASE PRICE | TARGET'S BOOK VALUE OF NET ASSETS |
            INDUSTRY | PRIMARY INTANGIBLE ASSET CATEGORIES | ERP PREMIUM USED]

title: The Bridgewater Global Macro Portfolio Construction Engine
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Portfolio Strategist at Bridgewater Associates — the world's
largest hedge fund — applying Ray Dalio's "All Weather" and "Pure Alpha"
frameworks to construct a macro portfolio that performs across all economic
environments.

I need a rigorous global macro portfolio framework built on economic machine
principles, with explicit risk factor budgeting and scenario robustness.

Design the portfolio:

Economic Machine Framework:
- Decompose the global economy into its three core forces: (1) Long-term
  debt / productivity cycle, (2) Short-term debt / business cycle,
  (3) Political / geopolitical cycle — identify the current phase of each
  and the dominant market-moving force
- Risk factor identification: map all asset classes to 4 underlying
  economic environments (Rising Growth, Falling Growth, Rising Inflation,
  Falling Inflation); show historical returns for each asset class in
  each quadrant
- "All Weather" logic: construct a portfolio where the 4 economic
  environments are equally risk-weighted — calculate the risk contribution
  of each asset class using historical volatility and correlation

Risk Parity Portfolio Construction:
- Target portfolio: equal risk contribution from each economic quadrant;
  show the resulting asset weights (will be heavily bond-weighted vs.
  naive equal-weight)
- Leverage rationale: risk parity requires leverage to achieve equity-like
  returns at target volatility; calculate the required gross leverage and
  financing cost assumption
- Volatility targeting: set portfolio to 10% annualized volatility target;
  dynamic leverage adjustment mechanism

Pure Alpha Overlay (Active Macro Bets):
- Current macro views: translate the economic cycle diagnosis into 5
  specific macro trades with asset class, direction, sizing, and catalyst
- Carry trades: identify the highest carry opportunities adjusted for
  crash risk across rates, FX, and credit
- Correlation assumptions: which correlations are at risk of breaking down?
  (e.g., stock-bond correlation in stagflation)
- Stress scenarios: portfolio performance in 2008 GFC replay, 1970s
  stagflation replay, and 1994 bond market massacre

Format as a Bridgewater Macro Strategy Memorandum with:
  • Economic Quadrant Asset Return Table
  • Risk Parity Portfolio Weights (Current Positioning)
  • Active Macro Trade Book (5 trades with entry/exit/sizing)
  • Stress Test Results Table
  • Portfolio Risk Attribution (% risk from each factor)

My inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | CURRENT ASSET ALLOCATION | TARGET VOLATILITY |
            LEVERAGE CONSTRAINTS | GEOGRAPHIC FOCUS | BIGGEST MACRO CONVICTION]

title: The Elliott Management Event-Driven & Activist Hedge Fund Playbook
prompt_text:
Act as a Portfolio Manager at Elliott Management — the most feared and
successful activist hedge fund in the world — specializing in event-driven
investments including corporate activism, merger arbitrage, and special
situations.

I need a complete event-driven investment strategy framework covering the
four core sub-strategies of the event-driven hedge fund universe.

Design the strategy:

1. Corporate Activism:
   - Target screening criteria: identify under-valued companies with
     identifiable catalysts that management is unwilling to pursue
     (asset sales, buybacks, spin-offs, CEO change, strategic review)
   - "Activist Thesis Construction": build the activist investment thesis
     in the format Elliott uses — identify the value gap, quantify the
     opportunity, and design the specific asks
   - 13D filing strategy: ownership threshold triggers, public vs. private
     engagement sequencing, and coalition-building with other shareholders
   - Return attribution: how activist campaigns generate returns
     (multiple re-rating, earnings improvement, capital return, M&A)
   - Historical success rates: what % of Elliott campaigns achieve their
     stated objectives? What factors predict success?

2. Merger Arbitrage:
   - Spread analysis: cash deal spread (annualized) = (Deal Price −
     Current Price) ÷ Current Price × (365 ÷ Days to Close)
   - Risk assessment: deal break probability estimation; the 5 key
     break risks (regulatory, financing, MAC clause, shareholder vote,
     target performance)
   - Portfolio construction: optimal number of positions, position
     sizing based on deal break probability and spread, correlation
     between positions in a deal break scenario
   - Downside protection: where does the stock trade if the deal breaks?
     Estimate the "break price" for each position

3. Distressed / Special Situations:
   - Credit catalyst investing: stressed credits where a near-term event
     (refinancing, asset sale, covenant waiver) closes the price gap
   - Fulcrum security identification and distressed-to-control strategy
   - Post-reorganization equity: companies that emerged from Chapter 11
     with clean balance sheets and depressed valuations

4. Convertible Arbitrage:
   - Convertible bond valuation: parity value, conversion premium, credit
     spread, and theoretical floor
   - Delta-neutral hedge construction and gamma capture

Format as an Elliott-Style Event-Driven Strategy Framework with:
  • Activism Target Screening Scorecard
  • Merger Arbitrage Risk/Return Calculator Framework
  • Special Situations Opportunity Matrix
  • Portfolio Construction Guidelines
  • Scenario Analysis: Portfolio Return in Risk-Off Environment

My inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | PRIMARY EVENT-DRIVEN SUB-STRATEGY FOCUS |
            RISK TOLERANCE | CONCENTRATION LIMITS | CURRENT OPPORTUNITY SET |
            TARGETED ANNUAL RETURN]

title: The Two Sigma Quantitative Factor Strategy Design & Backtesting Framework
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Quantitative Researcher at Two Sigma — one of the world's most
sophisticated systematic hedge funds — who designs, tests, and implements
data-driven equity factor strategies with rigorous statistical validation.

I need a comprehensive quantitative factor strategy design and backtesting
framework to generate systematic alpha in equity markets.

Design the strategy:

Factor Universe & Selection:
- Factor taxonomy: classify factors into 5 categories:
  (1) Value: P/E, P/B, EV/EBITDA, FCF yield, dividend yield
  (2) Momentum: 12-1 month price momentum, earnings revision momentum,
      analyst estimate revision
  (3) Quality: ROE, ROIC, gross margin stability, earnings quality (accruals)
  (4) Low Volatility: realized vol, beta, idiosyncratic vol
  (5) Alternative Data: web traffic, satellite imagery, credit card spend,
      NLP sentiment from earnings call transcripts
- Factor construction: describe the exact calculation methodology for 5
  specific factors; importance of sector-neutralization and
  winsorization to avoid outlier contamination
- Factor decay analysis: at what holding period does each factor's
  predictive power decay? (Momentum: days/weeks; Value: months/years)

Backtesting Methodology:
- Point-in-time data: why using restated/revised data introduces look-ahead
  bias; how to source and validate point-in-time financial data
- Transaction cost modeling: realistic estimates for market impact,
  bid-ask spread, and borrow costs for short positions by market cap
- Portfolio construction: long/short portfolio with target factor exposure,
  risk model neutralization (beta, sector, country), and turnover constraints
- Statistical validation: t-statistic of alpha (need t > 2.0), information
  ratio, Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, and hit rate
- Overfitting avoidance: out-of-sample testing, walk-forward validation,
  multiple testing correction (Bonferroni / BHY), and factor decay
  monitoring in live trading

Multi-Factor Model Combination:
- Equal-weight vs. IC-weighted (Information Coefficient-weighted) factor
  combination; rank combination vs. z-score combination
- Factor correlation matrix: identify which factors diversify each other
  and which are redundant
- Regime-conditional factor performance: which factors work in bull vs.
  bear markets, high vs. low volatility regimes?

Format as a Two Sigma Quantitative Research Specification with:
  • Factor Construction Methodology Table
  • Backtesting Framework Checklist (15 quality checks)
  • Factor Performance Summary (IC, IR, Sharpe by factor)
  • Multi-Factor Model Combination Approach
  • Live Trading Implementation Checklist

My inputs: [TARGET UNIVERSE (US LARGE CAP / SMALL CAP / GLOBAL / EM) |
            TARGET HOLDING PERIOD | LONG/SHORT OR LONG-ONLY | AUM SIZE |
            AVAILABLE DATA SOURCES | PRIMARY FACTOR HYPOTHESIS]

title: The Tiger Global Long/Short Equity Deep Research Process
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Analyst at Tiger Global Management — the premier long/short
equity hedge fund known for deep fundamental research in technology, internet,
and consumer businesses globally — who conducts exhaustive bottom-up research
to build high-conviction long and short positions.

I need a structured deep-dive research process for evaluating a technology
or consumer company as a potential long or short position.

Research Process Design:

Industry & Business Model Analysis:
- Industry structure: Porter's Five Forces with quantitative scoring;
  market growth rate (TAM CAGR), cyclicality, capital intensity, and
  winner-take-all dynamics
- Business model quality rating: assess on 6 dimensions: (1) Revenue
  predictability/recurrence, (2) Pricing power, (3) Operating leverage,
  (4) Capital intensity, (5) Network effects, (6) Competitive moat durability
- Unit economics: build a cohort-level P&L from customer acquisition
  through full lifetime; LTV/CAC by channel and customer segment;
  payback period and gross margin by product line

Proprietary Research Channels (Tiger's Edge):
- Expert network calls: design 10 specific questions to ask ex-management,
  ex-employees, and industry consultants that would not be answered in
  public filings
- Customer due diligence: net promoter score survey design; churn
  interview guide; questions to reveal switching costs and competitive
  vulnerability
- Channel checks: distributor/retailer feedback on sell-through, inventory
  levels, and competitive dynamics
- Alternative data: web traffic trends (SimilarWeb), app rankings, job
  postings as a hiring/investment signal, patent filings

Financial Model Deep-Dive:
- Revenue quality decomposition: distinguish organic vs. inorganic growth;
  price vs. volume; new vs. existing customers
- Accounting quality flags: check for aggressive revenue recognition,
  deferred revenue trends, days sales outstanding creep, large
  non-cash charges that may be recurrent, and stock comp as % of revenue
- Earnings power analysis: "owner earnings" (Buffett's concept) vs.
  GAAP earnings; mid-cycle normalized margins vs. current margins

Variant View Crystallization:
- State the single most important thing the market is wrong about
  (the "Pivotal Question")
- Identify the specific data point or event that will prove or disprove
  the thesis within 12 months
- Quantify the variant view: if right, what does the stock do?
  If wrong, what is the loss?

Format as a Tiger Global Research Process Template with:
  • Business Model Quality Scorecard (6 dimensions)
  • Expert Network & Channel Check Question Guide
  • Financial Model Quality Checklist
  • Variant View Statement & Validation Framework
  • Position Sizing Matrix (Conviction Level × Risk/Reward → % Portfolio)

            MARKET CAP | YOUR INITIAL HYPOTHESIS | TIME HORIZON]

title: The Goldman Sachs Bank Equity Research Fundamental Analysis
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Equity Research Analyst at Goldman Sachs covering large-cap
US banks (JPMorgan, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Citigroup) for institutional
investors managing $500B+ in AUM.

I need a comprehensive fundamental analysis framework for bank stocks that
addresses the unique financial statement structure, regulatory capital
framework, and valuation methodology specific to financial institutions.

Analyze:

Bank Financial Statement Framework:
- Income statement unique items: Net Interest Income (NII) = earning
  assets × NIM; Non-Interest Income (fees, trading, wealth management);
  Provision for Credit Losses (PCL) — explain the CECL methodology and
  how to forecast PCL through the credit cycle
- Balance sheet analysis: earning asset mix (loans, securities, cash);
  funding mix (deposits vs. wholesale); loan portfolio composition by
  type (C&I, CRE, residential mortgage, consumer) with credit quality metrics
- Efficiency Ratio = Non-Interest Expense ÷ Net Revenue (target < 55%
  for top-quartile banks); identify drivers of efficiency ratio improvement

Capital & Regulatory Framework:
- Basel III/IV capital ratios: CET1, Tier 1, Total Capital — current
  levels vs. regulatory minimums and internal targets; stress capital
  buffer (SCB) implications
- DFAST / CCAR stress test: how the Fed stress test determines capital
  return capacity; estimate the maximum buyback + dividend under the
  current capital framework
- RWA optimization: explain Risk-Weighted Assets and how management
  can reduce RWA without reducing loans

Bank Valuation Methodology:
- Price-to-Tangible Book Value (P/TBV): why TBV matters for banks;
  the ROTCE / (Ke − g) justified P/TBV formula; build a regression
  of P/TBV vs. ROTCE across the bank universe
- Dividend Discount Model (DDM): applicable to mature banks with
  stable payout ratios; sensitivity to ROTCE and payout ratio
- P/E and P/Pre-Provision Net Revenue (PPNR): through-the-cycle
  earnings normalization methodology
- Excess capital return analysis: how much capital above the target
  CET1 ratio can be returned over the next 3 years?

Scenario Analysis:
- Rate sensitivity: NII impact of +100bps / −100bps parallel shift;
  which loan and deposit categories are asset-sensitive vs. liability-
  sensitive?
- Credit cycle stress: PCL assumptions in a mild recession (NCO rate
  of 75bps) vs. severe recession (150bps) → EPS and CET1 impact
- Loan growth and deposit beta assumptions in the current rate environment

Format as a Goldman Sachs Bank Research Initiation Report Framework with:
  • Key Financial Metrics Dashboard (NIM, ROTCE, CET1, Efficiency Ratio)
  • P/TBV vs. ROTCE Regression Analysis
  • Rate Sensitivity & Credit Stress Scenario Table
  • Capital Return Capacity Analysis
  • Price Target Derivation with Methodology

My inputs: [BANK NAME | TICKER | CURRENT STOCK PRICE | CURRENT CET1 RATIO |
            CURRENT ROTCE | NIM | EFFICIENCY RATIO | PRIMARY INVESTMENT THESIS]

title: The Morgan Stanley Insurance Company Valuation & Embedded Value Analyst
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Equity Research Analyst at Morgan Stanley covering life insurance,
P&C insurance, and specialty insurance companies for institutional investors.

I need a comprehensive insurance company analysis framework covering the unique
accounting, business model, and valuation methodology for insurance stocks.

Analyze:

Insurance Business Model by Type:

Life Insurance:
- Embedded Value (EV) methodology: explain Traditional EV, Market-Consistent
  EV (MCEV), and Economic Value of New Business (VNB); how to read and
  interpret the EV disclosure
- Value of New Business (VNB): new business strain vs. long-term VNB
  creation; VNB margin and how it drives intrinsic value growth
- Investment portfolio analysis: ALM (Asset-Liability Management) approach;
  duration mismatch risk; credit quality of the investment portfolio;
  unrealized gain/loss sensitivity to rates

P&C Insurance:
- Combined Ratio = Loss Ratio + Expense Ratio; what drives underwriting
  profitability; through-the-cycle vs. current year combined ratio
- Reserve adequacy: development triangles analysis; favorable vs.
  unfavorable prior-year development and what it signals
- Catastrophe exposure: modeled PML (Probable Maximum Loss) at 1-in-100
  year and 1-in-250 year events; reinsurance program design and
  net retention
- Rate environment: current pricing cycle phase (hardening vs. softening);
  which lines of business are over/under-priced

Insurance Valuation:
- Price-to-Embedded Value (P/EV) for life insurance: justified P/EV based
  on ROE, VNB growth, and discount rate
- Price-to-Book (P/B) for P&C: regression vs. ROE like banks; normalized
  ROE using 10-year average combined ratio and investment return
- Sum-of-Parts (SOTP): life + P&C + asset management + distribution
  subsidiaries valued separately
- Dividend capacity: how much capital can be upstreamed from regulated
  insurance subsidiaries to the holding company?

Format as a Morgan Stanley Insurance Research Framework with:
  • Business Type Comparison Matrix (Life vs. P&C vs. Specialty)
  • Key Metrics Dashboard (Combined Ratio, ROE, EV, VNB Margin)
  • Valuation Methodology Grid (P/EV, P/B, SOTP)
  • Rate Cycle Positioning Analysis
  • Investment Recommendation Framework

My inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INSURANCE TYPE (LIFE/P&C/SPECIALTY/MULTI-LINE) |
            TICKER | CURRENT COMBINED RATIO OR EV | CURRENT P/B OR P/EV |
            PRIMARY INVESTMENT THESIS OR CONCERN]

title: The Oliver Wyman Bank Strategic Planning & NIM Optimization Framework
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Partner at Oliver Wyman's Banking practice who has advised
Tier-1 banks on strategic planning, balance sheet optimization, and Net
Interest Margin (NIM) management in rapidly changing rate environments.

I need a comprehensive bank strategic plan framework covering balance sheet
optimization, revenue diversification, and efficiency transformation.

Design the strategic plan:

Balance Sheet Strategy:
- Asset mix optimization: shift from lower-yield to higher-yield assets
  within regulatory capital constraints; model the NIM impact of rotating
  $1B from US Treasuries into C&I loans
- Deposit franchise value analysis: core deposit intangible value; deposit
  beta by product type (checking: 0–20%, savings: 30–50%, money market:
  60–80%); strategy to grow stickier, lower-beta deposits
- Loan portfolio construction: target mix by type (CRE, C&I, consumer)
  based on risk-adjusted return on capital (RAROC) for each loan type;
  concentration limit management
- Securities portfolio management: held-to-maturity vs.
  available-for-sale designation strategy; AOCI (Accumulated Other
  Comprehensive Income) risk management; duration management in the
  current rate environment

Revenue Diversification Strategy:
- Fee income growth levers: wealth management, treasury management,
  commercial card, and capital markets cross-sell — revenue potential
  for each from existing commercial banking relationships
- Bancassurance and investment product distribution: fee revenue
  opportunity from existing depositor base
- Fintech partnership revenue: embedded finance, BaaS (Banking-as-a-
  Service), and API banking fee structures

Efficiency Transformation:
- Branch network rationalization: transaction migration to digital channels;
  branch cost-income ratio analysis; optimal branch density model
- Operations automation: RPA and AI in loan processing, KYC/AML, and
  back-office reconciliation; FTE reduction potential and NPV of automation
- Technology investment prioritization: core banking modernization
  (legacy system risk), cloud migration, and digital channels

Format as an Oliver Wyman Bank Strategic Plan with:
  • Balance Sheet Optimization Opportunities Table
  • NIM Sensitivity Analysis (+/−100bps rate scenarios)
  • RAROC by Loan Type Matrix
  • Revenue Diversification Roadmap
  • Efficiency Ratio Improvement Bridge (Current → Target)

My inputs: [BANK NAME | ASSET SIZE | CURRENT NIM | CURRENT EFFICIENCY RATIO |
            LOAN PORTFOLIO MIX | DEPOSIT MIX | PRIMARY STRATEGIC CHALLENGE]

title: The Credit Suisse SPAC Analysis & De-SPAC Transaction Evaluator
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director in Credit Suisse's SPAC and Special Purpose
Acquisition Company Advisory group who has advised on $50B+ in SPAC
transactions from IPO through business combination (De-SPAC).

I need a comprehensive SPAC structure analysis and de-SPAC transaction
evaluation framework for a SPAC seeking a target or for a target company
evaluating a SPAC merger.

Analyze both perspectives:

For the SPAC Sponsor:
- SPAC structure mechanics: trust account (100% of IPO proceeds), sponsor
  promote (20% founder shares), private placement warrants, redemption
  right mechanics, and the economic impact of redemptions on the
  remaining shareholders
- Sponsor economics: calculate sponsor IRR under 0%, 30%, 70%, and 100%
  redemption scenarios; identify the "promote dilution" impact on
  public shareholders at each redemption level
- Target identification criteria: ideal de-SPAC target profile (capital-
  intensive growth company that wants certainty of proceeds, PE-backed
  company seeking liquidity, company wanting to avoid traditional IPO
  process)
- PIPE structuring: why a PIPE (Private Investment in Public Equity) is
  required in most de-SPAC transactions; typical PIPE discount and
  terms; how to identify PIPE investors

For the Target Company:
- SPAC vs. Traditional IPO: compare on: valuation certainty, speed,
  disclosure requirements, forward projection ability, dilution, and
  post-close trading dynamics; under what conditions is a SPAC
  preferable to a traditional IPO?
- De-SPAC valuation analysis: SPAC mergers often involve forward-year
  projections — how to assess whether the projected valuation is
  achievable; red flags in SPAC target financial projections
- Dilution analysis: map all sources of dilution for target company
  shareholders post-close: founder shares, warrants, PIPE shares,
  earnout shares
- Post-merger trading performance: historical analysis — what % of
  de-SPAC transactions have outperformed the Russell 2000 at
  1-month, 6-month, and 12-month post-close?

Format as a SPAC Advisory Memorandum with:
  • SPAC Economic Structure Diagram (Trust, Promote, PIPE, Warrants)
  • Sponsor Returns Under Redemption Scenarios Table
  • SPAC vs. IPO Comparison Matrix
  • De-SPAC Dilution Analysis

title: The Barclays IPO Aftermarket Strategy & Price Stabilization Advisor
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director in Barclays' Equity Capital Markets and Stabilization
group who manages the aftermarket trading and price stabilization activities
for IPOs in the weeks following pricing.

I need a comprehensive IPO aftermarket management strategy covering price
stabilization, greenshoe management, and long-term trading performance.

Deliver:

Pre-IPO Pricing Strategy:
- IPO pricing discipline: why underpricing (leaving money on the table)
  actually serves the issuer's long-term interest; the optimal first-day
  "pop" range (5–15%) that maximizes long-term institutional ownership
- Book-building intelligence: what order book quality signals (institutional
  vs. retail mix, concentrated orders, price sensitivity of demand)
  indicate a high-quality vs. fragile book
- Price range setting: how to anchor the range to create demand while
  pricing at the top; the psychology of the final pricing decision

Stabilization Mechanics:
- Over-allotment option (greenshoe): how it works — underwriters allocate
  115% of the offering, covering the short position either through open
  market purchases (if stock drops) or exercising the greenshoe (if
  stock rises)
- Stabilization bid mechanics: SEC Rule 10b-7 parameters; price limits
  on stabilization bids; how long the stabilization period lasts
  (typically 30 days post-IPO)
- Lock-up expiry management strategy: communication plan to prevent
  excessive selling pressure at the 180-day lock-up expiry

Post-IPO Investor Relations Strategy:
- First earnings call post-IPO: the unique challenges of the first quarter
  as a public company (setting expectations, internal controls readiness)
- Sell-side research initiation timing: typical 25-day quiet period;
  how to coordinate initiation coverage from IPO underwriters and
  independent research firms
- Index inclusion pathway: S&P 500, Russell 2000/1000, and MSCI inclusion
  criteria; timeline and estimated passive fund demand on inclusion

IPO Performance Diagnostics:
- Key performance drivers at 3-month post-IPO: what predicts strong vs.
  weak aftermarket performance? (Revenue growth execution, margin
  delivery vs. prospectus, management credibility, peer sector performance)
- Red flags that predict post-IPO underperformance

Format as a Barclays ECM Aftermarket Strategy Playbook with:
  • IPO Pricing Decision Framework
  • Greenshoe & Stabilization Mechanics Diagram (described)

title: The Jefferies Special Situations Spin-Off & Rights Offering Analyzer
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director in Jefferies' Special Situations and Event-Driven
Equity group who identifies and monetizes investment opportunities created by
corporate events: spin-offs, rights offerings, Dutch tenders, odd-lot tenders,
and exchange offers.

I need a comprehensive special situations investment framework covering the
most common corporate event-driven investment opportunities.

Analyze each event type:

1. Spin-Off Investment Strategy:
   - Why spin-offs outperform: academic evidence (Cusatis, Miles, Woolridge);
     the 3 drivers of spin-off alpha (management focus, index-selling pressure,
     forced selling by non-natural holders, improved incentive alignment)
   - Parent vs. SpinCo investment decision: which entity is more attractive
     post-separation? Analyze the financial profile of both
   - Spin-off timing: when to buy (before record date, at spin, or 3–6 months
     post-spin when forced sellers have exited)
   - SpinCo quality checklist: 8 factors that predict spin-off outperformance
     (management incentive alignment, clean balance sheet, no stranded costs,
     independent growth strategy)

2. Rights Offering Arbitrage:
   - Rights offering mechanics: subscription price, subscription ratio, rights
     trading period, over-subscription privilege
   - Theoretical ex-rights price (TERP): calculate and compare to actual
     market price to identify arbitrage opportunities
   - Decision framework: subscribe, sell rights, or do nothing?

3. Dutch Tender Offer & Odd-Lot Tender:
   - Dutch tender mechanics: company specifies a price range; shareholders
     tender at their desired price; company pays the clearing price to all
   - Odd-lot tender opportunity: holders of fewer than 100 shares often
     receive priority treatment — systematic strategy to exploit this
   - Return profile: calculate expected return on odd-lot tender strategy
     given tender premium and execution probability

4. Exchange Offer Analysis:
   - Debt-for-equity and equity-for-debt exchange offers — when and why
     companies use them; investor decision framework

Format as a Jefferies Special Situations Investment Framework with:
  • Spin-Off Opportunity Screening Criteria
  • Spin-Off Quality Checklist
  • Rights Offering Decision Tree
  • Dutch Tender Return Analysis Template
  • Event Calendar: how to track upcoming corporate events systematically

My inputs: [SPECIFIC EVENT OR COMPANY IF KNOWN | EVENT TYPE | PORTFOLIO SIZE |

title: The Franklin Templeton Emerging Markets Equity Strategy
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Portfolio Manager at Franklin Templeton Emerging Markets
— one of the pioneering EM investment franchises — who manages a $10B+
diversified EM equity portfolio with a bottom-up, value-oriented approach.

I need a comprehensive emerging markets equity investment strategy covering
country allocation, sector selection, and individual stock research.

Design the EM strategy:

EM Country Allocation Framework:
- Country attractiveness scorecard (score each of the major EM countries
  on a 1–10 scale for each factor):
  (a) Macro fundamentals: GDP growth, inflation, current account, fiscal
      balance, debt level
  (b) Valuation: MSCI Country P/E and P/B vs. own history and vs. DM
  (c) Currency: real effective exchange rate (REER) overvaluation or
      undervaluation; FX reserve adequacy
  (d) Political and institutional quality: governance, rule of law,
      property rights protection
  (e) Earnings growth: consensus EPS growth for next 12 months
  (f) Positioning and flows: institutional ownership vs. benchmark;
      recent fund flows
- Country rotation signals: which macro indicators predict EM country
  returns best? (Hint: current account improvement, currency cheapness,
  and earnings revisions are historically powerful)

EM vs. DM Relative Valuation:
- MSCI EM vs. MSCI World relative P/E and P/B historical spread;

- The EM earnings cycle: why EM earnings are more volatile than DM;

- DM vs. EM ROE gap: structural reasons for EM ROE discount and

EM-Specific Risk Management:
- Currency risk: hedging EM FX exposure — cost, availability, and

- Liquidity risk: daily trading volume analysis; position sizing
  in EM small/mid-cap stocks
- Corporate governance risk: related-party transactions, minority
  shareholder treatment, state-owned enterprise (SOE) risks
- Political event risk: election calendar analysis, nationalisation
  risk, capital controls risk

Format as a Franklin Templeton EM Strategy Blueprint with:
  • Country Attractiveness Scorecard (Top 10 EM countries ranked)
  • EM vs. DM Valuation Dashboard
  • Currency Risk Assessment by Country
  • Portfolio Construction Guidelines (Country limits, liquidity rules)
  • Top 5 EM Country Overweight / Underweight Recommendations
