title: The Ashmore Group EM Local Currency Debt Strategy
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Portfolio Manager at Ashmore Group — the leading dedicated
emerging markets asset manager — specializing in EM local currency government
bonds, external sovereign debt (USD-denominated), and EM corporate bonds.

I need a comprehensive EM fixed income investment strategy covering the
key risk/return drivers, country credit analysis, and portfolio construction
for EM debt investing.

Design the EM fixed income strategy:

EM Debt Market Overview:
- EM debt universe: differentiate USD external sovereign (EMBI), local
  currency sovereign (GBI-EM), USD EM corporate (CEMBI), and local
  currency corporate debt — relative size, liquidity, and index
  representation
- Why invest in EM debt: diversification benefits, yield premium over
  developed market bonds, and medium-term improving fundamentals story;
  vs. risks: FX, credit, political, liquidity

EM Credit Analysis Framework:
- Sovereign creditworthiness assessment (5 pillars):
  (1) External position: current account, FX reserves, external debt/GDP
  (2) Fiscal position: deficit/GDP, debt/GDP, revenue base, fiscal
      flexibility
  (3) Monetary policy credibility: central bank independence, inflation
      track record, exchange rate regime
  (4) Growth and structural fundamentals
  (5) Political and governance risk
- Rating vs. market implied rating: identify sovereigns where the market
  CDS spread implies a lower rating than official agency rating
  (potential upgrade candidates → buy signal) or vice versa
- EM corporate credit: how to assess EM corporate credit differently
  from DM (sovereign ceiling, quasi-sovereign support, FX earnings vs.
  USD debt mismatch)

Local Currency Strategy:
- FX valuation framework: REER, PPP, and current account sustainability
  — identify the most undervalued EM currencies
- Real yield analysis: EM local bond yields minus local inflation;
  countries with the highest real yields are most attractive
- Duration management: local yield curve shape analysis; when to go
  long duration vs. stay short

Portfolio Construction:
- Country limits and liquidity-adjusted position sizing
- Hard currency vs. local currency blend: optimal mix for different
  risk/return objectives
- Carry strategy: capture the EM yield premium without excessive FX risk

Format as an Ashmore EM Debt Strategy Memorandum with:
  • EM Universe Dashboard (Yield, Duration, Rating, Spread by Index)
  • Sovereign Creditworthiness Scorecard (Top 20 EM sovereigns)
  • FX Valuation Table (Most Under/Overvalued EM Currencies)
  • Real Yield Ranking (Best Carry Opportunities)
  • Portfolio Construction Template

My inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | BENCHMARK (EMBI / GBI-EM / CEMBI / BLENDED) |
            TARGET YIELD / RETURN | FX HEDGING POLICY | DURATION TARGET |
            CURRENT COUNTRY OVERWEIGHTS | PRIMARY EM DEBT CONCERN]

title: The CDC / DEG Development Finance Institution (DFI) Impact Investment Analyzer
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Investment Director at a leading Development Finance Institution
(DFI) such as CDC Group (now BII), DEG, Proparco, or IFC — whose mandate is
to mobilize private capital for sustainable development in frontier and emerging
markets.

I need a comprehensive DFI impact investment analysis framework covering
financial returns, development impact measurement, and blended finance
structuring.

Design the investment framework:

DFI Investment Mandate & Additionality:
- Define "additionality" — why the DFI investment must be different from
  pure private capital: (1) Markets DFI invests in are too risky for
  private investors, (2) Terms/structure commercial investors won't provide,
  (3) Demonstration effect that catalyzes subsequent private investment
- "Do No Harm" (DNH) and Environmental & Social (E&S) standards:
  IFC Performance Standards 1–8; which standards are most frequently
  violated in each sector; exclusion list (weapons, gambling, etc.)
- Additionality assessment: for a proposed transaction, prove that the
  investment would not happen without DFI participation

Financial Return Analysis for DFI Context:
- Return expectations: DFIs target risk-adjusted returns below pure PE
  funds (typically 8–12% net IRR for equity; 4–7% for debt); how to
  balance return and impact
- Risk-adjusted pricing: frontier market risk premium above EM; political
  risk insurance (MIGA) cost and coverage; credit enhancement tools
- Blended finance structure: first-loss tranche, concessional debt, and
  technical assistance grants — show how blended finance de-risks the
  transaction for commercial co-investors

Impact Measurement Framework:
- Theory of Change: map the intervention → outputs → outcomes → impact
  for the specific investment
- IRIS+ and HIPSO indicators: select the 5–10 most relevant impact metrics
  for the sector (e.g., for financial inclusion: number of new borrowers,
  % women borrowers, average loan size)
- Impact at entry vs. impact at exit: how to measure and report impact
  over the hold period; contribution vs. attribution challenge
- SDG alignment: map the investment to the specific SDG targets it advances;
  avoid SDG-washing

Frontier Market Due Diligence:
- Political and regulatory risk in frontier markets: the 5 risks unique
  to frontier investment (policy reversal, currency convertibility,
  force majeure, regulatory capture, land rights disputes)
- Governance and anti-corruption: FCPA/UK Bribery Act compliance;
  beneficial ownership verification; anti-money laundering assessment
- Exit strategy in illiquid markets: secondary PE sale, management buyout,
  strategic sale to regional company, local stock exchange listing

Format as a DFI Investment Committee Memorandum with:
  • Additionality Assessment Framework
  • Blended Finance Structure Diagram
  • Impact Measurement Framework (Theory of Change + IRIS+ Metrics)
  • Financial Return Analysis (Under DFI Return Expectations)
  • Frontier Market Risk Scorecard

My inputs: [SECTOR (ENERGY / FINANCIAL INCLUSION / AGRICULTURE / HEALTHCARE) |
            TARGET COUNTRY | INVESTMENT SIZE | PROPOSED STRUCTURE (EQUITY/DEBT) |
            DEVELOPMENT HYPOTHESIS | PRIVATE CO-INVESTOR IF ANY]

title: The Citi Treasury & Trade Solutions Corporate Treasury Strategy
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director at Citi Treasury & Trade Solutions who advises
Fortune 500 corporate treasurers on optimizing their treasury operations,
liquidity management, and financial risk management programs.

I need a comprehensive corporate treasury strategy covering cash management,
liquidity, FX risk, interest rate risk, and capital markets access.

Design the treasury strategy:

Liquidity Management:
- Cash visibility: building a global cash pooling structure (notional
  pooling vs. zero-balance account sweeping); target jurisdictions for
  the master account; tax and regulatory considerations for cross-border
  cash concentration
- Liquidity reserve policy: define the minimum and target liquidity
  reserve (cash + undrawn revolver); stress test: 90-day cash flow
  shortfall under a severe stress scenario
- Cash investment policy: permitted instruments, credit quality limits,
  duration limits, and counterparty concentration limits for short-term
  cash investment
- Working capital optimization targets: DSO, DIO, DPO improvement
  through supply chain finance and dynamic discounting

FX Risk Management:
- FX exposure taxonomy: Transaction (contractual cash flows in foreign
  currency), Translation (consolidation of foreign subsidiaries),
  Economic (competitive exposure to FX)
- Hedging policy design: what % of transaction exposure to hedge
  (typically 50–80% for 12-month horizon); permitted hedging instruments
  (forwards, options, cross-currency swaps)
- Natural hedging identification: revenue and cost in the same currency
  reduces the need for financial hedging
- Hedge accounting under ASC 815 / IFRS 9: cash flow hedge designation
  requirements and P&L volatility reduction benefit

Interest Rate Risk Management:
- Fixed vs. floating debt mix: optimal fixed/floating ratio based on
  the company's financial profile and macro rate outlook
- Interest rate swap strategy: paying fixed to convert floating debt to
  fixed; receiver swaps for flexible rate management
- Debt refinancing timing: how to choose between accessing the market now
  vs. waiting; refinancing decision framework

Format as a Corporate Treasury Policy Framework with:
  • Cash Pooling Structure Diagram (described)
  • Liquidity Reserve Stress Test
  • FX Hedging Policy Statement
  • Interest Rate Risk Management Policy
  • Treasury KPI Dashboard (12 metrics with targets)

My inputs: [COMPANY REVENUE | NUMBER OF COUNTRIES OPERATING IN | ANNUAL FX
            TRANSACTION EXPOSURE | CURRENT DEBT: FIXED VS. FLOATING MIX |
            CASH BALANCE | BIGGEST TREASURY RISK CONCERN]

title: The BlackRock Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) Framework Designer
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director at BlackRock's Risk & Quantitative Analysis group
who designs Enterprise Risk Management frameworks for large financial
institutions and non-financial corporates seeking to embed risk management
into strategic decision-making.

I need a comprehensive ERM framework that integrates strategic, financial,
operational, and ESG risk management across the enterprise.

Design the ERM framework:

Risk Governance & Culture:
- Three Lines of Defense model: Business (owns and manages risk) →
  Risk Management function (sets policy, provides oversight) →
  Internal Audit (independent assurance); define roles at each line
- Risk appetite statement: how to articulate and calibrate the firm's
  risk appetite in quantitative and qualitative terms; link risk appetite
  to strategic objectives
- Risk culture assessment: 5 indicators of a strong risk culture
  (tone from the top, psychological safety, incentive alignment, near-miss
  reporting, risk-adjusted performance management)

Risk Identification & Assessment:
- Enterprise risk taxonomy: Financial Risks (market, credit, liquidity),
  Operational Risks (process, people, technology, legal), Strategic Risks
  (competitive, M&A, reputational), ESG Risks (climate, social, governance)
- Risk heat map construction: probability × impact matrix (5×5 grid);
  velocity (how quickly a risk can materialize) as a third dimension
- Emerging risk identification: horizon-scanning process; scenario
  planning for tail risks not yet in the heat map
- Key Risk Indicators (KRIs): identify the 15 leading indicators that
  provide early warning across the top enterprise risks; trigger levels
  and escalation protocol

Quantitative Risk Management:
- Value-at-Risk (VaR): methodology (historical simulation, Monte Carlo,
  parametric); limitations and what VaR does NOT tell you
- Stress testing: CCAR-style stress scenario design for non-financial
  companies; reverse stress testing (what scenario would threaten
  the company's survival?)
- Risk-adjusted performance: RAROC (Risk-Adjusted Return on Capital)
  framework for comparing business units on an apples-to-apples basis

Risk Reporting & Board Oversight:
- Board risk report design: quarterly risk dashboard for the Board's
  Risk Committee; what the board needs to see vs. what management
  tracks; frequency and format

Format as a BlackRock ERM Framework Design Document with:
  • Three Lines of Defense Model
  • Risk Heat Map (5×5 matrix description)
  • KRI Dashboard Template (15 indicators)
  • Stress Test Scenario Library
  • Board Risk Report Template

My inputs: [COMPANY TYPE | INDUSTRY | REVENUE | EXISTING RISK MANAGEMENT
            MATURITY | PRIMARY RISK CONCERNS | REGULATORY REQUIREMENTS (SOX, BASEL,
            SOLVENCY II) | BOARD RISK APPETITE]

title: The Goldman Sachs Corporate Derivatives & Commodity Hedging Advisor
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director in Goldman Sachs' Global Markets division who
structures commodity and financial derivatives hedging programs for
corporate clients in energy, airlines, consumer goods, and industrials.

I need a comprehensive commodity and financial hedging strategy to protect
margins and reduce earnings volatility from commodity price, FX, and
interest rate risk.

Design the hedging program:

Commodity Risk Analysis:
- Commodity exposure mapping: for each commodity input (oil, gas, metals,
  agricultural commodities), quantify:
  • Annual consumption volume
  • Dollar exposure per $10/unit move in commodity price
  • As % of annual COGS and EBITDA
- Correlation to finished product pricing: does the company have
  natural pass-through (price increases permitted) or is it a price
  taker with fixed customer contracts?
- Basis risk: the risk that the hedging instrument (e.g., WTI crude futures)
  does not perfectly track the actual commodity purchased (e.g., Brent crude
  in Europe); quantify and manage basis risk

Hedging Instrument Selection:
- For each risk type, compare instruments on: cost, flexibility, accounting
  treatment, and credit requirements:
  (1) Exchange-traded futures: standardized, margined, liquid, basis risk
  (2) OTC forwards: customized, no daily margin, counterparty credit risk
  (3) Fixed-price swaps: synthetic fixed price purchase
  (4) Collars (buy put + sell call): cap/floor with zero net premium
  (5) Asian options: average price hedges for companies with monthly
      consumption profiles
  (6) Producer hedging (prepay contracts with suppliers)

Hedging Program Design:
- Hedging horizon and ratio: recommend % of exposure to hedge at each
  time horizon (e.g., 80% of 12-month forward consumption, 60% of
  13–24 months, 30% of 25–36 months); rationale for layered approach
- Hedge accounting qualification: designate as cash flow hedge under
  ASC 815 to avoid P&L mark-to-market volatility; effectiveness testing
- Credit support: CSA (Credit Support Annex) negotiation for OTC
  derivatives; threshold, minimum transfer amounts, and collateral types
- Cost-benefit analysis: expected savings from hedging vs. cost of
  premium and opportunity cost (foregone upside)

Format as a Goldman Sachs Commodity Hedging Advisory Memo with:
  • Commodity Exposure Quantification Table
  • Hedging Instrument Comparison Matrix
  • Recommended Hedging Program (by commodity, tenor, and instrument)
  • Hedge Accounting Treatment Summary
  • Annual P&L Volatility Reduction Estimate (hedged vs. unhedged)

My inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INDUSTRY | PRIMARY COMMODITY EXPOSURES |
            ANNUAL COMMODITY SPEND | CURRENT HEDGING POLICY (IF ANY) |
            BIGGEST HEDGING CONCERN | HEDGE ACCOUNTING APPETITE]

title: The Ares Management Direct Lending Credit Underwriting Framework
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director at Ares Management's Credit Group — the world's
largest publicly traded credit manager — who underwrites direct lending
investments to middle-market companies (EBITDA $10M–$75M) typically backing
private equity sponsors.

I need a comprehensive direct lending credit underwriting framework covering
credit analysis, deal structuring, and portfolio management.

Underwrite the credit:

Business Quality Assessment:
- Revenue and EBITDA quality: % of recurring revenue, contract duration,
  customer concentration, revenue cyclicality, and EBITDA add-back
  legitimacy (flag aggressive add-backs)
- Competitive position: niche market leadership (a key direct lending
  criterion — typically top-2 in a defensible niche market)
- Management team assessment: sponsor track record with this management
  team; management equity rollover as an alignment signal
- Sponsor quality: tier-ranking the PE sponsor (Tier 1: large established
  PE firms; Tier 2: mid-market specialists; Tier 3: smaller or first-time
  funds) — how does sponsor quality affect pricing and covenant protection?

Credit Metrics & Structuring:
- Entry leverage: Total Debt/EBITDA; Senior Secured Debt/EBITDA — compare
  to sector standards; coverage ratios: EBITDA/Interest, EBITDA−Capex/
  Interest, FCF/Debt Service
- Loan structure design: first-lien senior secured (most common in direct
  lending), unitranche, second lien, or mezzanine; explain the risk/return
  trade-off of each
- Pricing: reference rate (SOFR) + credit spread; upfront fees (OID);
  PIK toggle option and when it's appropriate; expected all-in yield
- Covenant package: maintenance covenants (Total Leverage, Interest
  Coverage, Minimum Liquidity — set at meaningful headroom levels);
  incurrence covenants (anti-accordion basket, acquisition limitations)
  — importance of maintenance covenants in direct lending vs. cov-lite
  broadly syndicated loans
- Collateral package: first priority lien on all assets (real property,
  IP, accounts receivable, inventory); borrowing base if applicable

Scenario & Stress Analysis:
- Base case: EBITDA grows at sponsor model; loan fully repaid at exit
- Stress case: EBITDA declines 20%; model DSCR breach timing and recovery
  value in a restructuring (liquidation value vs. going-concern value)
- Loan-to-Value (LTV) analysis: enterprise value cushion above the loan
  amount at entry; minimum acceptable entry LTV threshold

Format as an Ares Direct Lending Investment Committee Memo with:
  • Credit Metrics Summary (Leverage, Coverage, LTV)
  • Covenant Package Recommendation
  • Stress Test Scenario Table
  • Expected Return Analysis (Base / Stress → IRR and Loss Given Default)
  • Portfolio Fit Assessment (Sector concentration, sponsor concentration)

My inputs: [BORROWER NAME | INDUSTRY | SPONSOR | LTM EBITDA | PROPOSED LOAN
            AMOUNT | PROPOSED LEVERAGE | BUSINESS DESCRIPTION | PRIMARY CREDIT RISK]

title: The Blackstone Credit & Insurance (BXCI) Private Credit Portfolio Strategy
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Portfolio Manager at Blackstone Credit & Insurance (BXCI) —
one of the world's largest credit managers — responsible for constructing and
managing a diversified private credit portfolio for insurance company
general accounts, pension funds, and sovereign wealth funds.

I need a comprehensive private credit portfolio construction strategy
covering all sub-asset classes within the private credit universe.

Design the portfolio:

Private Credit Universe Mapping:
- Direct Lending: senior secured middle-market loans (EBITDA $10M–$75M
  backed by PE sponsors); typical return 10–12% all-in yield; floating rate
- Leveraged Loans (Broadly Syndicated): larger loans ($500M+) to larger
  sponsors; more liquid but tighter spreads (7–9% all-in)
- High Yield Bonds: fixed rate, public, liquid; 6–9% yield
- Mezzanine / Subordinated Debt: junior debt behind senior secured;
  12–15% return (cash + PIK); equity upside via warrants
- Real Estate Debt: commercial mortgage loans, CRE CLOs, CMBS B-pieces;
  targeted returns 8–12% depending on subordination
- Infrastructure Debt: investment-grade senior secured project finance
  and infrastructure loans; 4–7% yield with very low default rates
- Specialty Finance: consumer loans, SME loans, receivables finance,
  CLOs — asset-backed credit with structural protections

Allocation & Portfolio Construction:
- Return/risk/liquidity matrix: rank each sub-asset class on: expected
  net return, default rate, recovery rate, and liquidity (time to exit)
- Recommended portfolio weights for: (a) Insurance general account
  (capital efficiency, RBC charges per sub-asset class), (b) Pension
  fund (liability-matching, long duration preference), (c) SWF
  (pure return maximization with illiquidity premium capture)
- Vintage year diversification: importance of committing consistently
  across market cycles; avoid concentration in one vintage
- Correlation analysis: how do the sub-asset classes perform relative
  to each other in credit downturns (2008, 2020)?

Credit Cycle Positioning:
- Late cycle vs. early cycle positioning: which sub-asset classes to
  overweight/underweight at each phase of the credit cycle
- Defensive positioning signals: spread compression, covenant erosion,
  leverage creep — when these are observed, rotate to senior/secured
  and reduce subordinated exposure

Format as a BXCI Private Credit Portfolio Strategy with:
  • Sub-Asset Class Universe Table (Return / Risk / Liquidity Matrix)
  • Recommended Portfolio Weights by Investor Type
  • Vintage Year Diversification Strategy
  • Credit Cycle Positioning Guide
  • Expected Portfolio Yield, Duration, and Default Rate

My inputs: [INVESTOR TYPE (INSURANCE / PENSION / SWF / ENDOWMENT) |
            PORTFOLIO SIZE | TARGET NET RETURN | LIQUIDITY REQUIREMENTS |
            CURRENT PRIVATE CREDIT ALLOCATION | LEVERAGE APPETITE]

title: The Golub Capital Unitranche & One-Stop Financing Structuring Advisor
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director at Golub Capital — one of the most respected
direct lenders in the US middle market — specializing in unitranche and
one-stop financing solutions for PE-backed leveraged buyouts.

I need a comprehensive unitranche financing structure and credit analysis
for a PE-backed LBO transaction, explaining the unitranche product and
its advantages vs. a traditional senior/junior split-capital structure.

Structure and analyze:

Unitranche Mechanics:
- Definition: a single blended loan that combines first and second lien
  debt into one tranche with one interest rate and one lender relationship
- Agreement Among Lenders (AAL): how unitranche actually works — the
  synthetic split into "first out" (FO) and "last out" (LO) pieces within
  the unitranche, with different pricing and repayment priority
- Blended interest rate calculation: FO rate + LO rate weighted by size
  = effective blended rate for the borrower; show an example calculation
  (e.g., 60% FO at SOFR+500 + 40% LO at SOFR+800 = SOFR+620 blended)
- Comparison to traditional senior + mezz structure: same total leverage,
  but unitranche has: (a) one lender relationship, (b) faster execution,
  (c) flexible documentation, (d) typically covenant-lite below traditional
  direct lending thresholds

Unitranche Sizing & Terms:
- Typical sizing: 4.5x–6.0x EBITDA total unitranche; some one-stop
  providers go to 7.0x+ in hot markets for high-quality sponsors
- Pricing: current market all-in rate for unitranche by leverage tier
  (< 4.5x, 4.5–5.5x, > 5.5x) and EBITDA size
- Covenant package: single financial maintenance covenant (Leverage Ratio),
  typically set at 50–75bps headroom to closing leverage
- Accordion feature: uncommitted accordion that allows the borrower to
  upsize the facility post-close for acquisitions
- Equity commitment: PE sponsor equity check (typically 40–50% of total
  capitalization in direct lending deals)

Credit Underwriting for This Transaction:
- EBITDA quality assessment: identify top 5 add-backs and whether they
  are defensible; adjusted EBITDA vs. Golub's credit EBITDA (typically
  more conservative than sponsor EBITDA)
- Leverage analysis: entry leverage, DSCR, and required EBITDA growth
  to de-lever below 5.0x by Year 3
- Exit analysis: what PE sponsor exit scenarios generate full repayment
  plus fee income for Golub?

Format as a Golub Capital Unitranche Credit Memo with:
  • Unitranche vs. Senior/Junior Structure Comparison Table
  • Blended Rate Calculation Example
  • Deal Terms Summary (Sizing, Pricing, Covenant, Maturity)
  • Credit Metrics at Close and Year 3 Projection
  • Stress Analysis: EBITDA -20% → DSCR and Covenant Headroom

My inputs: [BORROWER NAME | SPONSOR | INDUSTRY | LTM EBITDA | PROPOSED LEVERAGE
            (X EBITDA) | ACQUISITION MULTIPLE | EQUITY % | BUSINESS DESCRIPTION]

title: The Norway Government Pension Fund (GPFG) Sovereign Wealth Fund
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Portfolio Strategist at Norges Bank Investment Management
(NBIM) — which manages the $1.7 trillion Norway Government Pension Fund
Global (GPFG), the world's largest sovereign wealth fund — responsible for
advising on strategic asset allocation, factor investing, and governance
standards.

I need a comprehensive sovereign wealth fund asset allocation and
governance framework applicable to a newly established or restructuring SWF.

Design the framework:

SWF Mandate & Design:
- SWF typology: stabilization fund, savings fund (intergenerational
  wealth transfer), reserve investment corporation, pension reserve fund,
  or development fund — each requires a different asset allocation
- Spending rule design: fiscal rule linking SWF withdrawals to government
  budget needs (e.g., Norway's 3% real return rule; Abu Dhabi's inflation+
  return objective); prevent procyclical drawdowns
- Time horizon and liability profile: if the fund has a defined liability
  (e.g., pension obligations) vs. a perpetual savings mandate — how this
  drives the risk/return trade-off

Strategic Asset Allocation:
- Equity allocation: global equities with factor tilts (value, quality,
  small cap as per GPFG's factor strategy); home bias avoidance
- Fixed income: global government bonds as a liquidity and risk buffer;
  inflation-linked bonds for real return protection; credit allocation
  limitations for large SWFs (market impact)
- Alternatives: real estate, infrastructure, and private equity allocation
  rationale; why GPFG historically avoided PE (fee transparency, benchmarking
  difficulty) vs. why Abu Dhabi ADIA, GIC, and Temasek embrace PE
- Factor investing at scale: GPFG's documented equity factor premium
  harvesting approach (value, momentum, size, quality); implementation
  challenges at $1T+ scale (capacity constraints, market impact)

Governance & Transparency:
- Governance structure: Ministry of Finance (mandate setter) → Central
  Bank Board → NBIM (investment manager) → External managers;
  clear accountability at each level
- Transparency and reporting: annual report, voting records, and
  exclusion/observation list disclosure (GPFG is the gold standard)
- Responsible Investment Policy: exclusion criteria (weapons, tobacco,
  human rights violations), engagement priorities, and ESG integration
  in investment decisions
- Cost management: why low cost is a competitive advantage for a SWF;
  GPFG's < 5bps total cost ratio as a benchmark

Format as a SWF Asset Allocation & Governance Blueprint with:
  • SWF Mandate & Spending Rule Design
  • Strategic Asset Allocation (Target Weights with Rationale)
  • Factor Investing Strategy
  • Governance Structure Diagram
  • Responsible Investment Policy Framework
  • Performance Measurement & Benchmarking Framework

My inputs: [FUND SIZE | FUND TYPE (STABILIZATION/SAVINGS/PENSION/DEVELOPMENT) |
            SPONSORING GOVERNMENT | EXISTING ALLOCATION | SPENDING RULE IN PLACE |
            TIME HORIZON | PRIMARY OBJECTIVE AND CONSTRAINTS]

title: The Goldman Sachs Healthcare Investment Banking Biotech Valuation
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director in Goldman Sachs' Healthcare Investment Banking
group who has led $100B+ in biotech M&A, IPOs, and equity follow-ons for
companies spanning clinical-stage biotechs to large-cap pharma.

I need a rigorous biotech/pharma company valuation using the risk-adjusted
Net Present Value (rNPV) methodology — the industry-standard approach for
valuing drug pipelines.

Build the valuation:

rNPV Pipeline Valuation Methodology:
- Explain why traditional DCF fails for clinical-stage companies (no
  current revenue, binary outcomes, long development timelines) and
  why rNPV is the appropriate methodology
- For each pipeline asset, build an rNPV model:
  • Peak sales estimate: patient population × diagnosis rate × treatment
    rate × market share × price (net of rebates) × launch year
  • Revenue ramp: S-curve adoption model from launch to peak (typically
    3–5 years); plateau duration; loss-of-exclusivity (LOE) cliff
  • Cost of goods and operating expenses: COGS (10–30% for biologics),
    SG&A (20–30% of sales), and ongoing R&D for lifecycle management
  • Probability of Technical and Regulatory Success (PTRS) by phase:
    Phase 1→2: 60–70%, Phase 2→3: 30–40%, Phase 3→Approval: 50–70%,
    NDA/BLA Approval: 85–90%; compound all phases to get overall PoS
  • Discount rate: WACC for approved products (8–10%); higher for
    clinical-stage (12–15%) to reflect binary risk
  • NPV per asset × PTRS = rNPV per asset
  • Sum all pipeline rNPVs + net cash − debt = equity value

Comparable Biotech Valuation:
- EV/Pipeline rNPV multiple: compare to peer biotechs at similar stage
- Price/Sales for commercial-stage biotech: NTM and Year+2 P/S multiples
- Precedent M&A transactions: acquisition premiums paid for assets at
  each development stage (Phase 2, Phase 3, pre-NDA, commercial)

Catalyst & Binary Event Mapping:
- Map all upcoming binary events (clinical readouts, FDA decisions,
  PDUFA dates) with probability-weighted stock price scenarios
- Implied valuation for each event outcome: success vs. failure price
  target and the stock move expected in each scenario

Format as a Goldman Sachs Biotech Valuation Memo with:
  • rNPV Model by Pipeline Asset (table with all assumptions)
  • Sum-of-Parts Equity Value Waterfall
  • Comparable Company & Transaction Analysis
  • Catalyst Calendar with Probability-Weighted Scenarios
  • Investment Recommendation: Buy / Hold / Sell with Price Target

My inputs: [COMPANY NAME | TICKER | PIPELINE ASSETS (INDICATION, PHASE) |
            NET CASH | ANNUAL BURN RATE | PRIMARY INVESTMENT CATALYST |
            BIGGEST RISK TO THE THESIS]

title: The JPMorgan Healthcare Services & Hospital System Financial Advisor
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director in JPMorgan's Healthcare Investment Banking group
covering hospitals, health systems, managed care organizations (MCOs), and
healthcare services companies.

I need a comprehensive financial analysis and strategic advisory framework
for a healthcare system evaluating a major strategic transaction (acquisition,
joint venture, or affiliation).

Deliver:

Healthcare System Financial Analysis:
- Revenue quality: payor mix analysis (Medicare %, Medicaid %, Commercial %, 
  Self-Pay %); case mix index (CMI); volume trends by service line
  (inpatient, outpatient, surgical, emergency); revenue cycle KPIs
  (days in AR, denial rate, clean claim rate)
- Margin analysis: net patient revenue margin; EBITDA margin vs. sector
  benchmarks (nonprofit vs. for-profit); operating expenses per adjusted
  discharge; labor cost as % of revenue (the primary driver in healthcare)
- Balance sheet: days cash on hand (DCOH) vs. rating agency thresholds
  (Moody's Aa: >200 days, A: >150 days, Baa: >100 days); debt-to-
  capitalization ratio; unrestricted vs. board-designated vs. restricted
  cash; defined benefit pension obligations
- Capital structure & ratings: nonprofit bond rating (Moody's / S&P /
  Fitch); tax-exempt bond capacity; management's financial flexibility

Strategic Transaction Analysis:
- Merger & affiliation rationale: scale economies (supply chain, IT,
  overhead), geographic market complementarity, access to capital,
  clinical program enhancement, physician alignment
- Synergy analysis adapted for healthcare: supply chain savings
  (GPO leverage), duplicative management layers, revenue cycle
  integration, clinical program rationalization
- Regulatory & Certificate of Need (CON) considerations: antitrust
  review for hospital mergers; state CON requirements; FTC scrutiny
  of hospital consolidation; community benefit obligations for nonprofits
- Integration risk factors unique to healthcare: physician alignment
  post-merger, culture of clinical excellence, union labor agreements,
  Epic/Cerner EHR integration complexity

Valuation of Healthcare Systems:
- EV/EBITDA and EV/Revenue multiples for health systems; price per bed
  as a cross-check; DCF using long-term operating projections

Format as a JPMorgan Healthcare M&A Advisory Memorandum with:
  • Financial Performance Dashboard (Key Operating & Financial Metrics)
  • Payor Mix & Revenue Quality Analysis
  • Synergy Identification Table
  • Regulatory Risk Assessment
  • Transaction Valuation Summary

My inputs: [HEALTH SYSTEM NAME | GEOGRAPHY | ANNUAL NET PATIENT REVENUE |
            EBITDA MARGIN | BOND RATING | STRATEGIC OBJECTIVE |
            POTENTIAL PARTNER OR ACQUIRER]

title: The Leerink Partners Medtech & Life Sciences Equity Research Framework
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Equity Research Analyst at Leerink Partners — the leading
independent healthcare investment bank and research firm — covering medical
devices, diagnostics, and life sciences tools companies.

I need a comprehensive equity research framework for analyzing medtech and
life sciences tools companies with sector-specific valuation and KPI analysis.

Analyze:

Medtech Business Model & Quality Assessment:
- Revenue model classification: capital equipment + disposables/consumables
  (razor/razorblade model), pure consumables, software/services, or
  diagnostic test volumes — assess the recurring revenue % and its
  margin profile
- Installed base analysis: total installed base of capital equipment;
  annual replacement cycle; pull-through revenue per installed unit
  (the key revenue predictability metric for medtech)
- Clinical evidence quality: number of published clinical studies, level
  of evidence (RCT vs. observational), regulatory approval pathway
  (510(k) vs. PMA); reimbursement status (covered by CMS, commercial
  payors — CPT code and reimbursement rate)
- Market penetration: current penetration rate of target patient

  market share dynamics
- Hospital capital budget sensitivity: is the product a "must have"
  or a "nice to have"? How does it perform in hospital capex freeze
  environments?

Life Sciences Tools Specific Framework:
- Funding environment sensitivity: % of revenue from NIH-funded academic
  labs, pharma/biotech customers, and clinical/applied markets;
  academic/government funding as a risk factor
- Bioprocessing exposure: biomanufacturing capacity expansion cycle;
  exposure to mRNA/cell & gene therapy growth themes
- Instrument vs. reagent/consumable revenue split; recurring reagent
  attach rate per instrument

Valuation Methodology for Medtech:
- EV/Revenue and EV/EBITDA vs. sector comps (segmented by growth rate)
- DCF with terminal value based on sustainable FCF conversion
- Revenue growth vs. FCF margin scatter plot: where does the company
  sit on the "Rule of X" framework for medtech?
- M&A comps: precedent device and life sciences tools acquisitions;
  premium paid and EV/Revenue multiples for strategics vs. PE

Regulatory & Reimbursement Risk:
- FDA pipeline: 510(k) pending, PMA supplements, De Novo — timing risk
- CMS coverage decisions: CED (Coverage with Evidence Development),
  NCD (National Coverage Determination) — how they affect revenue ramp

Format as a Leerink Medtech Equity Research Report Framework with:
  • Business Model Quality Scorecard
  • Installed Base & Pull-Through Revenue Analysis
  • Valuation Benchmarking Table
  • Regulatory & Reimbursement Risk Matrix
  • Investment Thesis with Bull/Base/Bear Price Targets

My inputs: [COMPANY NAME | TICKER | PRODUCT DESCRIPTION | PRIMARY INDICATION |
            REVENUE SPLIT (CAPITAL/CONSUMABLES) | INSTALLED BASE SIZE |

title: The Evercore ISI Managed Care & Health Insurance Sector Analyst
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Equity Research Analyst at Evercore ISI covering managed care
organizations (MCOs) and health insurance companies including UnitedHealth,
CVS/Aetna, Cigna, Humana, Centene, and Molina.

I need a comprehensive analytical framework for managed care companies covering
the unique financial metrics, regulatory drivers, and valuation methodology.

Analyze:

Managed Care Financial Metrics:
- Medical Loss Ratio (MLR): medical costs ÷ premium revenue; the core
  profitability metric; explain statutory MLR minimums (80–85% for ACA
  plans), how MLR is managed, and the earnings impact of 100bps MLR change
- Membership growth and revenue per member per month (PMPM): organic vs.
  acquired growth; government vs. commercial mix; Medicare Advantage (MA)
  growth vs. Medicaid managed care vs. commercial
- Premium yield: price increases vs. medical trend; how MCOs price for
  medical cost inflation with a 12–18 month lag; the "pricing cycle"
- Operating leverage: SG&A as % of premium revenue; the scalability of
  MCO platforms at higher membership volumes
- Star Ratings (Medicare Advantage): CMS Star Ratings drive MA bonus
  payments worth $600–$1,000 per member per year; 4-star threshold
  significance; impact of Star Rating changes on earnings

Regulatory & Policy Drivers:
- ACA and exchange enrollment: federal subsidies driving enrollment;
  cliff risk if subsidies expire; risk corridor and reinsurance mechanisms
- Medicare Advantage secular growth: demographic tailwind, MA penetration
  expansion; CMS risk adjustment methodology changes and their earnings
  impact (V28 model transition — the largest near-term headwind for MA)
- Medicaid redetermination cycles: the periodic unwinding of continuous
  enrollment protections and its impact on Medicaid MCO membership
- Drug pricing reform: IRA drug negotiation provisions and impact on PBM
  subsidiaries (CVS Caremark, Optum Rx, Express Scripts)

MCO Valuation:
- P/E multiple analysis: MCOs trade on P/E (not EV/EBITDA) because
  they are asset-light businesses with capital return stories
- Earnings growth decomposition: membership growth + PMPM growth + MLR
  management + operating leverage + capital deployment (buybacks)
- DCF using sustainable mid-cycle earnings power
- Sum-of-parts: health benefits + pharmacy benefits management (PBM) +
  care delivery / Optum-like services — each segment valued separately

Format as an Evercore ISI MCO Research Framework with:
  • MLR Sensitivity Analysis (EPS impact per 100bps MLR change)
  • Medicare Advantage Growth Model
  • P/E vs. EPS Growth Regression
  • Regulatory Risk Dashboard
  • Price Target Derivation with Multiple Methodologies

My inputs: [COMPANY NAME | TICKER | MEMBERSHIP BY SEGMENT | CURRENT MLR |
            MA STAR RATING | CURRENT P/E | PRIMARY INVESTMENT THESIS OR CONCERN]

title: The Morgan Stanley Technology Equity Research: Enterprise SaaS Initiation
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Equity Research Analyst at Morgan Stanley's Technology group
who covers enterprise software and SaaS companies for institutional investors,
known for the "Morgan Stanley CIO Survey" and in-depth SaaS framework research.

I need a comprehensive enterprise SaaS company initiation report framework
covering business quality, financial model, and valuation.

Build the initiation framework:

SaaS Business Quality Tier Assessment:
- Tier 1 (Best-in-Class): >120% NRR, >75% gross margin, durable 20%+ ARR
  growth, category leadership, platform with ecosystem — assign premium
  multiple
- Tier 2 (High Quality): 110–120% NRR, 70–75% gross margin, 15–20% growth,
  strong competitive position in a growing market
- Tier 3 (Developing Quality): <110% NRR or <70% gross margin or growth
  decelerating; requires a specific recovery catalyst to own

GTM (Go-to-Market) Model Analysis:
- Sales-led: enterprise ACV, quota attainment rates, pipeline coverage,
  sales cycle length — how to assess sales productivity and scalability
- Product-led growth (PLG): viral coefficient, free-to-paid conversion
  rate, bottom-up land-and-expand mechanics; why PLG companies have
  structurally lower CAC and faster payback
- Channel and partner ecosystem: % of ARR sourced through partners;
  GSI (Global System Integrator) relationships as a moat for enterprise SaaS
- International expansion: % of ARR from international markets; the S-curve
  of geographic expansion and what it means for TAM and margin compression

Cohort & Revenue Quality Analysis:
- ARR bridge: opening ARR + new logo ARR + expansion ARR − churn ARR
  = closing ARR; analyze each component and its trend
- S&M efficiency by cohort: do newer cohorts have better or worse unit
  economics vs. older cohorts? (Deterioration = sign of market saturation)
- Customer segmentation: SMB vs. mid-market vs. enterprise — margin
  profile, churn profile, and growth potential for each

SaaS Valuation Framework:
- EV/NTM ARR or EV/NTM Revenue multiple vs. NTM ARR/Revenue growth rate
  (the "Rule of 40 adjusted" valuation framework)
- DCF using ARR build-up → implied FCF in Year 5 → terminal value
- Mean reversion analysis: where multiples have compressed/expanded
  and what level is sustainable at this growth rate
- Acquisition value: at what price would a strategic acquirer (Salesforce,

title: The HSBC Semiconductor & Semiconductor Equipment Sector Research
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Equity Research Analyst at HSBC's Global Technology Research
team covering semiconductors, semiconductor equipment, and electronic design
automation (EDA) across US, Taiwan, South Korea, and Europe.

I need a comprehensive semiconductor sector research framework covering
the industry cycle, competitive dynamics, and company-specific analysis.

Analyze:

Semiconductor Industry Cycle Analysis:
- Industry structure: fabless design (Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm), IDM
  (integrated device manufacturer: Intel, Samsung, TI), and pure-play
  foundry (TSMC, GlobalFoundries); how each model performs differently
  in up-cycles vs. down-cycles
- Inventory cycle: the semiconductor inventory correction playbook —

- Pricing power and ASP trends: commodity-like products (DRAM, NAND) vs.

AI & Data Center Semiconductor Theme:

- Memory demand for AI: HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) attach rates to

Semiconductor Valuation:
- Through-the-cycle P/E and EV/Sales multiples: why normalized earnings
  matter more than current-year earnings in a cyclical industry
- P/B for memory companies at cycle bottom vs. cycle peak
- FCF yield for mature semiconductor companies (TI, Analog Devices)
- Fabless vs. IDM vs. equipment valuation differences

Format as an HSBC Semiconductor Research Framework with:

  • End-Market Exposure Matrix by Company
  • AI Semiconductor TAM Model
  • Valuation Comparison Table (Through-Cycle P/E vs. Current P/E)

title: The Bernstein AI & Cloud Infrastructure Investment Framework
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Equity Research Analyst at Bernstein Research — known for
contrarian, deeply researched views — covering hyperscalers (Microsoft,
Amazon, Google, Meta) and AI infrastructure companies.

I need a comprehensive AI infrastructure investment framework covering
capex cycle analysis, monetization models, and valuation implications.

AI Capex Cycle Analysis:

title: The UBS Fintech & Payments Equity Research Deep-Dive
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Equity Research Analyst at UBS covering financial technology,
digital payments, and payment network companies (Visa, Mastercard, PayPal,
Stripe, Block, Adyen, Nubank).

I need a comprehensive fintech and payments sector research framework
covering business model economics, competitive dynamics, and valuation.

Analyze:

Payment Network Economics (Visa/Mastercard Framework):
- Four-party network model: cardholder → issuing bank → network →
  acquiring bank → merchant; explain the economics at each node
- Net revenue: gross revenue − volume incentives (the "rebate" paid to
  large issuers and merchants to incentivize volume)
- Key metrics: payment volumes (PCE), transactions per card, cross-border
  volume (highest-margin segment), and service fee economics
- Network effects moat: why Visa and Mastercard are the definition of
  a two-sided platform moat; quantify the switching cost
- Threat analysis: real-time payment rails (RTP, FedNow, UPI, PIX),
  BNPL (Buy Now Pay Later), cryptocurrency payments, and big tech
  digital wallets — rate the threat level to the network model

Fintech Payments Business Models:
- PayFac model (Stripe, Square): software-led payment facilitation;
  monetization through interchange + software SaaS fees; GPV (Gross
  Payment Volume) as the key top-of-funnel metric
- BNPL economics: merchant discount rate, consumer credit risk (loss
  rates), and the interest rate sensitivity of BNPL funding models
- Embedded finance: the convergence of software and financial services;
  revenue opportunity for vertical SaaS companies embedding payments,
  lending, and insurance (e.g., Toast, Shopify, ServiceTitan)
- Neobanks: customer acquisition cost in digital banking; the path from
  loss-making growth phase to profitability; monetization beyond
  interchange (lending, premium subscriptions, wealth management)

Fintech Valuation Framework:
- Payments network: EV/Revenue and EV/EBITDA vs. growth rate; FCF
  yield for mature networks
- High-growth fintech: EV/TPV (Total Payment Volume) or EV/Revenue;
  how to normalize for take rate differences across business models
- Embedded finance: blended fintech + software multiple framework
- M&A multiples in fintech: historical deal premiums; strategic value
  of distribution + data to acquiring banks or networks

Format as a UBS Fintech & Payments Research Framework with:
  • Payment Network Economics Model (Revenue per $1,000 of TPV)
  • Fintech Business Model Comparison Matrix
  • Threat Assessment Dashboard (RTP, Crypto, BNPL, BigTech)
  • Valuation Benchmarking Table by Business Model Type
  • Top 3 Investment Ideas with Catalysts

My inputs: [COMPANY NAME OR SECTOR FOCUS | CURRENT EV/REVENUE MULTIPLE |
            TPV OR PAYMENT VOLUME | TAKE RATE | PRIMARY COMPETITIVE CONCERN |
            INVESTMENT HORIZON]

title: The Bernstein Consumer Staples & Brand Equity Research Framework
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Equity Research Analyst at Bernstein Research covering global
consumer staples — P&G, Unilever, Nestlé, Colgate, Reckitt — as well as
premium consumer brands (LVMH, Hermès, L'Oréal).

I need a comprehensive consumer staples and brand equity research framework
covering pricing power, volume resilience, and brand value quantification.

Analyze:

Consumer Staples Business Quality Framework:
- Pricing power assessment: historical price elasticity of demand for
  key categories; ability to take price above inflation without volume
  loss; private label penetration risk by category (cereal: high risk,
  baby care: low risk, luxury: no risk)
- Organic growth decomposition: pricing + volume + mix for the last
  8 quarters; identify whether growth is driven by durable market share
  gains or temporary pricing recovery
- Portfolio quality: % of revenue from "must have" daily-use categories
  vs. "nice to have" discretionary; category growth vs. market growth
  (gaining or losing share?)
- Geographic exposure: developed market (DM) vs. emerging market (EM)
  split; EM penetration opportunity vs. DM market saturation dynamics
- FMCG cost structure: commodity input exposure (soy, palm oil, PET
  resin, pulp); gross margin trajectory in periods of commodity inflation
  and deflation

Brand Equity Quantification:
- Interbrand / BrandZ methodology: explain the financial basis of brand
  value measurement; how brand equity translates to pricing premium and
  lower customer acquisition cost
- Premium-to-private-label price gap: is the brand's premium justified
  and sustainable? Has the price gap widened beyond consumer tolerance?
- Share of wallet: brand loyalty metrics — repeat purchase rate, basket
  penetration, household penetration; NPS vs. category average

Premium & Luxury Consumer Analysis (LVMH/Hermès Framework):
- Aspirational vs. true luxury: different demand dynamics; true luxury
  is price inelastic (Hermès Birkin appreciates with higher price)
- Chinese consumer sensitivity: luxury sector exposure to China GDP and
  consumer confidence; channel mix (mainland China, DFS, travel retail)
- Organic revenue growth = volume + price + mix + FX; for luxury,
  price and mix typically drive 60–70% of organic growth

Valuation:
- EV/EBITDA and P/E for staples; premium for pricing power and defensive
  characteristics; luxury EV/EBIT with justified premium multiple
- FCF yield and dividend growth as valuation anchors for mature staples

Format as a Bernstein Consumer Research Framework with:
  • Pricing Power & Volume Resilience Scorecard
  • Organic Growth Decomposition (8 quarters)
  • Brand Equity Dashboard
  • Commodity Cost Sensitivity Analysis
  • Valuation Table (EV/EBITDA vs. Organic Growth vs. FCF Yield)

            RECENT PRICING VS. VOLUME TREND | CURRENT EV/EBITDA |

title: The AlixPartners Retail Sector Transformation & Omnichannel Strategy
prompt_text:
Act as a Senior Managing Director at AlixPartners' Retail & Consumer Products
practice who has led retail transformation programs for distressed and
performing retailers navigating the omnichannel revolution.

I need a comprehensive retail business transformation strategy covering
store economics, e-commerce profitability, and supply chain adaptation.

Design the transformation:

Retail Financial Diagnostic:
- Four-wall store economics: for the average store and the bottom quartile
  — Revenue, Gross Margin, Labor, Occupancy, Other Controllable Costs →
  Four-Wall EBITDA; identify the store contribution threshold below which
  closure is value-enhancing
- Same-store sales (SSS) decomposition: traffic × conversion × average
  transaction value; identify which driver is the primary problem
- E-commerce unit economics: gross merchandise value (GMV), revenue
  (GMV × take rate or direct sales), fulfillment cost per order (last-
  mile delivery is the key variable cost), return rate and cost, and
  marketing cost per order → e-commerce contribution margin
- The profitability paradox: why e-commerce is often less profitable
  than physical retail per transaction; how to reach e-commerce
  profitability (AOV growth, return reduction, fixed cost absorption)

Store Network Optimization:
- Store classification: A-stores (profitable, strategic), B-stores
  (profitable but not strategic), C-stores (marginally profitable),
  D-stores (money-losing) — recommend action for each class
- Real estate liability management: negotiate lease modifications with
  landlords (rent reduction, co-tenancy relief, early termination);
  sale-leaseback opportunities for owned real estate
- Right-sizing the store: reduce square footage, sublease excess space,
  repurpose as fulfillment hub (BOPIS, ship-from-store)

Omnichannel Integration:
- Inventory visibility and unified inventory: single view of inventory
  across all channels; enable ship-from-store without cannibalizing
  store margin
- BOPIS (Buy Online, Pick Up In Store) and BORIS (Buy Online, Return
  In Store): economics of each; incremental in-store spend from
  BOPIS pick-up traffic
- Customer data and loyalty: unified customer ID across channels;
  personalization ROI; loyalty program economics (cost per point,
  redemption rate, incremental spend lift)

Format as an AlixPartners Retail Transformation Plan with:
  • Four-Wall Economics by Store Class
  • Store Network Optimization Recommendation
  • E-Commerce Unit Economics Model
  • Omnichannel Integration Roadmap
  • 3-Year Financial Bridge (Revenue + EBITDA improvement)

My inputs: [RETAILER NAME | FORMAT (SPECIALTY/DEPT/GROCERY/DTC) | NUMBER OF
            STORES | E-COMMERCE AS % OF REVENUE | CURRENT EBITDA MARGIN |
            PRIMARY TRANSFORMATION CHALLENGE]

title: The KKR Consumer & Retail PE Investment Thesis Builder

title: The Lazard Renewable Energy Project Finance & LCOE Analyzer
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director at Lazard's Power, Energy & Infrastructure group —
who publishes the annual Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) analysis, the global
standard for renewable energy economics — advising utilities, developers, and
infrastructure funds on renewable energy project financing.

I need a comprehensive renewable energy project finance analysis covering
LCOE, project economics, and optimal financing structure.

Analyze:

Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) Methodology:
- LCOE definition: the NPV of total lifecycle costs ÷ total lifetime
  energy production ($/MWh); makes different generation technologies
  comparable on a like-for-like basis
- LCOE components:
  (1) Capital Cost ($/kW installed): module/turbine cost, BOS
      (Balance of System: inverters, racking, wiring), EPC contractor
      margin, soft costs (permits, interconnection, development)
  (2) Operating & Maintenance Cost ($/MWh): fixed O&M ($/kW-year),
      variable O&M ($/MWh), insurance, land lease
  (3) Capacity Factor: % of hours per year the plant generates at
      full capacity — solar utility: 20–30%, onshore wind: 25–45%,
      offshore wind: 35–55%
  (4) Discount Rate (WACC): how to set WACC for renewable projects
      (lower than corporate WACC due to contracted cash flows)
  (5) Project Life: typically 25–35 years; degradation rate (solar:
      0.5% per year)
- LCOE comparison: solar, onshore wind, offshore wind, CCGT, nuclear,
  coal — current ranges and 10-year trajectory (learning curves)

Project Finance Structure:
- Non-recourse project finance: why projects use ring-fenced SPV
  structures; the role of the offtake agreement (PPA) in enabling
  low-cost debt financing
- Capital structure: typical 70:30 debt/equity split; senior secured
  project finance debt terms (DSCR covenant ≥ 1.25×, 15–20 year tenor)
- Revenue contract analysis: PPA terms ($/MWh fixed price or index-
  linked, duration, curtailment provisions); merchant revenue risk if
  partially uncontracted
- Tax equity: the critical role of US tax equity in ITC/PTC monetization
  (IRA enhanced credits); tax equity structure (partnership flip, sale-
  leaseback); effective return to tax equity investor (7–9% after-tax)
- Construction risk: EPC fixed-price lump-sum contract; performance
  bonds; delay liquidated damages; completion guarantee from sponsor

Returns Analysis:
- Project IRR (unlevered) and equity IRR (levered): target equity IRR
  for utility-scale solar (8–10%), onshore wind (10–12%), offshore wind
  (10–14%); DSCR sensitivity to merchant price assumptions
- Refinancing upside: "back-leverage" refinancing once construction risk
  is resolved typically increases equity returns 200–400bps

Format as a Lazard Renewable Energy Project Finance Memo with:
  • LCOE Build-Up Table (by technology, current and projected)
  • Project Finance Sources & Uses
  • Revenue Waterfall (PPA revenue → DSCR → equity cash flow)
  • Tax Equity Structure Diagram
  • Equity IRR Sensitivity (Capacity Factor × PPA Price)

My inputs: [PROJECT TYPE (SOLAR/WIND/STORAGE/HYBRID) | LOCATION | PROJECT SIZE
            (MW) | CAPITAL COST ($/W) | OFFTAKE STRUCTURE (PPA OR MERCHANT) |
            PPA PRICE IF APPLICABLE | TARGET EQUITY IRR]

title: The Goldman Sachs Energy Transition M&A & Corporate Strategy Advisor
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director in Goldman Sachs' Natural Resources Investment Banking
group who advises oil & gas majors (ExxonMobil, Shell, TotalEnergies, BP) and
independent E&P companies on energy transition strategy, portfolio optimization,
and clean energy M&A.

I need a comprehensive energy transition strategy for an oil & gas company
navigating decarbonization pressures while maximizing shareholder value.

Design the strategy:

Integrated Energy Company Strategy Framework:
- Business model options along the energy transition spectrum:
  (1) Integrated Energy Company (IEA): balanced portfolio of hydrocarbons
      + renewables + power + trading (Shell, TotalEnergies model)
  (2) Focused E&P with returns discipline: maximize FCF from hydrocarbons,
      return capital to shareholders, minimal low-carbon investment
      (ConocoPhillips, Pioneer model)
  (3) Radical transformation: divest hydrocarbons, pivot to renewables
      (Orsted, NextEra model — but requires access to low-cost capital)
  Evaluate each against: TSR potential, ESG credentials, cost of capital,
  and management capability requirements

Capital Allocation Framework:
- Upstream: maintained-for-value vs. growth capex; break-even oil price
  for each project in the portfolio; carbon cost embedded in project economics
- Clean energy investments: evaluate the risk-adjusted returns of
  renewable energy, hydrogen, carbon capture (CCS/CCUS), and EV charging
  vs. the E&P business; why many oil majors earn lower returns on
  renewable investments (competition from financial capital, lower leverage)
- Share buybacks vs. investment: at what oil price should the company
  prioritize buybacks vs. investment? FCF breakeven analysis

Stranded Asset Risk:
- Carbon budget analysis: how much of the company's proved reserves
  are "burnable" under a 1.5°C vs. 2.0°C scenario?
- Asset impairment risk: which long-dated, high-cost assets (oil sands,
  deep-water, LNG) face stranded asset risk under various carbon pricing
  scenarios?
- M&A implications: divest high-carbon-intensity assets to reduce
  transition risk and improve ESG credentials; identify buyers (NOCs,
  smaller E&P companies)

Clean Energy M&A Strategy:
- Build vs. buy in clean energy: developing greenfield renewables vs.
  acquiring an established renewable developer/IPP; make vs. buy analysis
- Hydrogen strategy: green H2 (electrolysis) vs. blue H2 (SMR + CCS);
  which markets have the near-term demand (industrial decarbonization)
- Carbon offset and CCUS investment: cost per tonne of CCS; credibility
  for corporate net-zero claims

Format as a Goldman Sachs Energy Transition Strategy Report with:
  • Business Model Strategic Options Matrix (TSR vs. ESG vs. Risk)
  • Capital Allocation Framework (Oil Price Scenarios)
  • Stranded Asset Risk Quantification
  • Clean Energy M&A Target Screening Criteria
  • 5-Year Financial Projection Under Each Strategy

My inputs: [COMPANY NAME | OIL EQUIVALENT PRODUCTION (BOE/DAY) | RESERVE LIFE |
            CURRENT CLEAN ENERGY % OF CAPEX | NET-ZERO COMMITMENT |
            SHAREHOLDER RETURN HISTORY | PRIMARY STRATEGIC DILEMMA]

title: The Macquarie Green Infrastructure & Battery Storage Investment Analyzer
prompt_text:
Act as a Managing Director at Macquarie's Green Investment Group (GIG) —
the world's largest green infrastructure investor — specializing in energy
storage, grid modernization, and emerging clean energy technologies.

I need a comprehensive investment analysis for a battery energy storage
system (BESS) project or clean energy infrastructure platform.

Analyze:

Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Investment Framework:
- Revenue streams for BESS: (1) Capacity payments ($/MW-year from ISOs:
  PJM, CAISO, ERCOT), (2) Energy arbitrage (buy cheap off-peak electricity,

  commercial/industrial customers, (5) Paired with renewable (solar +

- Revenue stacking strategy: rank the value streams by reliability and
  margins; model the combined revenue per MWh of storage installed
- Technology economics: lithium-ion (LFP vs. NMC); $/kWh installed cost
  trend (from $1,500/kWh in 2010 to $150–250/kWh today); degradation
  rate per cycle; expected life (3,000–6,000 cycles); replacement cycle
- Merchant vs. contracted revenue: contracted capacity payments provide

Grid Modernization Investment Theme:
- Aging grid infrastructure: the $2T US grid investment need over 20 years;

- Transmission investment: regulated return on equity for transmission
  assets (FERC-regulated: 10–12% ROE); predictable, inflation-linked

- Smart grid and digital grid: advanced metering infrastructure (AMI),

  energy transition (OSIsoft, AutoGrid, Itron)

Clean Energy Infrastructure Platform Strategy:
- Portfolio construction: combination of solar, wind, storage, and

- Development pipeline value: how to value a development pipeline vs.

- Platform M&A: acquiring multiple developers to build scale; synergies

Format as a Macquarie Green Infrastructure Investment Memo with:
  • BESS Revenue Stack Model ($/MWh by service type)

  • Technology Cost Curve (Historical and Projected)
  • Grid Investment Opportunity Sizing
  • Platform Development Strategy

My inputs: [INVESTMENT TYPE (BESS / SOLAR / WIND / TRANSMISSION / PLATFORM) |
