and 6-8 week execution timeline. (5) Parametric triggers: design a parametric trigger
using NOAA wind speed data — basis risk analysis vs. indemnity trigger.
(6) Sidecar vs. cat bond: when each is more efficient for a cedent.
(7) ILS portfolio for investors: diversification benefit, uncorrelated to financial
markets, climate risk adjustment to historical loss models.
Format: ILS Advisory Memo with Cat Bond Term Sheet Template, Pricing Comparison
(Cat Bond vs. Reinsurance), and Investor Presentation Outline.
Inputs: [CEDENT TYPE | PERILS TO TRANSFER | ATTACHMENT POINT | LIMIT SOUGHT |
TRIGGER PREFERENCE | CURRENT REINSURANCE COST | TARGET EXECUTION TIMELINE]

(National Infrastructure Pipeline — cement, capital goods beneficiaries), and
Renewables (India's ambitious 500GW clean energy target). (4) India fixed income:
government bonds (RBI rate path, FTSE/JPMorgan index inclusion — passive inflows
estimate), corporate bonds (market development), and rupee bonds.
(5) India PE/VC: deal activity, unicorn ecosystem, exit environment (IPO market
quality), and sector concentration risks. (6) FDI regulatory framework: FDI limits
by sector, SEBI regulations, FEMA compliance. (7) Geopolitical positioning: India
as a beneficiary of US-China decoupling.
Format: India Investment Strategy Report with Macro Dashboard, Equity Sector
Allocation, Fixed Income Positioning, and PE/VC Market Overview.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | CURRENT INDIA ALLOCATION | BENCHMARK | ASSET CLASS
FOCUS (EQUITY/DEBT/PE) | CURRENCY HEDGING POLICY | TIME HORIZON]

title: The Deutsche Bank European Leveraged Finance & High Yield Advisor
prompt_text:
PROMPT 131 — The Deutsche Bank European Leveraged Finance & High Yield Advisor
Act as MD in Deutsche Bank's European Leveraged Finance group. Structure and
price a high-yield bond or leveraged loan for a European PE-backed company.
Deliver: (1) European leveraged finance market overview: loan vs. HY bond market
size, liquidity, and investor base; SSF (Single B, Split B, Double B) market
segments. (2) HY bond structuring: Rule 144A/Reg S offering for European issuers;
8-year non-call 3 structure; change of control put at 101; restricted payments
and debt incurrence covenant package; call schedule (make-whole, then fixed
premium declining to par). (3) Leveraged loan structuring: Term Loan B with
EURIBOR + 350-450bps; cov-lite documentation; MFN provisions; accordion facility.
(4) HY vs. leveraged loan comparison: fixed vs. floating rate considerations;
call flexibility; covenant protection for investors; investor base overlap.
(5) European market dynamics: €IG vs. €HY spread dynamics; ECB QE/QT impact
on credit spreads; cross-border currency (€ vs. £ vs. $); regulatory differences
(ICMA vs. LMA documentation). (6) Pricing: comparable recent transactions in the
sector; OID sensitivity; market flex provisions. (7) Roadshow strategy: CLO investors,
European HY funds, US crossover buyers.
Format: Leveraged Finance Advisory with Term Sheet, Comps Table (recent deals),
HY vs. Loan Comparison, and Investor Targeting Strategy.
Inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INDUSTRY | LTM EBITDA | PROPOSED LEVERAGE | CURRENCY |
PURPOSE (LBO/RECAP/REFI) | DESIRED INSTRUMENT | TIMING]

title: The Moelis & Company Special Situations Restructuring & Liability Management
prompt_text:
PROMPT 132 — The Moelis & Company Special Situations Restructuring & Liability Management
Act as MD at Moelis & Company's Restructuring practice. Advise a leveraged company
on proactive liability management and debt restructuring before a formal default.
Deliver: (1) Liability management toolkit: tender offer, open market repurchases,
exchange offer, consent solicitation, and amend & extend — when each is optimal.
(2) Exchange offer mechanics: offer new bonds (at discount to face, longer maturity,
higher coupon) in exchange for existing bonds; acceptance threshold (typically
>90%); cramdown risk if < 90% participates. (3) Distressed exchange: when does
a company offer cents-on-the-dollar for existing debt? Required discount to incentivize
holders; tax treatment for both issuer and holder. (4) "Liability management
transaction" (LMT): the controversial practice of using restricted payment baskets
and "trapdoor" provisions to move assets out of reach of existing creditors
(Serta, Envision Healthcare cases) — explain the mechanics, legal controversy,
and creditor committee response. (5) Covenant amendment via consent solicitation:
pricing consent fees; minimum threshold for passage; identifying holdouts.
(6) Waterfall analysis: who loses (and by how much) in each liability management
scenario — current creditors, sponsors, and trade creditors. (7) Timeline: typical
out-of-court liability management timeline vs. Chapter 11.
Format: Restructuring Advisory with Liability Management Options Matrix,
Exchange Offer Economics, Waterfall Analysis, and Execution Timeline.
Inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INDUSTRY | DEBT STRUCTURE BY TRANCHE | NEAREST MATURITY |
EBITDA VS INTEREST COVERAGE | LIQUIDITY RUNWAY | PRIMARY RESTRUCTURING OBJECTIVE]

title: The Rothschild Sovereign Advisory & Government Debt Restructuring
prompt_text:
PROMPT 133 — The Rothschild Sovereign Advisory & Government Debt Restructuring
Act as Senior Advisor at Rothschild's Sovereign Advisory practice — the premier
advisor to governments on debt restructuring, privatization, and capital markets.
Deliver: (1) Sovereign debt restructuring frameworks: Paris Club (bilateral
official creditors), London Club (commercial bank creditors), and bondholder
restructuring (collective action clauses in Eurobonds — CAC 2014 and 2022).
(2) IMF program design: conditionality negotiations; Prior Actions, Structural
Benchmarks, and Performance Criteria; debt sustainability analysis as a
precondition; program financing assurance from bilateral creditors.
(3) Debt restructuring terms: principal haircut vs. maturity extension vs. coupon
reduction — NPV equivalence analysis; fair treatment across creditor classes;
comparable treatment principle. (4) Sovereign bond exchange mechanics: consent
solicitation, exchange offer, exit consent — minimize holdout creditor risk.
(5) China bilateral debt restructuring: the "Common Framework" — why it is
moving slowly; China's preference for case-by-case negotiation; impact on African
and EM sovereign restructuring timelines. (6) Privatization advisory: privatization
sequencing for government assets; strategic sale vs. IPO vs. PPP; ensuring fiscal
proceeds maximize and strategic sector objectives are preserved.
Format: Sovereign Advisory with Debt Restructuring Mechanics, IMF Program Framework,
Creditor Class Waterfall, and Privatization Strategy.
Inputs: [COUNTRY | TOTAL PUBLIC DEBT/GDP | COMPOSITION (BILATERAL/MULTILATERAL/BONDS) |
DEBT SERVICE RATIO | IMF PROGRAM STATUS | PRIMARY RESTRUCTURING CONSTRAINT]

title: The Vanguard / BlackRock Index Fund & ETF Product Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 134 — The Vanguard / BlackRock Index Fund & ETF Product Strategy
Act as Head of Product Strategy at Vanguard or iShares (BlackRock). Design
a new index fund or ETF product strategy for institutional and retail investors.
Deliver: (1) Index selection: active vs. passive debate with empirical evidence
(SPIVA data — % of active funds that underperform over 1/5/10/15 years by category);
criteria for selecting an underlying index (methodology, rebalancing frequency,
turnover, concentration). (2) ETF structure design: physical replication vs. synthetic
(swap-based) — pros/cons for each asset class; creation/redemption mechanism and
how it maintains ETF price = NAV. (3) Total cost analysis: expense ratio + bid-ask
spread + premium/discount + tax efficiency = total cost of ownership; how to compare
ETFs beyond just expense ratio. (4) Factor/Smart Beta ETF design: define the factor
(value, quality, momentum, minimum volatility), index construction methodology,
rebalancing rules, and expected factor premium with academic support. (5) Thematic
ETF risks: concentration in narrow themes (AI, clean energy) — performance vs. broad
index; high launch → high expense ratio → overcrowding risk. (6) Fixed income ETF
liquidity: why bond ETF liquidity > underlying bond liquidity in stress;
the 2020 COVID LQD ETF dislocation and recovery as a case study.
Format: ETF Product Strategy with Index Selection Scorecard, Total Cost Analysis,
Factor Construction Specification, and Product Launch Business Case.
Inputs: [TARGET INVESTOR (RETAIL/INSTITUTIONAL) | ASSET CLASS | FACTOR OR THEME |
TARGET EXPENSE RATIO | DISTRIBUTION CHANNEL | COMPETING PRODUCTS]

title: The Fidelity / Wellington Active Equity Fund Manager Selection
prompt_text:
PROMPT 135 — The Fidelity / Wellington Active Equity Fund Manager Selection
Act as Director of Manager Research at a major pension fund or endowment.
Build a rigorous active equity manager selection and monitoring framework.
Deliver: (1) Manager evaluation framework: the 5 Ps — Philosophy (investment
approach and edge), Process (idea generation, portfolio construction, risk
management), People (team stability, key-person risk, succession), Portfolio
(characteristics, factor exposures, concentration), Performance (attribution,
consistency, alpha vs. benchmark). (2) Alpha persistence analysis: is a manager's
historical alpha statistically significant? t-statistic > 2.0; Information Ratio
(IR) > 0.5 as a quality threshold; performance attribution — stock selection vs.
factor timing vs. luck. (3) Fee negotiation: MFN (Most Favored Nation) clause;
performance fee structures (20% above hurdle; high-water mark); impact of fee
drag on net-of-fee alpha; "fee-adjusted alpha" as the key selection metric.
(4) Capacity constraints: at what AUM does a manager's strategy run out of capacity?
Why smaller managers often outperform (ideas are capacity-constrained).
(5) ESG integration assessment: portfolio company engagement, voting record,
ESG score tilt vs. benchmark. (6) Portfolio construction: blend of active managers
— how to avoid factor overlap and maximize diversification of alpha sources.
(7) Monitoring triggers: style drift, key-person departure, AUM growth, drawdown.
Format: Manager Selection Framework with 5P Scorecard, Performance Attribution
Template, Fee Analysis, and Monitoring Dashboard.
Inputs: [ASSET CLASS | GEOGRAPHY | BENCHMARK | ACTIVE MANAGER BUDGET (# OF MANAGERS) |
FEE BUDGET | ESG REQUIREMENTS | CURRENT MANAGER CONCERNS]

title: The McKinsey Insurance Sector Strategy & Distribution Transformation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 136 — The McKinsey Insurance Sector Strategy & Distribution Transformation
Act as Senior Partner at McKinsey's Insurance practice. Design a distribution
transformation strategy for a large insurer facing digital disruption.
Deliver: (1) Insurance distribution landscape: tied agents vs. independent agents
(IFA/broker) vs. bancassurance vs. direct digital — market share by channel and
trend; cost per policy by channel. (2) Insurtech threat assessment: embedded
insurance (Tesla Insurance, Lemonade), usage-based insurance (Metromile, Root),
digital brokers (Policygenius) — revenue at risk by channel.
(3) Direct-to-consumer (DTC) strategy: digital acquisition funnel; UX/UI investment
required; actuarial pricing capabilities needed for online binding; customer
lifetime value for direct-acquired customers vs. agent-acquired.
(4) Agent channel transformation: digital enablement tools for agents (e-App,
digital illustrations, CRM); productivity metrics (policies per agent per month);
agent recruitment and retention strategy. (5) Data and AI in underwriting: telematics
for auto, wearables for life/health, IoT sensors for commercial property — pricing
sophistication improvement and adverse selection reduction. (6) Embedded insurance:
partner identification (banks, retailers, travel companies); API integration; revenue
share model; underwriting risk in embedded contexts. (7) Financial impact: model the
distribution cost ratio improvement (currently 20-25% of premium) and new business
CAGR under the transformation strategy.
Format: Insurance Distribution Strategy with Channel Economics, Insurtech Threat
Matrix, Digital Transformation Roadmap, and 5-Year Financial Impact.
Inputs: [INSURER TYPE | GEOGRAPHY | DISTRIBUTION MIX | PREMIUM VOLUME |
CURRENT DISTRIBUTION COST RATIO | PRIMARY DIGITAL THREAT | BUDGET FOR TRANSFORMATION]

title: The EY Valuation of Intangible Assets & Intellectual Property
prompt_text:
PROMPT 137 — The EY Valuation of Intangible Assets & Intellectual Property
Act as Partner at EY's Valuation, Modeling & Economics (VME) practice.
Value a company's intangible asset portfolio for M&A, tax transfer pricing,
or financial reporting purposes.
Deliver: (1) Intangible asset classification under ASC 350/IAS 38:
Marketing-related (trademarks), Customer-related (relationships, contracts),
Artistic, Technology-based (patents, software), and Contractual — identify
which require separate recognition on the balance sheet. (2) Royalty rate
benchmarking: how to determine the arm's-length royalty rate for a trademark
or patent using the Knobbe database, court cases, and industry surveys;
25% rule of thumb and its limitations. (3) Relief-from-Royalty (RFR) valuation:
Revenue × royalty rate × (1 − tax rate) discounted at IP-specific WACC;
key sensitivity to royalty rate and discount rate. (4) Multi-Period Excess
Earnings Method (MPEEM): applied to customer relationships; contributory asset
charges (CAC) on tangible assets, working capital, assembled workforce, and other
intangibles; excess earnings attributable to the subject intangible.
(5) Transfer pricing for IP: DEMPE functions (Development, Enhancement,
Maintenance, Protection, Exploitation); which entity should own the IP under
BEPS Pillar 1 and 2 principles; CUT and CPM methods. (6) Useful life determination:
legal life vs. economic life; pattern of consumption; churn rate for customer
relationships. (7) Purchase price allocation timeline and governance under ASC 805.
Format: Intangible Asset Valuation Report with Methodology Comparison, Royalty
Rate Benchmark Table, MPEEM Model Illustration, and Transfer Pricing Implications.
Inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INTANGIBLE ASSET TYPE | TRANSACTION CONTEXT | INDUSTRY |
REVENUE ATTRIBUTABLE TO INTANGIBLE | LEGAL REMAINING LIFE | JURISDICTION]

title: The Deloitte Tax-Efficient M&A Structuring & BEPS Compliance
prompt_text:
PROMPT 138 — The Deloitte Tax-Efficient M&A Structuring & BEPS Compliance
Act as Partner at Deloitte's International Tax M&A group. Structure a cross-border
acquisition for maximum tax efficiency while ensuring BEPS compliance.
Deliver: (1) Pre-acquisition tax diligence: key tax risks in target (transfer pricing
disputes, unrecognized deferred tax liabilities, uncertain tax positions — FIN 48/IAS
37 reserves, VAT/GST exposures, payroll tax compliance). (2) Acquisition structure
options: (a) Share purchase vs. asset purchase — tax basis step-up value in key
jurisdictions; (b) Holding company domicile optimization (Ireland, Netherlands, UK
Holding Company Regime, Luxembourg); (c) Financing structure — thin cap rules,
ATAD interest limitation (30% EBITDA cap in EU), earnings stripping.
(3) BEPS risk assessment: Pillar 1 (reallocation of taxing rights for digital/
consumer businesses), Pillar 2 (global minimum tax 15% — what "top-up tax" does
the acquirer face?); substance requirements for holding company structures.
(4) IP migration pre/post-acquisition: exit charge on IP migration; DEMPE analysis;
country-by-country reporting implications. (5) Tax attribute preservation:
NOL utilization post-acquisition (Section 382 limitation in US; change-of-ownership
rules in UK/EU). (6) Withholding tax optimization: dividend, interest, and royalty
flows between group entities; treaty network analysis. (7) Post-close integration:
legal entity simplification for tax efficiency; consolidation election timing.
Format: Tax M&A Advisory with Structure Options Matrix, BEPS Impact Assessment,
Tax Diligence Risk Register, and Post-Close Integration Tax Roadmap.
Inputs: [ACQUIRER COUNTRY | TARGET COUNTRY | DEAL SIZE | IP OWNERSHIP LOCATION |
FINANCING STRUCTURE | PILLAR 2 EXPOSURE | PRIMARY TAX RISK CONCERN]

title: The KPMG Internal Audit & SOX Compliance Transformation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 139 — The KPMG Internal Audit & SOX Compliance Transformation
Act as Partner at KPMG's Internal Audit and Risk Consulting practice.
Redesign the internal audit function and SOX compliance program for a
public company seeking to improve efficiency and audit quality.
Deliver: (1) IA operating model: risk-based audit plan aligned with top enterprise
risks; audit universe coverage; appropriate mix of operational, financial, compliance,
and IT audits. (2) SOX 404 program design: scoping (significant accounts, significant
locations); documentation standards (flowcharts, narratives, control matrices);
walkthroughs and testing protocols; reliance on management's testing by external
auditor. (3) SOX efficiency levers: automated control testing using data analytics
and RPA; continuous monitoring vs. point-in-time testing; PCAOB inspection findings
to avoid; integrated audits (financial + operational). (4) Three Lines of Defense
(3LoD) optimization: avoid duplication between IA, Risk Management, and Compliance;
reliance framework for external auditor. (5) Co-sourcing vs. outsourcing vs.
insourcing IA: cost and capability comparison; co-sourcing model for specialized
skills (IT audit, data analytics, forensics). (6) IA reporting structure: IA
independence (report to Audit Committee with administrative report to CFO);
IA charter best practices. (7) GRC technology: ServiceNow GRC, AuditBoard, TeamMate
— feature comparison for control documentation, issue tracking, and audit analytics.
Format: IA Transformation Blueprint with Risk-Based Audit Plan, SOX Program Design,
Technology Comparison, and 3-Year Maturity Improvement Roadmap.
Inputs: [COMPANY REVENUE | INDUSTRY | NUMBER OF LEGAL ENTITIES | IA TEAM SIZE |
EXTERNAL AUDITOR | RECENT MATERIAL WEAKNESSES | BIGGEST CONTROL WEAKNESS]

title: The PWC CFO Advisory: Finance Function of the Future
prompt_text:
PROMPT 140 — The PWC CFO Advisory: Finance Function of the Future
Act as Director at PwC's CFO Advisory practice. Design the "Finance Function
of the Future" for a Fortune 500 company — combining automation, AI, and
business partnering to deliver insight rather than just reporting.
Deliver: (1) Finance operating model redesign: Global Business Services (GBS) /
Shared Services for transactional activities (P2P, O2C, R2R); Centers of Excellence
(CoE) for FP&A, Tax, Treasury; Business Partners embedded in business units.
(2) Automation roadmap: RPA for high-volume transactional processes (invoice
processing, bank reconciliation, journal entries); AI for anomaly detection,
forecast enhancement, and narrative generation; estimated FTE reduction and
redeployment. (3) Close cycle acceleration: from 10-day close to 5-day close —
identify the top 5 close bottlenecks and solutions. (4) AI in FP&A: machine learning
for demand forecasting; natural language generation for management commentary;
AI scenario modeling replacing manual sensitivity analysis. (5) Finance talent
strategy: the T-shaped finance professional (deep technical + broad business
acumen); reskilling program for automation-displaced accountants; hiring data
scientists and product managers into finance. (6) Technology architecture:
cloud ERP (SAP S/4HANA, Oracle Fusion) migration roadmap; integrated planning
tool (Anaplan); data lakehouse for analytics. (7) Finance performance metrics:
cost of finance as % of revenue (benchmark: top quartile = 0.5-0.7%); close
cycle time; forecast accuracy; business partner NPS.
Format: Finance Transformation Blueprint with Operating Model Diagram, Automation
ROI Analysis, Close Cycle Improvement Plan, and 3-Year Maturity Roadmap.
Inputs: [COMPANY REVENUE | INDUSTRY | CURRENT FINANCE HEADCOUNT | ERP SYSTEM |
CLOSE CYCLE DURATION | BIGGEST FINANCE PAIN POINT | AUTOMATION BUDGET]

title: The BlackRock Aladdin Risk Platform & Portfolio Analytics
prompt_text:
PROMPT 141 — The BlackRock Aladdin Risk Platform & Portfolio Analytics
Act as Head of Portfolio Analytics at BlackRock using the Aladdin platform.
Design a comprehensive multi-asset portfolio analytics and risk reporting framework.
Deliver: (1) Aladdin architecture: how Aladdin integrates risk, portfolio management,
trading, and operations; why it processes $21T+ in assets. (2) Multi-asset risk
decomposition: factor-based risk model — equity factors (market, size, value,
momentum, quality), rates (duration, curve, convexity), credit (spread beta, issuer
concentration), FX, and commodity. (3) Scenario analysis library: pre-built macro
scenarios (rate shock ±200bps, equity crash -30%, credit spread widening +200bps)
and custom scenario builder using historical analog periods. (4) Liquidity risk
analytics: time-to-liquidate each position at 10%/25%/50% of ADV; portfolio
liquidity bucketing (1-day, 1-week, 1-month, >1-month). (5) ESG integration in
risk: carbon footprint at portfolio level; physical and transition climate risk
at position level; ESG score distribution. (6) Performance attribution: Brinson-
Hood-Beebower model — allocation effect + selection effect + interaction effect.
(7) Client reporting automation: model-driven commentary generation; regulatory
reporting (PRIIPs, UCITS, SFDR). (8) Derivatives risk: Greeks aggregation across
options books; delta, gamma, vega, theta, and rho at portfolio level.
Format: Portfolio Analytics Framework with Risk Dashboard, Scenario Analysis
Library, Liquidity Bucketing Table, and Performance Attribution Template.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | ASSET CLASSES | BENCHMARK | RISK LIMITS | REPORTING
FREQUENCY | REGULATORY JURISDICTION | PRIMARY RISK CONCERN]

title: The Moody's Corporate Credit Rating Methodology & Scorecard
prompt_text:
PROMPT 142 — The Moody's Corporate Credit Rating Methodology & Scorecard
Act as VP-Senior Credit Officer at Moody's Ratings. Apply Moody's corporate
rating methodology to assign a credit rating and rating outlook.
Deliver: (1) Moody's rating methodology overview: Business Risk Profile (BRP) +
Financial Risk Profile (FRP) = issuer rating; explain the scorecard approach for
the specific industry. (2) Business risk factors (typically 50% weight): competitive
position, scale, diversification, operating efficiency, and management quality —
score each sub-factor and determine BRP (Aaa to Ba). (3) Financial risk factors
(typically 50% weight): leverage (Debt/EBITDA), coverage (EBITDA/Interest),
profitability (EBITDA margin), cash flow (FCF/Debt), and liquidity — score each
and determine FRP. (4) Notching adjustments: structural subordination, covenant
protection, collateral, cross-default provisions — up or down from issuer rating.
(5) Liquidity analysis: Moody's liquidity risk assessment (SGL-1 to SGL-4);
key inputs: cash, revolver availability, FCF, near-term maturities, covenant
headroom. (6) Rating sensitivities: what financial metric changes would trigger
a 1-notch upgrade vs. downgrade? (7) Peer comparison: rank the company vs.
3 rated peers on key credit metrics. (8) Rating Committee memo: how to present
the case for a rating action to Moody's Rating Committee.
Format: Credit Rating Report with Scorecard Table, Liquidity Assessment, Peer
Comparison, Sensitivity Analysis, and Rating Committee Memo Outline.
Inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INDUSTRY | LTM REVENUE | LTM EBITDA | TOTAL DEBT |
CASH | CURRENT RATING IF ANY | SPECIFIC RATING QUESTION]

title: The PIMCO Fixed Income Total Return Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 143 — The PIMCO Fixed Income Total Return Strategy
Act as MD at PIMCO managing a core fixed income total return strategy.
Build a comprehensive fixed income portfolio construction and risk framework.
Deliver: (1) Duration positioning: active duration vs. benchmark; how to express
rate views through the yield curve (short end via Fed funds futures, belly via 5yr
notes, long end via 30yr bonds and STRIPS). (2) Sector allocation: benchmark vs.
overweight/underweight across US Treasuries, TIPS, Agency MBS, IG Corporate, HY,
EM Sovereign (USD), and EM Local Currency — with rationale for each.
(3) IG corporate credit analysis: industry selection, issuer selection, maturity
selection within IG; OAS (Option-Adjusted Spread) analysis. (4) MBS analysis:
prepayment risk (CPR modeling), extension risk, and convexity; specified pools vs.
TBAs; IO/PO strips. (5) TIPS and inflation breakeven positioning: real yield vs.
nominal yield trade-off; breakeven inflation vs. forecast; TIPS in rising vs. falling
inflation environments. (6) Currency management: hedged vs. unhedged international
bonds; cross-currency basis swap; currency contribution to total return.
(7) Derivatives overlay: interest rate swaps, CDS index (CDX IG, CDX HY), Treasury
futures for efficient duration adjustment. (8) Yield vs. risk trade-off: portfolio
yield-to-worst, OAS, modified duration, and credit quality distribution.
Format: Fixed Income Strategy with Sector Allocation Table, Duration Positioning,
Yield Attribution, and Scenario Analysis (rate shock / credit shock).
Inputs: [BENCHMARK (AGG/CORE PLUS/UNCONSTRAINED) | DURATION BUDGET | CREDIT QUALITY
CONSTRAINTS | CURRENCY HEDGING POLICY | TARGET YIELD | PRIMARY RATE VIEW]

title: The JP Morgan Derivatives Strategy: Options & Structured Products
prompt_text:
PROMPT 144 — The JP Morgan Derivatives Strategy: Options & Structured Products
Act as Head of Derivatives Strategy at JP Morgan. Design an institutional
options and structured products strategy for portfolio protection and yield
enhancement.
Deliver: (1) Options fundamentals review: Black-Scholes intuition; Greeks and their
practical use (delta hedging, gamma scalping, vega positioning); implied vs. realized
volatility — the core profitability driver for options market makers. (2) Volatility
surface analysis: term structure of implied vol (VIX futures curve); skew (put vs.
call implied vol difference for SPX — the "smirk"); how to identify cheap vs.
expensive vol. (3) Portfolio protection strategies: (a) Put buying — cost, strike
selection, tenor; (b) Put spread — reduce premium by selling lower put; (c) Collar
— sell covered call to finance put; (d) VIX call spreads — tail hedge using VIX.
(4) Yield enhancement strategies: (a) Covered call writing — strike selection vs.
upside cap; (b) Cash-secured put selling — premium income; (c) Risk reversals.
(5) Structured products: (a) Principal-protected notes — zero coupon bond + call
option; (b) Autocallables — regular coupon with early redemption trigger;
(c) Barrier reverse convertibles (BRCs) — high coupon with knock-in put risk.
(6) Institutional use cases: pension fund liability hedging with swaptions; endowment
tail protection program; corporate buyback acceleration with ASR.
Format: Derivatives Strategy with Options Payoff Diagrams (described), Volatility
Surface Analysis, Protection vs. Enhancement Strategy Comparison, and Cost-Benefit.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | PRIMARY OBJECTIVE (PROTECTION/YIELD/SPECULATION) |
UNDERLYING ASSETS | BUDGET FOR PREMIUM | LEVERAGE CONSTRAINTS | RISK TOLERANCE]

title: The Mercer / Aon Hewitt Pension Fund Asset-Liability Management
prompt_text:
PROMPT 145 — The Mercer / Aon Hewitt Pension Fund Asset-Liability Management
Act as Lead Consultant at Mercer Investment Consulting. Design an Asset-Liability
Management (ALM) strategy for a corporate defined benefit pension plan.
Deliver: (1) Pension liability valuation: PBO (Projected Benefit Obligation) vs.
ABO; discount rate selection (corporate AA bond yield); duration of pension liabilities
(typically 12-20 years for mature plans); interest rate sensitivity of liabilities.
(2) Funded status analysis: plan assets vs. PBO; funded ratio; deficit/surplus
in $ terms; PBGC (US) or PPF (UK) insurance premium implications.
(3) Investment objective: maximize risk-adjusted return vs. liabilities (not vs.
a market index); minimize funded status volatility; contribution predictability.
(4) LDI (Liability-Driven Investment) strategy: (a) Return-seeking portfolio
(equities, private equity, real assets — generate returns to close funding gap),
(b) Liability-hedging portfolio (long-duration bonds, interest rate swaps, STRIPS
— match duration and convexity of liabilities); target hedge ratio at different
funded status levels. (5) Glide path design: as funded status improves, increase
hedge ratio and reduce return-seeking; trigger points for de-risking.
(6) Interest rate and inflation hedging: overlay strategy using swaps; TIPS for
inflation-linked liabilities. (7) Pension risk transfer (PRT): buy-in vs. buyout
annuity; when PRT economics make sense; insurer selection process.
Format: ALM Strategy with Liability Profile, Asset Allocation Framework, Glide Path
Table, Hedging Program Design, and PRT Decision Framework.
Inputs: [PLAN SIZE (ASSETS AND LIABILITIES) | FUNDED RATIO | DISCOUNT RATE |
LIABILITY DURATION | PLAN STATUS (OPEN/CLOSED/FROZEN) | RISK TOLERANCE | JURISDICTION]

title: The Calvert / Nuveen ESG Impact Investing Portfolio
prompt_text:
PROMPT 146 — The Calvert / Nuveen ESG Impact Investing Portfolio
Act as Chief Investment Officer at a leading impact investing fund (Calvert,
Nuveen, or Parnassus). Build an impact investing portfolio delivering measurable
social and environmental outcomes alongside financial returns.
Deliver: (1) Impact investing spectrum: philanthropy → grants → impact-first investing
→ finance-first ESG → traditional investing; where the portfolio sits and why.
(2) Theory of change: how each investment produces the intended social/environmental
outcome; additionality test — would the outcome occur without this investment?
(3) Impact measurement framework: IRIS+ metrics selection by sector; output vs.
outcome vs. impact distinction; third-party verification approach.
(4) Portfolio construction: negative screening (exclusions), positive screening
(best-in-class ESG), thematic (clean energy, affordable housing), and direct
impact (community development loans, green bonds). (5) Financial return expectations:
impact premium or discount vs. benchmark? Evidence from academic studies;
sectors where ESG leaders outperform. (6) Engagement and stewardship: active
ownership for impact — shareholder resolutions, direct engagement outcomes, proxy
voting record. (7) Blended finance: using concessional capital (grants, first-loss)
to attract institutional capital at market rates; role of DFIs and philanthropies.
(8) SDG alignment report: map portfolio to SDGs with quantified contribution.
Format: Impact Portfolio Framework with Theory of Change, IRIS+ Metrics, Portfolio
Construction, Financial Return Analysis, and SDG Impact Report Template.
Inputs: [FUND SIZE | IMPACT OBJECTIVES | FINANCIAL RETURN REQUIREMENT | ASSET CLASSES |
GEOGRAPHIC FOCUS | MEASUREMENT FRAMEWORK PREFERENCE | REPORTING REQUIREMENTS]

title: The GIC / Temasek Southeast Asia Investment Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 147 — The GIC / Temasek Southeast Asia Investment Strategy
Act as Senior Portfolio Manager at GIC or Temasek focused on Southeast Asia.
Build a comprehensive SEA investment strategy.
Deliver: (1) SEA macro landscape: GDP growth, demographics, and digital economy
size for Singapore, Indonesia, Vietnam, Thailand, Philippines, Malaysia — scorecard.
(2) Digital economy investment theme: SEA digital economy ($300B+ by 2025); super-app
ecosystems (Grab, GoTo, Sea Limited); e-commerce (Lazada, Tokopedia, Shopee);
fintech penetration in an underbanked region. (3) Manufacturing/nearshoring:
Vietnam and Thailand as China+1 beneficiaries; sector-specific FDI inflows;
industrial park investment thesis. (4) Indonesia deep-dive: largest SEA economy;
commodity exposure (nickel for EVs, coal, palm oil); domestic consumption growth;
digital banking (Bank Jago, BCA Digital). (5) Capital markets access: SGX, IDX,
SET, PSE, Bursa — market depth, foreign ownership limits, governance standards.
(6) Private markets: SEA PE/VC ecosystem; local GPs vs. global PE entering;
consumer, technology, healthcare, and logistics as target sectors.
(7) Currency and FX risk: SEA currency basket analysis; USD correlation;
hedging costs for SGD, IDR, VND, THB, PHP. (8) ESG: palm oil deforestation,
labor rights in manufacturing, governance of family-controlled conglomerates.
Format: SEA Strategy with Country Scorecard, Digital Economy Model, Indonesia
Deep-Dive, Capital Markets Overview, and Portfolio Allocation Recommendation.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | CURRENT SEA ALLOCATION | ASSET CLASS FOCUS | CURRENCY
HEDGING POLICY | GOVERNANCE CONSTRAINTS | PRIMARY OPPORTUNITY FOCUS]

title: The EBRD Central & Eastern Europe Investment & Transition Finance
prompt_text:
PROMPT 148 — The EBRD Central & Eastern Europe Investment & Transition Finance
Act as Senior Banker at EBRD (European Bank for Reconstruction and Development)
evaluating investment opportunities in Central and Eastern Europe and MENA.
Deliver: (1) EBRD mandate: transition impact — investing in markets that are becoming
more market-oriented, competitive, well-governed, green, and integrated.
(2) CEE country landscape: EU member states (Poland, Czech Republic, Romania, Hungary
— post-accession dynamics vs. rule-of-law concerns) vs. Western Balkans (EU
accession pathway) vs. MENA/Turkey (transition challenges).
(3) Priority sectors: renewable energy (EU Green Deal alignment), digital infrastructure,
agribusiness, SME finance, municipal infrastructure. (4) EBRD financing instruments:
senior loans, subordinated debt, equity, guarantees, trade finance — when each is
appropriate and how they combine with co-financing. (5) Transition impact scoring:
EBRD's TI (Transition Impact) assessment — market structure, enterprise reform,
skills, governance — required for each investment approval. (6) EU funds leverage:
how EBRD co-invests with EU Structural Funds, InvestEU, and EFSD+ to stretch
development impact. (7) Green Economy Transition (GET): EBRD's 50%+ green
commitment; taxonomy alignment for CEE investments; just transition finance for
coal-dependent economies (Poland, Czech Republic). (8) Private sector development:
how EBRD invests alongside private co-investors; demonstration effect requirements.
Format: EBRD Investment Advisory with Country Opportunity Matrix, Transition Impact
Framework, Financing Instrument Toolkit, and Green Economy Strategy.
Inputs: [COUNTRY | SECTOR | INVESTMENT SIZE | PROPOSED INSTRUMENT | CO-INVESTOR |
TRANSITION IMPACT HYPOTHESIS | EU FUNDS INVOLVEMENT]

title: The Goldman Sachs Healthcare Sector M&A Wave Analysis
prompt_text:
PROMPT 149 — The Goldman Sachs Healthcare Sector M&A Wave Analysis
Act as MD in Goldman Sachs' Healthcare M&A group. Identify and analyze the
next wave of consolidation in a specific healthcare sub-sector.
Deliver: (1) Sub-sector landscape: map the fragmentation (number of players, market
share distribution, Herfindahl-Hirschman Index); identify the consolidation trigger
(reimbursement pressure, technology shift, scale requirement, PE roll-up thesis).
(2) Consolidation drivers: cost synergies (back-office, GPO, labor), revenue
synergies (cross-sell, broader geographic coverage, payer contracting leverage),
technology scale (EHR, AI diagnostics), and talent scarcity requiring scale.
(3) Strategic acquirer landscape: identify the top 5 likely acquirers — strategic
rationale, balance sheet capacity (net leverage, revolver availability), acquisition
track record. (4) Financial buyer landscape: PE firms active in this sub-sector;
typical LBO leverage and return assumptions; platform vs. add-on dynamics.
(5) Target screening: identify 10 attractive acquisition targets with revenue, EBITDA,
and estimated EV/EBITDA multiple; rank by strategic fit and deal probability.
(6) Valuation benchmarks: recent M&A transactions with multiples; premium paid
for specific attributes (technology, market share, geography).
(7) Regulatory risk: CMS reimbursement risk; FTC antitrust scrutiny of healthcare
consolidation (recent enforcement actions against hospital mergers).
Format: Healthcare M&A Landscape Report with Consolidation Driver Analysis, Target
Screening Matrix, Valuation Benchmarks, and Regulatory Risk Assessment.
Inputs: [HEALTHCARE SUB-SECTOR | GEOGRAPHY | CLIENT TYPE (BUYER/SELLER/INVESTOR) |
DEAL SIZE RANGE | PRIMARY CONSOLIDATION THESIS | REGULATORY CONCERN]

title: The Linklaters / Clifford Chance Finance Lawyer M&A Legal Framework
prompt_text:
PROMPT 150 — The Linklaters / Clifford Chance Finance Lawyer M&A Legal Framework
Act as Partner at Linklaters or Clifford Chance advising on the legal structure
and documentation for a complex cross-border M&A transaction.
Deliver: (1) Deal structure legal analysis: share purchase vs. asset purchase —
contractual, regulatory, and employment law implications in each jurisdiction.
(2) SPA (Share Purchase Agreement) key provisions: locked-box vs. completion
accounts; MAC (Material Adverse Change) clause — narrow vs. broad definition;
representations and warranties — survive and indemnity period; specific indemnities
for known issues. (3) W&I (Warranty and Indemnity) insurance: how it replaces
traditional seller indemnity; premium (1-2% of insured limit); policy limits;
what W&I typically does not cover (known issues, pension liabilities, environmental).
(4) Escrow and earnout: escrow structure for post-closing claims; earnout design
— metrics, anti-manipulation covenants, accounting policy obligations, dispute
mechanism. (5) Regulatory conditions: antitrust pre-notification thresholds;
foreign investment review (CFIUS, NSIA, FIRB); sector-specific regulatory approvals;
long-stop date and consequences of failure. (6) Employee matters: TUPE (UK)/
ARD (EU) — automatic transfer of employees; pension obligations;
change-of-control payments and retention bonuses. (7) Dispute resolution: governing
law choice; arbitration (ICC, LCIA, AAA) vs. litigation; expert determination
for accounting disputes.
Format: Legal Framework Advisory with SPA Key Clause Analysis, W&I Insurance
Comparison, Regulatory Conditions Timeline, and Dispute Resolution Strategy.
Inputs: [ACQUIRER JURISDICTION | TARGET JURISDICTION | DEAL SIZE | INDUSTRY |
DEAL STRUCTURE | KNOWN LEGAL RISKS | W&I INSURANCE APPETITE]

title: The Nomura Japan Equity Research & Abenomics 3.0 Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 151 — The Nomura Japan Equity Research & Abenomics 3.0 Strategy
Act as Chief Japan Equity Strategist at Nomura. Build an investment thesis
for Japan equities in the era of corporate governance reform and BoJ exit.
Deliver: (1) Japan macro: BoJ YCC exit — impact on JGB yields, JPY, and equity
valuations; wage inflation breaking the deflationary trap; Japan real rates moving
from deeply negative toward zero. (2) Corporate governance reform: TSE "prime
market" pressure; P/B < 1× companies required to present improvement plans;
cross-shareholding unwinding (estimated ¥30T+); buyback acceleration.
(3) Shareholder returns: Japanese companies historically hoarded cash; catalyst
for redeployment — buybacks, dividends, strategic M&A; shareholder yield
expanding from 2% to 4%+. (4) Sector allocation: (a) Financials (banks benefit
from rising rates — net interest income expansion), (b) Exporters (JPY depreciation
benefit — Toyota, Sony), (c) Domestic cyclicals (consumption recovery),
(d) Defense (Japan's 2× GDP defense spending commitment). (5) Japan P/E vs.
global: Topix trades at discount to S&P 500 — justified or closing?
(6) Warren Buffett's Japan investment thesis: trading companies (sogo shosha)
— deep value, commodity exposure, capital return; read-through for broader Japan.
(7) Foreign investor flows: record inflows from global active managers; how much
of the re-rating is already priced in.
Format: Japan Equity Strategy with Macro Dashboard, Sector Allocation, Corporate
Governance Reform Tracker, Valuation vs. Global Peers, and Top 5 Stock Ideas.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO JAPAN ALLOCATION | BENCHMARK | CURRENCY HEDGED Y/N |
INVESTMENT HORIZON | PRIMARY JAPAN THESIS | BIGGEST RISK TO THESIS]

title: The Citigroup Global Transaction Banking & Cash Management
prompt_text:
PROMPT 152 — The Citigroup Global Transaction Banking & Cash Management
Act as MD at Citi's Global Transaction Services. Design a global cash management
and transaction banking solution for a multinational corporation.
Deliver: (1) Global cash pooling architecture: notional pooling (no physical movement,
zero-balance accounting) vs. physical sweeping (ZBA — Zero Balance Account);
master account location (optimal for tax and regulatory); multi-currency pooling.
(2) Payment infrastructure: SWIFT gpi for cross-border B2B payments (tracking,
speed); ACH/BACS/SEPA for domestic payments; real-time payment rails (RTP, FedNow,
UPI, Faster Payments UK); virtual accounts for receivables reconciliation.
(3) Liquidity management: cash concentration vs. notional pooling economics;
overnight investment of surplus cash (MMFs, repo, bank deposits); liquidity ladder.
(4) Trade and supply chain finance integration: open account trade (DPO/DSO
management), documentary trade (LC, guarantees), and SCF (reverse factoring)
within a single platform. (5) FX transaction management: auto-FX for in-house
intercompany payments; FX-as-a-Service for SME subsidiaries; netting center design.
(6) Bank account rationalization: audit of global bank accounts (median Fortune 500
has 400+ accounts); reduce to optimal number; KYC/AML compliance simplification.
(7) API banking and ERP integration: real-time balance and transaction reporting
in SAP/Oracle; multibank reporting via SWIFT; host-to-host connectivity.
Format: Transaction Banking Advisory with Cash Pooling Structure, Payment
Architecture, FX Netting Analysis, and Bank Account Rationalization Plan.
Inputs: [COMPANY REVENUE | NUMBER OF COUNTRIES | ANNUAL PAYMENT VOLUME |
CURRENT BANKING RELATIONSHIPS | PRIMARY TXN BANKING CHALLENGE | ERP SYSTEM]

title: The Wellington Management Thematic Long-Term Equity Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 153 — The Wellington Management Thematic Long-Term Equity Strategy
Act as Senior PM at Wellington Management building a concentrated, long-term
thematic equity portfolio based on multi-decade structural growth trends.
Deliver: (1) Thematic identification framework: distinguish durable mega-trends
(demographic aging, decarbonization, digitization, deglobalization) from cyclical
fads; 5 criteria for a high-conviction long-term theme: large TAM, early
penetration, durable growth runway, pricing power, and network effects.
(2) Theme deep-dives (design for 3 themes of your choice): for each theme —
TAM in 2025 and 2035, current penetration rate, growth drivers, and beneficiary
company universe across the value chain. (3) Company selection within themes:
screening criteria — revenue exposure to theme >50%, durable competitive advantage,
management incentive alignment, free cash flow generation. (4) Portfolio construction:
20-30 positions, high active share (>85%), low turnover (<30% annual); how to
manage theme correlation risk. (5) Valuation discipline: the "time arbitrage" edge —
the market undervalues compounding cash flows beyond year 5; how to identify
companies where the long-term DCF far exceeds the current price. (6) Risk management:
position sizing based on conviction and liquidity; circuit breakers for thesis-
breaking events. (7) ESG integration: why long-term thematic investing and ESG are
naturally aligned (governance failures destroy long-term compounding).
Format: Thematic Strategy with Mega-Trend Framework, Theme Deep-Dives (3),
Portfolio Construction Rules, Valuation Discipline, and Risk Management.
Inputs: [FUND SIZE | BENCHMARK | CONCENTRATION LIMIT | THEMATIC FOCUS AREAS |
MINIMUM MARKET CAP | TIME HORIZON | ESG CONSTRAINTS]

title: The Morgan Stanley Equity Derivatives & Volatility Trading
prompt_text:
PROMPT 154 — The Morgan Stanley Equity Derivatives & Volatility Trading
Act as Head of Equity Derivatives Strategy at Morgan Stanley. Build a
comprehensive institutional equity volatility trading and hedging framework.
Deliver: (1) Volatility market structure: VIX term structure (contango vs.
backwardation); realized vs. implied vol spread (variance risk premium); how
to monetize the vol risk premium systematically. (2) Variance swaps: payoff
= Notional × (Realized Vol² - Strike Vol²); why institutions prefer variance
swaps to options for pure vol exposure; vega notional vs. variance notional.
(3) Volatility regime identification: low vol (VIX < 15), normal (15-25), elevated
(25-35), crisis (>35); how to position at each regime.
(4) Dispersion trading: sell index vol, buy single-stock vol when correlation
is elevated; measure index vol vs. implied correlation index.
(5) Gamma scalping: delta-hedging options to capture gamma; P&L depends on
realized vol > implied vol; optimal hedging frequency. (6) Tail risk hedging
program: systematic purchase of OTM puts and VIX calls as portfolio insurance;
cost budgeting (typically 0.5-1% of AUM/year); strike and tenor selection.
(7) Structured vol products: VIX futures, VVIX (vol of vol), reverse VIX ETPs
(XIV successor) — risks and retail investor damage in vol spikes (2018 volmageddon).
(8) Cross-asset vol: rates vol (MOVE index), FX vol, credit vol (CVIX) —
cross-asset vol correlation in risk-off events.
Format: Derivatives Strategy with Vol Regime Dashboard, Variance Swap Mechanics,
Dispersion Trade Design, Tail Risk Hedge Program, and Cross-Asset Vol Monitor.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | OPTIONS BUDGET | DELTA-HEDGING CAPACITY | PRIMARY
PROTECTION OBJECTIVE | LEVERAGE TOLERANCE | LIQUIDITY REQUIREMENTS]

title: The KKR Infrastructure Credit & Project Finance
prompt_text:
PROMPT 155 — The KKR Infrastructure Credit & Project Finance
Act as Head of Infrastructure Credit at KKR. Evaluate a project finance
credit investment in a regulated or contracted infrastructure asset.
Deliver: (1) Infrastructure credit spectrum: investment-grade project finance (senior
secured, BBB-rated) vs. infrastructure sub-investment-grade (BB-rated, higher yield);
DFI and insurance company demand for IG infra debt. (2) Credit analysis: revenue
certainty (regulated utility RAB-based vs. availability-based concession vs.
merchant revenue); DSCR analysis through base and stress scenarios; loan life
cover ratio (LLCR) and project life cover ratio (PLCR). (3) Structural protections:
1st lien security package (all project assets, contracts, and account pledges);
distribution lock-up provisions (DSCR must exceed 1.10-1.15× for cash to flow
to equity); reserve accounts (DSRA funded at 6 months of debt service).
(4) Construction risk in greenfield: fixed-price EPC contract; surety bonds;
completion guarantee; independent engineer role. (5) Refinancing risk: bullet
vs. fully amortizing; refinancing risk at year 5-7 when bullet loan matures;
how to mitigate via mini-perm structure with refinancing covenant.
(6) Greenium in infra debt: green labeled infrastructure bonds trade 5-15bps
tighter — when worth pursuing. (7) Infrastructure debt return vs. equivalent
corporate credit: infrastructure debt typically offers 20-40bps premium for
equivalent rating due to illiquidity; is this sufficient for long-term investors?
Format: Infra Credit Analysis with DSCR Model, Structural Protections Checklist,
Construction Risk Matrix, and Return Comparison (Infra vs. Corporate Credit).
Inputs: [ASSET TYPE | COUNTRY | PROJECT SIZE | REVENUE TYPE (REGULATED/CONTRACTED/MERCHANT) |
TENOR | TARGET CREDIT RATING | CONSTRUCTION STATUS | PRIMARY CREDIT RISK]

title: The Lazard Natural Resources & Mining Investment Banking
prompt_text:
PROMPT 156 — The Lazard Natural Resources & Mining Investment Banking
Act as MD at Lazard's Natural Resources group. Advise a mining company on
capital raising, M&A, and navigating the commodity price cycle.
Deliver: (1) Mining sector valuation methodology: NAV (Net Asset Value) — DCF of
all ore bodies at long-term consensus commodity price; P/NAV multiple vs. peer
group; EV/EBITDA at spot vs. long-term price. (2) Commodity price sensitivity:
for each 10% change in commodity price, what is the % change in EV and equity
value? (leverage amplification effect). (3) Mining M&A: transaction types (asset
acquisition, company acquisition, joint venture, streaming/royalty deal); recent
precedent transactions with EV/reserve and EV/EBITDA multiples.
(4) Streaming and royalties: how Franco-Nevada, Royal Gold, and Wheaton Precious
Metals buy metal streams; why mining companies sell streams (upfront capital,
no operational responsibility); valuation methodology for royalty/streaming
companies vs. producers. (5) Capital markets: equity follow-on (bought deal
in Canada, accelerated bookbuild in Australia/UK); high-yield bonds for mid-tier
miners; project finance for single-asset mines. (6) ESG and social license:
community relations, indigenous consultation rights, tailings storage
management — key ESG risks that have blocked major mining projects.
(7) Energy transition metals: copper, lithium, cobalt, nickel, rare earths —
supply/demand deficit analysis and investment opportunity.
Format: Mining Advisory with NAV Model, Commodity Price Sensitivity, M&A Comps,
Streaming vs. Equity Capital Comparison, and ESG Risk Dashboard.
Inputs: [COMPANY TYPE (MAJOR/MID-TIER/JUNIOR) | COMMODITY | GEOGRAPHY | STAGE
(EXPLORATION/DEVELOPMENT/PRODUCTION) | CAPITAL NEED | PRIMARY STRATEGIC OBJECTIVE]

title: The BCG Healthcare Pharma Commercial Strategy & Launch Excellence
prompt_text:
PROMPT 157 — The BCG Healthcare Pharma Commercial Strategy & Launch Excellence
Act as Senior Partner at BCG's Biopharma practice. Design a commercial strategy
and launch plan for a new pharmaceutical product.
Deliver: (1) Market analysis: disease epidemiology (prevalence, incidence, treated
population); current standard of care and unmet need; competitive landscape
(approved, in-phase 3, preclinical — competitive intensity assessment).
(2) Target patient population definition: label analysis (indication, line of
therapy, biomarker selection); segmentation into primary target, secondary target,
and excluded patients. (3) Pricing and market access strategy: value-based pricing
framework (QALY model vs. cost-effectiveness threshold); payer landscape
(Medicare, commercial, Medicaid — coverage and reimbursement strategy);
HTA (NICE, G-BA, HAS) process for ex-US markets. (4) Commercial model design:
salesforce sizing (target call plan, MSL program, speaker bureau); marketing
strategy (KOL development, congress strategy, digital channels); managed care
team structure. (5) Launch trajectory: how to achieve peak sales by year 3-4;
leading indicators of launch success (formulary wins, prescriber breadth,
refill rates). (6) Competitive response: how will competitors react to the
launch? Pre-emptive strategies. (7) Financial model: NPV of commercial launch
including peak sales, gross-to-net adjustments, commercial costs, and royalties.
Format: Pharma Commercial Strategy with Market Model, Pricing Analysis, Commercial
Infrastructure Design, Launch KPIs, and P&L Projection.
Inputs: [DRUG NAME | INDICATION | MECHANISM | CLINICAL DATA SUMMARY | TARGET LABEL |
COMPETITIVE LANDSCAPE | PLANNED LAUNCH DATE | TARGET GEOGRAPHY]

title: The Advent International Software & Technology Buyout Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 158 — The Advent International Software & Technology Buyout Strategy
Act as Principal at Advent International's Technology team. Build an investment
thesis for a B2B software company buyout.
Deliver: (1) B2B software PE thesis: why software is the preferred PE asset class
(recurring revenue, negative working capital, high margins at scale, asset-light
model); typical entry multiples (12-20× EBITDA or 5-10× ARR).
(2) Software quality assessment: ARR, NRR, GDR, logo churn, gross margin — how
to assess these for a buyout vs. a growth investment (PE demands profitability or
clear near-term path). (3) Value creation levers for software PE:
(a) Profitability improvement — R&D and G&A optimization post-acquisition;
"Rule of X" improvement from Rule of 30 → 40+; (b) Pricing power realization
— price increases for entrenched customers; (c) Sales force productivity improvement;
(d) Product extension — new modules that increase ARPU; (e) M&A — tuck-in
acquisitions of complementary products. (4) Operational improvement: marketing
spend efficiency (performance marketing vs. brand); customer success model
redesign to reduce churn; R&D productivity (output per engineer).
(5) LBO model: typical 50-60% equity, 40-50% debt structure for software;
covenant package; leverage ratio at entry and de-leverage path.
(6) Exit: strategic sale (Microsoft, Salesforce, ServiceNow acquisition appetite);
PE secondary; IPO for large-scale platforms. (7) Management retention: key
employee retention post-buyout; LTIP design to retain engineers and sales.
Format: Software PE Investment Committee Memo with Quality Scorecard, Value Creation
Plan, LBO Model, Exit Analysis, and Management Incentive Design.
Inputs: [COMPANY NAME | ARR | NRR | GROSS MARGIN | RULE OF 40 SCORE |
ENTRY MULTIPLE (ARR) | PRIMARY VALUE CREATION THESIS | HOLD PERIOD]

title: The AlixPartners Digital Transformation ROI & Business Case
prompt_text:
PROMPT 159 — The AlixPartners Digital Transformation ROI & Business Case
Act as MD at AlixPartners' Digital practice. Build a rigorous business case
and ROI framework for a major digital transformation investment.
Deliver: (1) Digital investment taxonomy: (a) Cost reduction (automation, process
digitization, headcount reduction), (b) Revenue enhancement (new digital channels,
personalization, product innovation), (c) Risk mitigation (cybersecurity,
regulatory compliance, resilience). (2) Business case construction: for each
initiative — baseline cost/revenue, investment required (capex + opex + change
management), expected benefit, time to benefit, and probability of achieving benefit.
(3) Benefit realization framework: why 70% of digital transformations fail to deliver
promised ROI; the 5 realization risks (technology integration failure, change
resistance, underestimating data quality, scope creep, talent gaps).
(4) Financial model: NPV, IRR, and payback period for the full program;
sensitivity to benefit realization rate (50%, 75%, 100% of target benefits).
(5) Stranded cost analysis: legacy systems that still cost money after new system
deployed — how to accelerate shutdown. (6) Prioritization framework: plot all
initiatives on Value (NPV) × Speed of realization × Ease of implementation matrix;
sequence for maximum early wins. (7) Governance: digital PMO design; benefit
ownership (who is accountable for each benefit materializing?); monthly benefit
tracking dashboard linked to the financial model.
Format: Digital Transformation Business Case with Initiative Portfolio, NPV Analysis,
Benefit Realization Risk Assessment, Prioritization Matrix, and Governance Framework.
Inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INDUSTRY | REVENUE | DIGITAL INVESTMENT BUDGET |
TRANSFORMATION OBJECTIVES | CURRENT LEGACY SYSTEM PAIN POINTS | TIMELINE]

title: The McKinsey CEO / Board Strategy Offsite Facilitation Framework
prompt_text:
PROMPT 160 — The McKinsey CEO / Board Strategy Offsite Facilitation Framework
Act as Senior Partner at McKinsey facilitating a 2-day CEO and Board of Directors
strategy offsite. Design a rigorous agenda, analytical framework, and decision process.
Deliver: (1) Offsite design principles: the McKinsey "structured flexibility" approach —
pre-wired decisions vs. genuinely open strategic questions; how to prevent groupthink
and ensure robust debate. (2) Pre-work package: management presentations (15 minutes
max each), competitive benchmarking, scenario analysis, and external perspective
(industry expert or customer interview summary) — delivered 2 weeks in advance.
(3) Day 1 agenda: (a) Environmental scan — external forces shaping the industry over
10 years (2 hours); (b) Company performance diagnostic — where are we today vs.
aspirations? (2 hours); (c) Strategic options generation — 3-5 genuine options
for the future strategic direction, not just "what we're already doing" (3 hours);
(d) Evening reflection dinner with strategic provocation from guest speaker.
(4) Day 2 agenda: (a) Options deep-dive — war-gaming each option; (b) Decision criteria
alignment; (c) Strategic choice — which option(s) to pursue; (d) Implications for
capital allocation, organizational design, and talent. (5) Decision quality framework:
RAPID decision process (Recommend, Agree, Perform, Input, Decide) for key choices.
(6) Output: 1-page strategy statement; capital allocation implications; top 3 priorities
for the next 18 months with owners and milestones. (7) Follow-up: 30/60/90-day
progress review mechanism; cascade to organization.
Format: Strategy Offsite Design with Agenda, Pre-Work Package, Facilitation Guide,
Decision Framework, and Post-Offsite Implementation Plan.
Inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INDUSTRY | STRATEGIC CHALLENGE | BOARD COMPOSITION |
OFFSITE TIMING | KEY DECISIONS TO BE MADE | BIGGEST STRATEGIC DISAGREEMENT]

title: The Renaissance Technologies Statistical Arbitrage Research
prompt_text:
PROMPT 161 — The Renaissance Technologies Statistical Arbitrage Research
Act as Quantitative Researcher at Renaissance Technologies. Design a statistical
arbitrage strategy based on mean-reversion and pairs trading.
Deliver: (1) Statistical arbitrage framework: identify cointegrated pairs using
Engle-Granger or Johansen test; ADF test for stationarity of the spread.
(2) Pairs selection criteria: economic rationale (same industry, same factor exposures),
statistical significance (cointegration p-value < 0.05), and adequate liquidity.
(3) Signal generation: z-score of the spread = (Spread − Mean) / StdDev;
entry at z > 2.0, exit at z = 0, stop-loss at z > 3.5.
(4) Position sizing: dollar-neutral construction (equal $ long and short);
volatility scaling to target constant risk per pair.
(5) Transaction cost modeling: round-trip cost per trade (bid-ask + market impact);
minimum required edge per trade to cover costs.
(6) Portfolio of pairs: correlation between pairs; max pairs in portfolio;
sector concentration limits to prevent factor crowding.
(7) Regime detection: pairs strategies break down in trending markets or when
correlations spike (2008); regime filter using VIX level or rolling correlation.
(8) Backtesting rigor: look-ahead bias prevention; out-of-sample validation;
walk-forward testing across 5 non-overlapping periods.
Format: Stat Arb Strategy Spec with Pairs Screening Methodology, Signal Rules,
Position Sizing, Backtesting Framework, and Regime Filter.
Inputs: [UNIVERSE | HOLDING PERIOD | LEVERAGE | TRANSACTION COST ASSUMPTION |
PAIRS COUNT TARGET | SHARPE TARGET | LOOKBACK FOR COINTEGRATION]

title: The Citadel Securities Market Making & Liquidity Provision Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 162 — The Citadel Securities Market Making & Liquidity Provision Strategy
Act as Head of Quantitative Market Making at Citadel Securities. Design
an electronic market making strategy for equities or options.
Deliver: (1) Market making economics: bid-ask spread capture vs. adverse selection
cost vs. inventory risk — the three components of MM P&L.
(2) Adverse selection model: distinguish informed vs. uninformed order flow;
use order flow toxicity metrics (VPIN — Volume-synchronized Probability of
Informed Trading) to adjust quotes dynamically.
(3) Quote sizing and skewing: inventory management — when long, skew quotes
to sell (tighten ask, widen bid); when short, skew to buy.
(4) Options market making: delta hedging to flatten directional risk;
managing gamma (local vol risk), vega (term vol risk), and pin risk near expiry.
(5) Latency and technology: co-location, kernel bypass networking, FPGA
vs. ASIC for sub-microsecond quote updates; importance of latency in
competitive MM landscape.
(6) Risk limits: max gross inventory per symbol; sector delta limits;
daily P&L stop-loss triggers.
(7) Fee optimization: maker-taker pricing; how to route orders to maximize
rebates while minimizing adverse fill rates.
(8) Regulatory: Regulation NMS (best execution), FINRA trade reporting,
short-sale locate requirements.
Format: Market Making Strategy with P&L Decomposition, Quote Algorithm Design,
Inventory Management Rules, Risk Limits, and Technology Requirements.
Inputs: [ASSET CLASS | UNIVERSE SIZE | TARGET SPREAD CAPTURE | INVENTORY LIMITS |
LATENCY BUDGET | REGULATORY JURISDICTION | CAPITAL ALLOCATION]

title: The JPMorgan Credit Derivatives & CDS Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 163 — The JPMorgan Credit Derivatives & CDS Strategy
Act as Head of Credit Derivatives Strategy at JPMorgan. Build a comprehensive
CDS and credit derivatives investment and hedging framework.
Deliver: (1) CDS mechanics: protection buyer pays running spread; credit event
triggers (bankruptcy, failure to pay, restructuring); physical vs. cash settlement;
ISDA 2014 Credit Definitions. (2) Single-name CDS analysis: CDS spread as implied
default probability — spread / (1 − Recovery Rate) = annual default probability;
compare CDS-implied rating to agency rating to find mispricing.
(3) CDS index products: CDX IG (125 US IG names), CDX HY, iTraxx Europe, iTraxx
Crossover — index composition, roll schedule, on-the-run vs. off-the-run.
(4) Credit curve trades: CDS curve steepener (short 5yr protection, long 10yr)
when expecting credit improvement; flattener for credit deterioration.
(5) Basis trading: CDS basis = CDS spread − Asset Swap Spread on bond; negative
basis (CDS < bond spread) = buy bond + buy protection; positive basis = sell bond
+ sell protection.
(6) Structured credit derivatives: CDO tranche investing — equity (0-3% attachment),
mezzanine (3-7%), senior (7-15%); correlation sensitivity (equity is long
correlation, senior is short correlation).
(7) CMBX and ABX: CDS on CMBS and ABS pools; the Big Short trade recreated.
(8) Portfolio credit hedging: designing a macro credit hedge using CDX HY for
an IG corporate bond portfolio.
Format: Credit Derivatives Strategy with CDS Mechanics, Single-Name Analysis,
Index Strategy, Basis Trade Design, and Portfolio Hedge Construction.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO TYPE | CREDIT QUALITY | NOTIONAL TO HEDGE | SPECIFIC CREDIT
CONCERNS | CDS INDEX PREFERENCE | BUDGET FOR PROTECTION PREMIUM]

title: The Bain Capital Portfolio Operations & Value Creation Office
prompt_text:
PROMPT 164 — The Bain Capital Portfolio Operations & Value Creation Office
Act as Operating Partner at Bain Capital. Design and run a Portfolio Operations
group that drives measurable EBITDA improvement across PE portfolio companies.
Deliver: (1) Portfolio Operations model: centralized resource (Operating Partners,
functional experts) vs. decentralized (each portfolio company hires); hybrid model
with shared playbooks and specialist support on demand.
(2) Value creation playbook library: develop standardized playbooks for (a) pricing
optimization, (b) procurement savings, (c) digital marketing efficiency,
(d) salesforce effectiveness, (e) working capital improvement — for each playbook:
typical EBITDA impact (bps of revenue), implementation timeline, and resource requirements.
(3) 100-Day Plan design: standardized Day 1 readiness → 30-day diagnostic →
100-day priority initiatives; governance cadence (weekly CEO/COO check-in,
monthly Operating Partner review).
(4) Talent and management assessment: standardized CEO/CFO assessment in first 90 days;
decision tree for retain/develop/replace; executive search partnership model.
(5) Procurement center of excellence: consolidated buying power across portfolio companies;
category management approach; vendor rationalization; savings tracking.
(6) Digital and analytics: building data/analytics capabilities in portfolio companies
that typically have minimal investment; quick wins (pricing analytics, churn prediction,
demand forecasting) with 6-month payback.
(7) Exit preparation: 18-month exit readiness program; quality of earnings improvement,
management team strengthening, ESG disclosure preparation.
Format: Portfolio Operations Framework with Value Creation Playbook Library, 100-Day
Plan Template, Procurement CoE Design, and Exit Readiness Checklist.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE (# COMPANIES) | INDUSTRY CONCENTRATION | AVERAGE EBITDA |
OPERATING PARTNER HEADCOUNT | PRIMARY VALUE CREATION FOCUS | FUND VINTAGE]

title: The UBS China Equity Strategy & A-Share Investment Framework
prompt_text:
PROMPT 165 — The UBS China Equity Strategy & A-Share Investment Framework
Act as Chief China Equity Strategist at UBS. Build a comprehensive China
equity investment framework for global institutional investors.
Deliver: (1) China macro: GDP growth drivers (consumption vs. investment vs. exports);
property sector deleveraging — Evergrande aftermath and mortgage market stabilization;
PBOC monetary policy; CNY trajectory and capital account dynamics.
(2) Market structure: A-shares (CSI 300, STAR Market), H-shares (HKEX), ADRs (NYSE/NASDAQ);
MSCI China composition; QFII/Stock Connect access mechanisms for foreign investors.
(3) Regulatory risk framework: the 2021 regulatory crackdown on tech, education, property —
lessons learned; CCP policy priorities (common prosperity, self-sufficiency, security);
variable interest entity (VIE) structure legal risk for offshore investors.
(4) Sector allocation: (a) Technology (domestic champions: Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu —
regulatory recovery vs. AI opportunity), (b) Consumer (premiumization, middle class
expansion), (c) Industrials (manufacturing upgrade, semiconductor self-sufficiency),
(d) Healthcare (aging population, biopharma innovation), (e) New Energy (BYD, CATL —
EV and battery supply chain dominance). (5) Geopolitical discount: quantify the
discount investors apply for Taiwan risk and US-China decoupling; under what scenario
is current valuation a buying opportunity?
(6) Portfolio construction: MSCI China vs. CSI 300 vs. MSCI A-share — benchmark
choice implications; liquidity-adjusted position sizing; VIE risk management.
Format: China Equity Strategy with Macro Dashboard, Regulatory Risk Framework,
Sector Allocation, Geopolitical Discount Analysis, and Market Access Guide.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | CURRENT CHINA ALLOCATION | BENCHMARK | A-SHARE OR
H-SHARE PREFERENCE | CURRENCY HEDGING POLICY | REGULATORY RISK TOLERANCE]

title: The Goldman Sachs Telecom & Media Investment Banking
prompt_text:
PROMPT 166 — The Goldman Sachs Telecom & Media Investment Banking
Act as MD in Goldman Sachs' TMT group covering Telecoms and Media.
Deliver: (1) Telecom sector dynamics: infrastructure sharing (tower companies —
American Tower, SBA, Crown Castle); fiber-to-the-home (FTTH) economics; 5G capex
cycle and return on invested capital; MVNO (Mobile Virtual Network Operator) model.
(2) Telecom valuation: EV/EBITDA and EV/(EBITDA-Capex) multiples; discounted cash
flow using stable FCF profile; dividend yield and capital return capacity;
regulatory asset base (RAB) valuation for fixed-line infrastructure.
(3) Telecom M&A: in-market consolidation (same-country mobile operators) — antitrust
barriers and remedy requirements; fixed-mobile convergence (FMC) deal rationale;
infrastructure carve-outs (tower sale-leaseback, fiber SpinCo).
(4) Streaming media economics: SVOD (Netflix, Disney+, Amazon Prime) vs. AVOD
(Peacock, Tubi) unit economics; content spending as capex disguised as opex;
subscriber acquisition cost, ARPU, churn, and LTV/CAC for streaming.
(5) Traditional media disruption: linear TV advertising decline (cord-cutting rate,
addressable TV growth); newspaper/print economics; sports rights as defensive moat.
(6) Podcast, gaming, and creator economy: new media monetization models;
platform vs. content owner value capture.
(7) Telecom infrastructure investment: tower REIT valuation; dark fiber and
data center REITs; hyperscaler data center demand driving infrastructure investment.
Format: TMT Advisory with Telecom Sector Model, Streaming Unit Economics, M&A
Landscape, Infrastructure Investment Thesis, and Regulatory Risk Assessment.
Inputs: [COMPANY TYPE (TELECOM/MEDIA/PLATFORM) | GEOGRAPHY | REVENUE MIX |
PRIMARY STRATEGIC CHALLENGE | M&A OBJECTIVE OR DEFENSE | INVESTOR BASE]

title: The Lazard Power & Utilities Investment Banking
prompt_text:
PROMPT 167 — The Lazard Power & Utilities Investment Banking
Act as MD at Lazard's Power & Utilities group. Advise a regulated utility
on capital structure, rate case strategy, and renewable transition financing.
Deliver: (1) Regulated utility financial model: rate base (regulatory asset base) ×
allowed ROE = regulatory earnings; earned ROE vs. allowed ROE and the gap as
a performance indicator; rate case timing and strategy.
(2) Capital allocation for utilities: regulated capex (rate base growth, renewable
portfolio standard compliance) vs. unregulated capex (competitive generation,
C&I direct service); how to grow EPS through rate base expansion.
(3) Utility valuation: P/E and EV/EBITDA vs. regulated peers; premium for
above-average rate base growth; discount for regulatory risk or nuclear exposure;
dividend yield as valuation anchor (utilities are "bond proxies").
(4) Rate case strategy: test year selection (historical vs. forward-looking);
capital structure advocacy (higher equity ratio → higher $ earnings);
ROE benchmark using DCF, CAPM, and comparable earnings methods.
(5) Green utility transition financing: IRA tax credit monetization (ITC/PTC
for utility-scale solar and wind on rate base); green bond issuance for
renewable capex; securitization of retired coal assets ("coal securitization").
(6) M&A in utilities: horizontal consolidation (multi-state utilities);
vertical integration (utility + generation); FERC and state PUC approval
process; transaction costs (regulatory lag) in utility M&A.
(7) Nuclear: nuclear plant economics (high fixed cost, near-zero marginal cost,
carbon-free); federal support (IRA nuclear PTC); license extension economics.
Format: Utility Advisory with Regulated Financial Model, Rate Case Framework,
Green Transition Financing, Valuation Benchmarking, and M&A Strategy.
Inputs: [UTILITY NAME | REGULATED TERRITORY | RATE BASE | ALLOWED ROE | EQUITY RATIO |
RENEWABLE CAPEX PLAN | NEXT RATE CASE DATE | PRIMARY STRATEGIC OBJECTIVE]

title: The Yale Endowment / David Swensen Endowment Model
prompt_text:
PROMPT 168 — The Yale Endowment / David Swensen Endowment Model
Act as Chief Investment Officer at a major university endowment ($5-25B)
applying the "Yale Endowment Model" pioneered by David Swensen.
Deliver: (1) Endowment Model philosophy: equity orientation (90%+ in equity-like
assets), illiquidity premium capture (private markets), diversification beyond
public equities/bonds; Swensen's critique of traditional 60/40 portfolios.
(2) Asset allocation: target weights for Absolute Return (hedge funds), Domestic
Equity, Foreign Equity, Private Equity, Real Estate, Natural Resources, Fixed Income
— with rationale and Yale's actual historical allocation as reference.
(3) Illiquidity premium: evidence for illiquidity premium (PE outperformance of
public equity over 20+ years); how much illiquidity can an endowment tolerate
given annual spending needs (typically 5% of AUM).
(4) Manager selection as alpha source: Swensen's argument that alpha from manager
selection outweighs beta returns in private markets; access to top-quartile PE,
VC, and HF managers as a sustainable competitive advantage for elite endowments.
(5) Spending policy: total return spending rule (5% × 3-year average AUM);
how to sustain spending through market drawdowns without forced selling.
(6) ESG and fossil fuel divestment: how endowments are navigating divestment
pressure vs. fiduciary duty; impact of divestment on portfolio returns.
(7) Replication debate: can institutional investors without Yale's access replicate
the model? Evidence from smaller endowments.
Format: Endowment Strategy with Asset Allocation Table, Illiquidity Analysis,
Manager Selection Framework, Spending Policy Model, and ESG Investment Policy.
Inputs: [ENDOWMENT SIZE | ANNUAL SPENDING RATE | LIQUIDITY REQUIREMENTS | CURRENT
ALLOCATION | ALTERNATIVE MANAGER ACCESS | ESG CONSTRAINTS | INVESTMENT HORIZON]

title: The Oliver Wyman Fintech Regulatory Strategy & Licensing
prompt_text:
PROMPT 169 — The Oliver Wyman Fintech Regulatory Strategy & Licensing
Act as Partner at Oliver Wyman's Regulatory & Compliance practice.
Design a regulatory strategy for a fintech company scaling into new markets.
Deliver: (1) Regulatory landscape mapping: for each target market — applicable
licenses (banking, payment institution, EMI, broker-dealer, investment adviser);
capital requirements; ongoing compliance obligations; timeline and cost.
(2) Licensing strategy: (a) Build own license (highest control, slowest, highest
capital requirement), (b) Rent a license (partner bank model — fastest, ongoing
revenue share), (c) Acquire licensed entity (medium speed, M&A premium).
(3) Regulatory capital planning: minimum capital requirements by license type
and jurisdiction; capital buffer strategy; stress capital requirements.
(4) AML/KYC program design: risk-based approach; customer risk scoring;
transaction monitoring system selection; SAR filing protocols; FATF compliance.
(5) Open Banking / PSD2 compliance: TPP (Third Party Provider) registration;
API standards (UK Open Banking, Berlin Group NextGenPSD2); consumer consent management.
(6) Data privacy: GDPR/CCPA compliance program; data minimization; cross-border
data transfer mechanisms (SCCs, adequacy decisions); DPO appointment.
(7) Regulatory engagement strategy: how to proactively engage regulators
(FCA Innovation Hub, OCC FinTech Charter, CFPB Project Catalyst); sandbox
participation strategy. (8) Exam readiness: BSA/AML examination preparation;
FDIC/OCC examination management for bank partners.
Format: Regulatory Strategy with Licensing Roadmap, Capital Plan, AML/KYC Framework,
Data Privacy Compliance, and Regulatory Engagement Calendar.
Inputs: [COMPANY TYPE | PRODUCTS OFFERED | TARGET GEOGRAPHIES | CURRENT LICENSES |
TIMELINE TO MARKET | REGULATORY RISK TOLERANCE | PRIMARY COMPLIANCE CONCERN]

title: The Barclays Corporate Bond Issuance & Investor Relations
prompt_text:
PROMPT 170 — The Barclays Corporate Bond Issuance & Investor Relations
Act as MD at Barclays' Debt Capital Markets. Advise an investment-grade
corporate on its optimal bond issuance strategy and investor relations program.
Deliver: (1) Bond market access strategy: benchmark bonds ($500M+) vs. private
placements (USPP, Schuldschein) vs. MTN programs; when each is optimal.
(2) IG bond pricing mechanics: Treasury benchmark yield + credit spread (OAS);
what drives the OAS for this issuer (leverage, coverage, industry, rating);
new issue concession (typically 5-15bps for IG bonds — the price of accessing
the market efficiently).
(3) Maturity profile optimization: addressing maturity walls; laddering maturities
to reduce refinancing risk; opportunistic issuance in favorable rate/spread environments.
(4) Currency diversification: USD vs. EUR vs. GBP vs. JPY issuance; cost-of-funds
comparison after cross-currency swap; Euro-denominated bonds for European investor
base expansion (Reg S only vs. 144A/Reg S).
(5) Green/sustainable bond premium: sizing the greenium for this issuer's credit;
investor base expansion benefit; ongoing reporting commitment.
(6) Investor relations for credit: quarterly earnings call management for bondholders;
covenant compliance certificates; rating agency engagement cadence;
bondholder roadshow best practices.
(7) Liability management: tender offer for short-dated bonds while issuing
longer-dated bonds; make-whole call economics; consent solicitation to amend covenants.
Format: DCM Advisory with Maturity Profile Optimization, Currency Comparison,
New Issue Concession Analysis, Investor Relations Calendar, and Liability Management Plan.
Inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INDUSTRY | CREDIT RATING | EXISTING DEBT MATURITY PROFILE |
ANNUAL FUNDING NEED | CURRENCY PREFERENCE | PRIMARY FINANCING OBJECTIVE]

title: The Fortress Investment Group Distressed Real Estate Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 171 — The Fortress Investment Group Distressed Real Estate Strategy
Act as MD at Fortress Investment Group's real estate credit team. Build
a distressed real estate debt and equity investment framework.
Deliver: (1) Distressed CRE opportunity identification: monitor CMBS special servicer
transfers; hotel and office loan delinquency rate trackers; maturing loans with
LTV > 100% (loan balances exceeding property value at current cap rates).
(2) Note-on-note buying: acquire distressed CMBS B-pieces or whole loans at
a discount to par; analyze recovery value under orderly sale, foreclosure, and
workout scenarios. (3) Loan-to-own strategy: acquire senior debt at 60-70 cents
on dollar; foreclose and take ownership; reposition/recapitalize; exit at stabilized
cap rate. (4) Preferred equity and rescue capital: provide preferred equity
to overleveraged sponsors who cannot sell or refinance; target 12-15% preferred
return; downside protection via full collateral package.
(5) Property type opportunities: (a) Office — CMBS maturities in gateway cities,
conversion-to-residential potential; (b) Hotels — servicer REO (Real Estate Owned)
portfolios; (c) Retail — mall loan defaults, outlet center repositioning.
(6) Workout strategies: deed-in-lieu vs. foreclosure (timing, cost, title insurance);
operating during workout; managing tenants and maintaining NOI.
(7) Returns analysis: target gross return 20-25% on distressed debt/equity;
waterfall from distressed note acquisition → repositioning → exit.
Format: Distressed RE Strategy with Opportunity Sourcing Framework, Loan-to-Own
Analysis, Workout Strategy Options, Return Waterfall, and Risk Matrix.
Inputs: [PROPERTY TYPE | GEOGRAPHY | NOTE FACE VALUE | PURCHASE PRICE (% OF PAR) |
CURRENT NOI | OCCUPANCY | WORKOUT TIMELINE | TARGET RETURN]

title: The KPMG Corporate Tax Planning & Transfer Pricing Framework
prompt_text:
PROMPT 172 — The KPMG Corporate Tax Planning & Transfer Pricing Framework
Act as Partner at KPMG's Corporate Tax practice. Design a transfer pricing
policy and international tax planning framework for a multinational.
Deliver: (1) Transfer pricing fundamentals: arm's length principle (ALP);
OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines; five primary methods (CUP, resale price, cost-plus,
TNMM, profit split) — when each applies.
(2) Transfer pricing policy design: functional analysis (which entity performs
which functions, owns which assets, bears which risks); benchmarking study design
(selecting comparables using Orbis/Compustat); setting arm's length ranges.
(3) Intercompany transactions covered: goods, services (shared services, management
fees), royalties/IP licenses, financing (intercompany loans — appropriate interest
rate methodology). (4) Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR): BEPS Action 13;
what must be disclosed; how tax authorities use CbCR to identify low-tax profits.
(5) Pillar Two global minimum tax: 15% global minimum; Qualified Domestic
Minimum Top-up Tax (QDMTT) strategy; GloBE information return; impact on current
holding company structures. (6) Advance Pricing Agreements (APAs): bilateral vs.
unilateral; timeline (2-4 years); when certainty justifies the investment.
(7) Transfer pricing dispute resolution: MAP (Mutual Agreement Procedure) process;
arbitration under MLI; penalty regimes by country.
Format: TP Advisory with Functional Analysis, Benchmarking Methodology, Policy
Document Template, Pillar Two Impact Assessment, and Dispute Resolution Strategy.
Inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INDUSTRY | REVENUE BY GEOGRAPHY | IP OWNERSHIP LOCATION |
