INTERCOMPANY TRANSACTION TYPES | CURRENT ETR | PILLAR TWO EXPOSURE | DISPUTE HISTORY]

title: The Oaktree Capital Distressed Credit & Special Situations
prompt_text:
PROMPT 173 — The Oaktree Capital Distressed Credit & Special Situations
Act as Managing Director at Oaktree Capital. Apply Howard Marks' distressed
credit philosophy to build a distressed investment thesis.
Deliver: (1) Oaktree philosophy: "the most important thing" for distressed investing
is buying at the right price — value investing in credit; the role of the credit
cycle in creating opportunity. (2) Credit cycle framework: identify the current
phase (expansion, deterioration, distress, recovery); which phase generates the
best distressed investment entry points (maximum pessimism ≠ maximum opportunity).
(3) Fulcrum security identification: the tranche of debt that will be converted
to equity in a restructuring; analytical approach to identifying fulcrum position
across capital structures of different complexity. (4) Distressed-to-control
investing: build a position in fulcrum debt; take board seats post-restructuring;
operate the company as a private equity owner; exit when EBITDA recovers.
(5) Non-control distressed: buy distressed bonds at deep discount; benefit from
either (a) recovery above purchase price if company stabilizes, or (b) negotiated
recovery in restructuring above market price.
(6) Chapter 11 claims trading: buying bankruptcy claims (trade payables,
supplier credits) at a discount; recovery rate analysis.
(7) Secondary loan market: buying performing but deeply discounted leveraged loans;
LSTA market mechanics; clearing price dynamics in credit dislocation.
(8) Portfolio construction: position sizing in high-convexity distressed situations;
diversification across vintages, industries, and recovery scenarios.
Format: Distressed Investment Framework with Credit Cycle Dashboard, Fulcrum Security
Analysis, Returns Analysis (Non-Control vs. Control), and Portfolio Construction.
Inputs: [COMPANY NAME OR SECTOR | CAPITAL STRUCTURE | CURRENT TRADING LEVELS |
LTM EBITDA | PRIMARY CATALYST | TARGET HOLD PERIOD | TARGET RETURN]

title: The Fitch Ratings Structured Finance & ABS Rating Methodology
prompt_text:
PROMPT 174 — The Fitch Ratings Structured Finance & ABS Rating Methodology
Act as Senior Director at Fitch Ratings' Structured Finance group. Apply
Fitch's rating methodology to analyze an ABS or MBS transaction.
Deliver: (1) Structured finance rating methodology: credit enhancement (over-
collateralization, reserve account, subordination, excess spread) sized to withstand
Fitch's rating stress scenarios. (2) Cash flow modeling: stressed prepayment speeds
(CPR), default rates (CDR), and loss severity — for auto ABS, credit card ABS,
or RMBS. (3) Asset quality analysis: pool composition (obligor concentration,
geographic concentration, seasoning, credit score distribution); static pool
analysis vs. dynamic pool.
(4) Structural features: sequential vs. pro-rata pay; trigger events that
switch payment priority; clean-up call (10% pool factor); prefunding period risks.
(5) Legal analysis: true sale of receivables; bankruptcy remoteness of the SPV;
commingling risk; servicer replacement provisions.
(6) Operational risk: servicer quality assessment (financial strength, systems,
track record); backup servicer designation; servicer transition risks.
(7) Rating sensitivity: what increase in defaults or decrease in prepayments
causes a 1-notch downgrade for the AAA tranche? For the BBB tranche?
(8) ESG in structured finance: how climate risk affects geographic concentrations
(coastal properties in RMBS; carbon-intensive auto fleets in auto ABS).
Format: ABS Rating Analysis with Credit Enhancement Sizing, Cash Flow Model Summary,
Legal Structure Review, Operational Risk Assessment, and Rating Sensitivity Analysis.
Inputs: [ASSET CLASS | POOL SIZE | COLLATERAL QUALITY METRICS | PROPOSED STRUCTURE |
RATING TARGET (AAA/AA/A/BBB) | ISSUER NAME | JURISDICTION]

title: The BCG Healthcare System Efficiency & Clinical Operations
prompt_text:
PROMPT 175 — The BCG Healthcare System Efficiency & Clinical Operations
Act as Senior Partner at BCG's Healthcare practice. Design an operational
efficiency program for a hospital or integrated health system.
Deliver: (1) Clinical operations benchmarking: length of stay (LOS) by DRG vs.
peer hospitals; readmission rate (30-day) vs. CMS national average; operating
room utilization (% of prime time utilized); ED throughput (door-to-disposition).
(2) Staffing optimization: nurse-to-patient ratios by unit; overtime and agency
labor as % of total labor cost; flexible staffing models (float pools, cross-training).
(3) Revenue cycle optimization: days in AR; first-pass claim acceptance rate; denial
rate by payer; underpayment recovery; payer contract optimization.
(4) Supply chain: physician preference items (PPIs) standardization; value analysis
committee governance; GPO utilization rate; consignment inventory.
(5) Service line strategy: contribution margin by service line; invest/maintain/divest
framework; high-growth service lines (oncology, orthopedics, neuroscience).
(6) Digital health: EHR optimization (Epic/Cerner workflow efficiency); AI-powered
scheduling, sepsis prediction, imaging AI; remote patient monitoring economics.
(7) Financial improvement: EBITDA bridge from current state to target;
prioritized initiatives by impact and timeline; FTE savings vs. revenue enhancement.
Format: Health System Efficiency Program with Clinical Benchmarking Dashboard,
Staffing Model, Revenue Cycle Analysis, Service Line Strategy, and EBITDA Bridge.
Inputs: [HEALTH SYSTEM NAME | BEDS | NET PATIENT REVENUE | EBITDA MARGIN |
PAYOR MIX | PRIMARY OPERATIONAL CHALLENGE | IMPROVEMENT TARGET]

title: The Accenture Finance Digital Transformation & AI in Finance
prompt_text:
PROMPT 176 — The Accenture Finance Digital Transformation & AI in Finance
Act as Managing Director at Accenture's Finance & Risk practice. Design an
AI-powered finance transformation leveraging Gen AI and machine learning.
Deliver: (1) Gen AI use cases in finance: (a) Automated management commentary
generation from financial data (reduce narrative drafting from 4 hours to 20 mins);
(b) Conversational financial analytics (CFO asks questions in plain English);
(c) Intelligent variance analysis (AI identifies drivers without manual investigation);
(d) Contract review and covenant monitoring for treasury; (e) AI-powered audit
sampling and anomaly detection. (2) ML in FP&A: revenue forecasting using ML
(gradient boosting vs. ARIMA vs. neural networks — accuracy comparison);
driver-based planning with AI-identified leading indicators.
(3) Automation roadmap: classify processes by automation potential (RPA vs. ML
vs. Gen AI vs. human judgment required); phased implementation by value and complexity.
(4) Data foundation: why AI in finance fails without clean data; data governance
requirements; ERP data quality; master data management for finance.
(5) Build vs. buy: build custom models vs. use off-the-shelf finance AI products
(Workday Illuminate, Oracle AI, Anaplan AI, Pigment) — evaluation framework.
(6) Change management: finance talent reskilling; prompt engineering for accountants;
managing anxiety about AI replacing finance jobs.
(7) ROI: quantify the time savings, error reduction, and insight quality improvement;
typical 3-year ROI for AI-in-finance investment.
Format: AI Finance Transformation Blueprint with Use Case Portfolio, Automation
Roadmap, Data Requirements, Build vs. Buy Analysis, and ROI Model.
Inputs: [COMPANY REVENUE | FINANCE HEADCOUNT | ERP | CURRENT AUTOMATION LEVEL |
PRIMARY PAIN POINTS | AI INVESTMENT BUDGET | RISK TOLERANCE FOR AI DEPLOYMENT]

title: The Kohlberg Kravis Roberts (KKR) Global Macro & Asset Allocation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 177 — The Kohlberg Kravis Roberts (KKR) Global Macro & Asset Allocation
Act as Senior Strategist at KKR's Global Macro & Asset Allocation team
(Henry McVey's team). Build a forward-looking asset allocation framework.
Deliver: (1) KKR macro framework: the "New Regime" thesis — higher nominal growth,
higher inflation, higher interest rates, and greater geopolitical fragmentation
vs. the 2010s "Great Moderation"; implications for asset class returns.
(2) Asset class return forecasts: 10-year expected returns for US equities, Int'l DM,
EM, IG bonds, HY bonds, PE, infra, real estate, private credit — using building
blocks (inflation + real growth + valuation change).
(3) Portfolio construction for the new regime: higher allocations to real assets
(infrastructure, real estate, commodities) as inflation hedges; private credit over
public credit; international equity over US equity based on valuation.
(4) "Regime-aware" allocation: how optimal allocation shifts across economic regimes
(high growth/low inflation, low growth/high inflation, stagflation); dynamic overlay.
(5) Alternatives allocation sizing: why institutional investors should allocate
30-50% to alternatives in the current environment; liquidity stress test for high
alternatives allocation.
(6) Geopolitical scenarios: multipolar world → portfolio positioning; reshoring
trends → sector implications; dollar hegemony risk → gold and commodity exposure.
(7) Tactical vs. strategic: which asset class views are long-term structural vs.
near-term tactical; portfolio review frequency.
Format: KKR-Style Asset Allocation Report with Return Forecasts, Regime Analysis,
Portfolio Construction Recommendations, Geopolitical Scenario Analysis, and
Alternatives Allocation Case.
Inputs: [INVESTOR TYPE | PORTFOLIO SIZE | CURRENT ALLOCATION | RETURN TARGET |
LIQUIDITY CONSTRAINTS | INVESTMENT HORIZON | PRIMARY MACRO CONCERN]

title: The Andreessen Horowitz Enterprise AI Startup Investment
prompt_text:
PROMPT 178 — The Andreessen Horowitz Enterprise AI Startup Investment
Act as General Partner at a16z evaluating an enterprise AI startup at Series B.
Deliver: (1) Enterprise AI market landscape: horizontal AI platforms (OpenAI API,
Anthropic, Google Gemini) vs. vertical AI applications (legal AI, medical AI,
financial AI, coding AI); where defensibility lies.
(2) Defensibility analysis: AI startups face commoditization risk as foundation
models improve — assess defensibility through: (a) proprietary data moat,
(b) workflow integration depth, (c) switching costs, (d) network effects,
(e) distribution advantage.
(3) Revenue quality: ARR, NRR (AI companies should show >120% NRR from expansion
as customers add more seats/usage), and usage-based pricing dynamics (consumption
vs. seat-based).
(4) AI model strategy: build own models vs. fine-tune open source vs. call
foundation model APIs — cost, quality, and differentiation implications.
(5) Gross margin: AI companies face unique COGS pressure (GPU inference costs);
model efficiency improvements (distillation, quantization) — gross margin
trajectory to SaaS-like levels (70%+).
(6) Foundation model risk: OpenAI / Google / Anthropic adding similar features
natively — how to assess existential risk from foundation model feature creep.
(7) Team assessment: AI research talent (publications, citations, prior companies);
enterprise sales motion (early customer proof); product-market fit signals.
Format: Enterprise AI Investment Memo with Defensibility Analysis, Unit Economics,
Foundation Model Risk Assessment, Gross Margin Path, and Investment Recommendation.
Inputs: [COMPANY NAME | AI APPLICATION | CURRENT ARR | NRR | GROSS MARGIN |
PROPRIETARY DATA ASSETS | FOUNDATION MODEL DEPENDENCY | PROPOSED VALUATION]

title: The Deloitte Mergers & Acquisitions Human Capital Integration
prompt_text:
PROMPT 179 — The Deloitte Mergers & Acquisitions Human Capital Integration
Act as Partner at Deloitte's Human Capital practice. Design a people and
culture integration program for a major acquisition.
Deliver: (1) Day 1 people readiness: employee communication cascade (who hears what,
when, and from whom); HR service continuity (payroll, benefits, HRIS — no employee
disruption); org structure announcement timeline.
(2) Culture assessment: pre-close cultural due diligence — values, decision-making
styles, performance management philosophy, communication norms; culture clash risk rating.
(3) Organizational design: determine target operating model within 90 days; avoid
prolonged uncertainty (the #1 talent retention risk); RACI for key decisions.
(4) Talent retention: identify critical talent (top 10% by role impact); design
retention agreements (typically 12-24 month; 50-100% of annual compensation);
departure risk assessment for key executives.
(5) Compensation harmonization: benchmark combined entity vs. market; address
pay gaps between legacy companies; equity refresh grants for acquired employees.
(6) Benefits integration: harmonize benefit plans (healthcare, retirement, PTO) —
typically 12-18 months to fully harmonize; costs and employee experience trade-offs.
(7) Change management: the "change curve" (Kübler-Ross model for organizational
change); communication frequency and content by employee segment; manager
enablement (managers as primary change agents).
(8) Integration success metrics: employee engagement score at 6 and 12 months post-close;
voluntary attrition rate vs. pre-deal baseline; cultural alignment score.
Format: HR Integration Playbook with Day 1 Readiness Checklist, Culture Assessment,
Talent Retention Program, Compensation Harmonization Plan, and Integration KPIs.
Inputs: [ACQUIRER | TARGET | INDUSTRY | COMBINED HEADCOUNT | CLOSE DATE |
CULTURAL SIMILARITY ASSESSMENT | PRIMARY TALENT RETENTION CONCERN]

title: The IMF World Economic Outlook Global Forecast & Policy Analysis
prompt_text:
PROMPT 180 — The IMF World Economic Outlook Global Forecast & Policy Analysis
Act as Senior Economist at IMF's Research Department contributing to the
World Economic Outlook (WEO). Build a rigorous global growth forecast
and risk assessment for the next 2 years.
Deliver: (1) Global growth forecast: real GDP growth for G7 (US, Eurozone, Japan,
UK, Canada) and BRICS+ (China, India, Brazil, Russia, South Africa) — explain
the drivers and divergences. (2) Inflation outlook: headline vs. core PCE/CPI;
last-mile inflation challenge (services vs. goods); central bank credibility
and inflation expectations anchoring.
(3) Monetary policy path: Fed, ECB, BoE, BoJ rate path; divergence risks;
financial conditions index and its impact on growth.
(4) Fiscal sustainability: debt-to-GDP trajectories for major economies;
fiscal dominance risk (where monetary policy is constrained by fiscal pressures);
IMF's Article IV recommendations for fiscal consolidation.
(5) Global trade and supply chains: trade fragmentation (friend-shoring,
near-shoring) impact on global growth; services trade expansion offsetting
goods trade slowdown.
(6) EM vulnerability: identify the 5 most vulnerable EM economies (high external
debt, fiscal deficit, inflation above target, currency pressure); financing risk.
(7) Downside scenarios: (a) China hard landing — impact on global growth and
commodity prices; (b) Persistent inflation — higher-for-longer rates causing
financial stability stress; (c) Geopolitical escalation — energy price spike.
(8) Multilateral policy recommendations: G20 coordinated action areas; debt
relief for low-income countries; global minimum tax implementation.
Format: WEO-Style Report with Global Growth Table, Inflation Outlook, Central Bank
Path, Fiscal Sustainability, Downside Scenarios, and Policy Recommendations.
Inputs: [GEOGRAPHIC FOCUS | FORECAST HORIZON | PRIMARY DOWNSIDE CONCERN |
POLICY QUESTION TO ADDRESS | AUDIENCE (IMF BOARD / FINANCE MINISTERS / PUBLIC)]

title: The Goldman Sachs Ayco Executive Financial Planning
prompt_text:
PROMPT 181 — The Goldman Sachs Ayco Executive Financial Planning
Act as Senior Financial Advisor at Goldman Sachs Ayco serving C-suite executives.
Design a holistic financial plan integrating equity compensation, tax, and estate.
Deliver: (1) Equity compensation analysis: RSUs (income on vest, tax withholding
choices), NSOs (spread = ordinary income; exercise timing strategy), ISOs (AMT trap,
qualifying disposition holding period), and PSUs (performance vesting scenarios —
model threshold/target/maximum payouts). (2) Concentrated stock management:
10b5-1 plan design (pre-scheduled sales to avoid insider trading risk); exchange
fund contribution eligibility; charitable strategies (CLAT, CRT, DAF) for
high-basis shares. (3) Tax planning: marginal rate optimization across vesting events;
state tax nexus for executives with multiple residences; deferral through NQDC
(Non-Qualified Deferred Compensation) plans. (4) Net worth diversification: illiquid
equity compensation vs. liquid portfolio — target no single asset > 25% of NW.
(5) Retirement income planning: tax-efficient withdrawal sequencing (Roth vs.
traditional vs. taxable); defined benefit pension optimization; Social Security
timing. (6) Insurance review: D&O liability, umbrella, disability income, life
insurance (ILIT structure for estate liquidity). (7) Estate planning integration:
annual gifting ($18K/year per donee), 529 superfunding, GRATs timed to RSU vesting.
Format: Executive Financial Plan with Equity Comp Tax Model, Concentrated Stock
Strategy, Retirement Projection, and Estate Planning Summary.
Inputs: [EXECUTIVE AGE | COMPANY | ANNUAL COMP | EQUITY COMP TYPES AND AMOUNTS |
CONCENTRATED STOCK VALUE | ESTIMATED NW | STATE OF RESIDENCE | ESTATE PLANNING OBJECTIVES]

title: The Federal Reserve Bank Senior Economist: Inflation Dynamics
prompt_text:
PROMPT 182 — The Federal Reserve Bank Senior Economist: Inflation Dynamics
Act as Senior Economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York researching
modern inflation dynamics and the effectiveness of monetary policy.
Deliver: (1) Inflation decomposition: separate headline CPI/PCE into tradeable goods,
non-tradeable services (shelter, healthcare, education), energy, and food; identify
the most persistent components. (2) Labor market and wage-price dynamics: wage growth
decomposition (employment cost index); the NAIRU concept and whether the current
unemployment rate is above or below; productivity-adjusted wage pressure.
(3) Shelter inflation mechanics: rent CPI lags private-market rents by 12-18 months
(Zillow Observed Rent Index as leading indicator); when will shelter disinflation
show up in official CPI? (4) Supply-side vs. demand-side inflation: the 2021-23
episode — how much was pandemic supply shock vs. fiscal stimulus demand?
Implications for optimal monetary policy response. (5) Inflation expectations:
Michigan Survey (short-term), NY Fed SCE, TIPS breakevens (market-based),
SPF (Survey of Professional Forecasters) — which measure is most reliable?
(6) International comparison: why US, UK, and Eurozone experienced different
inflation peaks despite common supply shocks (energy, semiconductor) —
fiscal policy differences, labor market structures, commodity exposure.
(7) Lessons for future policy: should the Fed adopt a higher inflation target
(3% vs. 2%)? Evidence for and against.
Format: Fed Research Paper Structure with Inflation Decomposition, Labor Market
Analysis, Expectations Monitoring, International Comparison, and Policy Implications.
Inputs: [GEOGRAPHIC FOCUS | POLICY QUESTION | TIME PERIOD OF ANALYSIS |
DATA SOURCES AVAILABLE | AUDIENCE (FOMC / ACADEMIC / PUBLIC)]

title: The Sequoia Capital Global Venture Portfolio Construction
prompt_text:
PROMPT 183 — The Sequoia Capital Global Venture Portfolio Construction
Act as Managing Partner at Sequoia Capital. Design a global venture fund
portfolio construction strategy across stages and geographies.
Deliver: (1) Fund strategy: Sequoia's multi-fund structure (seed fund, early-stage fund,
growth fund, public equities) — why separate vehicles for each stage; cross-fund
co-investment governance. (2) Portfolio construction math: seed fund ($200M) —
target 50-60 investments at $2-4M; expect 10% to become Series A fund investments;
calculate the required return from winners to deliver 3× fund.
(3) Entry stage optimization: seed (pre-product, idea stage, 1-5% ownership for
$1-2M), Series A (product-market fit signals, 15-20% ownership for $10-15M), growth
(scaling, 5-10% for $50-100M); return dilution from pro-rata rights decisions.
(4) Sector and geography: global vs. regional mandate; how Sequoia manages US,
Europe (Peak XV), India, and Southeast Asia (Peak XV) as separate franchises.
(5) Portfolio support: Sequoia Academy, network effects from portfolio companies
helping each other; talent network for recruiting into portfolio companies.
(6) Reserve strategy: follow-on capital allocation in winners (pro-rata rights vs.
super-pro-rata to double down); opportunity cost of following losers vs. concentrating
in winners. (7) Exit strategy: secondary sales for liquidity; IPO timing (when does
an IPO maximize long-term value vs. short-term liquidity?); lock-up expiry management.
Format: Venture Portfolio Construction with Stage Math, Reserve Allocation Model,
Expected Return Distribution, and Fund Return Scenario Analysis.
Inputs: [FUND SIZE | TARGET STAGE | SECTOR FOCUS | GEOGRAPHIC MANDATE |
CHECK SIZE RANGE | TARGET OWNERSHIP % | EXPECTED FUND LIFE]

title: The Citi Wealth Management Tax-Loss Harvesting & After-Tax Alpha
prompt_text:
PROMPT 184 — The Citi Wealth Management Tax-Loss Harvesting & After-Tax Alpha
Act as Head of Wealth Tax Strategy at Citi Private Bank. Design a systematic
after-tax investment strategy for UHNW clients.
Deliver: (1) After-tax alpha sources: tax-loss harvesting (systematic realization of
losses to offset gains), tax-lot optimization (specify which shares to sell: HIFO
vs. FIFO), asset location (place high-yield/high-turnover assets in tax-deferred
accounts), and municipal bond allocation in taxable accounts.
(2) Tax-loss harvesting mechanics: identify positions with unrealized losses > $10K;
sell and immediately reinvest in a highly correlated substitute (avoid wash sale);
track the tax alpha generated; reset cost basis for future liability.
(3) Direct indexing: own individual securities instead of an ETF to enable
continuous tax-loss harvesting at the position level; expected annual TLH alpha
50-150bps vs. ETF holding; when direct indexing beats ETFs (high tax rate + high
portfolio turnover + concentrated stock overlay).
(4) Long-term capital gains management: hold period optimization; donation of
appreciated stock to charity or DAF vs. selling; Qualified Opportunity Zone
investments to defer/eliminate capital gains.
(5) Estate planning and step-up: strategic holding of appreciated securities
until death (step-up in basis at death eliminates embedded gain); gifting strategy
for assets with low basis.
(6) Portfolio rebalancing tax efficiency: rebalance using dividends and new contributions
before selling; rebalance across tax lots to minimize gains recognized.
(7) Alternative minimum tax (AMT) planning: ISO exercise planning; preference items.
Format: After-Tax Strategy with TLH Alpha Quantification, Direct Indexing Decision
Framework, Asset Location Optimization, and Multi-Year Tax Scenario Analysis.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | FEDERAL + STATE TAX RATE | ANNUAL CAPITAL GAINS BUDGET |
CONCENTRATED POSITIONS | INVESTMENT OBJECTIVE | TAX LOSS CARRYFORWARD BALANCE]

title: The Pimco / T. Rowe Price Asset Allocation for Insurance Companies
prompt_text:
PROMPT 185 — The Pimco / T. Rowe Price Asset Allocation for Insurance Companies
Act as Head of Insurance Asset Management at PIMCO or T. Rowe Price.
Design an investment strategy for an insurance company general account.
Deliver: (1) Insurance investment mandate: liability-matching (duration, convexity,
and cash flow matching for policy reserves) vs. return enhancement (spread over
liability cost of funds). (2) NAIC risk-based capital (RBC) charges: how each
asset class's RBC charge affects after-RBC-cost return; optimization of the
portfolio to maximize yield/RBC charge. (3) Life insurance: liability duration
10-20 years; investment-grade long-duration corporate and municipal bonds; NAIC 1
vs. NAIC 2 designation and capital implications. (4) P&C insurance: shorter liability
duration (1-5 years); taxable vs. tax-exempt bond allocation; liquidity required
for catastrophe claims. (5) Alternative investments for insurance: private credit
(direct lending, CLOs — higher spread, efficient RBC treatment), infrastructure
debt (IG, long-duration, low default), commercial real estate debt.
(6) Duration gap management: measure and manage the A-L duration gap; interest rate
sensitivity of surplus; strategies to close the gap (receiver swaptions, long-duration
bonds, annuity product mix).
(7) Investment grade credit: insurance company credit research emphasis on
fallen angel risk and issuer-specific concentration.
Format: Insurance Investment Strategy with A-L Duration Analysis, RBC Optimization,
Asset Allocation Recommendation by Insurance Type, and Yield Enhancement Roadmap.
Inputs: [INSURANCE TYPE (LIFE/P&C/MULTI) | TOTAL INVESTED ASSETS | LIABILITY DURATION |
CURRENT PORTFOLIO YIELD | RBC RATIO | INVESTMENT GRADE CONSTRAINT | PRIMARY OBJECTIVE]

title: The Perella Weinberg Partners Hostile Takeover — Target Perspective
prompt_text:
PROMPT 186 — The Perella Weinberg Partners Hostile Takeover — Target Perspective
Act as financial advisor to the CEO of a company that received an unsolicited
$X per share proposal (30% premium) that the Board believes undervalues the company.
Deliver: (1) Fiduciary duty framework: Revlon duties triggered? Business judgment rule
protection for rejecting a premium offer; Delaware courts' standard of review.
(2) Standalone value creation plan: what would the stock price be worth in 18 months
under an accelerated standalone value creation plan? Build the case with specific
initiatives and financial targets. (3) Strategic alternatives process: should the
Board run a formal process? Risk that opening the process confirms the company is "for
sale" and reduces negotiating leverage. (4) White knight search: identify 3-5
alternative acquirers who might pay more; how to approach them without triggering
a bidding war that forces an outcome. (5) Poison pill analysis: does one exist?
Should a new shareholder rights plan be adopted at 15% trigger?
(6) Investor communications: script the Board Chair's message to top 10 institutional
holders; pre-empt activist accumulation of a blocking stake.
(7) Negotiation strategy: if the Board decides to engage — minimum acceptable price,
form of consideration preference (cash vs. stock), deal certainty requirements
(reverse break fee), and regulatory conditions that would allow walking away.
Format: Target Defense Advisory with Standalone Value Case, White Knight Map,
Poison Pill Analysis, Investor Comm Script, and Negotiation Framework.
Inputs: [TARGET COMPANY | HOSTILE BIDDER | OFFER PRICE | CURRENT STOCK PRICE |
52-WEEK RANGE | STRATEGIC RATIONALE CLAIMED BY BIDDER | BOARD COMPOSITION]

title: The Bain & Company Net Promoter Score & Customer Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 187 — The Bain & Company Net Promoter Score & Customer Strategy
Act as Senior Manager at Bain & Company's Customer Strategy practice.
Design a comprehensive NPS and customer loyalty measurement system.
Deliver: (1) NPS methodology: promoters (9-10) − detractors (0-6) = NPS; statistical
significance requirements; frequency of measurement (transactional vs. relational).
(2) NPS by customer segment: enterprise vs. SMB vs. consumer; by product/service
line; by geography; identify where NPS improvement drives the most revenue.
(3) Closed-loop feedback system: how to act on every detractor response within 48
hours; frontline employee empowerment to resolve issues; the ROI of closed-loop.
(4) NPS → revenue linkage: econometric model linking NPS to churn, expansion revenue,
and referrals; "NPS-value linkage" framework showing $-value of a 1-point NPS increase.
(5) Customer lifetime value (CLV) by NPS segment: promoters have 3-5× higher CLV
than detractors; segment the customer base by NPS × CLV to prioritize investments.
(6) Inner loop vs. outer loop: inner loop (individual feedback → immediate resolution)
vs. outer loop (aggregated insights → systemic improvements); process design for both.
(7) NPS governance: who owns NPS? How to prevent gaming (survey cherry-picking);
NPS as a KPI in executive compensation.
Format: Customer Strategy with NPS Measurement Design, Closed-Loop Process, Revenue
Linkage Model, CLV Segmentation, and Governance Framework.
Inputs: [COMPANY TYPE | INDUSTRY | CURRENT NPS (IF KNOWN) | CUSTOMER SEGMENTS |
REVENUE PER CUSTOMER | CHURN RATE | PRIMARY CUSTOMER PAIN POINT]

title: The Warburg Pincus Growth Stage Technology Investment
prompt_text:
PROMPT 188 — The Warburg Pincus Growth Stage Technology Investment
Act as MD at Warburg Pincus evaluating a $100-500M growth equity investment
in a technology company at Series D/E or pre-IPO stage.
Deliver: (1) Growth stage investment criteria: differentiated from VC (profitability
path required or near-term achievable); from buyout (no control, growth not yield);
target profile: $100-500M ARR, 25-50% growth, approaching or at Rule of 40.
(2) Commercial due diligence: customer reference calls (10+ calls); win/loss analysis;
competitive displacement rate; ICP (ideal customer profile) definition and penetration.
(3) Technology due diligence: architecture review (cloud-native, API-first, scalable?);
technical debt assessment; engineering team quality; IP protection.
(4) Financial model: revenue bridge, margin expansion path, FCF breakeven timeline;
scenario analysis (bull/base/bear) with specific assumption ranges.
(5) Public company comparables: identify 5-7 public comps; EV/NTM Revenue and
Rule of 40 adjusted multiple; where does this company fit vs. the public market
trading range?
(6) Pre-IPO positioning: what needs to be true for a successful IPO in 18-24 months?
S-1 readiness: financial reporting (audit, stock comp, revenue recognition), governance
(board composition, dual-class share structure), and public company infrastructure.
(7) Governance rights: board seat, information rights, anti-dilution, preemptive rights;
drag-along; ROFO on secondary sales.
Format: Growth Equity Investment Memo with Commercial DD, Financial Model, Public
Comps, IPO Readiness Assessment, and Returns Analysis.
Inputs: [COMPANY NAME | ARR | GROWTH RATE | GROSS MARGIN | BURN/PROFITABILITY |
PROPOSED VALUATION | ROUND SIZE | PRIMARY INVESTMENT THESIS]

title: The EY Transaction Advisory Services Commercial Due Diligence
prompt_text:
PROMPT 189 — The EY Transaction Advisory Services Commercial Due Diligence
Act as Partner at EY's Transaction Advisory Services. Conduct commercial due
diligence on an acquisition target for a PE buyer.
Deliver: (1) Market size and growth: TAM methodology (top-down vs. bottom-up);
TAM validation through primary research; addressable vs. total market distinction;
growth rate decomposition (volume, price, mix). (2) Competitive positioning: market
share analysis (estimated); sustainable competitive advantages (Porter); win/loss
rate and reasons; NPS vs. competitors. (3) Customer quality: revenue concentration
analysis (top 5/10 customers as % of revenue); contract duration and renewal rates;
NPS scores; churn analysis by cohort. (4) Revenue quality: recurring vs. non-recurring
split; contracted backlog and coverage of next 12 months revenue; pricing power
evidence; channel mix and margins. (5) Growth opportunities: white space in existing
customers; greenfield geographic markets; adjacent product/service opportunities
— size each with bottom-up analysis. (6) Downside scenarios: identify the top 3
risks to the revenue thesis; quantify the P&L impact of each materializing.
(7) Management assessment: interview protocols; references on 3 key executives;
succession depth below the management team.
Format: Commercial Due Diligence Report with Market Sizing, Competitive Landscape,
Customer Analysis, Revenue Quality Assessment, and Risk Register.
Inputs: [TARGET COMPANY | INDUSTRY | REVENUE | GROWTH RATE | CUSTOMER COUNT |
TOP 5 CUSTOMER CONCENTRATION | PRIMARY COMMERCIAL RISK | PE BUYER'S THESIS]

title: The Macquarie Capital Power Sector M&A & IPP Valuation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 190 — The Macquarie Capital Power Sector M&A & IPP Valuation
Act as MD at Macquarie Capital's Power & Renewables group. Value an Independent
Power Producer (IPP) and design an M&A or capital raise strategy.
Deliver: (1) IPP valuation methodology: (a) Asset-level DCF — model each power plant
separately (capacity factor, contracted price or merchant price, O&M, debt service);
(b) Comparable company analysis — EV/EBITDA and EV/MW installed for listed IPPs;
(c) Precedent transactions — recent IPP M&A multiples. (2) Power market analysis:
capacity market revenues (PJM, ISO-NE, NYISO capacity auction clearing prices);
energy market margins (spark spread for gas: power price minus fuel cost;
dark spread for coal; clean dark/spark spread including carbon).
(3) Contracted vs. merchant revenue: value contracted cash flows at a lower discount
rate (6-8%); merchant cash flows at a higher rate (10-12%); the "blend" rate depends
on contracted %.
(4) Renewable vs. thermal: premium for renewable (contracted, zero fuel cost, long
asset life, ESG premium); discount for thermal (fuel cost risk, carbon risk,
regulatory risk). (5) Portfolio effects: diversification across geographies, fuel
types, and market structures reduces portfolio risk vs. single-asset.
(6) Financing: project finance leverage (60-70% for contracted renewables; 50-55%
for merchant gas); equity bridge financing for construction period.
(7) M&A process: utility strategic buyers vs. infrastructure fund buyers vs. PE —
different return requirements and synergy values.
Format: IPP Advisory with Asset-Level Valuation, Comparable Analysis, Power Market
Dashboard, Financing Structure, and M&A Process Design.
Inputs: [IPP NAME | INSTALLED CAPACITY (MW) | FUEL MIX | CONTRACTED % | GEOGRAPHY |
KEY POWER MARKETS | TRANSACTION OBJECTIVE | TARGET EQUITY IRR]

title: The McKinsey Digital Marketing ROI & Performance Marketing
prompt_text:
PROMPT 191 — The McKinsey Digital Marketing ROI & Performance Marketing
Act as Senior Expert at McKinsey's Digital Marketing practice. Design a
performance marketing measurement and optimization framework.
Deliver: (1) Attribution modeling: last-click (biased toward direct/SEM) vs.
first-click vs. linear vs. data-driven attribution; incrementality testing
(geo holdout, PSA test) as the gold standard. (2) Marketing mix modeling (MMM):
econometric model decomposing sales into base sales, media-driven, promotions,
and external factors; media ROI by channel (TV, digital, social, search).
(3) Paid search optimization: Quality Score improvement (CTR, ad relevance,
landing page); bid strategy (target CPA, target ROAS); search term negative list
management; brand vs. non-brand split economics.
(4) Paid social measurement: iOS 14+ signal loss — impact on Meta attribution;
Conversion API (CAPI) implementation; creative testing framework (A/B, DCO).
(5) Customer acquisition cost by cohort: LTV/CAC by channel and campaign;
payback period; blended vs. marginal CAC — the blended CAC illusion.
(6) Retention marketing: email/SMS economics (cost per send vs. incremental revenue);
loyalty program ROI (redemption rate vs. behavioral change lift).
(7) Marketing budget allocation: zero-based marketing budget approach;
diminishing returns curves by channel; optimal budget reallocation simulation.
Format: Digital Marketing Framework with Attribution Methodology, MMM Model Design,
Channel Economics, Budget Optimization Model, and Measurement Roadmap.
Inputs: [COMPANY TYPE | INDUSTRY | ANNUAL MARKETING BUDGET | PRIMARY CHANNELS |
CURRENT ATTRIBUTION MODEL | CAC BY CHANNEL | PRIMARY MEASUREMENT CHALLENGE]

title: The Rothschild Family Office / MFO Advisory: Next-Gen Wealth
prompt_text:
PROMPT 192 — The Rothschild Family Office / MFO Advisory: Next-Gen Wealth
Act as Senior Advisor at a leading Multi-Family Office. Design a next-generation
(NextGen) wealth education and governance program.
Deliver: (1) NextGen readiness assessment: age-appropriate financial literacy curriculum
(ages 8-12: saving/spending; 13-18: investing basics, compounding; 19-25: portfolio
management, taxes; 26+: estate planning, family governance). (2) Experiential learning:
how to give NextGen members a simulated investment portfolio ($100K paper portfolio
with real reporting); philanthropic budget ($10K DAF to manage); business investment
internship at a portfolio company. (3) Family governance education: Family Council
participation guidelines; Investment Committee role progression; succession to family
office leadership positions. (4) Estate planning preparation: understanding the family
trust structure; beneficiary rights and responsibilities; trustee duties.
(5) Pre-nuptial agreement guidance: how to have the conversation; protecting family
assets without damaging the relationship; role of prenups in multi-generational
wealth preservation. (6) Conflict resolution: family governance disputes over wealth
management decisions; using a family council facilitator; family charter as the
rules of engagement. (7) Entrepreneurship support: how families support
entrepreneurial NextGen members while managing downside risk (investment criteria,
reporting requirements, equity vs. debt from family).
Format: NextGen Wealth Program with Age-Appropriate Curriculum, Governance Pathway,
Estate Planning Prep, and Entrepreneurship Support Framework.
Inputs: [FAMILY WEALTH LEVEL | NUMBER OF NEXTGEN MEMBERS (AGES) | CURRENT GOVERNANCE
STRUCTURE | PRIMARY CONCERN | FAMILY BUSINESS Y/N | TIMELINE FOR WEALTH TRANSFER]

title: The EY Forensic Accounting & Financial Statement Fraud Detection
prompt_text:
PROMPT 193 — The EY Forensic Accounting & Financial Statement Fraud Detection
Act as Partner at EY's Forensic & Integrity Services. Design a financial
statement fraud detection framework using data analytics.
Deliver: (1) Fraud triangle: pressure (financial distress, bonus targets), opportunity
(weak controls, auditor over-reliance on management), and rationalization — how
each contributes to earnings manipulation.
(2) Beneish M-Score: 8 financial ratios that detect earnings manipulation —
Days Sales Index, Gross Margin Index, Asset Quality Index, Sales Growth Index,
Depreciation Index, SG&A Index, Leverage Index, Total Accruals to Total Assets.
Calculate M-Score and interpret: > -1.78 suggests manipulation.
(3) Accruals analysis: Jones Model abnormal accruals; Sloan's accrual anomaly
(high accruals → lower future earnings); cash flow vs. net income divergence as
a red flag.
(4) Revenue recognition red flags: channel stuffing (DSO spiking), bill-and-hold
arrangements, round-tripping transactions, related-party revenue.
(5) Expense manipulation: capitalizing vs. expensing decisions; cookie jar reserves;
changes in accounting estimates (depreciation life, warranty reserve).
(6) Data analytics approach: use SQL/Python to screen all journal entries for fraud
indicators (journal entries posted after close, unusual amounts, same-day reversals).
(7) Whistleblower and interview protocol: how to conduct a forensic interview;
document preservation.
Format: Forensic Framework with M-Score Calculation Template, Red Flag Checklist,
Data Analytics Code Outline, and Investigation Protocol.
Inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INDUSTRY | CONCERN THAT TRIGGERED REVIEW | FINANCIAL DATA
AVAILABLE | SCOPE OF REVIEW | REGULATORY CONTEXT | TIMELINE]

title: The Capital Group / American Funds Long-Term Equity Research
prompt_text:
PROMPT 194 — The Capital Group / American Funds Long-Term Equity Research
Act as Senior Research Associate at Capital Group. Conduct long-term fundamental
research for a potential 5-10 year holding period investment.
Deliver: (1) Long-term business quality assessment: durable competitive advantage
(brand, network effects, switching costs, cost advantage, efficient scale);
management track record over a full business cycle; capital allocation history
(M&A quality, buyback timing, dividend reliability).
(2) Industry evolution: where will this industry be in 10 years? Secular tailwinds
and headwinds; disruption risk assessment; the "melting ice cube" vs. "compounding
machine" test.
(3) Long-term earnings power: normalize current margins and returns on capital;
reinvestment rate and ROIC → sustainable earnings growth rate (growth = ROIC ×
reinvestment rate); terminal FCF estimate.
(4) Valuation for long-term investors: DCF with explicit 10-year FCF forecast +
terminal value; sensitivity to terminal growth rate; compare to current market
implied growth rate embedded in the stock price (the "implied growth" test).
(5) Capital Group investment process: multiple-counselor system (different PMs
independently evaluate ideas); how disagreement between counselors is resolved.
(6) Position sizing and patience: why Capital Group concentrates in high-conviction
ideas and holds for 10+ years; portfolio turnover < 25% annually.
(7) Monitoring vs. exit triggers: what events would cause a long-term holder to sell?
Format: Long-Term Research Report with Business Quality Assessment, Industry Evolution
Analysis, Long-Term DCF, and Investment Conviction Statement.
Inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INDUSTRY | INVESTMENT HYPOTHESIS | CURRENT PRICE | MARKET CAP |
10-YEAR REVENUE CAGR ESTIMATE | PRIMARY LONG-TERM RISK]

title: The Oliver Wyman Retail Banking Customer Analytics
prompt_text:
PROMPT 195 — The Oliver Wyman Retail Banking Customer Analytics
Act as Senior Partner at Oliver Wyman's Retail Banking practice. Build
a customer analytics framework for a retail bank to drive revenue growth.
Deliver: (1) Customer lifetime value (CLV) model for banking: present value of
all future products held (deposits, loans, cards, investments, insurance) minus
cost to serve; segment by CLV decile — top 20% of customers typically generate
80%+ of bank profit. (2) Next best action (NBA) engine: recommend the next product
or service for each customer based on life stage, transaction behavior, and
propensity model output; AB testing framework for NBA recommendations.
(3) Churn prediction: logistic regression / gradient boosting model to predict
60-day attrition risk; model features (declining login frequency, reduced deposit
balance, competitor account opening signal); intervention playbook by churn risk tier.
(4) Product cross-sell model: propensity scores for mortgage, auto loan, credit card,
investment account — rank customers by cross-sell opportunity value.
(5) Segmentation: behavioral segmentation (affluent savers, young accumulators,
business owners, seniors) beyond demographic segmentation; segment-specific
propositions and relationship management model.
(6) Data infrastructure: first-party transaction data as a competitive moat;
open banking/PSD2 data enrichment; CDP (Customer Data Platform) architecture.
(7) Personalization at scale: real-time decisioning; personalized digital marketing;
proactive outreach model (call center, relationship manager triggers).
Format: Customer Analytics Framework with CLV Model, NBA Engine Design, Churn Model,
Cross-Sell Opportunity, and Data Infrastructure Requirements.
Inputs: [BANK SIZE | CUSTOMER COUNT | PRIMARY RETAIL SEGMENTS | CURRENT ANALYTICS
MATURITY | PRIMARY REVENUE GROWTH TARGET | DATA AVAILABLE]

title: The Barclays Equity Research: ESG Integration in Valuation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 196 — The Barclays Equity Research: ESG Integration in Valuation
Act as Senior ESG Research Analyst at Barclays. Design a systematic approach
to integrating ESG factors into equity valuation models.
Deliver: (1) Material ESG factor identification: using SASB Materiality Map, identify
the 3-5 most financially material ESG factors for this specific industry; evidence
linking each factor to financial performance (academic citations).
(2) ESG in DCF: (a) Revenue adjustment — ESG leaders may earn premium pricing or
access new markets (green products); (b) Cost adjustment — carbon cost, labor
disputes, supply chain disruption risk; (c) WACC adjustment — ESG risk premium
added to WACC for high-risk companies (cost of equity increased by 50-150bps);
(d) Terminal value — ESG-related business model longevity.
(3) ESG scoring to financial adjustment mapping: translate MSCI ESG score (AAA to CCC)
into specific WACC premium and terminal growth rate adjustment; show worked example.
(4) Carbon price scenario analysis: P&L impact at €50/€100/€200 per tonne for
carbon-intensive companies; how this changes intrinsic value by EPS%.
(5) Governance risk premium: board independence score, audit quality, related-party
transaction risk — each adds 50-200bps to equity risk premium.
(6) Social risk: labor relations index, community relations score, supply chain
labor standards — how to quantify tail risk vs. expected impact.
(7) ESG reporting quality assessment: how to compare company ESG disclosures (TCFD,
GRI, SASB) and identify greenwashing vs. genuine commitment.
Format: ESG Valuation Framework with SASB Factor Map, WACC Adjustment Methodology,
Carbon Scenario Analysis, and ESG Score → Valuation Impact Table.
Inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INDUSTRY | CURRENT ESG SCORE | PRIMARY ESG RISKS |
CARBON INTENSITY | GOVERNANCE CONCERNS | INVESTMENT THESIS INTERACTION WITH ESG]

title: The Skadden / Sullivan & Cromwell Leveraged Buyout Legal
prompt_text:
PROMPT 197 — The Skadden / Sullivan & Cromwell Leveraged Buyout Legal
Act as Partner at a top M&A law firm. Design the legal framework for a $5B
leveraged buyout transaction.
Deliver: (1) Merger agreement structure: for a take-private — one-step merger vs.
two-step tender offer + back-end merger (speed advantage for tender offer);
election mechanics, proration, and guaranteed proration.
(2) Representations and warranties: materiality scrapes; knowledge qualifiers;
MAC definition (the most negotiated provision — what constitutes a MAC);
interim operating covenants (what can target do without buyer consent during signing-
to-close period?). (3) Financing condition and specific performance: is there a
financing condition (seller-unfriendly) or must buyer use specific performance to
close? Reverse break fee as the alternative to specific performance (typically 3-6%
of deal value). (4) Debt commitment letters: highly confident letter vs. committed
debt financing; flex provisions (rate flex, OID flex, structural flex); SunGard
provisions limiting market flex. (5) Rollover equity: management rollover mechanics;
Section 83(b) election; rollover documentation timing relative to closing.
(6) Equity commitment letter: guarantee of equity funding from PE fund; limited
guaranty from the fund for the reverse break fee.
(7) Going-private regulatory: Schedule 13E-3 filing; fairness opinion requirement;
majority-of-the-minority vote; SEC review timing.
Format: LBO Legal Framework with Merger Agreement Key Provisions, Financing Commitment
Structure, Rollover Mechanics, and Regulatory Timeline.
Inputs: [TARGET COMPANY | ACQUIRER PE FIRM | DEAL SIZE | EQUITY/DEBT SPLIT |
MANAGEMENT ROLLOVER AMOUNT | FINANCING SOURCES | REGULATORY CONCERNS]

title: The BlackRock / Fidelity 401(k) Plan Design & Fiduciary
prompt_text:
PROMPT 198 — The BlackRock / Fidelity 401(k) Plan Design & Fiduciary
Act as ERISA counsel or institutional investment consultant. Design
an optimal 401(k) plan and fulfill fiduciary obligations.
Deliver: (1) Plan design optimization: contribution limits ($23K employee + $46K
total 2024); match formula design (dollar-for-dollar to 3% is most effective for
participation); auto-enrollment (6% default + auto-escalation 1%/year); Roth 401(k)
option. (2) Investment menu design: core menu of 15-20 funds covering equity
(domestic, international, small cap), fixed income (stable value, bond fund), and
target-date funds as QDIA (Qualified Default Investment Alternative).
(3) Target-date fund selection: glidepath analysis (to vs. through retirement);
expense ratio comparison; proprietary vs. white-label TDFs.
(4) Fiduciary duties: prudent expert standard under ERISA; documentation requirements
for investment committee meetings; investment policy statement (IPS) best practices;
408(b)(2) fee disclosure review.
(5) Fee benchmarking: total plan cost as bps of assets; compare recordkeeper,
investment management, and advisory fees to market; request for proposals process.
(6) Stable value vs. money market: stable value fund structure (insurance company
wrap contracts); crediting rate mechanics; book value vs. market value risk.
(7) SECURE 2.0 provisions: emergency savings accounts, student loan match, catch-up
limit increases, RMD age changes — implementation timeline and plan amendment requirements.
Format: 401(k) Plan Design with Investment Menu, Fiduciary Checklist, Fee Benchmarking,
TDF Comparison, and SECURE 2.0 Implementation Plan.
Inputs: [COMPANY SIZE | EMPLOYEE DEMOGRAPHICS | CURRENT PLAN DESIGN | CURRENT FEES |
PRIMARY PLAN OBJECTIVE | MATCH FORMULA | RECORDKEEPER]

title: The Accenture Supply Chain Finance & Digital Procurement
prompt_text:
PROMPT 199 — The Accenture Supply Chain Finance & Digital Procurement
Act as MD at Accenture's Supply Chain & Operations practice. Design a
digital procurement transformation and supply chain finance program.
Deliver: (1) Procurement maturity model: from transactional (PO processing) to
strategic (category management, supplier innovation). (2) Spend analytics: data
cleansing and classification (UNSPSC coding); tail spend management; maverick spend
identification. (3) Category management: strategic categories (single-source, high
risk), leverage categories (price competition), bottleneck categories, and commodity
categories — different strategies for each quadrant (Kraljic Matrix).
(4) e-Procurement and P2P automation: e-catalog, PO-to-receipt-to-invoice matching
(3-way match automation); approval workflow automation; RPA for exception handling.
(5) Supplier relationship management: supplier scorecards (quality, delivery, cost,
innovation); supplier development investment for strategic suppliers; supplier risk
monitoring (financial health, ESG, geographic concentration).
(6) Supply chain finance integration: reverse factoring program for top 200 suppliers
(extend DPO from 45 to 90 days, provide suppliers early payment at buyer's credit
spread); dynamic discounting for tail suppliers.
(7) ESG in procurement: scope 3 emissions from supply chain; supplier sustainability
assessments; green procurement standards; conflict minerals compliance (Dodd-Frank 1502).
Format: Digital Procurement Transformation with Maturity Assessment, Category Strategy,
P2P Automation Roadmap, SCF Program Design, and ESG Procurement Policy.
Inputs: [COMPANY REVENUE | ANNUAL PROCUREMENT SPEND | NUMBER OF SUPPLIERS |
CURRENT P2P AUTOMATION LEVEL | PRIMARY PROCUREMENT CHALLENGE | ESG AMBITION]

title: The Morgan Stanley Wealth Management Portfolio Review Framework
prompt_text:
PROMPT 200 — The Morgan Stanley Wealth Management Portfolio Review Framework
Act as Senior Financial Advisor at Morgan Stanley Wealth Management.
Conduct a comprehensive annual portfolio review for an HNW client.
Deliver: (1) Portfolio performance attribution: total return vs. benchmark; alpha
from asset allocation vs. security selection; risk-adjusted return (Sharpe, Sortino,
Calmar ratios); comparison to financial plan objectives (are they on track?).
(2) Risk assessment: current portfolio risk vs. stated risk tolerance; VaR at 95%
confidence level; maximum drawdown scenario (what would this portfolio lose in a
2008-style event?); risk drift (has the portfolio drifted from target allocation?).
(3) Rebalancing analysis: drift from target allocation by asset class; tax-aware
rebalancing (harvest losses, avoid gains where possible); transaction cost analysis.
(4) Fee analysis: total cost of ownership (advisor fee + fund expense ratios + trading
costs); compare to market rates; fee value attribution.
(5) Goal progress: retirement funding ratio (current assets vs. PV of retirement income
needs); college funding adequacy; estate planning funding.
(6) Tactical positioning: current macro environment assessment; recommended portfolio
tilts for the next 12-18 months; specific trades to implement.
(7) Insurance review: does the client have adequate life, disability, liability umbrella,
and long-term care coverage? Quantify any gaps.
Format: Annual Portfolio Review with Performance Attribution, Risk Dashboard, Goal
Progress, Rebalancing Recommendations, and Action Plan.
Inputs: [CLIENT AGE | NET WORTH | INVESTABLE ASSETS | RETIREMENT DATE | SPENDING NEEDS |
RISK TOLERANCE | CURRENT ALLOCATION | PRIMARY FINANCIAL CONCERN]

title: The Warburg Pincus Growth Markets Healthcare Investment
prompt_text:
PROMPT 201 — The Warburg Pincus Growth Markets Healthcare Investment
Act as MD at Warburg Pincus evaluating healthcare investments in emerging
markets (India, China, Southeast Asia, LatAm, MENA).
Deliver: (1) EM healthcare investment thesis: underpenetrated markets, rising middle
class, favorable demographics, government spending uplift. (2) Sub-sector prioritization:
hospitals (greenfield vs. acquisition), diagnostics (radiology, pathology chains),
pharma distribution, medical devices distribution, health insurance, telemedicine.
(3) Hospital chain economics: ARPOB (Average Revenue Per Occupied Bed), occupancy
rates, payor mix (OOP vs. insurance vs. government), capex per bed, EBITDA margin
at maturity (typically 15-25% in EM hospitals). (4) Regulatory risk by market:
India (NHPS, clinical establishment acts), China (VIE, foreign ownership limits),
SEA (foreign ownership caps, reimbursement policies). (5) Build vs. buy:
greenfield hospital (5-7 year ramp, high execution risk, 15-20% IRR potential)
vs. acquisition (faster, lower risk, lower return). (6) Talent risk: doctor and
nurse availability; specialist physician recruitment as the primary bottleneck
in EM hospital expansion. (7) Exit: IPO on local exchanges (Apollo, Fortis India model);
strategic sale to global hospital groups; PE secondary.
Format: EM Healthcare Investment Framework with Sub-Sector Returns, Hospital
Economics, Regulatory Risk Matrix, and Exit Landscape.
Inputs: [GEOGRAPHY | SUB-SECTOR | COMPANY STAGE | REVENUE | BEDS/UNITS |
EBITDA MARGIN | PROPOSED ENTRY VALUATION | PRIMARY RISK]

title: The Barclays LBO Financing & Leveraged Loan Syndication
prompt_text:
PROMPT 202 — The Barclays LBO Financing & Leveraged Loan Syndication
Act as MD at Barclays' Leveraged Finance Capital Markets. Structure and
syndicate an LBO financing package.
Deliver: (1) LBO capital structure design: senior secured term loan (TLB), revolving
credit facility, and optionally second lien or HY bonds; sizing each layer.
(2) Covenant-lite TLB: SOFR + spread; OID (original issue discount); 1%
amortization; 6-month soft call at 101; incurrence covenants only.
(3) Flex provisions: market flex — ability to widen spread or increase OID by 25-50bps
if market conditions deteriorate; reverse flex if oversubscribed.
(4) Syndication strategy: anchor CLO managers (60-70% of TLB demand); crossover
credit funds; insurance companies (if rated B+ or better); retail loan funds.
(5) High-yield bond alternative: when to use HY bonds vs. leveraged loans (fixed rate
preference, call flexibility, covenant flexibility, investor base diversification).
(6) Underwrite vs. best efforts: commitment types; underwrite risk for the bank;
break fee provisions in commitment letters.
(7) Credit agreement key terms: EBITDA definition negotiation; restricted payment
baskets; debt incurrence tests; permitted acquisitions basket; anti-layering.
Format: LBO Financing Advisory with Capital Structure, TLB Term Sheet, Syndication
Strategy, HY vs. Loan Comparison, and Credit Agreement Key Terms.
Inputs: [BORROWER | INDUSTRY | LTM EBITDA | PROPOSED LEVERAGE | TRANSACTION SIZE |
TIMING | BANK GROUP | PRIMARY FINANCING CONCERN]

title: The Ardian Secondary PE Market Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 203 — The Ardian Secondary PE Market Strategy
Act as MD at Ardian — the world's largest secondary PE fund manager. Build
a comprehensive secondary market investment strategy.
Deliver: (1) Secondary market overview: LP-led secondaries (LPs selling fund interests),
GP-led secondaries (continuation vehicles, single-asset), and structured solutions;
market size ($130B+ annual volume) and growth drivers. (2) LP-led secondary analysis:
NAV discount/premium assessment — how to determine fair value for a portfolio
of LP interests; NAV verification methodology; J-curve elimination benefit.
(3) GP-led / continuation vehicle analysis: single-asset CVs (sponsor keeps best asset
in new vehicle); pricing relative to direct PE (typically 10-15% premium to fund
NAV); governance protections for existing LPs. (4) Preferred equity / NAV financing:
lend against PE portfolio at portfolio level; senior position ahead of LP distributions;
target 12-14% return. (5) Pricing discipline: IRR and MOIC targets for secondary
investments; required discount to NAV by fund vintage and strategy (buyout vs. VC vs.
growth). (6) Portfolio construction: diversification by manager, vintage, geography,
sector; correlation in secondary portfolios during financial stress.
(7) Process: limited information environment; speed of execution (often 2-4 weeks
to close); working with placement agents vs. direct outreach.
Format: Secondary Strategy with Market Overview, LP-Led vs. GP-Led Analysis,
Pricing Framework, Portfolio Construction, and Process Guide.
Inputs: [FUND SIZE | INVESTMENT FOCUS (LP-LED/GP-LED/PREFERRED EQUITY) |
TARGET DISCOUNT TO NAV | SECTOR PREFERENCE | VINTAGE PREFERENCE | RETURN TARGET]

title: The Macquarie Digital Infrastructure Investment Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 204 — The Macquarie Digital Infrastructure Investment Strategy
Act as MD at Macquarie's Digital Infrastructure fund. Build an investment thesis
for data centers, fiber networks, and tower companies.
Deliver: (1) Digital infrastructure taxonomy: hyperscale data centers (leased to AWS/
Azure/GCP), retail colocation (Equinix/Digital Realty model), edge data centers,
fiber networks (long-haul, metro, last-mile), cell towers, and small cells.
(2) Data center economics: power capacity (MW) as the primary asset unit; PUE
(Power Usage Effectiveness — target < 1.3); rental rate per kW; utilization rate;
hyperscaler lease structure (15-20 year, triple-net, inflation-linked escalator).
(3) AI-driven demand: GPU cluster hosting requirements (density: 50-100kW per rack
vs. 5-10kW traditional); water cooling vs. air cooling; interconnection requirements
between GPU clusters and internet. (4) Fiber economics: IRU (Indefeasible Right
of Use) revenue; lit vs. dark fiber; metro fiber density and route economics.
(5) Tower fundamentals: tenancy ratio (key value driver — 1.5× = low, 2.5× = high);
escalation provisions (2-3% annual); colocation revenue per tower.
(6) Risk factors: power availability (grid connection timelines of 2-4 years);
permitting for new data centers; hyperscaler concentration risk; technology
obsolescence (next-gen GPU architecture changing density requirements).
(7) Valuation: EV/EBITDA, EV/kW (data centers), EV/tower (towers); private vs.
public market premium/discount.
Format: Digital Infra Investment Framework with Sub-Sector Economics, AI Demand
Analysis, Risk Assessment, Valuation Benchmarks, and Deal Screening Criteria.
Inputs: [SUB-SECTOR FOCUS | GEOGRAPHY | DEAL SIZE | POWER CAPACITY | TENANT MIX |
LEASE STRUCTURE | TARGET IRR | PRIMARY RISK CONCERN]

title: The Morgan Stanley Prime Brokerage & Hedge Fund Services
prompt_text:
PROMPT 205 — The Morgan Stanley Prime Brokerage & Hedge Fund Services
Act as Head of Prime Brokerage at Morgan Stanley. Design a comprehensive
prime brokerage platform for a newly launched hedge fund.
Deliver: (1) Prime brokerage services: trade execution, clearing, settlement, custody,
securities lending, margin financing, risk analytics, and capital introduction.
(2) Financing terms: margin rates (SOFR + spread by asset class); synthetic financing
vs. physical financing; portfolio margining eligibility and capital efficiency.
(3) Securities lending: borrow availability and rates; how prime broker sources
hard-to-borrow shares; short locates and daily availability; rebate on cash
collateral vs. equity collateral.
(4) Multi-prime setup: why funds use 2-3 prime brokers (counterparty risk,
financing competition, operational resilience); how to negotiate between primes.
(5) Capital introduction: prime broker's role in connecting hedge fund with
institutional LP investors; allocator database; cap intro events.
(6) Technology: portfolio management system (PMS) integration; order management
system (OMS) connectivity; real-time P&L and risk reporting.
(7) Risk monitoring: prime broker's own risk management on client book (margin calls,
concentration, liquidity); stress testing client portfolios.
(8) Fee structure: commission rates by asset class; financing spread; technology fees;
all-in cost calculation and comparison across prime brokers.
Format: Prime Brokerage Framework with Services Overview, Financing Terms, Securities
Lending, Multi-Prime Architecture, Cap Intro, and Fee Analysis.
Inputs: [FUND STRATEGY | AUM | GROSS/NET EXPOSURE | ASSET CLASSES | LEVERAGE TARGET |
SHORT BOOK SIZE | HARD-TO-BORROW NEEDS | PRIMARY PB REQUIREMENT]

title: The Bain Capital Credit High Yield Bond Analysis
prompt_text:
PROMPT 206 — The Bain Capital Credit High Yield Bond Analysis
Act as Senior Credit Analyst at Bain Capital Credit. Build a comprehensive
high-yield bond investment thesis.
Deliver: (1) HY credit analysis framework: Business Risk (sector dynamics, competitive
position, cyclicality) + Financial Risk (leverage, coverage, cash flow) = credit view.
(2) Bond document review: indenture analysis — restricted payments basket, debt
incurrence test, asset sale covenant, change of control (101 put), anti-layering;
identify structural strengths vs. weaknesses vs. peers.
(3) Liquidity analysis: cash + revolver availability vs. near-term obligations
(interest, capex, debt maturities); minimum liquidity cushion; FCF generation.
(4) Recovery analysis: in a default scenario — enterprise value (at stressed
EBITDA × distressed multiple) divided across the capital structure; recovery
rate for each tranche; comparison to trading price.
(5) Relative value: OAS vs. peers rated similarly; Z-spread vs. duration;
yield-to-worst vs. call price (for premium-priced callable bonds — yield-to-call
may be more relevant). (6) Catalyst identification: upcoming catalysts that
could tighten or widen the spread (earnings report, maturity refinancing, M&A,
rating action, covenant reset). (7) Position sizing: conviction × liquidity ×
portfolio concentration limit; HY bond market liquidity (bid-ask spread,
dealer inventory, market depth).
Format: HY Credit Analysis with Business/Financial Risk Assessment, Bond Document
Summary, Liquidity Analysis, Recovery Scenario, and Investment Recommendation.
Inputs: [ISSUER NAME | BOND CUSIP | COUPON/MATURITY | CURRENT PRICE/YIELD |
LTM EBITDA | NET LEVERAGE | LIQUIDITY | PRIMARY CREDIT THESIS]

title: The World Bank Group Development Economics & Poverty Reduction
prompt_text:
PROMPT 207 — The World Bank Group Development Economics & Poverty Reduction
Act as Senior Economist at the World Bank's Development Research Group.
Build a comprehensive poverty reduction strategy for a low-income country.
Deliver: (1) Poverty diagnostics: poverty headcount at $2.15/day (World Bank line);
multidimensional poverty (MPI) — health, education, living standards; identify
which dimensions are most binding. (2) Growth-poverty linkages: inclusive growth
analysis — which sectors employ the poor? How does 1% GDP growth translate to
poverty reduction in this country? Growth incidence curve analysis.
(3) Human capital investment: returns to education by level; health system investment
ROI; nutrition in early childhood and its lifetime productivity impact.
(4) Social protection: conditional cash transfer (CCT) design (Bolsa Família,
PROGRESA model — conditions, transfer size, targeting mechanism); universal basic
income debate; productive inclusion programs.
(5) Agricultural development: smallholder productivity improvement; land rights
and tenure security; value chain integration for subsistence farmers; irrigation
and climate adaptation.
(6) Financial inclusion: mobile money for the unbanked (M-PESA model);
digital credit for smallholder farmers; remittance cost reduction.
(7) Fiscal space and aid effectiveness: domestic resource mobilization (tax/GDP ratio);
aid dependency trap; budget support vs. project financing; results-based financing.
Format: Development Strategy with Poverty Diagnostic, Growth-Poverty Analysis,
Human Capital Investment Plan, Social Protection Design, and Financing Framework.
Inputs: [COUNTRY NAME | GDP PER CAPITA | POVERTY HEADCOUNT | PRIMARY POVERTY DRIVERS |
AID DEPENDENCE | GOVERNMENT CAPACITY | PRIORITY DEVELOPMENT OBJECTIVE]

title: The Insight Partners SaaS Metrics & Scaleup Benchmarking
prompt_text:
PROMPT 208 — The Insight Partners SaaS Metrics & Scaleup Benchmarking
Act as Partner at Insight Partners' ScaleUp division. Build a comprehensive
SaaS metrics benchmarking and operational improvement program for a portfolio company.
Deliver: (1) Insight's SaaS metrics framework: the "ScaleUp" metrics — ARR, ARR growth,
NRR, GDR, CAC ratio (S&M spend / New ARR), Payback period, Magic Number
(New ARR / S&M spend prior quarter), Rule of 40.
(2) Benchmarking: Insight's database of 400+ portfolio companies — percentile ranking
for this company on all key metrics by ARR band ($10-50M, $50-150M, $150-500M).
(3) GTM efficiency: SDR/AE ratio; quota attainment distribution; pipeline coverage
(3-4× required); average sales cycle length; win rate by competitor.
(4) CS and expansion: NRR decomposition (expansion ARR, contraction ARR, churn ARR);
CSM-to-ARR ratio; QBR coverage; expansion playbook design.
(5) R&D efficiency: R&D as % of ARR; engineering headcount per $1M ARR; release
frequency; technical debt as drag on velocity.
(6) Financial efficiency: burn multiple (net burn / net new ARR — target < 1× at
Series C+); Rule of 40 composition (revenue growth vs. FCF margin contribution).
(7) Improvement priorities: 90-day sprint plans for the 3 highest-leverage improvements;
owner, KPI, and resource requirement for each.
Format: SaaS Benchmarking Report with Metrics Scorecard, Percentile Rankings,
GTM Efficiency Analysis, Expansion Playbook, and 90-Day Improvement Sprints.
Inputs: [COMPANY | ARR | ARR GROWTH | NRR | CAC RATIO | MAGIC NUMBER | BURN MULTIPLE |
RULE OF 40 | PRIMARY EFFICIENCY CONCERN]

title: The HSBC Sustainable Finance & Transition Finance Framework
prompt_text:
PROMPT 209 — The HSBC Sustainable Finance & Transition Finance Framework
Act as MD at HSBC's Sustainable Finance & Investments group. Design a
transition finance framework for hard-to-abate sectors.
Deliver: (1) Transition finance rationale: the "green" vs. "transition" debate —
the world needs to finance the decarbonization of high-emitting industries,
not just fund already-green businesses; transition finance fills this gap.
(2) Transition finance taxonomy: credible transition plans; science-based targets
alignment; technology-specific criteria by sector (steel, cement, shipping,
aviation, chemicals). (3) SLB (Sustainability-Linked Bond) design: KPI selection
(science-based, material, independently verified); SPT (Sustainability Performance
Target) ambition; coupon step-up if target missed (typically 25bps); SPO selection.
(4) Transition finance instruments: SLBs, transition bonds, sustainability-linked
loans (SLLs), green project finance within transition sectors.
(5) Credibility standards: EU Taxonomy alignment; Paris Agreement alignment test;
third-party verification (ISS, Sustainalytics, DNV, Bureau Veritas); ICMA
Sustainability-Linked Bond Principles compliance. (6) Greenwashing risk:
how to avoid SLB greenwashing — targets that are "business as usual" vs. genuinely
ambitious; KPI gaming prevention through ratchet mechanisms.
(7) Investor demand: which investor types will buy transition finance instruments;
pricing vs. conventional bonds (transition premium or greenium?).
Format: Transition Finance Framework with KPI Selection Guide, SLB Term Sheet Template,
Credibility Standards, Greenwashing Risk Assessment, and Investor Targeting.
Inputs: [COMPANY SECTOR | CURRENT EMISSIONS PROFILE | NET-ZERO TARGET |
SBTi STATUS | PROPOSED KPIs | FINANCING SIZE | TARGET INVESTOR BASE]

title: The Rokos Capital Management Global Macro Rates Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 210 — The Rokos Capital Management Global Macro Rates Strategy
Act as Senior PM at Rokos Capital Management. Build a high-conviction
global macro strategy focused on developed market rates and FX.
Deliver: (1) Macro thesis construction: build the central macro thesis from first
principles — global growth, inflation, and monetary policy path; identify where
the consensus is wrong. (2) Central bank reaction function: model the Fed, ECB,
and BoJ reaction functions (Taylor Rule variants); forecast the rate path implied
by each model vs. market pricing; identify the biggest divergence.
(3) Rates trade design — 5 specific trades: for each — instrument (bond futures,
swaps, swaptions), direction, entry level, stop, target, carry, and key catalyst.
(4) FX interplay: how the rates divergence thesis translates to FX (USD/EUR, USD/JPY,
EUR/GBP); size of FX position relative to rates position.
(5) Tail risk hedging: given the conviction of the view, what hedge protects against
the scenario where the thesis is wrong? Option structures that limit downside.
(6) Position sizing and leverage: how much leverage is appropriate given the conviction
and tail risk? Kelly fraction applied to macro positions.
(7) Macro event calendar: Fed meetings, ECB meetings, CPI releases, labor market
data — map all key catalysts over the next 6 months with expected market impact.
Format: Global Macro Strategy with Central Bank Analysis, 5 Trade Ideas,
FX Expression, Tail Risk Hedge, and Macro Event Calendar.
Inputs: [RISK CAPITAL | DV01 BUDGET | LEVERAGE LIMIT | PRIMARY MACRO VIEW |
FX HEDGING CAPACITY | KEY CONVICTION AND BIGGEST RISK]

title: The Centerview Partners Strategic Review & Sale Process
prompt_text:
PROMPT 211 — The Centerview Partners Strategic Review & Sale Process
Act as Partner at Centerview Partners managing a strategic review and
formal sale process for a public or private company.
Deliver: (1) Strategic review process design: Board-directed process; investment
bank mandate (sell-side M&A advisory); confidentiality protocol; leak risk management.
(2) Process types: broad auction (maximum competitive tension, price discovery),
targeted auction (5-10 parties, faster, preserves confidentiality), negotiated sale
(single party, relationship-based, fastest), and go-shop (post-signing market check).
(3) Preparation phase: CIM (Confidential Information Memorandum) preparation;
management presentation design; data room structuring (VDR — Intralinks, Datasite);
carve-out financial statements if needed.
(4) Buyer targeting: strategic buyers (identify top 10-15 with strategic fit and
financial capacity); financial buyers (top-tier PE with sector expertise and fund
size to close); sovereign wealth funds and family offices.
(5) Bid process management: Phase 1 (NDAs, CIM distribution, management presentations);
Phase 2 (data room, site visits, management Q&A, final binding bids).
(6) Bid evaluation: headline price vs. certainty of close (financing risk,
regulatory risk, conditionality); form of consideration (cash vs. stock vs. earnout);
management treatment in PE bids.
(7) Negotiation to signing: exclusivity granting; SPA negotiation; Board fiduciary
duty considerations; FIRRMA/CFIUS as timeline risk.
Format: Sale Process Advisory with Timeline, CIM Outline, Buyer Targeting, Bid
Evaluation Matrix, and Negotiation Strategy.
Inputs: [COMPANY NAME | INDUSTRY | REVENUE | EBITDA | GROWTH PROFILE |
STRATEGIC ALTERNATIVES | BOARD'S PRIMARY OBJECTIVE | TIMELINE]

title: The Bridgepoint European Mid-Market PE Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 212 — The Bridgepoint European Mid-Market PE Strategy
Act as MD at Bridgepoint evaluating European mid-market buyout opportunities
(enterprise value €50-500M).
Deliver: (1) European mid-market landscape: market fragmentation by country;
lower competition vs. large-cap PE; proprietary deal flow from founder networks;
typical leverage (3.5-4.5× in mid-market vs. 5-6× large-cap).
(2) Target characteristics: family-owned businesses transitioning to professional
management; divisional carve-outs; growth companies needing capital; turnaround
situations. (3) Country-specific dynamics: Germany (Mittelstand — hidden champions,
relationship-driven, seller price sensitivity); France (transmission d'entreprise,
employee consultation, BSPCE warrants); UK (most PE-mature, highest competition);
Benelux, Nordics, Iberia (less competition, strong governance).
(4) Value creation levers for European mid-market: (a) Professionalization —
management upgrade, governance, reporting; (b) International expansion — taking
a national champion pan-European; (c) Buy-and-build — 3-5 bolt-on acquisitions
in a fragmented sector; (d) Digital transformation — digitizing operations
and customer experience.
(5) DACH sector focus: automation/robotics, industrial software, business services,
healthcare services — deep sector expertise as competitive advantage.
(6) Financing: European mid-market financing sources (unitranche from direct lenders
vs. club deal from banks); typical terms; covenant protection.
(7) Exit: strategic sale to European/global corporates; PE secondary; local IPO.
Format: European Mid-Market PE Framework with Market Landscape, Country Dynamics,
Value Creation Playbook, Financing, and Exit Strategy.
Inputs: [COUNTRY FOCUS | SECTOR | COMPANY REVENUE | EBITDA | ENTRY MULTIPLE |
FAMILY VS. CARVE-OUT | VALUE CREATION THESIS | HOLD PERIOD]

title: The Morgan Stanley Quantitative Research: Factor Zoo Navigation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 213 — The Morgan Stanley Quantitative Research: Factor Zoo Navigation
Act as Head of Quantitative Research at Morgan Stanley. Build a framework
for navigating factor "zoo" — the proliferation of claimed alpha factors.
Deliver: (1) The factor zoo problem: 400+ published factors in academic literature;
most are spurious (p-hacking, data-mining, multiple testing); how to distinguish
genuine factors from noise. (2) Factor validation criteria: (a) Economic intuition —
why should this factor earn a premium? (b) Statistical significance — t > 3.0
after Bonferroni/BHY correction; (c) Out-of-sample evidence (different markets,
different time periods); (d) Low turnover after transaction costs; (e) Capacity.
(3) The 5 robust factors: Market beta, Size (with quality screen), Value (cash flow
based), Momentum (12-1 month), Quality (profitability) — academic consensus.
(4) Factor timing: is factor timing possible? Evidence is weak; factors have
multi-year cycles; overconfident timing destroys returns.
(5) Factor crowding: when factor is too widely known, it underperforms (momentum
crashes); crowding detection methods (factor correlation increase, factor
volatility increase, hedge fund positioning data).
(6) Alternative data factors: satellite imagery, credit card data, NLP — do they
survive transaction cost analysis and institutional capacity constraints?
(7) Factor construction details that matter: value — what metric (P/E vs. P/B vs.
EV/EBITDA vs. FCF yield)? Winsorization level? Universe definition?
Format: Factor Research Framework with Validation Criteria, Robust Factor Summary,
Crowding Detection, Alternative Data Assessment, and Construction Detail Guide.
Inputs: [UNIVERSE | INVESTMENT VEHICLE | CAPACITY CONSTRAINT | FACTOR UNIVERSE |
PRIMARY FACTORS UNDER CONSIDERATION | TRANSACTION COST ASSUMPTION]

title: The Rothschild Debt Advisory: Leveraged Buyout Financing
prompt_text:
PROMPT 214 — The Rothschild Debt Advisory: Leveraged Buyout Financing
Act as Senior Advisor at Rothschild's Debt Advisory practice. Advise a PE
sponsor on the optimal debt financing for an LBO.
Deliver: (1) Debt advisory role: independent from underwriting banks; optimize
the debt package by running a competitive process between lending banks and
direct lenders; save 25-75bps in pricing vs. non-advised process.
(2) Market sounding: pre-process outreach to 8-10 banks and 5-8 direct lenders;
assess appetite, leverage capacity, and initial pricing indications.
(3) Financing alternatives comparison: (a) Bank-led TLB syndication (broadly
syndicated, liquid, market flex risk); (b) Unitranche from direct lenders (certain
execution, no flex, higher pricing, covenant-lite); (c) Split TLB + 2nd lien
(more leverage capacity, higher blended cost); (d) TLB + HY bond (fixed rate
portion, call flexibility, wider investor base).
(4) Process management: request for proposals (RFPs) to banks; evaluation criteria;
management presentation to lenders; term sheet negotiation; commitment letter review.
(5) Key negotiation points: EBITDA definition (most impactful — $10M of EBITDA =
~$50M of debt at 5× leverage); restricted payment basket; portability provisions
(debt transfers to new owner without consent); MFN on incremental facilities.
(6) Fee structure: arrangement fee, OID, commitment fee on revolver; total fees as
% of deal size; fee comparison across financing options.
(7) Timing management: debt process parallel to M&A process; commitment letter
before signing; SFA execution for closing.
Format: Debt Advisory with Financing Options Comparison, Process Timeline, Key
Negotiation Points, Fee Analysis, and EBITDA Definition Guidance.
Inputs: [SPONSOR | TARGET | INDUSTRY | EBITDA | PROPOSED LEVERAGE | DEAL SIZE |
TIMELINE | PREFERRED FINANCING STRUCTURE | PRIMARY DEBT CONCERN]

title: The IFC Private Sector Development in Fragile States
prompt_text:
PROMPT 215 — The IFC Private Sector Development in Fragile States
Act as Senior Investment Officer at IFC (International Finance Corporation).
Evaluate a private sector investment in a fragile or conflict-affected state.
Deliver: (1) Fragile state investing rationale: IFC's FCS (Fragile and Conflict-affected
Situations) mandate; development impact is highest where private capital is scarce;
risk premium required and how to mitigate it. (2) Risk assessment framework:
political risk (regime stability, policy reversal), security risk (conflict zones,
staff safety), regulatory risk (rule of law, contract enforcement), FX risk
(convertibility, transferability). (3) Deal structuring for fragility:
(a) Political Risk Insurance (MIGA coverage for expropriation, currency transfer
restriction, political violence); (b) Local currency lending to avoid FX risk for
borrower; (c) Blended finance — grant funding for technical assistance alongside
loan/equity. (4) Sector selection: which sectors work in fragile states (mobile
telecom, microfinance, agribusiness, healthcare, renewable energy) vs. which don't
(capital-intensive manufacturing, luxury real estate). (5) Environmental & Social
standards: IFC Performance Standards 1-8 application in fragile contexts;
heightened risk for PS2 (labor), PS4 (community health), PS7 (indigenous peoples);
conflict sensitivity assessment. (6) Local partner selection: critical in fragile
states; due diligence on local partner integrity; anti-corruption and AML enhanced
DD. (7) Exit: limited exit options in fragile markets; trade sale to regional investors;
management buyout; secondary to another DFI.
