Format: Fragile State Investment Framework with Risk Assessment, Deal Structure,
MIGA Coverage, Sector Selection, E&S Standards, and Exit Analysis.
Inputs: [COUNTRY | FRAGILITY INDEX SCORE | SECTOR | INVESTMENT SIZE | LOCAL PARTNER |
DEVELOPMENT HYPOTHESIS | PRIMARY RISK CONCERN | BLENDED FINANCE AVAILABILITY]

title: The Blackstone Real Estate Debt Strategies (BREDS)
prompt_text:
PROMPT 216 — The Blackstone Real Estate Debt Strategies (BREDS)
Act as MD at Blackstone Real Estate Debt Strategies. Build a real estate
debt investment strategy across the capital structure.
Deliver: (1) RE debt universe: senior construction loans, senior bridge loans,
subordinate/mezzanine debt, preferred equity, CMBS B-pieces, and CRE CLOs;
return targets: senior (7-9%), mezzanine (10-13%), preferred equity (12-15%).
(2) Construction loan underwriting: spec vs. pre-leased; LTV at completion
(target <65%); interest reserve adequacy; cost overrun contingency; developer
track record. (3) Bridge loan underwriting: transitional assets (lease-up, renovation);
business plan feasibility; exit strategy (stabilized sale or permanent loan refi);
debt yield at stabilization target (>8%).
(4) Mezzanine debt structuring: intercreditor agreement with senior lender;
cure rights; equity kicker warrants; preferred return vs. current pay.
(5) Property type focus: industrial (strongest fundamentals), multifamily (supply
concern in some markets), office (distress opportunity vs. structural headwind),
retail (selective — grocery-anchored vs. secondary mall).
(6) CMBS B-piece investing: buying the most junior rated or unrated portion of CMBS;
influence on loan underwriting during B-piece negotiation; yield target (10-15%).
(7) Market timing: credit market cycle and how it affects RE debt pricing;
rate environment impact on cap rates and collateral values.
Format: RE Debt Strategy with Capital Structure Map, Underwriting Standards by
Product, CMBS B-Piece Analysis, Property Type Allocation, and Market Timing.
Inputs: [INVESTMENT FOCUS | GEOGRAPHY | LOAN SIZE | PROPERTY TYPE | RATE ENVIRONMENT
ASSUMPTION | TARGET YIELD | RISK TOLERANCE | PREFERRED STRUCTURE]

title: The Standard Chartered Asia Pacific Corporate Banking Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 217 — The Standard Chartered Asia Pacific Corporate Banking Strategy
Act as Head of Corporate Banking Strategy at Standard Chartered for Asia Pacific.
Design a corporate banking strategy for multinational and regional corporates.
Deliver: (1) Asia Pacific corporate banking landscape: trade and transaction banking
dominance (StanChart's core); capital markets growth (bond issuance, ECM);
relationship banking vs. transactional banking economics.
(2) Target client segmentation: Global Multinationals (GMs — top 200 global
corporates), Local Corporates (top 500 in each market), and Emerging Corporates
(high-growth mid-market). (3) Trade finance revenue model: LC, guarantees, supply
chain finance — RORWA (Return on Risk-Weighted Assets) for trade finance products;
capital efficiency advantage of trade finance vs. corporate lending.
(4) Transaction banking cross-sell: cash management, FX, and trade finance
bundled as total relationship revenue maximization; wallet share by product.
(5) Asia intra-regional flows: China-ASEAN, India-Middle East, ASEAN-MENA trade
corridors; RMB internationalization opportunity; cross-border payment modernization.
(6) Digital corporate banking: digital trade finance (Contour, Marco Polo);
API integration with client ERP; virtual accounts; straight-through processing.
(7) Country risk management: concentration limits by country; political risk
overlay; regulatory capital by jurisdiction.
Format: Corporate Banking Strategy with Client Segmentation, Product Revenue Model,
Trade Finance Framework, Cross-Sell Playbook, and Digital Roadmap.
Inputs: [GEOGRAPHY | CLIENT SEGMENT | PRIMARY PRODUCT FOCUS | CURRENT MARKET SHARE |
DIGITAL CAPABILITY | PRIMARY COMPETITIVE CHALLENGE | GROWTH TARGET]

title: The GQG Partners Emerging & Frontier Market Stock Selection
prompt_text:
PROMPT 218 — The GQG Partners Emerging & Frontier Market Stock Selection
Act as Senior Portfolio Manager at GQG Partners. Apply GQG's quality-growth
philosophy to select EM/FM stocks.
Deliver: (1) GQG philosophy: high-quality businesses with sustainable growth at
reasonable valuations; avoid value traps and hype; concentrated portfolio (30-50 stocks);
long-term hold (3-5 year horizon). (2) Quality framework: (a) Financial quality
(high ROIC, low leverage, strong FCF conversion); (b) Business quality (pricing
power, competitive position, management integrity); (c) ESG quality (governance
as primary risk, environmental as material risk in EM).
(3) Growth assessment: revenue and earnings growth sustainability; is growth
driven by volume (durable) or price (less durable in EM)? Reinvestment rate
and ROIC on incremental capital. (4) EM valuation: how to value EM companies
correctly — currency-adjusted P/E; accounting quality adjustments; political
risk discount. (5) Portfolio construction: position sizing by conviction and
liquidity; EM country limits; sector concentration constraints.
(6) Sell discipline: when to exit — thesis broken, better opportunity, valuation
stretched, governance concern emerges.
(7) EM/FM specific risks: (a) Governance — related-party transactions, minority
rights; (b) Regulatory — policy reversal, nationalization; (c) FX — earnings in
local currency with USD reporting; (d) Liquidity — bid-ask in frontier markets.
Format: GQG-Style Stock Selection Framework with Quality Scorecard, Growth
Assessment, EM Valuation, Portfolio Construction, and Sell Discipline.
Inputs: [UNIVERSE (EM/FM/SPECIFIC COUNTRY) | BENCHMARK | PORTFOLIO SIZE |
SECTOR FOCUS | GOVERNANCE RISK TOLERANCE | LIQUIDITY MINIMUM | TIME HORIZON]

title: The Alvarez & Marsal CRO Assessment & Financial Restructuring
The Ark Invest Disruptive Innovation Investment Framework
prompt_text:
PROMPT 220 — The Ark Invest Disruptive Innovation Investment Framework
Act as Research Director at ARK Invest. Build a disruptive innovation
investment thesis using ARK's "convergence" framework.
Deliver: (1) ARK's framework: "Big Ideas" — identify technologies whose costs are
declining exponentially (Wright's Law) and whose adoption will be non-linear;
convergence of multiple technologies amplifies disruption.
(2) Technology cost curve analysis: Wright's Law — costs drop by a fixed % for every
doubling of cumulative production volume; calculate expected cost in 5 years for:
AI compute (GPU cost per FLOP), energy storage ($/kWh), gene sequencing ($/genome),
3D printing ($/part). (3) Total addressable market (TAM) in 5 years: bottom-up TAM
from adoption curve modeling (S-curve); why traditional analysts underestimate TAM
by extrapolating linearly in a non-linear adoption world.
(4) Convergence example: autonomous vehicles require AI, sensors, mapping, 5G,
and electric vehicles simultaneously — cost declines compound across all 5 dimensions.
(5) Winner identification: which companies are positioned to capture value from each
platform technology; first-mover advantage vs. fast-follower risk.
(6) Valuation: DCF with 5-year revenue scenario; Monte Carlo simulation across
adoption curve outcomes; expected value calculation across bull/base/bear scenarios.
(7) Risk factors: adoption slower than expected; regulatory intervention; incumbent
response; technology path veers differently than expected.
Format: Disruptive Innovation Framework with Technology Cost Curve, TAM Model,
Convergence Analysis, Winner Identification, and Monte Carlo Valuation.
Inputs: [TECHNOLOGY PLATFORM | COMPANY | CURRENT ADOPTION % | WRIGHT'S LAW SLOPE |
TIME HORIZON | BULL/BEAR ADOPTION SCENARIOS | INVESTMENT SIZE]

title: The Veritas Capital Defense & Government Services PE
prompt_text:
PROMPT 221 — The Veritas Capital Defense & Government Services PE
Act as MD at Veritas Capital. Build an investment thesis for a government
services or defense technology company.
Deliver: (1) Government services PE thesis: recession-resistant revenue (mandatory
government spending), predictable contract cash flows, high switching costs (FedRAMP
certification, security clearances, incumbent advantage). (2) Contract analysis:
CPFF (Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee) vs. FFP (Firm-Fixed-Price) vs. T&M — risk profile and
margin characteristics of each; contract ceiling vs. funded backlog distinction.
(3) LPTA vs. best value procurement: lowest-price-technically-acceptable contracts
compress margins; best-value criteria reward differentiated capabilities.
(4) Security clearance workforce: cleared personnel as a strategic asset;
attrition rates; time to clear new hires (6-24 months by level); facility clearances.
(5) M&A in defense tech: DoD as a "partner" not customer; ITAR/EAR compliance;
CFIUS sensitivity for defense companies with foreign interest; organic vs.
inorganic capability expansion. (6) Cybersecurity/C4ISR/AI themes: growth
sub-sectors within defense tech; CMMC 2.0 compliance requirement creating
consulting demand. (7) Exit: SPAC (used extensively in defense tech 2020-22,
now out of favor), strategic sale to prime contractors (Raytheon, L3Harris, Leidos),
or IPO.
Format: Government Services PE Framework with Contract Analysis, Cleared Workforce
Assessment, CFIUS Risk, Sub-Sector Prioritization, and Exit Strategy.
Inputs: [COMPANY | CONTRACT MIX | CLEARANCE LEVEL | REVENUE | EBITDA |
PRIMARY GROWTH DRIVER | PRIMARY ACQUISITION RISK]

title: The Andreessen Horowitz Bio + Health Investment Framework
prompt_text:
PROMPT 222 — The Andreessen Horowitz Bio + Health Investment Framework
Act as General Partner at a16z's bio + health fund. Evaluate a digital health
or biotech investment at Series B/C.
Deliver: (1) Digital health market landscape: telehealth, mental health tech, chronic
disease management, AI diagnostics, pharmacy tech, benefits navigation — TAM and
current penetration by sub-sector. (2) Digital health business model quality:
B2B2C (sell to employer/payer, serve employee/member) vs. DTC (consumer pays);
B2B2C ARPU ($15-50 PMPM) vs. DTC ($30-100/month); enterprise sales cycle
(9-18 months) vs. DTC CAC ($80-300). (3) Clinical validation: FDA clearance pathway
(510k, De Novo, PMA); peer-reviewed outcomes data; how payers use clinical evidence
for coverage decisions. (4) Reimbursement strategy: CPT code coverage; value-based
contracts with risk-sharing; employer self-insured market as fastest path to scale.
(5) AI in health: diagnostic AI (radiology, pathology, ECG); clinical decision support;
prior authorization automation — FDA SaMD (Software as Medical Device) classification.
(6) Data moat: health data as competitive advantage; HIPAA compliance; interoperability
(HL7 FHIR); patient consent architecture. (7) Regulatory risk: CMS coverage policy
changes; FDA guideline evolution for AI/ML in healthcare.
Format: Digital Health Investment Memo with Business Model Analysis, Clinical
Validation Framework, Reimbursement Strategy, AI Assessment, and Returns.
Inputs: [COMPANY | PRODUCT | TARGET POPULATION | BUSINESS MODEL | CURRENT REVENUE |
NRR | FDA STATUS | CLINICAL EVIDENCE | PROPOSED VALUATION]

title: The Nomura Equity Capital Markets: Block Trade Execution
prompt_text:
PROMPT 223 — The Nomura Equity Capital Markets: Block Trade Execution
Act as ECM MD at Nomura. Design a block trade (accelerated bookbuild) strategy
for a large shareholder selling a significant stake in a public company.
Deliver: (1) Block trade mechanics: seller instructs bank overnight; bank "blocks" the
trade from research/sales until announcement; next morning launch and accelerated
bookbuild over 1-4 hours; pricing at discount to last close.
(2) Discount pricing: typical discount range (2-5% for liquid large-cap, 5-10% for
mid-cap); factors affecting required discount (liquidity, overhang concern, sector,
market conditions). (3) Risk to the bank: underwritten block (bank commits to buy
unsold shares) vs. best-efforts (bank doesn't guarantee); when to underwrite vs.
best-efforts based on market conditions and order book quality.
(4) Investor targeting: which institutional investors absorb large blocks (long-only,
hedge funds, crossover); building the book in 90-120 minutes; price sensitivity
of demand. (5) Stabilization: greenshoe option for block trades; when to use to
support aftermarket performance. (6) Coordination with M&A: how block trades interact
with change-of-control provisions; standstill periods post-block.
(7) Secondary sell-down coordination: structured program of block trades over
12-18 months to reduce stake without signaling distress.
Format: Block Trade Advisory with Execution Mechanics, Discount Pricing, Risk/
Underwriting Decision, Investor Targeting, and Multi-Trade Program Design.
Inputs: [SELLER | COMPANY | STAKE SIZE | CURRENT PRICE | DAILY VOLUME |
LOCK-UP STATUS | TIMING CONSTRAINTS | UNDERWRITING APPETITE]

title: The Fidelity Investments Retirement & Target Date Fund Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 224 — The Fidelity Investments Retirement & Target Date Fund Strategy
Act as Head of Asset Allocation at Fidelity. Design target date fund glide
path and retirement income strategy.
Deliver: (1) Target date fund mechanics: all-in-one fund shifting from aggressive
(equity-heavy) in early years to conservative (bond-heavy) at retirement; glide path
design (to vs. through retirement distinction). (2) Glide path construction: equity
allocation at age 25 (90%+), age 45 (70-75%), age 65 (50-55%), age 75 (30-35%);
academic research on optimal equity allocation in retirement.
(3) Asset class selection within TDF: equity (US, international, emerging markets
in declining proportions with age); fixed income (TIPS, Treasuries, short-duration
bonds increasing with age); alternatives (REITs, inflation protection).
(4) Sequence-of-returns risk: why a market crash at retirement is catastrophically
worse than the same crash 20 years earlier; bucket strategy and time-segmentation
as solutions. (5) Decumulation strategy: sustainable withdrawal rate (4% rule debate —
current research suggests 3.3-3.5% in low-return environment); required minimum
distributions (RMDs); Roth conversion strategy.
(6) Longevity risk: life expectancy at 65 = 20+ years; annuitization as partial
longevity hedge; deferred income annuity (DIA) embedded in TDF.
(7) Fee and performance benchmarking: expense ratio as primary driver of net returns;
passive vs. active TDF performance comparison.
Format: TDF Strategy with Glide Path Design, Asset Class Rationale, Decumulation
Framework, Longevity Risk Management, and Fee Benchmarking.
Inputs: [TARGET VINTAGE YEAR | RISK TOLERANCE | CURRENT AGE | RETIREMENT INCOME
NEED | SOCIAL SECURITY ESTIMATE | EXISTING SAVINGS | OTHER INCOME SOURCES]

title: The Mubadala / ADQ Gulf Sovereign Development Fund Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 225 — The Mubadala / ADQ Gulf Sovereign Development Fund Strategy
Act as Senior Investment Director at Mubadala or ADQ. Build a sovereign
development fund strategy balancing financial returns and national development.
Deliver: (1) SDF mandate: distinguish Mubadala (strategic investment + financial
return), ADQ (Abu Dhabi food security + diversification), PIF (Vision 2030
enablement + return) — how mandate shapes portfolio differently from pure SWF.
(2) Strategic sectors: advanced manufacturing (semiconductors, aerospace), food
security (agribusiness investments globally), healthcare, technology, clean energy
— rationale for each as strategic priority vs. financial investment.
(3) Co-investment with global PE: how Gulf SWFs co-invest alongside KKR, Blackstone,
Carlyle; co-investment terms (economics, governance, information rights);
relationship management with PE sponsors. (4) Direct investment program: SDF as
direct PE investor without fund layer; build internal team vs. outsource; sector
verticals approach. (5) International vs. domestic allocation: domestic economic
diversification mandate vs. international diversification; local content requirements
for investments. (6) Geopolitical dimensions: using investment for strategic
partnerships; technology transfer expectations; alignment with national industrial
policy. (7) Governance and transparency: SWF governance best practices (Santiago
Principles); reporting to ownership (Ruler's court vs. Board); accountability mechanisms.
Format: SDF Strategy with Mandate Framework, Sector Prioritization, Co-Investment
Model, Direct Investment Program, and Governance Structure.
Inputs: [FUND NAME | AUM | PRIMARY MANDATE | CURRENT ALLOCATION | RETURN TARGET |
DOMESTIC VS. INTERNATIONAL SPLIT | STRATEGIC PRIORITY SECTORS]

title: The Credit Suisse / UBS Wealth Management M&A Integration
prompt_text:
PROMPT 226 — The Credit Suisse / UBS Wealth Management M&A Integration
Act as Senior Partner at Oliver Wyman advising on the integration of two
major wealth management businesses (e.g., UBS acquisition of Credit Suisse).
Deliver: (1) Wealth management M&A rationale: scale in AUM ($), relationship
manager productivity, technology infrastructure, and brand. (2) Client retention risk:
#1 priority — wealthy clients leave during uncertainty; model expected AUM attrition
by client segment (UHNW most at risk); retention strategy by relationship manager.
(3) RM retention: relationship managers carry the client relationships; retention
program design (golden handcuffs — deferred comp, transition bonuses, clear career
path); risk of RM departure triggering client departure.
(4) Brand and client proposition: which brand survives? How to communicate proposition
change to clients without triggering moves; re-papering of client accounts.
(5) Platform rationalization: two wealth management platforms to one; technology
migration risk (client data, discretionary mandate continuity, reporting disruption).
(6) Synergy delivery: cost synergies (back office, technology, real estate);
revenue synergies (cross-sell of investment banking, expanded product shelf);
typical 3-year synergy achievement curve.
(7) Regulatory: simultaneous regulatory approvals in multiple jurisdictions;
FINMA, FCA, SEC coordination; SIPA concerns for broker-dealer combination.
Format: Wealth M&A Integration Playbook with AUM Retention Model, RM Retention
Program, Brand Strategy, Platform Migration Plan, and Synergy Tracking.
Inputs: [ACQUIRER | TARGET | COMBINED AUM | RM COUNT | PLATFORM OVERLAP |
GEOGRAPHIC PRESENCE | EXPECTED ATTRITION | SYNERGY TARGET]

title: The Cambridge Associates Endowment & Foundation Investment Policy
The Hines Real Estate Development Finance & Pro Forma
prompt_text:
PROMPT 228 — The Hines Real Estate Development Finance & Pro Forma
Act as Development Finance Director at Hines. Build a real estate development
pro forma and financing structure for a mixed-use project.
Deliver: (1) Development pro forma: total development cost (land + hard costs + soft
costs + financing costs + developer fee); stabilized NOI; cap rate at sale → total
project value; developer profit (margin and IRR).
(2) Hard cost budgeting: $/sqft by building type (office: $300-500, multifamily:
$250-400, industrial: $100-200); contingency reserve (5-10%); GC contract type
(GMP vs. lump-sum) and risk allocation. (3) Soft cost budgeting: architecture/
engineering (5-8% of hard costs), permits, legal, financing costs, pre-opening expenses.
(4) Construction loan: 65% LTC (Loan-to-Cost); SOFR + 250-350bps; interest reserve;
completion guarantee from developer; leasing milestones for draw downs.
(5) Permanent loan takeout: how construction loan transitions to permanent financing
at stabilization; DSCR requirement (1.25-1.30×); Debt Yield (>8%).
(6) Equity structure: developer co-invest (10-20%); LP equity (pension fund, REIT,
family office); waterfall — preferred return (6-8%), catch-up, then promote (20-30%).
(7) Entitlement and permitting risk: the most common cause of development delay;
community opposition management; environmental review timeline.
Format: Development Finance Model with Pro Forma, Construction Loan Structure,
Equity Waterfall, Sensitivity Analysis, and Risk Register.
Inputs: [PROPERTY TYPE | LOCATION | TOTAL SQFT | ESTIMATED DEVELOPMENT COST |
STABILIZED NOI | TARGET CAP RATE | EQUITY STRUCTURE | TIMELINE]

title: The Bain & Company Hospital & Healthcare System Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 229 — The Bain & Company Hospital & Healthcare System Strategy
Act as Senior Partner at Bain's Healthcare practice. Design a growth strategy
for a regional hospital system facing competitive and financial pressures.
Deliver: (1) Competitive landscape analysis: map all hospital systems, ambulatory
surgical centers, physician groups, and retail health clinics in the service area;
market share by service line; where the system is winning vs. losing patients.
(2) Service line portfolio: contribution margin by service line (oncology, orthopedics,
cardiology, neuroscience, women's health, primary care); invest/grow/maintain/exit
framework based on margin, volume, and strategic importance.
(3) Ambulatory strategy: hospital outpatient migration trend (payers incentivize lower-cost
settings); ASC development and physician joint ventures; freestanding ED and urgent
care strategy. (4) Physician integration: employment vs. independent vs. joint venture;
physician compensation model (RVU-based vs. salary + incentive); physician alignment
for referral capture. (5) Digital health and virtual care: telehealth integration
post-COVID; remote patient monitoring for chronic disease management; digital front
door strategy (app-based scheduling, triage, virtual visits). (6) Revenue cycle
transformation: net revenue per adjusted discharge improvement; denial prevention;
payer contract optimization; underpayment recovery program.
(7) Payer strategy: value-based care contracts (ACO, global capitation); risk-sharing
arrangements; managed care contract leverage from market share concentration.
Format: Health System Growth Strategy with Competitive Map, Service Line Portfolio,
Ambulatory Plan, Physician Strategy, Digital Health Roadmap, and Financial Impact.
Inputs: [SYSTEM NAME | GEOGRAPHY | BEDS | NET PATIENT REVENUE | MARKET SHARE |
EBITDA MARGIN | PRIMARY COMPETITIVE THREAT | STRATEGIC OBJECTIVE]

title: The Accenture Enterprise Technology M&A Integration
prompt_text:
PROMPT 230 — The Accenture Enterprise Technology M&A Integration
Act as MD at Accenture's M&A Services practice. Design a technology integration
plan for a large enterprise software or technology company acquisition.
Deliver: (1) Technology integration strategy: (a) Full integration (single platform
— highest synergy, highest risk), (b) Federated (keep separate systems, shared data),
(c) Best-of-breed (select best system from each company). Decision framework.
(2) ERP integration: SAP/Oracle integration — data migration, chart of accounts
harmonization, legal entity structure; why 50%+ of ERP integrations fail or go over budget.
(3) Cybersecurity integration: Day 1 security assessment; network segmentation until
security posture is verified; identity and access management (IAM) harmonization;
vulnerability scanning of acquired company's infrastructure.
(4) Data integration: master data management (MDM); customer and product data
deduplication; data governance for the combined entity; GDPR/CCPA compliance
for combined data sets. (5) Application rationalization: inventory of all applications
(typically 200-500 apps in mid-size company); rationalization to reduce count by 30-50%
over 3 years; cloud migration opportunity during integration.
(6) Technology synergies: eliminate duplicate SaaS subscriptions; renegotiate vendor
contracts using combined volume; consolidate data center footprint.
(7) Integration PMO: technology integration workstreams; Day 1 readiness testing;
cut-over planning; rollback procedures.
Format: Technology Integration Playbook with Strategy Decision, ERP Roadmap,
Security Framework, Data Integration, App Rationalization, and PMO Design.
Inputs: [ACQUIRER TECH STACK | TARGET TECH STACK | INDUSTRY | DEAL CLOSE DATE |
INTEGRATION TIMELINE | IT HEADCOUNT | PRIMARY TECH INTEGRATION RISK]

title: The Two Sigma Ventures Deep Tech Investment Framework
prompt_text:
PROMPT 231 — The Two Sigma Ventures Deep Tech Investment Framework
Act as Partner at Two Sigma Ventures evaluating a deep tech startup
(AI infrastructure, quantum computing, advanced materials, robotics).
Deliver: (1) Deep tech investment thesis: longer development timelines (5-10 years
vs. 3-5 for SaaS), higher technical risk, but defensible IP moats and large eventual
TAMs; how VC fund structure (10-year fund) fits or doesn't fit deep tech timelines.
(2) Technical due diligence: engaging domain expert advisors; assessing TRL
(Technology Readiness Level 1-9) and what capital is needed to reach TRL 7+;
IP landscape (freedom-to-operate, patent strength, trade secrets).
(3) Team assessment: PhD/research pedigree from top labs (MIT, Stanford, DeepMind,
Bell Labs spinouts); transition from researcher to commercial leader — the key risk;
industry advisory board quality. (4) Market timing: is the enabling technology
(compute, materials, regulatory) ready? Too-early companies fail even with superior
technology. (5) Capital intensity: deep tech companies require 10-100× more capital
than SaaS to reach revenue; co-investment with strategic partners (corporates,
government grants — NSF SBIR, DARPA, DoE) to extend runway.
(6) Revenue model: licensing (IP monetization) vs. product sale vs. service model —
how revenue model affects capital needs and defensibility.
(7) Exit: strategic acquisition (defense/industrial prime contractors, big tech);
IPO for at-scale platforms; government/public sector customer as anchor.
Format: Deep Tech Investment Framework with TRL Assessment, Technical DD Guide,
Capital Intensity Model, Market Timing Analysis, and Exit Strategy.
Inputs: [TECHNOLOGY | TRL LEVEL | TEAM BACKGROUND | TOTAL CAPITAL TO DATE |
NEXT MILESTONE | TARGET CUSTOMER | PROPOSED VALUATION | STRATEGIC PARTNER]

title: The Lazard Restructuring: Pre-Pack Administration
prompt_text:
PROMPT 232 — The Lazard Restructuring: Pre-Pack Administration
Act as MD at Lazard's Financial Restructuring group. Structure a pre-packaged
administration (UK) or pre-packaged Chapter 11 (US) for a distressed company.
Deliver: (1) Pre-pack rationale: speed (business value preservation), lower cost,
management continuity — vs. conventional in-court process. (2) US pre-pack:
plan of reorganization negotiated and votes solicited before filing; company files
and confirms plan in 30-60 days vs. 12-24 months for contested Chapter 11.
(3) UK pre-pack administration: sale of business is arranged pre-appointment;
administrator appointed and business sold on Day 1 (SIP 16 compliance required).
(4) Valuation: enterprise value determined for the debt/equity split; fulcrum
security analysis; "best interests" test (creditors recover more than liquidation).
(5) Creditor negotiation pre-filing: RSA (Restructuring Support Agreement) with
>2/3 in value and >1/2 in number of creditors (US) or majority by value (UK);
plan treatment for each class.
(6) DIP financing (US) or pre-pack financing (UK): bridge financing to fund
operations during restructuring; roll-up of pre-petition debt; new money terms.
(7) Connected party sales (UK): administrator selling to connected party (management
buyout) requires Phoenix Protocol compliance; independent valuation; marketing evidence.
Format: Pre-Pack Restructuring Framework with Process Timeline, Creditor Strategy,
RSA Design, DIP/Financing, Valuation Analysis, and Connected Party Protocol.
Inputs: [COMPANY | JURISDICTION | DEBT STRUCTURE | CASH RUNWAY | FULCRUM SECURITY |
KEY CREDITORS | PROPOSED RESTRUCTURING TRANSACTION | TIMELINE]

title: The Pimco Mortgage and Securitized Products Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 233 — The Pimco Mortgage and Securitized Products Strategy
Act as PM at PIMCO's Mortgage and Securitized Products team. Build a
comprehensive agency and non-agency mortgage investment framework.
Deliver: (1) Agency MBS: pass-through securities guaranteed by Fannie/Freddie/Ginnie;
prepayment risk (CPR — Conditional Prepayment Rate); convexity — negative convexity
means duration extends when rates rise, shortens when rates fall (worst of both worlds).
(2) TBA (To-Be-Announced) market: forward delivery mechanism; dollar roll economics
(implied financing rate); specialness and cheapness of TBA vs. specified pools.
(3) Specified pool investing: prepayment protection through pool attributes (loan balance,
geography, LTV, credit score); OAS analysis of specified pools vs. TBAs.
(4) CMOs (Collateralized Mortgage Obligations): PAC (Planned Amortization Class) bonds —
stable cashflows within a band; TAC (Targeted Amortization Class); IO/PO strips —
extreme convexity profiles.
(5) Non-agency RMBS: prime jumbo, non-QM (non-Qualified Mortgage), CRT
(Credit Risk Transfer — Fannie/Freddie risk sharing); credit analysis approach
for non-agency (no government guarantee). (6) HELOC and home equity ABS:
2nd lien risk; combined LTV analysis; borrower behavior in HELOCs.
(7) Macro overlay: rate sensitivity of MBS vs. Treasuries; spread widening in
risk-off (MBS are not risk-free despite agency guarantee — convexity selling
pressure); Fed MBS balance sheet runoff impact on spreads.
Format: Mortgage Strategy with Agency MBS Framework, TBA Roll Analysis, Specified
Pool Strategy, Non-Agency DD, and Macro Overlay.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO TYPE | DURATION TARGET | PREPAYMENT ASSUMPTION | CREDIT QUALITY
CONSTRAINT | AGENCY VS. NON-AGENCY SPLIT | OAS TARGET | LEVERAGE PERMITTED]

title: The Temasek Long-Term Portfolio Construction
prompt_text:
PROMPT 234 — The Temasek Long-Term Portfolio Construction
Act as Senior Portfolio Manager at Temasek Holdings. Build a long-term
(20-year horizon) portfolio construction framework for a state investment company.
Deliver: (1) Temasek's philosophy: "Temasek Charter" — wealth creation, wealth
steward, engaged shareholder, and forward-looking institution; shareholder return
target (TSR above 8% in SGD over 20 years). (2) Thematic portfolio construction:
Temasek's four trends — Digitisation, Sustainable Living, Future of Consumption,
Longer Lifespans — how to build a portfolio around durable structural trends.
(3) Portfolio structure: liquid portfolio (public equities, listed infrastructure)
vs. illiquid portfolio (PE, VC, direct investments); target mix and reasoning.
(4) Generational time horizon advantages: ability to hold through cycles without
redemption pressure; compounding of quality businesses over decades; when to exit
vs. hold indefinitely. (5) Singapore core assets: strategic holdings in Singapore
institutions (SingTel, DBS, ST Engineering) — strategic vs. financial rationale;
balancing national interest with global portfolio optimization.
(6) Emerging market focus: ASEAN, India, China concentration — how Temasek
builds regional relationships and proprietary deal flow vs. global investors.
(7) ESG as long-term value: Temasek's carbon-neutral portfolio by 2050 target;
halving portfolio carbon emissions by 2030; how decarbonization affects portfolio
construction today.
Format: Long-Term Portfolio Framework with Thematic Construction, Liquid/Illiquid
Mix, Generational Advantages, Singapore Core Strategy, and ESG Integration.
Inputs: [AUM | RETURN TARGET | TIME HORIZON | CURRENT ALLOCATION | DOMESTIC VS.
INTERNATIONAL MIX | LIQUID VS. ILLIQUID TARGET | ESG CONSTRAINTS]

title: The A.T. Kearney Automotive Industry Transformation Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 235 — The A.T. Kearney Automotive Industry Transformation Strategy
Act as Senior Partner at A.T. Kearney. Design a transformation strategy for
a traditional automotive OEM navigating electrification and software-defined vehicles.
Deliver: (1) Automotive disruption landscape: EV adoption curve (S-curve — inflection
point at 20% penetration expected mid-decade); BEV vs. PHEV vs. FCEV technology bet.
(2) Software-defined vehicle (SDV): cars as software platforms — OTA (over-the-air)
updates, software revenue (subscriptions, features on demand); Tesla vs. legacy OEM
software capability gap. (3) EV platform economics: dedicated BEV platform vs.
ICE-flexible platform (MEB, STLA Frame, Ultium); battery cost ($/kWh) and pack cost
as % of vehicle BOM; manufacturing cost parity with ICE expected 2026-2028.
(4) Battery strategy: cell chemistry (LFP for volume/cost vs. NMC for range/performance);
cell manufacturing — Tesla vs. BYD vertical integration vs. outsourcing to CATL/LG/SK;
gigafactory economics. (5) Dealer network transformation: agency model vs. traditional
franchise; EV service requirements vs. ICE; online direct sales strategy.
(6) China strategy: BYD and local EV brands threatening market share in China (VW,
GM, Ford losing share); joint venture restructuring; China-for-China product development.
(7) Financial restructuring: transitioning from ICE profit to funding EV losses;
Ford Model-e (EV) vs. Ford Blue (ICE) segment reporting; capex allocation.
Format: OEM Transformation Strategy with EV Adoption Model, SDV Roadmap, Battery
Strategy, China Assessment, Financial Transition Plan, and 5-Year Targets.
Inputs: [OEM NAME | GEOGRAPHY | CURRENT EV % OF SALES | BEV PLATFORM STATUS |
BATTERY PARTNER | CHINA MARKET SHARE TREND | EV INVESTMENT BUDGET]

title: The Neuberger Berman Private Equity Secondaries & Co-Investment
prompt_text:
PROMPT 236 — The Neuberger Berman Private Equity Secondaries & Co-Investment
Act as MD at Neuberger Berman's Alternatives team managing secondary PE
and co-investment programs for institutional LPs.
Deliver: (1) LP perspective on PE allocation: primary fund commitment, co-investment
(direct deals alongside GP at reduced/zero fees), and secondary purchases — how
to optimize the mix for net return and fee efficiency.
(2) Co-investment economics: primary fund (2% management fee, 20% carry) vs.
co-investment (0% fee, 0% carry typically) → net return differential of 300-500bps.
(3) Co-investment due diligence: limited time (often 2-3 weeks); relying on GP's
work but independently assessing; when to pass (concentrated position, GP conflict,
industry expertise gap). (4) Secondary market for LP interests: buying existing LP
interests in PE funds at a discount to NAV; pricing methodology; J-curve elimination.
(5) GP-led secondary transactions: continuation vehicles, strip sales, preferred
equity — when LPs should roll vs. cash out vs. sell in secondary.
(6) Portfolio construction for PE program: target # of GPs (20-30), vintage years
(2-4 commitments/year), strategies (buyout/VC/growth/credit), geographies.
(7) Governance: LP Advisory Committee (LPAC) seat strategy; key-person clause
triggers; term extension consent; GP removal provisions.
Format: PE Allocation Framework with Co-Investment Economics, Secondary Analysis,
GP-Led Secondary Assessment, Portfolio Construction, and LP Governance.
Inputs: [LP INSTITUTION | AUM | PE ALLOCATION TARGET | CURRENT PE PORTFOLIO |
CO-INVESTMENT CAPACITY | SECONDARY APPETITE | PRIMARY GP RELATIONSHIPS]

title: The BCG Digital Transformation ROI Measurement & CFO Toolkit
prompt_text:
PROMPT 237 — The BCG Digital Transformation ROI Measurement & CFO Toolkit
Act as Senior Partner at BCG's Digital practice. Build a rigorous ROI measurement
framework for a CFO evaluating digital transformation investments.
Deliver: (1) Digital investment categorization: (a) Cost reduction investments
(automation, headcount reduction) — ROI measured in cost savings/FTE eliminated;
(b) Revenue growth investments (new digital channels, personalization) — ROI in
incremental revenue; (c) Risk reduction (cyber, compliance, resilience) — ROI
in avoided expected loss. (2) Benefit realization office: who owns each benefit;
baseline measurement before implementation; post-implementation validation;
clawback if benefits not realized. (3) Total Cost of Ownership (TCO): software
license + implementation + change management + ongoing maintenance + training;
why TCO is always 3-5× the software license cost. (4) Time-to-value: staged benefit
realization (typically 10% in year 1, 40% in year 2, full benefits by year 3);
NPV impact of delayed realization. (5) Digital initiative sequencing: quick wins
first (6-month payback) to fund longer-horizon transformation; program portfolio
management. (6) Intangible benefits: speed of decision-making, employee experience,
data asset value — how to assign financial value to intangibles for investment cases.
(7) Common traps: underestimating change management cost (typically 15-20% of
total program budget); not decommissioning legacy systems post-migration (stranded cost).
Format: Digital ROI Framework with Investment Categorization, Benefit Realization
Office Design, TCO Model, Time-to-Value Analysis, and CFO Dashboard.
Inputs: [COMPANY | INDUSTRY | DIGITAL INVESTMENT SIZE | PRIMARY OBJECTIVES |
CURRENT TECH STACK | CHANGE MANAGEMENT MATURITY | BOARD RETURN EXPECTATIONS]

title: The KKR Real Estate Core+ Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 238 — The KKR Real Estate Core+ Strategy
Act as MD at KKR Real Estate's Core+ strategy. Build a core-plus real estate
investment framework for institutional investors seeking stable income.
Deliver: (1) Core-plus definition: stabilized assets with modest value-add potential;
target unlevered returns 7-9%; moderate leverage (40-55% LTV); income-oriented with
some appreciation upside. (2) Sector allocation: industrial/logistics (highest
conviction — e-commerce, nearshoring demand), multifamily (demographic tailwind,
rent growth persistence), office (deeply selective — trophy assets in supply-constrained
markets only), data centers (high growth but premium pricing).
(3) Asset selection criteria: occupancy >90% at acquisition; WALT >5 years for office/
industrial; rent mark-to-market potential; location quality (infill urban/suburban vs.
exurban).  (4) Operating platform integration: KKR's owned operating platforms
(Caliber, Globe Life) drive asset management alpha vs. passive ownership.
(5) ESG in core real estate: green building certification (LEED, BREEAM) requirement
for institutional capital; energy efficiency capex underwriting; GRESB rating target.
(6) Debt strategy: long-term fixed-rate financing (10-year agency for multifamily,
insurance company debt for industrial); interest rate hedge through fixed rate.
(7) Liquidity structure: open-end core-plus fund vs. closed-end; NAV-based pricing;
redemption queue management (2022-23 BREIT/BPREA episode lessons).
Format: Core-Plus RE Strategy with Sector Allocation, Asset Selection Criteria,
Operating Platform, ESG Standards, Debt Strategy, and Liquidity Management.
Inputs: [FUND SIZE | INVESTOR TYPE | TARGET UNLEVERED RETURN | SECTOR FOCUS |
GEOGRAPHY | LEVERAGE TARGET | ESG REQUIREMENTS | LIQUIDITY STRUCTURE]

title: The Goldman Sachs Equity Research: Initiating Coverage Framework
prompt_text:
PROMPT 239 — The Goldman Sachs Equity Research: Initiating Coverage Framework
Act as VP at Goldman Sachs Equity Research. Design a rigorous framework for
initiating coverage on a company in a new or unfamiliar sector.
Deliver: (1) Initiation research process: 4-6 weeks of intensive work; primary research
(management, customers, competitors, suppliers, industry experts); financial model build;
thesis development. (2) Industry framework: Porter's Five Forces for the sector;
industry growth drivers and headwinds; regulatory environment; technology disruption risk.
(3) Company-specific analysis: competitive positioning within industry; management track
record (revenue and EPS delivery vs. consensus over 5 years); capital allocation history
(M&A, buybacks, dividends — value creation or destruction?).
(4) Financial model: 3-statement model (income statement, balance sheet, cash flow);
5-year forecast; key driver assumptions explicitly stated and stress-tested.
(5) Valuation: primary methodology selection with rationale; EV/EBITDA, P/E, EV/Sales,
DCF, NAV — which applies to this sector and why; 12-month price target derivation.
(6) Bull/Base/Bear scenario: probability-weighted scenarios; key variant assumptions in
each; expected value price target = sum of probability-weighted scenario prices.
(7) Investment thesis statement: the single most important reason to own (or avoid)
the stock — the "elevator pitch" that can be stated in 2-3 sentences; the pivotal
question that, when answered, will determine stock performance.
Format: Initiation Report Framework with Industry Analysis, Financial Model, Valuation,
Scenario Analysis, and Investment Thesis.
Inputs: [COMPANY | SECTOR | CURRENT PRICE | MARKET CAP | ANALYST CONVICTION LEVEL |
PRIMARY INVESTMENT THESIS | BIGGEST RISK | COMPARABLE COMPANIES]

title: The Piper Sandler Technology M&A: Software Consolidation Wave
prompt_text:
PROMPT 240 — The Piper Sandler Technology M&A: Software Consolidation Wave
Act as MD at Piper Sandler's Technology M&A group. Analyze the software
sector consolidation wave and advise a software company on strategic options.
Deliver: (1) Software consolidation drivers: PE-backed consolidation (Vista, Thoma Bravo,
Francisco Partners model); strategic buyers building product suites (Salesforce,
SAP, Oracle M&A cadence); AI disruption forcing consolidation of point solutions.
(2) Thoma Bravo playbook: buy vertical SaaS leaders; implement operational rigor
(sales efficiency, R&D prioritization); bolt-on M&A to build product suite;
exit at premium multiple. (3) Valuation in current market: EV/ARR multiples
post-correction (public market NTM ARR multiples by growth rate); private market
lag to public comps; control premium for strategic vs. PE buyer.
(4) Strategic alternatives for a software company: (a) Remain independent (organic
growth + tuck-ins); (b) Sell to strategic buyer (product synergy premium);
(c) Sell to PE (financial buyer — operational improvement thesis);
(d) Merge with peer (consolidation, scale, public company currency).
(5) Sell-side positioning: how to maximize valuation — data room quality, forward
ARR momentum, NRR demonstration, strategic rationale for each buyer type.
(6) AI value creation story: how AI enhances the product and protects against
commoditization — critical for buyer confidence in sustained ARR growth.
(7) Transaction timing: optimal timing relative to ARR cohort trends, public
comparable valuations, and buyer appetite cycles.
Format: Software M&A Advisory with Consolidation Analysis, Valuation Framework,
Strategic Alternatives, Sell-Side Positioning, and Transaction Timing.
Inputs: [COMPANY | ARR | GROWTH RATE | NRR | VERTICAL | CURRENT VALUATION |
STRATEGIC RATIONALE | PRIMARY ACQUIRER TYPE PREFERENCE]

title: The Vista Equity Partners Vertical SaaS Operational Improvement
prompt_text:
PROMPT 241 — The Vista Equity Partners Vertical SaaS Operational Improvement
Act as Operating Principal at Vista Equity Partners. Apply Vista's operational
improvement playbook to a newly acquired vertical SaaS company.
Deliver: (1) Vista Consulting Group (VCG) model: centralized best practices library;
standardized KPIs across all portfolio companies; playbook for sales, marketing,
R&D, customer success, and finance. (2) Revenue operations (RevOps): unified data
from CRM, marketing automation, and CS platform; single source of truth for pipeline;
OKR cascade from company to rep level. (3) Sales productivity: quota attainment
analysis (top/middle/bottom thirds); territory redesign; sales process standardization
(Sandler, MEDDIC methodology); SDR-to-AE ratio optimization.
(4) Pricing optimization: willingness-to-pay analysis; tiering (Good/Better/Best);
annual vs. monthly pricing (12-15% discount for annual → improve cash flow, reduce churn);
price increase strategy for existing customers. (5) R&D efficiency: product roadmap
prioritization framework (customer value × ARR impact × build cost); technical debt
sprint allocation (20% of R&D capacity); engineering velocity metrics.
(6) Customer success redesign: CSM coverage model (high-touch >$50K ARR, tech-touch
<$10K ARR); QBR template and frequency; expansion playbook triggers.
(7) G&A optimization: shared services for HR, finance, legal across Vista portfolio;
typical G&A reduction of 200-400bps of ARR.
Format: Vista Operational Playbook with KPI Benchmarks, Sales Productivity Plan,
Pricing Strategy, R&D Efficiency, CS Redesign, and G&A Optimization.
Inputs: [COMPANY | ARR | SALES HEADCOUNT | QUOTA ATTAINMENT % | NRR | GROSS MARGIN |
PRIMARY OPERATIONAL BOTTLENECK | 100-DAY PRIORITY]

title: The Evercore Healthcare Biotech M&A & Licensing Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 242 — The Evercore Healthcare Biotech M&A & Licensing Strategy
Act as MD at Evercore's Healthcare group. Advise a mid-size biopharma on
its business development and M&A strategy.
Deliver: (1) BD/M&A strategic rationale: "patent cliff" management; pipeline gap
filling; platform technology acquisition; geographic expansion; therapeutic
area deepening. (2) Build vs. buy vs. license: when each is optimal for different
stages of drug development and company size; cost comparison.
(3) Licensing deal structures: upfront payment, milestones (development, regulatory,
commercial), and royalties; royalty stacking risk; typical deal terms by stage
(Phase 2: $20-100M upfront, Phase 3: $50-300M upfront, commercial: $100M+).
(4) Reverse merger / SPAC: for private biotechs seeking public currency for BD;
shell company selection criteria. (5) Bolt-on acquisition valuation: rNPV of
acquired pipeline + synergies − acquisition premium; maximum willingness to pay.
(6) Alliance management: post-deal governance (Joint Steering Committee, JDC, JCC);
milestone payment disputes; option exercise decisions.
(7) Large pharma acquirer identification: which pharma companies are most likely
to pay a premium for this asset (therapeutic area fit, pipeline gaps, geographic
need); track record of past acquisitions.
Format: Biopharma BD Strategy with Build/Buy/License Framework, Licensing Term
Structure, Acquisition Valuation, Alliance Management, and Acquirer Targeting.
Inputs: [COMPANY | PIPELINE ASSETS | STAGE | THERAPEUTIC AREA | CURRENT CASH |
BURN RATE | STRATEGIC OBJECTIVE | PRIMARY PARTNER OR ACQUIRER TARGET]

title: The Lazard Asset Management Global Multi-Asset Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 243 — The Lazard Asset Management Global Multi-Asset Strategy
Act as CIO at Lazard Asset Management's Multi-Asset team. Build a global
multi-asset portfolio for a risk-aware institutional investor.
Deliver: (1) Multi-asset investment philosophy: diversification across return drivers
(growth assets, defensive assets, real assets, alternative risk premia);
dynamic tactical asset allocation overlay on strategic weights.
(2) Strategic asset allocation: target weights for global equities (DM + EM),
global bonds (government + credit), real assets (infra, real estate, commodities),
and alternatives (hedge funds, private markets) — with expected return and risk.
(3) Tactical asset allocation process: monthly investment committee; conviction-based
deviations from SAA (±5-10% per asset class); signal framework (valuation,
momentum, macro, sentiment). (4) Correlation regime analysis: how equity-bond
correlation shifts across inflation regimes; portfolio construction implications
when stocks and bonds move together (2022 problem).
(5) Risk budgeting: contribution to portfolio risk (CVaR) by asset class; rebalancing
when any asset class risk contribution exceeds threshold.
(6) Currency management: hedged vs. unhedged international exposure; strategic
currency overlay for large currency tilts; tactical FX views.
(7) Client customization: liability-driven overlay for insurance/pension clients;
income-oriented variant; capital preservation variant.
Format: Multi-Asset Strategy with SAA, TAA Process, Risk Budget, Correlation
Regime Analysis, Currency Management, and Client Customization Options.
Inputs: [INVESTOR TYPE | AUM | RETURN TARGET | VOLATILITY LIMIT | HORIZON |
CURRENCY BASE | ALTERNATIVES ACCESS | PRIMARY RISK CONCERN]

title: The Clifford Chance Private Equity Fund Formation & LPPA
prompt_text:
PROMPT 244 — The Clifford Chance Private Equity Fund Formation & LPPA
Act as Partner at Clifford Chance's Investment Funds practice. Draft the
key terms of a PE fund limited partnership agreement.
Deliver: (1) Fund structure: Cayman LP (offshore) + Delaware LP (onshore) parallel
fund; GP entity structure; carried interest vehicle structure.
(2) Economics: management fee (2% on committed during investment period, 1.5-2%
on invested/cost after); carried interest (20% above 8% hurdle, with catch-up;
whole-fund vs. deal-by-deal carry — GP preference for deal-by-deal, LP preference
for whole-fund). (3) Key LP protections: LPAC (LP Advisory Committee) consent
for conflicts; key-person provisions (trigger suspension if 2+ named key-persons
leave); no-fault removal (75-80% LP vote); cause removal.
(4) Investment restrictions: concentration limits (25-35% max per single investment);
geographic restrictions; sector exclusions; co-investment rights (all LPs get pro-rata
right or tiered access). (5) Reporting: quarterly financial statements; annual audited
accounts; quarterly performance reports (IRR, MOIC, DPI, TVPI, RVPI).
(6) Clawback: GP must return carried interest if total distributions don't meet
the hurdle on a fund-wide basis; escrow mechanism (30-50% of carry escrowed).
(7) Recycling: can committed capital be recycled (reinvested after return)?
Limits on recycling to protect LP against overcommitment.
Format: LP Agreement Term Sheet with Economics, LP Protections, Investment
Restrictions, Reporting Standards, Clawback, and Recycling.
Inputs: [FUND SIZE | STRATEGY | GEOGRAPHY | MANAGEMENT FEE STRUCTURE | CARRY RATE |
HURDLE | KEY PERSONS | PRIMARY LP INVESTOR TYPE]

title: The Hercules Capital Venture Debt & Technology Lending
prompt_text:
PROMPT 245 — The Hercules Capital Venture Debt & Technology Lending
Act as MD at Hercules Capital. Build a venture lending framework for
growth-stage technology and life sciences companies.
Deliver: (1) Venture debt rationale: non-dilutive capital (warrants are typically 1-3%
of loan face value vs. 20-30% dilution for equity round); extends runway between
equity rounds; complements — not replaces — equity.
(2) Borrower profile: post-revenue, VC-backed companies with strong sponsors;
minimum 12-month liquidity post-financing; revenue quality (recurring, growing);
sponsor commitment to continue funding. (3) Loan structure: term loan (24-48 months);
interest only period (6-12 months); PIK toggle option; final payment fee (2-4%);
prepayment premium declining from 3% to 1% over loan life.
(4) Credit analysis: VC sponsor quality (tier-1 vs. tier-2 backers); cash runway
without the debt; revenue growth rate; burn multiple; path to profitability.
(5) Warrant coverage: warrants priced at the most recent equity round price; typical
coverage of 5-15% of loan amount → equity upside to enhance returns.
(6) Covenant package: minimum cash/liquidity covenant; material adverse change clause;
change of control put; no financial maintenance covenants (key differentiator from bank).
(7) Return profile: all-in yield (cash interest + OID + final payment + warrant value)
targeting 13-17% gross; credit losses in venture lending (historically 1-3% loss rate
for top-tier VD providers).
Format: Venture Debt Framework with Borrower Criteria, Loan Structure, Warrant Analysis,
Credit Assessment, Covenant Package, and Return Profile.
Inputs: [COMPANY | VC BACKERS | LTM REVENUE | REVENUE GROWTH | BURN RATE |
CASH RUNWAY | PROPOSED LOAN AMOUNT | STRATEGIC USE OF PROCEEDS]

title: The Lazard Middle East & Africa Advisory Practice
prompt_text:
PROMPT 246 — The Lazard Middle East & Africa Advisory Practice
Act as MD at Lazard's Middle East & Africa advisory practice. Advise on
a complex cross-border M&A or capital raising in the MENA/Africa region.
Deliver: (1) MENA M&A market: GCC consolidation (banking, telecoms, healthcare);
SWF investment trends (PIF, ADIA, QIA as acquirers vs. co-investors); strategic
rationale for cross-border MENA-Africa-Asia deals. (2) Africa M&A dynamics:
pan-African acquirers (MTN, Dangote, Equity Bank expanding regionally) vs.
global strategic buyers entering Africa; PE secondary wave.
(3) Sovereign wealth fund engagement: how to structure a deal that appeals to GCC
SWFs (co-investment alongside PE, minority stakes with governance protections,
strategic alignment with Vision 2030/Qatar National Vision).
(4) Legal and regulatory complexity: joint stock company requirements in Saudi Arabia;
foreign ownership restrictions in UAE/Qatar; COMESA competition clearance for
pan-African deals; bilateral investment treaties.
(5) Valuation in frontier/emerging markets: additional country risk premium in WACC;
political risk discount; liquidity discount for private companies; precedent
transaction multiples in regional context. (6) Currency and repatriation: USD
vs. local currency deal structure; UAE dirham peg stability; African currency
convertibility risk; repatriation controls.
(7) Cultural and relationship dynamics in MENA deal-making: relationship-first
culture; decision-making timeline; Ramadan/holiday timing considerations.
Format: MEA Advisory Framework with Market Landscape, SWF Engagement Strategy,
Legal Complexity, Valuation Adjustments, Currency Risk, and Cultural Dynamics.
Inputs: [DEAL TYPE | GEOGRAPHY | SECTOR | DEAL SIZE | BUYER/SELLER IDENTITY |
SOVEREIGN INVOLVEMENT Y/N | PRIMARY REGULATORY CONCERN | TIMELINE]

title: The Oaktree Real Estate Income & Value Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 247 — The Oaktree Real Estate Income & Value Strategy
Act as MD at Oaktree Real Estate. Build a real estate value and income
investment strategy in the current market environment.
Deliver: (1) Real estate cycle positioning: where are we in the RE cycle? Cap rate
expansion (values falling) — opportunity for new investment; cap rate stabilization
signals recovery entry. (2) Value opportunities: (a) Office distress — quality
building, distressed seller, significant cap rate reset; (b) Retail recovery plays
— necessity retail (grocery-anchored) at distressed pricing; (c) Multifamily
cap rate reset in high-supply markets (Sun Belt oversupply 2024-25 → opportunity).
(3) Income strategy: core stabilized assets with long WALT; sectors with inflation
linkage (industrial with annual CPI escalators, self-storage with monthly pricing power).
(4) Distressed real estate credit: buying senior loans at discount from regional banks
forced to reduce CRE exposure; note-on-note analysis; foreclosure timeline by state.
(5) Operational value creation: property management improvements; energy efficiency
(NOI uplift from OpEx reduction); amenity enhancement for multifamily rent premium.
(6) Leverage strategy: fixed-rate agency debt for multifamily (prepayment-protected);
floating-rate bridge for value-add (match floating income to floating cost); duration
matching to exit horizon. (7) Exit strategy: core buyer universe (pension funds, SWFs,
REITs); cap rate compression at exit assumption; hold period optimization.
Format: RE Value Strategy with Cycle Positioning, Opportunity Set, Income Strategy,
Distressed Credit Analysis, Operational Value Creation, and Exit Framework.
Inputs: [PROPERTY TYPE | GEOGRAPHY | INVESTMENT APPROACH | TARGET RETURN | LEVERAGE
LIMIT | HOLD PERIOD | CURRENT MARKET CONDITIONS ASSESSMENT | RISK TOLERANCE]

title: The Guggenheim Partners Insurance Asset Management
prompt_text:
PROMPT 248 — The Guggenheim Partners Insurance Asset Management
Act as Senior PM at Guggenheim Partners managing insurance company general accounts.
Design a bespoke fixed income strategy for an insurance general account.
Deliver: (1) Insurance investment objectives: ALM (match asset duration to reserve
liabilities); statutory capital efficiency (NAIC RBC charges by asset class);
income generation (support policyholder return assumptions); illiquidity premium capture.
(2) NAIC designation system: NAIC 1 (high quality) → NAIC 6 (in or near default);
RBC charge by NAIC designation; how to optimize the portfolio for capital efficiency.
(3) Asset class allocation: (a) IG corporate bonds (NAIC 1-2, low RBC); (b) Structured
credit (ABS, RMBS, CLO — risk-adjusted yields); (c) Private placements (144A,
USPP — illiquidity premium with investment-grade quality); (d) Commercial mortgage
loans (direct lending by insurance companies — NAIC CML designations).
(4) Private placement strategy: USPP (US Private Placement) market size and mechanics;
make-whole call protection; shelf registration exemption; 15-year average life.
(5) Duration management: target duration slightly shorter than liabilities (1-year
positive duration gap); impact of rate changes on statutory surplus.
(6) Yield enhancement: sector rotation to higher-yielding IG sectors (financials,
utilities, BBB corporates); structured credit allocation within RBC limits;
direct lending (private credit) allocation.
(7) Regulatory constraints: NAIC investment limitations by state; Regulation 130
(NYDFS); permitted investments schedule; prohibited investments.
Format: Insurance GA Strategy with RBC Optimization, Asset Class Allocation,
Private Placement Framework, Duration Management, and Regulatory Compliance.
Inputs: [INSURANCE TYPE (LIFE/P&C/HEALTH) | PORTFOLIO SIZE | LIABILITY DURATION |
TARGET YIELD | RBC TARGET RATIO | STATE DOMICILE | PRIMARY CONSTRAINT]

title: The Warburg Pincus Technology Infrastructure Investment
prompt_text:
PROMPT 249 — The Warburg Pincus Technology Infrastructure Investment
Act as MD at Warburg Pincus's Technology, Media & Telecom team. Build an
investment thesis for technology infrastructure (cloud, connectivity, data).
Deliver: (1) Tech infrastructure investment rationale: recurring revenue, high barriers
to entry, capex-intensive (moat-building), demand driven by digital transformation.
(2) Cloud infrastructure: hyperscaler supply chain investment (cooling equipment,
power infrastructure, fiber connectivity) — where to invest ahead of demand;
co-location data center operators as picks-and-shovels play.
(3) Connectivity infrastructure: fiber-to-the-home (FTTH) — overbuilder economics
vs. incumbent; ROI model for new FTTH network (cost per home passed, take rate,
ARPU, payback period); fixed wireless access (FWA) as last-mile alternative.
(4) Mission-critical software infrastructure: middleware, DevOps tools, security
infrastructure — high switching costs, recurring revenue; SaaS valuation with
infrastructure defensibility premium. (5) Subsea cable investment: backbone of
internet traffic; hyperscaler-funded vs. carrier-grade cables; capacity pricing trends.
(6) PE value creation in tech infra: organic growth (market growth) + capex deployment
(new nodes/routes) + operational efficiency + multiple expansion (transition from
telecom to tech multiple). (7) Exit: strategic sale to utilities, PE continuation
fund, infrastructure fund buyout, or listed YieldCo structure.
Format: Tech Infrastructure Investment Framework with Sub-Sector Analysis, Connectivity
ROI Model, PE Value Creation, and Exit Strategy.
Inputs: [SUB-SECTOR | GEOGRAPHY | ASSET TYPE | REVENUE | EBITDA | CAPEX PLAN |
TARGET IRR | STRATEGIC VS. INFRASTRUCTURE BUYER TARGET]

title: The McKinsey Financial Services Regulatory Response Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 250 — The McKinsey Financial Services Regulatory Response Strategy
Act as Senior Partner at McKinsey's Risk & Regulation practice. Design a
strategic response to a major new regulatory requirement.
Deliver: (1) Regulatory impact assessment: map the new regulation to affected business
lines, products, processes, and systems; quantify P&L impact (revenue at risk,
compliance cost, capital requirement change).
(2) Strategic options: (a) Full compliance (standard implementation); (b) Strategic
repositioning (exit regulated activity, restructure product); (c) Competitive
arbitrage (comply faster than peers to gain market share); (d) Regulatory engagement
(participate in consultation to shape final rules). (3) Implementation roadmap:
regulatory timeline → internal milestones → program workstreams (policy, process,
technology, data, reporting); regulatory examination readiness.
(4) Technology and data architecture: regulatory reporting factory design; data
lineage and audit trail requirements; vendor solutions vs. in-house build.
(5) Governance: regulatory change management office; Board and senior management
oversight structure; regulatory horizon scanning process.
(6) Cost-benefit analysis: total cost of compliance (one-time + ongoing) vs.
cost of non-compliance (fines, remediation, reputational damage, market access loss).
(7) Peer benchmarking: how are leading institutions approaching this regulation?
Where can the firm gain competitive advantage through superior implementation?
Format: Regulatory Response Strategy with Impact Assessment, Options Analysis,
Implementation Roadmap, Technology Architecture, Governance, and Cost-Benefit.
Inputs: [REGULATION NAME | JURISDICTION | EFFECTIVE DATE | BUSINESS LINES AFFECTED |
CURRENT COMPLIANCE GAP | BUDGET | PRIMARY STRATEGIC CONCERN]

title: The Sixth Street Specialty Lending & Asset-Backed Finance
prompt_text:
PROMPT 251 — The Sixth Street Specialty Lending & Asset-Backed Finance
Act as MD at Sixth Street Partners. Build an asset-backed finance investment
strategy for specialty lending opportunities.
Deliver: (1) Asset-backed finance (ABF) universe: consumer installment loans, auto
loans/leases, equipment finance, trade receivables, royalty streams, insurance
premium finance, litigation finance — returns 8-15% depending on asset quality.
(2) Structure: originator sells pool of assets to SPV (bankruptcy-remote); SPV
issues notes backed by asset cash flows; structural protections (OC, reserve account,
excess spread). (3) Originator assessment: underwriting standards, servicing
capabilities, track record (static pool analysis — vintage-by-vintage default
rates), financial health and skin-in-the-game retention.
(4) Asset quality analysis: credit score distribution, seasoning, geographic
diversification, concentration limits; underwriting policy compliance testing
via due diligence sample. (5) Yield and structure: senior notes at investment-grade
pricing (SOFR + 150-300bps); mezzanine (SOFR + 400-600bps); equity/residual
(15-25% IRR); which tranche to invest in based on risk appetite.
(6) Financing: warehouse facility during ramp-up (revolving, 75-80% advance rate);
securitization takeout or whole loan sale.
(7) Litigation finance: providing capital for plaintiffs in exchange for portion
of recovery; underwriting legal merit; portfolio diversification across cases.
Format: ABF Investment Framework with Originator Assessment, Structure Analysis,
Yield by Tranche, Warehouse Strategy, and Litigation Finance Sub-Strategy.
Inputs: [ASSET CLASS | ORIGINATOR | ORIGINATION VOLUME | UNDERWRITING STANDARDS |
PROPOSED STRUCTURE | TARGET TRANCHE | RETURN TARGET | PRIMARY RISK CONCERN]

title: The CBRE Real Estate Investment Management Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 252 — The CBRE Real Estate Investment Management Strategy
Act as Head of Strategy at CBRE Investment Management. Design a global real
estate investment strategy for a diversified institutional mandate.
Deliver: (1) Global RE market overview: sector performance divergence (industrial
outperformance, office underperformance); geographic comparison (US vs. Europe vs.
APAC cap rates and growth). (2) Core sectors deep dive: industrial/logistics
(rent growth drivers: supply chain reconfiguration, e-commerce); residential
(multifamily US, BTR UK/Europe, student housing); data centers; alternatives
(life science, healthcare, self-storage). (3) Opportunistic sectors: office
repositioning and conversion; distressed retail; hospitality recovery.
(4) Geographic allocation: US (most liquid, highest quality assets), Europe
(value relative to US, regulatory complexity), APAC (growth markets, Japan
value opportunity, Australia logistics). (5) Currency: local currency borrowing
to create natural hedge; cross-currency swaps for non-hedgeable currencies.
(6) ESG integration: GRESB benchmark target (top quartile); energy efficiency
improvement program; green certification capex ROI; carbon neutral portfolio target.
(7) Fund structure: open-end (core) vs. closed-end (value-add/opportunistic);
co-investment alongside fund for large mandates; separate account for largest LPs.
Format: RE Investment Strategy with Sector Allocation, Geographic Framework,
Opportunistic Opportunities, ESG Standards, and Fund Structure.
Inputs: [MANDATE TYPE (CORE/VALUE-ADD/OPPO) | AUM | GEOGRAPHY | SECTOR FOCUS |
LEVERAGE TARGET | ESG REQUIREMENTS | LIQUIDITY STRUCTURE | RETURN TARGET]

title: The Zurich Insurance Group Enterprise Risk & Capital Management
prompt_text:
PROMPT 253 — The Zurich Insurance Group Enterprise Risk & Capital Management
Act as Group CRO at Zurich Insurance Group. Design an enterprise risk and
economic capital management framework for a global P&C and life insurer.
Deliver: (1) Economic capital model: bottom-up capital requirement for each risk type
(underwriting, market, credit, operational) using a 99.95% VaR (1-in-2000 year event
consistent with AA financial strength target). (2) Risk aggregation: correlation
between risk types (market risk and credit risk are correlated in financial crises);
diversification benefit in economic capital.
(3) Solvency II (EU) / Bermuda BSCR: regulatory capital vs. economic capital;
SCR (Solvency Capital Requirement) components; Solvency II ratio target (>170% for
Zurich); impact of EIOPA volatility adjustment. (4) ORSA (Own Risk and Solvency
Assessment): annual forward-looking assessment; how strategy choices affect the
Solvency II ratio trajectory; management actions available.
(5) Reinsurance optimization: how reinsurance reduces required capital; risk transfer
vs. cost; optimal reinsurance program design (XL, quota share, aggregate stop-loss).
(6) Asset-liability matching: for life insurance reserves — duration matching;
currency matching; liquidity matching. (7) Capital allocation to business units:
RAROC (Risk-Adjusted Return on Capital) by BU; capital fungibility across geographies
(dividend upstream capacity, regulatory constraints).
Format: ERM Framework with Economic Capital Model, Solvency Ratio Management,
Reinsurance Optimization, ALM Design, and Capital Allocation.
Inputs: [INSURER TYPE | GEOGRAPHY | SOLVENCY RATIO | SCR COMPOSITION | TARGET RATING |
LARGEST RISK CONCENTRATIONS | PRIMARY CAPITAL CONCERN]

title: The Hudson Bay Capital Event-Driven Merger Arbitrage
prompt_text:
PROMPT 254 — The Hudson Bay Capital Event-Driven Merger Arbitrage
Act as PM at Hudson Bay Capital. Build a systematic event-driven merger
arbitrage strategy.
Deliver: (1) Merger arb mechanics: buy target at current price, short acquirer (for
stock deals); capture spread = deal price − current trading price; annualized return
= spread / days to close × 365. (2) Deal break probability estimation: build a
regression model using historical deal break rates (4-8% for cash deals, 8-15% for
stock deals) with predictors: deal type, size, acquirer financial condition, regulatory
complexity, MAC clause breadth, financing contingency. (3) Break price estimation:
where does target trade if deal breaks? Typically -20 to -35% from deal price;
estimate using: pre-announcement price + strategic value discount + market move.
(4) Risk/reward: spread earned if deal closes (e.g., +4%) vs. loss if deal breaks
(e.g., -25%) × respective probabilities → expected value calculation.
(5) Portfolio construction: 30-50 simultaneous arb positions; sizing inversely
proportional to break probability × break loss; correlation (all arb positions
correlate in a risk-off event when deals cluster to break simultaneously).
(6) Regulatory risk assessment: HSR second request probability; DOJ/FTC challenge
probability based on HHI change and enforcement philosophy; EU Phase II investigation.
(7) Event calendar: FTC/DOJ second request timeline; shareholder vote date; closing
conditions tracking.
Format: Merger Arb Strategy with Break Probability Model, Expected Value Analysis,
Portfolio Construction, Regulatory Risk, and Event Calendar Management.
Inputs: [DEAL NAME | ACQUIRER | TARGET | DEAL PRICE | CURRENT PRICE | SPREAD |
DEAL TYPE (CASH/STOCK) | REGULATORY RISK | EXPECTED CLOSE DATE]

title: The Booz Allen Hamilton Government Technology & Digital Transformation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 255 — The Booz Allen Hamilton Government Technology & Digital Transformation
Act as Principal at Booz Allen Hamilton. Design a digital transformation
program for a US federal government agency.
Deliver: (1) Government digital transformation context: federal IT modernization
mandate (FITARA, Cloud Smart, Zero Trust Architecture Executive Order); legacy
system risks (COBOL, mainframe dependencies); procurement complexity (FAR/DFARS).
(2) Cloud migration strategy: government cloud options (AWS GovCloud, Azure Government,
Google Government Cloud, Oracle Government Cloud); FedRAMP authorization process
(3-18 months); data sovereignty and IL (Impact Level) requirements (IL2/IL4/IL5/IL6).
(3) Zero Trust Architecture: CISA ZTA model (identity, device, network, application,
data); implementation roadmap by pillar; CDM (Continuous Diagnostics and Mitigation)
program integration. (4) Agile at scale in government: SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework)
for federal; managing agile within FAR Part 12 contracts; DevSecOps pipeline in
classified environments. (5) Data modernization: DOGE-era data visibility requirements;
data lakehouse architecture for federal analytics; interoperability across agency
systems (FHIR for HHS, ICAM for identity). (6) Program management: PMBOK for
government IT; EVM (Earned Value Management) reporting requirements; Congressional
budget cycle alignment. (7) Small business set-asides and teaming: 8(a), HUBZone,
SDVOSB programs; teaming with large primes; GSA Schedule positioning.
Format: Government Digital Transformation Program with Cloud Strategy, ZTA Roadmap,
Agile Implementation, Data Architecture, PM Framework, and Acquisition Strategy.
Inputs: [AGENCY | MISSION FUNCTION | LEGACY SYSTEMS | SECURITY CLASSIFICATION LEVEL |
BUDGET | TIMELINE | CONGRESSIONAL OVERSIGHT | PRIMARY MODERNIZATION OBJECTIVE]

title: The Pantheon Ventures Private Equity Primaries Program
prompt_text:
PROMPT 256 — The Pantheon Ventures Private Equity Primaries Program
Act as Head of PE Primaries at Pantheon Ventures. Design a primary fund
commitment program for an institutional LP.
Deliver: (1) Primary fund commitment rationale: access to top-quartile managers,
vintage year diversification, strategy diversification; J-curve as the main drawback.
(2) Manager universe construction: buyout (large, mid, lower-mid), venture, growth
equity, credit, real assets; total universe of ~4,000 PE managers → narrowed to
200-300 in investment grade → 50-70 active relationships.
(3) Manager selection process: track record analysis (net IRR, MOIC, PME — Public
Market Equivalent); fund manager interviews; reference checks; LP Advisory Committee
role; portfolio company visits. (4) Portfolio construction: number of funds (20-35
for $1B+ LP PE program), commitment sizing (no fund >10-15% of total PE allocation),
strategy weights, geographic weights, vintage year commitments.
(5) Commitment pacing: annual commitment budget to maintain full investment period;
managing overcommitment ratio (total commitments / target PE allocation — typically
120-130% to account for J-curve cash flows).
(6) Monitoring: quarterly reports, LP meeting attendance, LPAC representation;
monitoring flags for manager deviation (style drift, key-person departure, AUM growth).
(7) Portfolio reporting: IRR, MOIC, DPI, TVPI, RVPI; PME benchmarking (Cambridge
Associates, Burgiss); risk analytics (underlying company fundamentals aggregation).
Format: PE Primaries Program with Manager Universe, Selection Process, Portfolio
Construction, Commitment Pacing, Monitoring, and Performance Reporting.
Inputs: [LP INSTITUTION | TOTAL PE ALLOCATION | ANNUAL COMMITMENT BUDGET |
STRATEGY MIX | GEOGRAPHIC FOCUS | NUMBER OF MANAGER RELATIONSHIPS | RETURN TARGET]

title: The Credit Agricole Corporate & Investment Banking ESG-Linked Finance
prompt_text:
PROMPT 257 — The Credit Agricole Corporate & Investment Banking ESG-Linked Finance
Act as MD at Credit Agricole CIB's Sustainable Finance group. Structure
an ESG-linked financing for a corporate client.
Deliver: (1) SLL (Sustainability-Linked Loan) mechanics: revolving credit facility
with margin step-up/step-down linked to pre-agreed KPIs; LMA Sustainability-Linked
Loan Principles compliance.
(2) KPI selection: 2-3 KPIs must be material to borrower (not just PR KPIs);
independently verifiable (third-party assurance); ambitious but achievable;
linked to borrower's overall sustainability strategy. Examples: GHG emission intensity
reduction, renewable energy %, women in leadership %, safety incident rate.
(3) SPT (Sustainability Performance Target) calibration: based on science (SBTi),
regulatory requirements, or industry benchmarks; step-up/step-down of typically 5-10bps.
(4) Verification and assurance: external verifier selection (KPMG, EY Sustainability,
DNV, Bureau Veritas); annual KPI reporting requirement; what happens if borrower
fails to report (margin step-up regardless of KPI performance).
(5) Greenwashing safeguards: ICMAand LMA principles require genuine ambition;
regulatory scrutiny (EU Taxonomy verification, SEC climate disclosure); reputational
risk for both bank and borrower if KPIs are too easy.
(6) SLL vs. green loan: SLL = tied to borrower performance (use of proceeds unrestricted);
green loan = restricted use of proceeds for green projects; when each is appropriate.
(7) Pricing: greenium in SLL market? Evidence suggests minimal (<5bps) for loans
vs. more significant in bonds (8-15bps for genuine green bonds).
Format: SLL Advisory with KPI Framework, SPT Calibration, Verification Design,
Greenwashing Risk Assessment, and SLL vs. Green Loan Comparison.
Inputs: [COMPANY | SECTOR | FACILITY SIZE | CURRENT SUSTAINABILITY METRICS |
PROPOSED KPIs | CURRENT MARGIN | SUSTAINABILITY STRATEGY | VERIFICATION PREFERENCE]

title: The Neuberger Berman Multi-Asset Credit Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 258 — The Neuberger Berman Multi-Asset Credit Strategy
Act as PM at Neuberger Berman's Multi-Asset Credit team. Build a diversified
credit portfolio spanning investment-grade, high-yield, and private credit.
Deliver: (1) Multi-asset credit rationale: higher yield than IG bonds alone with lower
volatility than pure HY; diversification across credit quality, sectors, and liquidity.
(2) Portfolio construction: target allocation across: IG corporate bonds (30-40%),
BB-rated bonds (20-25%), B-rated bonds (15-20%), loans (10-15%), CLO tranches (5-10%),
private credit (5-10%); rebalancing triggers.
(3) Credit cycle positioning: early cycle (overweight HY and loans), mid-cycle
(hold balanced), late cycle (rotate to IG and short duration), downturn
(defensive positioning — reduce HY, add CDS protection).
(4) Duration management: multi-asset credit portfolio typically shorter duration
than IG bonds; active duration management relative to benchmark.
(5) Liquidity tiering: liquid (IG, liquid HY ETFs — can sell in days), semi-liquid
(HY bonds, loans — can sell in weeks), illiquid (private credit — locked up for years).
Target composition by liquidity tier based on fund structure.
(6) Default and recovery analysis: expected default rate and recovery rate by credit
quality; stress scenario analysis (2008-style default spike).
(7) Factor exposures: credit spread beta, duration, equity beta (HY has 0.3-0.5 equity
beta in downturns); how to hedge unwanted factor exposures.
Format: Multi-Asset Credit Strategy with Allocation Framework, Credit Cycle Guide,
Duration Management, Liquidity Analysis, and Stress Testing.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | BENCHMARK | TARGET YIELD | DURATION BUDGET | LIQUIDITY
REQUIREMENTS | CREDIT QUALITY LIMITS | PRIVATE CREDIT APPETITE]

title: The Greenhill & Co. Fairness Opinion & Board Advisory
prompt_text:
PROMPT 259 — The Greenhill & Co. Fairness Opinion & Board Advisory
Act as MD at Greenhill & Co. Provide a fairness opinion and board advisory
for a company receiving an acquisition offer.
Deliver: (1) Fairness opinion purpose: independent financial advisor's written opinion
that the consideration is fair from a financial point of view to shareholders;
protects board's business judgment rule defense.
(2) Methodologies used: (a) DCF — intrinsic value based on management projections;
(b) Comparable company analysis — public trading multiples;
(c) Precedent transactions — deal multiples from comparable M&A.
Weighted or range-of-value approach across all three.
(3) Sensitivity analysis: how does value change across WACC ±100bps and terminal
growth rate ±50bps? Document the full range of outputs.
(4) Key assumptions scrutiny: are management projections reliable? Has the Board
seen independent verification? Are synergies included or excluded?
(5) Go-shop vs. no-shop: did the company run a full process before signing?
If no-shop, is the deal price defensible without competitive tension?
(6) Board process evaluation: were conflicts of interest managed? Was the Special
Committee truly independent? Did management have conflicting interests in the outcome?
(7) Litigation risk: Delaware appraisal proceedings; class action shareholder suits
challenging fairness; role of fairness opinion in limiting litigation exposure.
Format: Fairness Opinion Framework with Methodology, Sensitivity Analysis, Process
Assessment, Assumption Scrutiny, and Litigation Risk Management.
Inputs: [TARGET COMPANY | ACQUIRER | DEAL PRICE | FORM OF CONSIDERATION |
DEAL PROCESS (AUCTION/NEGOTIATED) | CONFLICTS OF INTEREST | MANAGEMENT PROJECTIONS]

title: The Hamilton Lane Private Markets Portfolio Analytics
prompt_text:
PROMPT 260 — The Hamilton Lane Private Markets Portfolio Analytics
Act as Director of Portfolio Analytics at Hamilton Lane. Build a comprehensive
private markets portfolio analytics and monitoring system.
Deliver: (1) Private markets data aggregation: collecting fund-level and portfolio
company-level data from 50+ GP relationships; standardization challenge (each GP
reports differently); data normalization and quality control.
(2) Performance metrics: IRR (internal rate of return), MOIC, DPI (Distributed to
Paid-In), TVPI (Total Value to Paid-In), RVPI (Residual Value to Paid-In);
time-weighted vs. money-weighted returns for PE.
(3) Benchmarking: PME (Public Market Equivalent — what would $1 invested in PE have
earned if invested in public markets instead); Cambridge Associates, Burgiss, Preqin
benchmarks; why benchmark selection matters enormously.
(4) Risk analytics for PE: J-curve visualization; vintage year correlation; sector
concentration; geographic concentration; leverage concentration in portfolio companies.
(5) Cash flow modeling: commitment-weighted distribution pacing model; capital call
and distribution forecasting for liquidity management.
(6) Secondaries pricing: mark-to-model for portfolio LP interests; discount/premium
to NAV by strategy and vintage; bid-ask spread in current secondary market.
(7) Reporting: LP quarterly report design; regulator reporting (Form PF for fund
managers, ILPA reporting templates for LPs); carbon footprint of private market portfolio.
Format: PE Analytics Framework with Data Aggregation, Performance Metrics, PME
Benchmarking, Risk Analytics, Cash Flow Model, and Reporting Design.
Inputs: [LP INSTITUTION | NUMBER OF FUNDS | TOTAL PE ALLOCATION | AUM | REPORTING
