FREQUENCY | PME BENCHMARK | SECONDARY MARKET APPETITE | PRIMARY ANALYTICS NEED]

title: The Ares Capital Corporation BDC (Business Development Company) Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 261 — The Ares Capital Corporation BDC (Business Development Company) Strategy
Act as Head of Portfolio Management at Ares Capital (ARCC), the largest BDC.
Design an investment strategy for a publicly-traded BDC.
Deliver: (1) BDC structure: regulated investment company (RIC) that must distribute
90%+ of income; leverage limit 1.0× debt/equity (post-SBCAA 2018 allows 2.0×);
publicly traded on exchange — unique combination of daily liquidity + illiquid assets.
(2) Lending strategy: first-lien senior secured (>70% of portfolio), one-stop/unitranche,
second lien, subordinated debt, equity co-investments; target weighted average yield
(12-14% in current rate environment). (3) Credit underwriting: EBITDA $5-75M, PE-backed
companies, SOFR + 550-700bps for senior debt; DSCR, leverage, and liquidity assessment.
(4) Dividend sustainability: is the dividend covered by net investment income (NII)?
NII yield vs. dividend yield — undercovered dividends require return of capital.
(5) NAV analysis: book value per share; premium/discount to NAV (quality BDCs trade
at 1.1-1.2× NAV; stressed BDCs trade below NAV). (6) Manager economics: ARCC pays
Ares management fee (1.5% of assets) + incentive fee (20% above hurdle) — total fee
drag vs. direct lending fund. (7) BDC selection criteria for investors: asset quality,
fee structure, leverage, dividend coverage, manager track record.
Format: BDC Strategy with Lending Framework, Credit Underwriting, Dividend Analysis,
NAV Assessment, Manager Economics, and Investor Selection Criteria.
Inputs: [BDC NAME | PORTFOLIO SIZE | CURRENT YIELD | NAV/SHARE | STOCK PRICE |
LEVERAGE RATIO | PORTFOLIO COMPOSITION | PRIMARY INVESTMENT THESIS]

title: The TPG Rise Climate Clean Energy Investment
prompt_text:
PROMPT 262 — The TPG Rise Climate Clean Energy Investment
Act as MD at TPG Rise Climate. Build an investment thesis for a climate
technology PE investment.
Deliver: (1) Climate tech investment landscape: clean energy (solar, wind, storage),
sustainable food and agriculture, decarbonized industry (green steel, green cement),
sustainable transportation (EV, public transit), built environment (heat pumps,
building efficiency); expected TAM by sector in 2030. (2) Returns by climate tech
segment: infrastructure-like (contracted renewables: 10-12%), growth equity
(climate software, circular economy: 20-25%), venture (hard tech: VC returns needed).
(3) TPG's sector thesis: invest in sectors where climate solutions are achieving
cost parity with incumbent fossil alternatives; technology pull vs. regulatory push.
(4) Policy dependency risk: how IRA tax credits underpin returns; cliff risk if
credits are reduced; geopolitical risk for Chinese supply chains (solar panels,
batteries). (5) Measurement: TCFD-aligned impact reporting; tons of CO2e avoided
per dollar invested; Science-Based Target for the fund itself.
(6) Co-investment with corporates: strategic partners accelerate distribution;
how corporates become anchor customers for portfolio companies.
(7) Exit: strategic acquisitions by energy companies, industrials, or utilities;
IPO for scaled climate tech platforms; infrastructure fund buyout for mature operating assets.
Format: Climate Tech PE Framework with Sector Returns, Policy Risk Assessment,
Impact Measurement, Corporate Co-Investment, and Exit Strategy.
Inputs: [CLIMATE SECTOR | COMPANY | TECHNOLOGY MATURITY | REVENUE | EBITDA OR ARR |
IRA DEPENDENCY | PROPOSED ENTRY VALUATION | TARGET IRR | IMPACT METRICS]

title: The Apollo Global Management Insurance & Annuity Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 263 — The Apollo Global Management Insurance & Annuity Strategy
Act as Senior Strategist at Apollo Global Management / Athene Holding.
Build the integrated PE-insurance strategy.
Deliver: (1) Apollo-Athene model: how a PE firm owning a life insurer creates
a "perpetual capital" vehicle — Athene writes insurance (fixed annuities, funding
agreements), generating permanent liabilities that fund Apollo's private credit assets.
(2) Annuity economics: fixed indexed annuity (FIA) spread economics — crediting rate
to policyholder vs. investment yield on assets; surrender charges as optionality.
(3) Asset strategy: Athene's asset allocation is heavily private credit (Apollo-managed
direct lending, structured credit) vs. traditional insurers (public IG bonds);
yield advantage = 150-200bps above traditional insurers' portfolios.
(4) Capital efficiency: NAIC RBC charges for private credit vs. public bonds;
how Apollo structures private credit to minimize RBC charges (rated feeder funds,
investment-grade tranches of private deals). (5) Regulatory risk: NAIC's push for
tighter PE-insurance regulation; state insurance department scrutiny; Form E filings
for private equity ownership.
(6) Replication by competitors: how other PE firms (Blackstone/Resolution Life,
KKR/Global Atlantic, Carlyle/Fortitude) have adopted the Apollo-Athene model.
(7) Systemic risk concern: regulators' worry about illiquid private credit backing
insurance liabilities; liquidity stress scenarios.
Format: PE-Insurance Strategy with Business Model Mechanics, Asset Strategy,
Capital Efficiency, Regulatory Risk, and Peer Comparison.
Inputs: [PE FIRM | INSURANCE AFFILIATE | AUM | ANNUITY LIABILITIES | ASSET YIELD |
RBC RATIO | REGULATORY JURISDICTION | PRIMARY STRATEGIC OBJECTIVE]

title: The Societe Generale Structured Equity & Principal Finance
prompt_text:
PROMPT 264 — The Societe Generale Structured Equity & Principal Finance
Act as MD at SocGen's Structured Equity & Principal Finance group. Design
a structured equity solution for a corporate or financial institution.
Deliver: (1) Structured equity universe: equity-linked notes, mandatory convertibles,
contingent convertibles (AT1 CoCos for banks), exchangeable bonds, equity repos,
share-backed financing, delta-one products. (2) Mandatory convertible: converts to
equity at maturity regardless of share price; coupon paid; accounting as equity
(credit-friendly); use case — bridge to equity dilution.
(3) Equity repo financing: corporation repos its own treasury shares to a bank for
cash; bank holds shares as collateral; use cases for balance sheet optimization.
(4) Collar-wrapped share financing: bank lends against shares with put/call collar
limiting downside for bank; use for monetizing large concentrated positions
with tax deferral. (5) CoCo AT1 bonds: bank-issued; convert to equity or principal
write-down if CET1 falls below 5.125% (or 7%); investor receives high coupon
for absorbing this tail risk; Credit Suisse AT1 write-down case study (March 2023).
(6) Structured secondary offerings: equity accelerated bookbuild with embedded
derivative (floor price, distribution enhancement); use for PE sponsors managing
controlled exit. (7) Margin loan: lending against listed equity portfolio;
typical LTV 50-65%; margin call mechanics; recourse vs. non-recourse structure.
Format: Structured Equity Framework with Product Mechanics, Use Cases, Bank Risk,
CoCo Case Study, and Customized Solution Design.
Inputs: [CLIENT TYPE | OBJECTIVE (MONETIZE/FINANCE/CAPITAL) | UNDERLYING EQUITY |
SHARE PRICE | BLOCK SIZE | TAX SENSITIVITY | ACCOUNTING TREATMENT PREFERENCE]

title: The Canaccord Genuity Technology Growth Equity Capital Markets
prompt_text:
PROMPT 265 — The Canaccord Genuity Technology Growth Equity Capital Markets
Act as MD at Canaccord Genuity's Technology group. Advise a high-growth
technology company on accessing capital markets for the first time.
Deliver: (1) Pre-IPO capital markets options: late-stage VC (Series C-E), growth equity
from PE (minority stake), convertible notes (Nasdaq/NYSE pre-IPO bridge), venture debt.
(2) Dual-track process: running IPO preparation alongside M&A sale process; optionality
maximization; how banks manage both tracks simultaneously.
(3) IPO readiness assessment: SOX 404 internal controls, SEC-quality financial
statements (3 years audited PCAOB), investor-ready management team, predictable
revenue model (no revenue surprises post-IPO), IR capability.
(4) Exchange selection: NYSE vs. Nasdaq — fees, listing standards, specialist vs.
market maker system, index eligibility (S&P 500 requires NYSE or Nasdaq).
(5) Underwriter selection: bulge bracket (credibility, analyst coverage, distribution)
vs. tech-specialist boutiques (Canaccord, Cowen, Needham — sector expertise, smaller
deal focus); economics (gross spread 5-7% of IPO proceeds).
(6) Pre-IPO investor education: cornerstone investors for IPO book; PIPE alongside
IPO; directed share program for employees and customers.
(7) Post-IPO obligations: SEC periodic reporting (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K); Reg FD
compliance; insider trading policy; quiet periods and lockup management.
Format: Capital Markets Advisory with Pre-IPO Options, Dual-Track Design, IPO
Readiness, Exchange Selection, Underwriter Process, and Post-IPO Framework.
Inputs: [COMPANY | ARR OR REVENUE | GROWTH RATE | BURN | LAST VALUATION |
IPO TARGET TIMING | STRATEGIC ALTERNATIVES | PRIMARY CAPITAL OBJECTIVE]

title: The Advent/Bain Latin America Private Equity
prompt_text:
PROMPT 266 — The Advent/Bain Latin America Private Equity
Act as MD at a leading Latin America-focused PE firm (Advent International,
Bain Capital, Patria Investments). Build a LatAm PE investment strategy.
Deliver: (1) LatAm PE market: $20-25B annual deal volume; Brazil dominates (50%+);
Mexico second; Colombia, Chile, Peru, Argentina — each with different risk/return.
(2) Brazil PE: BRL currency risk (historical: 30-40% devaluation cycles);
political risk premium; agricultural and energy sector strengths; strong domestic
consumer market. (3) Mexico PE: USMCA proximity advantage; nearshoring beneficiary;
security/organized crime risk in some regions; US LP appetite for Mexico exposure.
(4) Deal sourcing: proprietary deal flow in family businesses (succession planning);
corporate carve-outs by Brazilian multinationals; management buyouts.
(5) Local execution advantage: Portuguese/Spanish language; regulatory navigation;
government relations; operational involvement in portfolio companies.
(6) Value creation: professionalizing family businesses; implementing technology
(ERP, e-commerce); regional expansion of national champions; accessing US/EU markets.
(7) Exit dynamics: Brazil B3 IPO (limited liquidity); strategic sale to multinationals
entering LatAm; PE secondary; sponsor-to-sponsor.
Format: LatAm PE Strategy with Country Risk/Return Matrix, Deal Dynamics, Value
Creation Playbook, Currency Management, and Exit Framework.
Inputs: [COUNTRY FOCUS | SECTOR | REVENUE | EBITDA | ENTRY MULTIPLE | FX EXPOSURE |
PRIMARY VALUE CREATION THESIS | HOLD PERIOD | EXIT PREFERENCE]

title: The GIC Global Portfolio Stress Testing & Scenario Analysis
prompt_text:
PROMPT 267 — The GIC Global Portfolio Stress Testing & Scenario Analysis
Act as Head of Risk at GIC (Singapore's sovereign wealth fund). Build a
comprehensive stress testing and scenario analysis framework for a global portfolio.
Deliver: (1) Scenario library: historical scenarios (2008 GFC, 2020 COVID, 2022 rate
shock, 1997 Asian financial crisis), hypothetical scenarios (China hard landing, US
recession, energy price spike, geopolitical escalation), and reverse stress tests
(what scenario would cause portfolio to fall below minimum funding level).
(2) Scenario design methodology: identify the macro shock → estimate asset class
returns under the shock using historical relationships → apply correlations →
calculate portfolio P&L. (3) Cross-asset correlation in stress: equity-bond
correlation breakdown in inflationary stress (2022); credit spread widening in
recession; commodity price behavior in geopolitical stress.
(4) Illiquid asset stress: PE and real estate carry book value; when do GPs
mark down? Liquidity stress — forced selling of liquid assets to meet obligations.
(5) Tail risk quantification: Expected Shortfall (CVaR) at 99% vs. 95%; portfolio
behavior in the worst 1% of scenarios.
(6) Management actions under stress: which assets to liquidate first (liquidity
ladder); FX hedging activation; derivative overlay trigger levels.
(7) Communication: how to present stress test results to the Board Investment
Committee; risk appetite calibration; when to de-risk.
Format: Stress Testing Framework with Scenario Library, Methodology, Cross-Asset
Correlation Model, Illiquid Asset Treatment, and Management Action Playbook.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | ASSET CLASS MIX | MINIMUM FUNDING REQUIREMENT | LIQUIDITY
LADDER | LARGEST RISK CONCENTRATIONS | PRIMARY TAIL RISK CONCERN]

title: The Societe Generale Natural Resources & Commodities Banking
prompt_text:
PROMPT 268 — The Societe Generale Natural Resources & Commodities Banking
Act as MD at SocGen's Natural Resources & Commodity Finance group. Structure
a commodity-backed financing for an energy or mining company.
Deliver: (1) Commodity finance structures: prepayment financing (offtaker prepays for
future commodity delivery — off-balance-sheet treatment if structured correctly);
reserve-based lending (RBL — oil & gas producing properties as collateral);
streaming (metal streaming financing for miners).
(2) RBL mechanics: borrowing base = NPV of proved developed producing (PDP) reserves
at commodity price deck × advance rate (typically 60-70%); semi-annual redetermination;
oil price deck used (typically 20-30% below strip prices for conservatism).
(3) Prepayment financing: commodity bank pays producer upfront; producer delivers
commodity over 3-7 years; bank marks to market; off-balance-sheet for producer if
structured as a sale. (4) Streaming agreement: streaming company pays upfront for
right to buy X% of mine production at below-market fixed price; long-term (life-of-mine);
NPV of stream vs. upfront payment.
(5) Covenant package: reserve replacement covenants; hedging requirements (25-50%
of production hedged for 12-24 months); senior leverage ratio.
(6) Commodity price risk: production economics at different commodity prices;
break-even analysis (WTI break-even for US shale: $45-60/bbl). 
(7) ESG considerations: transition risk for fossil fuel financing; IEA net-zero scenario
implications for reserves valuation; climate disclosure requirements.
Format: Commodity Finance Advisory with RBL Mechanics, Prepayment Structure,
Streaming Analysis, Covenant Package, and ESG Risk Assessment.
Inputs: [COMMODITY | COMPANY TYPE | PRODUCTION VOLUME | RESERVE LIFE | ASSET LOCATION |
PROPOSED FINANCING SIZE | COMMODITY HEDGE PERCENTAGE | PRIMARY FINANCING OBJECTIVE]

title: The Deloitte Restructuring: Financial Modeling Under Distress
prompt_text:
PROMPT 269 — The Deloitte Restructuring: Financial Modeling Under Distress
Act as Director at Deloitte's Restructuring Services. Build a financial model
for a distressed company evaluating restructuring options.
Deliver: (1) Distressed financial modeling requirements: extreme downside scenarios
(not management case); weekly/monthly granularity (not annual); covenant compliance
tracking; liquidity as the binding constraint.
(2) 13-week cash flow: receipts (AR collections using DSO assumption) vs. disbursements
(payroll, trade payables, debt service, rent) = net cash flow; ending cash balance
vs. minimum liquidity requirement; when does cash run out without action?
(3) Scenario modeling: (a) Status quo (no restructuring); (b) Out-of-court restructuring
(debt exchange, extended maturities); (c) Chapter 11 (additional costs but more tools);
(d) Liquidation (worst case recovery). Each scenario → cash flow → debt paydown
→ reorganization value → recovery by creditor class.
(4) Enterprise valuation: going concern (EBITDA × comparable company multiple) vs.
liquidation (orderly liquidation value of assets); fulcrum security determination.
(5) Waterfall analysis: enterprise value allocated across secured → unsecured →
equity; percentage recovery for each creditor class under each scenario.
(6) Debt capacity analysis: what sustainable leverage supports post-restructuring
operations? New debt terms (maturity, interest, covenants) that company can service.
(7) Sensitivity analysis: commodity price, volume, and margin sensitivity; which
variables most affect the waterfall and recovery rates.
Format: Distressed Financial Model Framework with 13-Week Cash Flow, Scenario Analysis,
Waterfall, Enterprise Valuation, Debt Capacity, and Sensitivity.
Inputs: [COMPANY | INDUSTRY | WEEKLY CASH BURN | DEBT STRUCTURE | NEAREST COVENANT
BREACH | EBITDA | LIQUIDATION ASSET VALUES | PRIMARY RESTRUCTURING OBJECTIVE]

title: The Wellington Management Emerging Markets Equity Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 270 — The Wellington Management Emerging Markets Equity Strategy
Act as Senior PM at Wellington Management's EM team. Build an active EM
equity strategy with a fundamental quality tilt.
Deliver: (1) Wellington EM philosophy: bottom-up fundamental research; quality companies
at reasonable prices; long-term ownership; proprietary research network advantage.
(2) Country framework: top-down country allocation based on macro stability, valuation,
growth, and sentiment — but company quality drives the overweight, not the country.
(3) Quality definition in EM: sustainable competitive advantage (often government
relationships, distribution monopoly, brand); clean governance (no related-party
abuse); FCF generation (not just accounting earnings); management track record.
(4) EM-specific research: field research importance — visiting companies, meeting
management, channel checks in local language; proprietary local analyst network.
(5) EM valuation: P/E adjusted for leverage; EV/EBITDA for capital-intensive EM
businesses; FCF yield adjusted for political risk discount; currency-adjusted returns.
(6) Risk management: single stock position limit (4-5% for high-conviction ideas);
country limits (max 2× index weight); liquidity-adjusted position sizing.
(7) Portfolio characteristics: benchmark-aware (active share 60-75%); tracking error
budget (4-6%); sector diversification despite bottom-up construction.
Format: EM Equity Strategy with Country Framework, Quality Scorecard, Research
Process, Valuation Methodology, Risk Management, and Portfolio Characteristics.
Inputs: [BENCHMARK | PORTFOLIO SIZE | ACTIVE SHARE TARGET | TRACKING ERROR BUDGET |
CURRENT COUNTRY OVERWEIGHTS | TOP HOLDINGS | PRIMARY INVESTMENT THESIS]

title: The Rothschild M&A: Takeover Defense & Staggered Board Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 271 — The Rothschild M&A: Takeover Defense & Staggered Board Strategy
Act as Senior Partner at Rothschild advising a Board on defending against
a hostile takeover approach.
Deliver: (1) Hostile takeover mechanics: unsolicited offer → Board rejects →
acquirer goes directly to shareholders (tender offer or proxy fight).
(2) Defensive measures already in place: staggered (classified) board — only 1/3
directors up for election each year → minimum 2 years to get full board control;
poison pill (rights plan) — dilutes acquirer above threshold. Assess strength.
(3) Poison pill design: 20% flip-in trigger; 364-day duration; "morning after"
pill for overnight creep; exempt threshold for existing large shareholders.
(4) White knight strategy: identify friendly alternative bidder; how to run a
confidential process while publicly rejecting the hostile; auction risk.
(5) "Just say no" defense: Board can simply reject if it has a credible standalone plan;
Delaware fiduciary duty (Revlon duties not triggered unless Board decides to sell);
when this defense is viable vs. legally risky.
(6) Value creation response: commit to specific financial targets that close the
valuation gap; accelerated share buyback; portfolio streamlining; dividend increase.
(7) Communications: shareholder letter disputing acquirer's valuation; analyst day;
media management; proxy fight preparation.
Format: Takeover Defense Playbook with Defensive Measures Assessment, Poison Pill
Design, White Knight Process, Value Creation Response, and Communications Plan.
Inputs: [TARGET COMPANY | HOSTILE BIDDER | BID PRICE | CURRENT PRICE | PREMIUM % |
EXISTING DEFENSES | INSTITUTIONAL SHAREHOLDER LIST | BOARD'S PRIMARY OBJECTIVE]

title: The Franklin Templeton Fixed Income Emerging Market Debt
prompt_text:
PROMPT 272 — The Franklin Templeton Fixed Income Emerging Market Debt
Act as Senior PM at Franklin Templeton's Fixed Income division. Build an EM
hard currency (USD) sovereign debt investment framework.
Deliver: (1) EMBI universe: 70+ sovereign issuers in the JP Morgan EMBI Global
index; spread duration; credit quality distribution (IG vs. HY EM sovereign).
(2) Sovereign credit analysis (5-pillar model): (a) External position (CA, FX reserves,
external debt/GDP), (b) Fiscal position (deficit, debt/GDP, revenue base), (c) Growth
prospects, (d) Political/governance risk, (e) Monetary policy credibility.
(3) Spread decomposition: credit spread = expected default loss + risk premium;
compare CDS-implied spread to bond spread (basis); identify mispricing.
(4) Country selection: overweight countries with improving fundamentals (ratings upgrade
candidates); underweight countries with deteriorating dynamics.
(5) Distressed sovereign opportunities: countries in IMF programs or near default;
recovery value analysis; timing entry into distressed credits (pre-IMF program,
post-default, during restructuring).
(6) New issue premium: EM sovereigns typically pay 20-40bps NIC (New Issue Concession);
how to capture NIC through primary market participation.
(7) Risk management: duration vs. benchmark; country concentration limits; liquidity
(bid-ask spreads in illiquid frontier markets); contagion risk.
Format: EM Sovereign Debt Framework with Credit Analysis Template, Spread Decomposition,
Country Selection, Distressed Opportunities, and Risk Management.
Inputs: [BENCHMARK (EMBI GLOBAL/EMBI+) | DURATION TARGET | IG VS. HY SPLIT |
CURRENT COUNTRY OVERWEIGHTS | DISTRESSED EXPOSURE LIMIT | LIQUIDITY REQUIREMENT]

title: The Boston Consulting Group Corporate Performance Transformation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 273 — The Boston Consulting Group Corporate Performance Transformation
Act as Senior Partner at BCG's Corporate Finance & Strategy practice. Design
a performance transformation program for an underperforming conglomerate.
Deliver: (1) Portfolio diagnosis: map all business units on a relative market share
vs. market growth matrix (BCG Matrix); identify Stars (high share, high growth),
Cash Cows (high share, low growth), Question Marks (low share, high growth), Dogs (both low).
(2) Value creation gaps: compare each BU's ROIC to WACC; quantify value destruction;
identify BUs where improvement programs can close the gap vs. divest.
(3) Portfolio restructuring options: (a) Active portfolio management — divest dogs,
invest in stars; (b) Pure-play spin-off — separate BUs to eliminate conglomerate
discount; (c) Strategic M&A — acquire to fill capability gaps.
(4) Performance improvement for retained BUs: prioritized value creation initiatives
by BU — margin improvement, growth acceleration, capital efficiency; 3-year
financial targets.
(5) Capital allocation transformation: move from BU-based budget requests to
zero-based capital allocation (fund the best opportunities regardless of history);
hurdle rate review.
(6) Organizational design: right-size corporate HQ (typically over-staffed in
underperforming conglomerates); redesign incentives to align BU leaders with
shareholder value (P&L ownership, equity-linked comp).
(7) Investor relations strategy: how to communicate the transformation to investors;
tracking metrics; timelines for value realization.
Format: Corporate Performance Transformation with BCG Matrix, ROIC/WACC Analysis,
Portfolio Restructuring Plan, BU Improvement Programs, Capital Allocation, and IR Strategy.
Inputs: [COMPANY | NUMBER OF BUS | REVENUE | EBITDA MARGIN | CURRENT ROIC VS. WACC |
PRIMARY UNDERPERFORMANCE DRIVER | ACTIVIST PRESENCE Y/N | TRANSFORMATION TIMELINE]

title: The Crestview Partners Media & Entertainment Investment
prompt_text:
PROMPT 274 — The Crestview Partners Media & Entertainment Investment
Act as MD at Crestview Partners' Media team. Build an investment thesis
for a traditional or digital media company.
Deliver: (1) Media landscape disruption: linear TV (cord-cutting rate, affiliate fee
pressure, advertising cyclicality); streaming (content cost inflation, subscriber
growth challenges post-COVID); digital advertising (Google/Meta duopoly);
sports rights (inflation, streaming migration). (2) Local TV consolidation:
Nexstar, Sinclair, Gray — scale advantages in retransmission consent negotiations;
political advertising windfall in election years; Big 4 network affiliation value.
(3) Digital media: attention economy metrics (MAU, DAU, time-on-platform);
monetization (CPM trends, branded content, commerce); distribution platforms
(Facebook/Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, podcasts).
(4) Sports media rights: the last "must-watch live" content; rights inflation
(NFL: $110B over 11 years); streaming fragmentation (Amazon, Apple bidding alongside
traditional broadcast networks). (5) Studio/IP value: franchise IP (superhero,
animation) vs. prestige drama; content library valuation (DCF of existing cash flows
+ option value of future sequels/spin-offs); PVOD/streaming vs. theatrical windows.
(6) Podcast/audio: Spotify's audio strategy; acquisition multiples for podcast networks;
advertising vs. subscription monetization.
(7) PE value creation in media: cost restructuring, digital transformation, M&A
consolidation, and ultimately exit to strategic.
Format: Media Investment Framework with Sector Landscape, Sub-Sector Thesis,
Value Creation Playbook, and Exit Strategy.
Inputs: [MEDIA SUB-SECTOR | COMPANY | REVENUE | EBITDA | DIGITAL TRANSITION STAGE |
ENTRY VALUATION | PRIMARY VALUE CREATION LEVER | EXIT HORIZON]

title: The JPMorgan Private Bank Investment Advisory for Family Offices
prompt_text:
PROMPT 275 — The JPMorgan Private Bank Investment Advisory for Family Offices
Act as Head of Investment Advisory at JPMorgan Private Bank. Design a
comprehensive family office investment program.
Deliver: (1) Family office investment policy: IPS tailored to family's values, tax
situation, liquidity needs, generational timeline, and philanthropic objectives.
(2) Asset allocation for family offices: typically more alternatives-heavy than
institutional investors (40-60% alternatives — PE, real estate, hedge funds, direct
investments); why illiquidity premium is appropriate for long-horizon families.
(3) Direct investment program: co-investing in PE deals directly alongside sponsors;
family office club deals; proprietary deal flow from family's operating companies.
(4) Tax optimization: carried interest benefit for family office PE investments;
opportunity zone investments; grantor trust structures for PE fund investments;
international tax planning for families with multi-jurisdictional presence.
(5) Operating company integration: investment management of non-operating cash
from family business; pre-liquidity event planning; ESOP strategy for business exit.
(6) Next generation: financial education program for next-gen family members;
training account for next-gen with supervised portfolio management; governance
for bringing next-gen into family office investment committee.
(7) Philanthropy: DAF (Donor Advised Fund) vs. private foundation vs. LLC;
impact investing program within philanthropic capital; impact measurement.
Format: Family Office Investment Program with IPS, Asset Allocation, Direct Investment
Framework, Tax Strategy, Next-Gen Plan, and Philanthropy Integration.
Inputs: [FAMILY NET WORTH | OPERATING COMPANY STATUS | LIQUIDITY EVENT HORIZON |
GEOGRAPHY | FAMILY STAGE (1ST/2ND/3RD GEN) | PRIMARY FAMILY OBJECTIVE | TAX SITUATION]

title: The EY Forensic & Integrity: Anti-Bribery Compliance Program
prompt_text:
PROMPT 276 — The EY Forensic & Integrity: Anti-Bribery Compliance Program
Act as Partner at EY Forensic & Integrity Services. Design an anti-bribery
and corruption (ABC) compliance program for a global company.
Deliver: (1) Regulatory framework: US FCPA (Foreign Corrupt Practices Act) — anti-bribery
and books & records provisions; UK Bribery Act (broader — includes private sector
bribery, no facilitation payment exception); OECD Anti-Bribery Convention ratification
status by key markets. (2) Risk assessment: FCPA/UKBA risk factors — country risk
(CPI score), industry risk (government contract dependence), third-party risk
(agents, distributors, JV partners), transaction risk (M&A, licensing).
(3) Third-party due diligence: enhanced DD for high-risk third parties;
risk-tiered approach; ongoing monitoring (not just onboarding); red flag database screening.
(4) Policy design: gifts & entertainment policy (monetary limits, documentation,
approval thresholds); facilitation payment prohibition; political contributions policy;
charitable donations vetting.
(5) Training program: mandatory annual anti-bribery training; enhanced training for
high-risk functions (sales, procurement, government affairs, M&A); tone from the top.
(6) Monitoring and audit: anti-corruption audit procedures (expense reimbursement
analytics, agent payment review); continuous monitoring using data analytics
(anomaly detection on high-risk transactions).
(7) Investigation: when and how to conduct internal investigations; voluntary disclosure
to DOJ/SEC; cooperation credit and declination agreements.
Format: ABC Compliance Program with Risk Assessment, Third-Party DD Framework,
Policy Design, Training Program, Monitoring, and Investigation Protocol.
Inputs: [COMPANY | INDUSTRIES | GEOGRAPHIES | HIGH-RISK MARKETS | THIRD-PARTY COUNT |
EXISTING COMPLIANCE PROGRAM | RECENT INVESTIGATIONS OR CONCERNS]

title: The Advent International Fintech PE Investment
prompt_text:
PROMPT 277 — The Advent International Fintech PE Investment
Act as MD at Advent International's Fintech team. Build an investment thesis
for a fintech company at the growth or buyout stage.
Deliver: (1) Fintech PE landscape: payments processing (high-margin infrastructure),
lending tech (cyclical, credit risk), wealth tech, insurance tech, banking software
(core banking modernization), and RegTech. PE prefers later-stage, profitable, or
near-profitable fintechs vs. VC's earlier-stage loss-making model.
(2) Payments as preferred PE sub-sector: recurring revenue, low credit risk, network
effects, high switching costs; merchant acquiring, ISOs, PayFac software.
(3) Banking software consolidation: core banking modernization wave (legacy systems
being replaced) — SaaS banking platforms (Temenos, Finastra, nCino) vs.
new entrants (Thought Machine, 10x Banking); PE consolidation opportunity.
(4) Credit underwriting for fintech companies: revenue growth sustainability;
NRR; gross margin trajectory; path to profitability (EBITDA positive at what ARR?).
(5) Regulatory risk: how pending regulation affects fintech valuation (CFPB rules,
OCC fintech charter, EU PSD3); regulatory advantage for licensed vs. unlicensed fintechs.
(6) Value creation: buy-and-build (acquire complementary fintech products);
geographic expansion; enterprise sales motion upgrade.
(7) Exit: strategic sale to banking group or payment network; PE secondary; IPO.
Format: Fintech PE Framework with Sub-Sector Preferences, Payments Deep-Dive,
Banking Software Thesis, Credit Underwriting, Regulatory Risk, and Exit Analysis.
Inputs: [COMPANY | SUB-SECTOR | ARR OR REVENUE | EBITDA | GROWTH RATE | NRR |
ENTRY MULTIPLE | PRIMARY VALUE CREATION THESIS | HOLD PERIOD]

title: The IMF Monetary Policy Framework Design
prompt_text:
PROMPT 278 — The IMF Monetary Policy Framework Design
Act as Senior IMF Economist advising a central bank on monetary policy
framework design and operational implementation.
Deliver: (1) Monetary policy framework options: (a) Inflation targeting (IT) —
explicit CPI target, instrument independence, transparent communication;
(b) Exchange rate targeting — peg or crawling peg, sacrifices monetary independence;
(c) Money targeting — quantity theory approach, less popular post-1990s;
(d) Average Inflation Targeting (AIT) — Fed's 2020 framework — allows inflation
above target after undershooting.
(2) Inflation target design: point target vs. range; symmetric vs. asymmetric;
headline vs. core vs. supercore; medium-term (2-year) horizon.
(3) Central bank independence: instrument independence (CB sets rates freely) vs.
goal independence (government sets inflation target); legal framework; appointment
process for governor and MPC members; fiscal dominance risk.
(4) Monetary transmission: interest rate channel, exchange rate channel, bank lending
channel, asset price channel — how strong is each channel in this country's context?
(5) Communication framework: forward guidance (calendar-based vs. state-contingent);
inflation report / monetary policy report design; press conference conduct; Fan charts.
(6) Unconventional monetary policy: QE applicability in EM; zero lower bound management;
FX intervention rules (when and how to intervene without compromising IT credibility).
(7) Fiscal-monetary coordination: avoiding fiscal dominance; emergency financing
of government (COVID lessons); fiscal council role.
Format: Monetary Policy Framework Advisory with Framework Options, Target Design,
Independence Governance, Communication Framework, and Unconventional Tools.
Inputs: [COUNTRY | CURRENT FRAMEWORK | INFLATION TARGET | CURRENT INFLATION |
EXCHANGE RATE REGIME | CENTRAL BANK INDEPENDENCE LEVEL | PRIMARY FRAMEWORK CHALLENGE]

title: The Cerberus Capital Management Distressed PE & Financial Institutions
prompt_text:
PROMPT 279 — The Cerberus Capital Management Distressed PE & Financial Institutions
Act as MD at Cerberus Capital Management's Financial Institutions team.
Build an investment thesis for a distressed bank or financial institution.
Deliver: (1) Distressed bank investing thesis: banks trade below book value when
market fears loan losses exceed reserves; opportunity when fear exceeds reality;
historical examples (S&L crisis 1990s, European banks 2012-15, regional banks 2023).
(2) Bank distress analysis: NPL ratio (non-performing loans / total loans);
NPL coverage ratio (loan loss reserves / NPLs); tangible book value per share;
CET1 ratio and distance to regulatory minimum; earnings power without elevated provisions.
(3) Recovery scenarios: base case (bank stabilizes, provisions normalize, book value
recovers); bull case (strategic buyer pays premium to TBV); bear case (regulatory
resolution, significant dilution or wipe-out). (4) Regulatory engagement: OCC, FDIC,
state banking department — relationship management for troubled institution investment;
FDIC-assisted acquisition structure; change-in-control approval.
(5) Workout and asset management: Cerberus's operating capability to manage distressed
loan portfolios; NPL servicing platforms; REO (real estate owned) management.
(6) Capital injection structure: preferred stock (convertible to common at TBV);
warrants; rights offering; government capital (TARP-like structure implications).
(7) European bank opportunities: EBA stress test disclosures; Italian NPL market;
Spanish bank consolidation; Deutsche Bank restructuring as case study.
Format: Distressed Bank Investment Framework with NPL Analysis, Recovery Scenarios,
Regulatory Strategy, Capital Structure, and European Opportunities.
Inputs: [BANK NAME | COUNTRY | TOTAL ASSETS | NPL RATIO | CET1 RATIO | P/TBV |
EARNINGS TRAJECTORY | PRIMARY DISTRESS DRIVER | PROPOSED INVESTMENT STRUCTURE]

title: The MSCI ESG Ratings Methodology & Portfolio ESG Integration
prompt_text:
PROMPT 280 — The MSCI ESG Ratings Methodology & Portfolio ESG Integration
Act as Head of ESG Research at MSCI. Build a comprehensive ESG ratings
methodology and portfolio integration framework.
Deliver: (1) MSCI ESG Rating methodology: Key Issue identification (34 key ESG issues
mapped to 10 ESG themes); industry-specific materiality (which issues are most
financially material for each GICS sub-industry); exposure and management score
for each key issue → weighted industry-adjusted score → AAA-CCC rating.
(2) Data sources: company disclosures (annual report, sustainability report, CDP),
regulatory filings, government databases, NGO/media controversy monitoring;
unverified vs. verified data and its treatment.
(3) Controversy monitoring: ESG rating downgrade triggers (major controversies —
bribery, environmental incidents, labor violations); how quickly MSCI adjusts ratings
vs. the slow adjustment that created controversy (Wirecard maintained BBB until bankruptcy).
(4) Portfolio ESG integration: portfolio weighted average ESG score vs. benchmark;
ESG factor contribution to portfolio risk; ESG score improvement trajectory.
(5) SFDR (EU) article classification: Article 6, 8, 9 criteria; PAI (Principal
Adverse Impacts) indicators required for Article 8/9 funds; entity-level SFDR disclosure.
(6) Carbon footprint metrics: WACI (Weighted Average Carbon Intensity — tCO2e per
$M revenue); absolute financed emissions; portfolio temperature alignment (°C above
pre-industrial).
(7) ESG performance attribution: has ESG integration added or detracted from returns?
Evidence on ESG alpha.
Format: ESG Framework with Rating Methodology, Data Sources, Controversy Monitoring,
Portfolio Integration, SFDR Compliance, and Performance Attribution.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO TYPE | BENCHMARK | ESG RATING PROVIDER | SFDR ARTICLE TARGET |
CARBON FOOTPRINT TARGET | KEY ESG ISSUES FOR SECTOR | REPORTING REQUIREMENTS]

title: The Warburg Pincus Financial Services & Fintech Global PE
prompt_text:
PROMPT 281 — The Warburg Pincus Financial Services & Fintech Global PE
Act as MD at Warburg Pincus's Financial Services team. Build an investment
thesis for a global financial services PE investment.
Deliver: (1) Warburg's FS philosophy: invest globally in financial inclusion, fintech
disruption, and emerging market financial services growth; long-term hold.
(2) Sub-sector priorities: digital payments (high growth, network effects), insurance
technology (massive underinsurance in EM), alternative asset management (secular growth),
specialty finance (credit cards, BNPL, auto finance in underpenetrated markets).
(3) Financial inclusion thesis: 1.4B unbanked adults globally; mobile money as
infrastructure (M-Pesa, Wave, Airtel Money); digital credit for MSMEs.
(4) Insurtech in EM: insurance penetration 1-3% of GDP in Africa/India vs. 7-10%
in developed markets; distribution through mobile and embedded channels;
parametric products for farmers and MSMEs.
(5) Alternative asset manager investments: secular shift from public to private markets;
fee economics of $1B AUM manager vs. $100B — smaller managers offer asymmetric
return potential; co-investment pipeline access.
(6) Regulatory considerations: financial services require licensing; change of control
approvals; capital requirements as constraint on leverage and returns.
(7) Exit: IPO (financial services businesses often trade well publicly — premium
for growth + recurring fees); strategic sale to incumbent bank or global FI.
Format: FS PE Investment Framework with Sub-Sector Map, Financial Inclusion Thesis,
Insurtech Analysis, Alt Manager Investment, Regulatory Strategy, and Exit.
Inputs: [GEOGRAPHY | SUB-SECTOR | REVENUE | EBITDA OR ARR | REGULATORY LICENSE |
GROWTH RATE | ENTRY VALUATION | PRIMARY INVESTMENT THESIS]

title: The PwC Digital Assets & Crypto Accounting Framework
prompt_text:
PROMPT 282 — The PwC Digital Assets & Crypto Accounting Framework
Act as Partner at PwC's Digital Assets practice. Build a comprehensive
accounting and tax framework for crypto and digital asset businesses.
Deliver: (1) Crypto accounting under US GAAP: FASB ASU 2023-08 (fair value accounting
for crypto assets effective Dec 2024); previously held at cost less impairment;
new standard requires mark-to-market with gains/losses in P&L.
(2) Asset classification: crypto as intangible asset (GAAP) vs. financial instrument
debate; stablecoin accounting; NFT accounting; DeFi protocol accounting.
(3) Mining and staking income: crypto mined/staked is ordinary income at fair market
value on receipt date; cost basis = FMV at receipt; subsequent sale triggers capital
gain/loss.
(4) Exchange and broker accounting: customer crypto custody — is it on or off balance
sheet? SAB 121 (SEC guidance requiring on-balance-sheet treatment) and its withdrawal.
(5) Transfer pricing for crypto businesses: IP holding company in crypto; cross-border
trading desk allocation; OECD guidance on taxing crypto businesses.
(6) Tax: IRS Notice 2014-21 (crypto as property); every transaction is a taxable event;
wash sale rules don't apply to crypto (vs. securities); DeFi transaction complexity.
(7) Audit considerations: custody verification; private key access controls;
blockchain analytics for transaction completeness; counterparty concentration.
Format: Digital Assets Accounting Framework with GAAP Standards, Tax Treatment,
Audit Procedures, Exchange Accounting, and Transfer Pricing.
Inputs: [BUSINESS TYPE (EXCHANGE/MINER/INVESTOR/DeFI PROTOCOL) | CRYPTO HOLDINGS |
PRIMARY ACCOUNTING CONCERN | JURISDICTION | TAX COMPLEXITY | AUDIT REQUIREMENTS]

title: The Mitsubishi UFJ (MUFG) Japan Outbound M&A Advisory
prompt_text:
PROMPT 283 — The Mitsubishi UFJ (MUFG) Japan Outbound M&A Advisory
Act as MD at MUFG's Investment Banking group. Advise a Japanese corporation
on an outbound cross-border M&A transaction.
Deliver: (1) Japanese outbound M&A context: Japan's cash-rich corporations with

(2) Target markets for Japanese outbound: US (technology, healthcare, consumer);
Southeast Asia (financial services, infrastructure, consumer); Europe (technology,
industrial, luxury); India (pharmaceuticals, IT services).
(3) Cultural and governance challenges: Japanese consensus-based decision making
(nemawashi) slows transaction timelines; post-close management style differences;

(4) Financing: Japanese banks provide low-cost acquisition financing (historically
near-zero yen rates); cross-currency swap for USD/EUR acquisition financing;

(6) Integration: Japanese language barrier in C-suite integration; cultural training;
expatriate assignment of Japanese managers; retaining target management.
(7) Governance: compliance with Japan's Revised Corporate Governance Code;

Format: Outbound M&A Advisory with Market Selection, Cultural Challenges, Financing,
Valuation Discipline, Integration Strategy, and Governance Framework.

RATIONALE | FINANCING STRUCTURE | PRIMARY INTEGRATION CHALLENGE]

title: The Blackrock Investment Institute: Geopolitical Risk Premium
prompt_text:
PROMPT 284 — The Blackrock Investment Institute: Geopolitical Risk Premium
Act as Head of Geopolitical Research at BlackRock Investment Institute.
Build a framework for pricing geopolitical risk into asset allocation.
Deliver: (1) Geopolitical risk taxonomy: interstate conflict (Russia-Ukraine, Taiwan
Strait), great power competition (US-China tech/trade war), regional instability
(Middle East, Korean Peninsula), domestic political risk (populism, policy reversal),
terrorism and non-state actors.
(2) Geopolitical risk premium quantification: historical asset returns during
geopolitical events; VaR contribution from geopolitical factor; how to price
geopolitical tail risk into expected returns.
(3) US-China decoupling scenarios: (a) Managed competition (current trajectory —
trade restrictions but no military conflict); (b) Technology cold war (semiconductor
export controls, TikTok-style app restrictions); (c) Taiwan kinetic conflict
(catastrophic scenario — $10T+ global GDP impact estimate).
(4) Portfolio implications: de-globalization → commodity supply chain disruption →
commodity price inflation; security of supply → defense spending → defense
sector overweight; friend-shoring → manufacturing in allied countries.
(5) Safe haven assets in geopolitical stress: gold (monetary hedge, geopolitical hedge);
USD (reserve currency premium); Swiss franc; short-duration US Treasuries.
(6) Resilient portfolio construction: geographic diversification beyond financial
optimization; avoiding extreme country concentration; options overlay for tail risk.
(7) Scenario planning: assign probability to each geopolitical scenario; stress test
portfolio under each; ensure portfolio can survive worst-case without permanent loss.
Format: Geopolitical Risk Framework with Risk Taxonomy, Premium Quantification,
US-China Scenarios, Portfolio Implications, Safe Havens, and Scenario Planning.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | GEOGRAPHIC EXPOSURES | PRIMARY GEOPOLITICAL CONCERN |
RISK TOLERANCE | SAFE HAVEN CURRENT ALLOCATION | TAIL RISK BUDGET]

title: The Allianz Global Investors Convertible Bond Arbitrage
prompt_text:
PROMPT 285 — The Allianz Global Investors Convertible Bond Arbitrage
Act as PM at Allianz Global Investors' Convertible Bond team. Build a
convertible bond arbitrage strategy.
Deliver: (1) CB arb mechanics: buy convertible bond (long gamma, long vol) + short
the underlying stock (hedge delta) = delta-neutral position that profits from
realized volatility exceeding implied volatility (gamma scalping).
(2) Theoretical edge: CB implied vol is often lower than listed options implied vol
for the same issuer — buy cheap vol in CB market, sell expensive vol in listed market.
(3) Delta hedging: calculate delta of CB (partial derivative of CB price vs. stock);
short stock at delta to become delta-neutral; re-hedge as stock moves (dynamic delta).
(4) Gamma scalping P&L: each time stock moves significantly, the arb trader buys
low and sells high on the delta hedge — capturing the gamma premium.
(5) Credit risk: the bond component of the CB carries issuer credit risk; credit
hedge via CDS or proxy hedge (short IG credit index if issuer is IG).
(6) Funding and leverage: CB arb funds typically use 2-4× leverage; repo market
for CB funding; short rebate on borrowed stock.
(7) Risk factors: vol compression (implied vol declines, CB cheap on delta basis);
takeover (instant delta=1, eliminates optionality); credit events; short squeeze.
Format: CB Arb Strategy with Delta Hedging Mechanics, Gamma Scalping, Vol Comparison,
Credit Hedge, Funding Structure, and Risk Factors.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | LEVERAGE | VOL TARGET | CREDIT HEDGE APPROACH |
UNIVERSE (US/EU/GLOBAL) | LIQUIDITY CONSTRAINTS | PRIMARY STRATEGY RISK]

global diversified portfolio (45% Singapore, 55% international today).
(5) Technology investments: global tech portfolio (Alibaba, Microsoft, PayPal historical);

title: The McKinsey Cybersecurity Risk & Resilience Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 287 — The McKinsey Cybersecurity Risk & Resilience Strategy
Act as Senior Partner at McKinsey's Cybersecurity practice. Build a
comprehensive cyber risk management and resilience strategy.
Deliver: (1) Cyber threat landscape: nation-state attacks (critical infrastructure,
IP theft), ransomware (RaaS — Ransomware-as-a-Service business model), supply chain
attacks (SolarWinds-style), and insider threats.
(2) Cyber risk quantification: FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk) model;
expected loss calculation (threat frequency × vulnerability × magnitude); cyber
VaR; how to present cyber risk in financial terms to the Board.
(3) Cybersecurity architecture: Zero Trust (never trust, always verify — replace
perimeter-based security); cloud security posture management; endpoint detection
and response (EDR); SIEM + SOAR for detection and response.
(4) Third-party risk: supply chain cyber risk management; vendor assessment program;
critical vendor monitoring; contractual security requirements.
(5) Incident response: playbook for ransomware (isolate, preserve, notify, negotiate vs.
restore from backup); regulatory notification requirements (SEC 4-day disclosure,
GDPR 72-hour, HIPAA, PCI-DSS); breach cost estimation.
(6) Cyber insurance: policy structure; sub-limits for ransomware, business interruption,
third-party liability; underwriting requirements (MFA, EDR, patching SLA).
(7) Regulatory compliance: SEC cybersecurity rules; NIS2 (EU); DORA (financial sector);
FedRAMP; SOC 2 Type II.
Format: Cybersecurity Strategy with Threat Landscape, Risk Quantification, Zero Trust
Architecture, Third-Party Risk, Incident Response, Insurance, and Compliance.
Inputs: [COMPANY TYPE | INDUSTRY | REVENUE | CURRENT SECURITY MATURITY |
REGULATORY REQUIREMENTS | CYBER INSURANCE STATUS | PRIMARY THREAT CONCERN]

title: The MSCI ESG Ratings & Index Construction Methodology
prompt_text:
PROMPT 288 — The MSCI ESG Ratings & Index Construction Methodology
Act as Director at MSCI ESG Research. Explain MSCI's ESG rating methodology
and its application in index construction for institutional investors.
Deliver: (1) MSCI ESG Rating methodology: industry-specific material ESG issues;
34 ESG key issues mapped to 10 themes; company scoring on each issue
(laggard, average, leader); weighted average score → CCC to AAA rating.
(2) Materiality framework: different industries have different material ESG issues
(oil & gas: carbon emissions, oil spills; banks: data privacy, governance;
retail: supply chain labor standards); explain how materiality is determined.
(3) ESG data collection: company disclosures (annual report, CDP, CSR reports);
media monitoring for controversies; government/regulatory data; alternative data.
(4) Controversy monitoring: immediate score impact for severe ESG controversies
(environmental violations, fraud, governance failures); distinction from rating.
(5) MSCI ESG Indexes: MSCI ESG Leaders (50% of each MSCI sector by ESG score);
MSCI SRI (rigorous exclusions + top 25% ESG score); MSCI Climate Paris Aligned.
(6) Criticism of ESG ratings: inter-rater disagreement (MSCI vs. Sustainalytics vs.
S&P ESG — correlation only 0.4-0.6); backward-looking; gaming by companies
with better disclosure teams; academic evidence on ESG alpha is mixed.
(7) Index impact on capital: MSCI index inclusion/exclusion drives passive capital
flows; ESG index weight changes trigger systematic rebalancing by passive managers.
Format: ESG Methodology with Rating Framework, Materiality Map, Controversy Scoring,
Index Construction, Methodology Critique, and Capital Flow Analysis.
Inputs: [COMPANY OR SECTOR | CURRENT ESG RATING | KEY ESG ISSUES | CONTROVERSY HISTORY |
TARGET INDEX INCLUSION | PRIMARY ESG IMPROVEMENT OBJECTIVE | INVESTOR BASE]

title: The Lazard Infrastructure Finance: US Water Utility Advisory
prompt_text:
PROMPT 289 — The Lazard Infrastructure Finance: US Water Utility Advisory
Act as MD at Lazard's Infrastructure Finance group advising a water utility
on financing, M&A, and rate case strategy.
Deliver: (1) Water utility financial model: rate base (regulated assets in service);
allowed ROE (WACC for water utilities — typically 9-10%); revenue requirement
(cost-plus tariff model); earned vs. allowed ROE gap.
(2) Water infrastructure investment need: $1T US water infrastructure investment
need over 20 years; lead pipe replacement (LCRR), PFAS remediation, meter modernization.
(3) Rate case strategy: forward test year advocacy; accumulated deferred income tax
(ADIT) treatment; AFUDC (Allowance for Funds Used During Construction); performance
incentive mechanisms for water quality.
(4) Infrastructure affordability: low-income customer assistance programs;
rate affordability analysis (benchmark: monthly water bill < 1% of median HHI);
EPA affordability constraints on rate case outcomes.
(5) M&A in water: consolidation of municipal systems (asset condition risk, operator
expertise gap, access to capital); fair market value (FMV) acquisition laws
(allow private utilities to pay FMV premium over book in rate base).
(6) Green financing: water revenue bonds for infrastructure projects; green bond
eligibility for water quality and conservation investments.
(7) Privatization: why municipalities sell water systems (capital needs, pension
obligations, operating efficiency); valuation premium for private acquirer.
Format: Water Utility Advisory with Regulatory Model, Rate Case Strategy, Infrastructure
Investment Plan, M&A Framework, and Green Financing.
Inputs: [UTILITY NAME | RATE BASE | ALLOWED ROE | NEXT RATE CASE | INFRASTRUCTURE
NEED | ACQUISITION INTEREST | BOND RATING | PRIMARY STRATEGIC OBJECTIVE]

title: The Pantheon Ventures Fund-of-Funds PE Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 290 — The Pantheon Ventures Fund-of-Funds PE Strategy
Act as Managing Partner at Pantheon Ventures. Build a PE fund-of-funds
strategy for a pension fund or endowment client.
Deliver: (1) Fund-of-funds rationale: diversification across top-tier managers
(access that individual LPs cannot achieve alone); economies of scale in LP operations;
fee drag (management fee on management fee) trade-off vs. access benefit.
(2) Manager selection methodology: quantitative (performance, ranking, quartile consistency)
+ qualitative (investment process, team stability, culture, portfolio management).
(3) Portfolio construction: vintage year diversification (3-4 year commitment pace);
strategy diversification (buyout, growth, venture, credit); geographic diversification;
fund size diversification (mega vs. mid-market).
(4) Access to top managers: oversubscribed top-tier funds (KKR, Sequoia, Accel);
how Pantheon earns allocation (LP tenure, co-investment commitment, secondary market
participation); relationship-based access vs. merit-based access.
(5) Secondaries integration: using secondary market purchases to accelerate deployment
and reduce J-curve; pricing secondary purchases within FoF.
(6) Co-investment program: allocating 20-30% of capital to co-investments alongside
GP fund investments; fee savings; portfolio concentration management.
(7) Performance reporting: TVPI, DPI, RVPI by vintage and strategy; PME (Public Market
Equivalent) benchmark comparison; attribution analysis.
Format: PE FoF Strategy with Manager Selection, Portfolio Construction, Access Strategy,
Secondaries/Co-Investment, Performance Reporting, and Fee Analysis.
Inputs: [INVESTOR TYPE | AUM TO ALLOCATE | RETURN TARGET | VINTAGE DIVERSIFICATION |
CO-INVESTMENT APPETITE | MANAGER CONCENTRATION LIMIT | REPORTING REQUIREMENTS]

title: The Goldman Sachs Asset Management (GSAM) Hedge Fund Solutions
prompt_text:

Act as Head of Hedge Fund Solutions at GSAM. Design a hedge fund allocation

(4) Terms negotiation: management fee (industry moving from 2/20 to 1.5/15 or flat);
lock-up and liquidity provisions; MFN clause; separately managed account negotiation.
(5) Portfolio monitoring: monthly return attribution; factor exposure monitoring (ensure
paying for alpha not disguised beta); transparency reporting.
(6) Operational due diligence: fund administrator independence; prime broker diversification;
valuation procedures; regulatory compliance (SEC RIA, CFTC registration).
(7) Redemption risk management: liquidity waterfall (liquid HFs first, locked-up HFs
with gate provisions); stress test for simultaneous redemption.
Format: Hedge Fund Solutions Framework with Strategy Allocation, Manager Selection,
Terms Negotiation, Portfolio Monitoring, Operational DD, and Liquidity Management.
