REQUIREMENTS | FEE BUDGET | TRANSPARENCY REQUIREMENTS | PRIMARY HF OBJECTIVE]

title: The Rothschild Fairness & Solvency Assessment: Dividend Capacity
prompt_text:
PROMPT 292 — The Rothschild Fairness & Solvency Assessment: Dividend Capacity
Act as Partner at Rothschild advising the Board of a holding company on
dividend upstream capacity and inter-company financial support.
Deliver: (1) Holding company dividend assessment: can subsidiaries legally and financially
upstream dividends to the parent? Analysis by jurisdiction (distributable reserves,
thin cap, transfer pricing, minority interest rights).
(2) Solvency tests: statutory solvency (balance sheet test — assets > liabilities);
cash flow solvency (ability to pay debts as they fall due); both must be satisfied
before dividends can be paid.
(3) Financial assistance rules: UK Companies Act s.678 and international equivalents;
restrictions on financial assistance for own share acquisition; whitewash procedure.
(4) Intragroup loan capacity: loan amount, interest rate (arm's length — benchmarked
to external credit), tenor, repayment capacity; intercompany interest deductibility
(thin cap, EBITDA interest limitation rules).
(5) Restricted payment covenants: analysis of existing debt covenants limiting upstreaming;
basket analysis (available restricted payment capacity); builder basket mechanics.
(6) Board fiduciary duties: directors' duty to consider interests of creditors when
near insolvency; wrongful trading risk in UK; fraudulent transfer risk in US.
(7) Waterfall modeling: track cash from operating subsidiary up through the group;
quantify the maximum extractable cash in compliance with all constraints.
Format: Dividend Capacity Analysis with Legal Solvency Tests, Jurisdiction Review,
RP Covenant Analysis, Intragroup Loan Framework, and Cash Waterfall Model.
Inputs: [HOLDING CO STRUCTURE | KEY SUBSIDIARIES | DEBT COVENANTS | JURISDICTION |
DIVIDENDS SOUGHT | MINORITY SHAREHOLDERS | PRIMARY CONSTRAINT CONCERN]

title: The Advent International Software-as-a-Service Emerging Markets
prompt_text:
PROMPT 293 — The Advent International Software-as-a-Service Emerging Markets
Act as MD at Advent International. Build an investment thesis for a B2B SaaS
company targeting emerging market businesses.
Deliver: (1) EM SaaS opportunity: formalization of EM SME sector creating ERP/accounting
demand; leapfrogging legacy software generation (cloud-native from start);
lower competition from global SaaS players (Salesforce, SAP priced for DM).
(2) EM SaaS characteristics: lower ACV ($1-5K/year vs. $10-50K in DM); higher
churn risk (SME mortality rate); local language requirements; local payment methods
(mobile money, bank transfer).
(3) Target geographies: India (massive SME base, English, digital-first), Nigeria
(fastest-growing SaaS market in Africa), LATAM (Brazil/Mexico formalization),
SEA (Indonesia, Vietnam).
(4) Unit economics in EM: CAC is lower (cheaper digital advertising, local sales);
ACV is lower; LTV may be lower or equivalent if churn is controlled; payback
period similar to DM if economics are managed.
(5) Distribution: channel partners (local accountants, banks, telcos as distributors
reach SMEs cost-effectively); embedded distribution (payments + ERP bundle).
(6) Localization requirements: local language, local tax compliance (GST/VAT complexity
in India, Brazil), local payment rails, local support.
(7) Exit: regional strategic acquirers (African telcos, Indian conglomerates); global
SaaS acquirers expanding into EM (Sage, Xero, Intuit); PE secondaries.
Format: EM SaaS Investment Framework with Opportunity Analysis, Unit Economics,
Distribution Strategy, Localization Requirements, and Exit.
Inputs: [GEOGRAPHY | VERTICAL (ACCOUNTING/ERP/HR/PAYMENTS) | ARR | NRR | CHURN |
CAC | PRIMARY DISTRIBUTION CHANNEL | ENTRY VALUATION | TARGET RETURN]

title: The HSBC Project Finance: LNG Terminal and Regasification
prompt_text:
PROMPT 294 — The HSBC Project Finance: LNG Terminal and Regasification
Act as MD at HSBC's Project Finance group. Structure the financing for
an LNG import terminal or export project.
Deliver: (1) LNG project finance overview: capital-intensive ($500M-$10B+);
long-lived assets (30+ years); supported by long-term offtake agreements (15-20 year
SPAs — Sale and Purchase Agreements).
(2) Revenue structure: tolling agreement (charge for regasification/liquefaction
capacity regardless of throughput) vs. merchant (volume risk); FSRU
(Floating Storage and Regasification Unit) vs. onshore terminal.
(3) Project finance structuring: SPV; 70-80% senior debt; ECA support (Export Credit
Agency — US Ex-Im, JBIC, K-EXIM for equipment from respective countries);
commercial banks; project bonds.
(4) DSCR analysis: DSCR > 1.4× required during loan life; debt service reserve account
(DSRA) at 6 months; LNG price and volume sensitivity to DSCR.
(5) Offtake credit analysis: creditworthiness of offtaker (gas utility, power company,
industrial user); S&P rating required for non-recourse lenders; parent guarantee.
(6) Construction risk: fixed-price EPC contract; performance bond; technical risk
insurance; independent engineer role; force majeure provisions.
(7) Environmental and social (E&S): IFC Performance Standards; ESIA (Environmental
and Social Impact Assessment); community engagement; Equator Principles compliance.
Format: LNG Project Finance with Revenue Structure, Debt Package, DSCR Analysis,
Offtake Credit, Construction Risk, and E&S Framework.
Inputs: [PROJECT LOCATION | CAPACITY | TECHNOLOGY (FSRU/ONSHORE) | OFFTAKER |
PROJECT COST | TARGET LEVERAGE | ECA SUPPORT | PRIMARY RISK CONCERN]

title: The Sequoia Heritage Family Investment Office Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 295 — The Sequoia Heritage Family Investment Office Strategy
Act as CIO at Sequoia Heritage (the family office arm for Sequoia partners).
Build a multi-generational family investment strategy.
Deliver: (1) Multi-generational framework: investment horizon of 20-30+ years; preservation
of real purchasing power across generations; liquidity for current generation needs.
(2) Asset allocation: 40-50% private markets (PE, venture, growth equity); 20-25%
public equity; 10-15% real assets (real estate, infrastructure); 10-15% credit
(private credit, bonds); 5% gold/commodity; 5-10% liquid alternatives.
(3) VC access: direct relationships with top-tier VCs (a16z, Benchmark, Greylock);
co-investment in late-stage growth rounds; secondary VC fund positions.
(4) Direct investment: principal investing alongside family relationships and deal flow;
management of concentrated single-stock positions from founder liquidity.
(5) Tax structure: dynasty trust for multi-generational transfer; irrevocable trusts
(GRAT, IDGT) for inter-generational transfer of appreciated assets; tax loss
harvesting program for public portfolio.
(6) Governance: investment committee composition (family + independent advisors);
voting rights for next-generation family members; family values statement
integrated into investment policy.
(7) Philanthropy: private foundation governance; DAF vs. foundation trade-offs;
impact investing integration (PRIs — Program-Related Investments).
Format: Family Office Strategy with Asset Allocation, VC Access, Direct Investment,
Tax Structure, Governance Framework, and Philanthropy Integration.
Inputs: [FAMILY NET WORTH | LIQUIDITY NEEDS | GENERATIONAL STAGE |
OPERATING BUSINESS CONCENTRATION | DOMICILE | PHILANTHROPIC GOALS | RISK TOLERANCE]

title: The Citadel Enterprise: Insurance Operations & Underwriting
prompt_text:
PROMPT 296 — The Citadel Enterprise: Insurance Operations & Underwriting
Act as Chief Risk Officer at a specialty insurance company. Build a
comprehensive underwriting and portfolio risk management framework.
Deliver: (1) Insurance value chain: product design → underwriting → pricing →
distribution → claims → reserving; where value is created and destroyed.
(2) Underwriting discipline: risk selection criteria; price adequacy testing
(loss ratio analysis by segment); capacity allocation by line of business;
technical underwriting standards.
(3) Pricing methodology: actuarial rate-making (loss development triangles, trend
analysis, credibility weighting); rate adequacy by class; pricing model validation.
(4) Reinsurance strategy: XL (excess of loss) vs. quota share; how reinsurance
changes the volatility and profitability of the portfolio; reinsurer credit risk.
(5) Reserve adequacy: loss reserves by accident year; IBNR (Incurred But Not Reported)
methodology; reserve development risk; actuarial review independence.
(6) CAT model management: RMS/AIR/Verisk probabilistic catastrophe models; EP curves
(Exceedance Probability); PML (Probable Maximum Loss) at 1-in-100 year;
capital requirement from CAT exposure.
(7) Capital allocation by line: risk-adjusted profitability (RAROC) by business line;
allocate capital based on VaR or TailVaR; identify lines earning below cost of capital.
Format: Insurance Risk Framework with Underwriting Standards, Pricing Methodology,
Reinsurance Structure, Reserve Adequacy, CAT Model, and Capital Allocation.
Inputs: [INSURER TYPE | LINES OF BUSINESS | PREMIUM VOLUME | LOSS RATIO HISTORY |
REINSURANCE PROGRAM | CAT EXPOSURE | CAPITAL POSITION | PRIMARY RISK CONCERN]

title: The Linklaters Private Equity Fund Formation & LP Terms
prompt_text:
PROMPT 297 — The Linklaters Private Equity Fund Formation & LP Terms
Act as Partner at Linklaters' Investment Funds group. Design the fund
terms and legal structure for a new PE fund.
Deliver: (1) Fund legal structure: Delaware LP (standard US); Cayman Islands LP
(offshore, tax neutral); Luxembourg SCSp (EU AIFMD compliant); parallel fund
structures for different investor bases.
(2) Key economic terms: management fee (1.5-2% of committed capital during investment period,
reducing to 1-1.25% on invested capital thereafter); carried interest (20%);
hurdle rate (8% preferred return); catch-up (100% GP catch-up to hurdle); waterfall
(European: whole-fund return before carry; American: deal-by-deal carry with clawback).
(3) LP protections: LPAC (Limited Partner Advisory Committee) — consent rights for
conflicts, key man provisions; key man suspension clause (pause investments if key
person departs); no-fault GP removal (75% LP vote); clawback provision.
(4) Investment restrictions: portfolio company size limits; sector and geography limits;
single-investment concentration (max % of fund); leverage limits; co-investment policy.
(5) Subscription mechanics: drawdowns (capital calls); distribution reinvestment period;
commitment period (3-5 years); fund life (10 years + 2 extensions).
(6) Regulatory: AIFMD registration (EU); SEC RIA registration (US); FATCA/CRS for
offshore funds; AML/KYC for LP subscriptions.
(7) Market terms evolution: ESG side letters; most favored nation clauses; fee offsets
from deal fees; subscription credit facilities and LP concerns.
Format: Fund Formation Advisory with Legal Structure, Economic Terms, LP Protections,
Investment Restrictions, Regulatory Compliance, and Market Evolution.
Inputs: [GP NAME | STRATEGY | TARGET SIZE | PRIMARY LP BASE | DOMICILE PREFERENCE |
KEY ECONOMIC TERMS | REGULATORY JURISDICTIONS | PRIMARY LP CONCERN]

title: The CPPIB Total Portfolio Approach & Risk Factor Framework
prompt_text:
PROMPT 298 — The CPPIB Total Portfolio Approach & Risk Factor Framework
Act as Managing Director at Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPPIB).
Build a total portfolio approach (TPA) investment framework.
Deliver: (1) CPPIB TPA philosophy: optimize the whole portfolio rather than managing
asset classes in silos; every investment competes for capital against all alternatives
on a risk-adjusted basis; reference portfolio (passive benchmark) as the hurdle.
(2) Risk factor framework: decompose all portfolio positions into underlying risk factors
(equity beta, duration, credit spread, illiquidity premium, inflation, FX);
monitor factor concentration across all assets — private and public.
(3) Absolute vs. relative return focus: TPA focuses on absolute return above the
reference portfolio; active risk budget is the sum of all active positions vs. reference.
(4) Private market integration: PE and infrastructure valued using fair value; how
CPPIB marks-to-market private assets quarterly; private asset factor exposure
mapped to public factor proxies for risk aggregation.
(5) Currency management: CPPIB's global currency hedging program; partial hedge
on non-CAD assets; currency as a separate risk factor allocation.
(6) Sustainable investing: CPPIB's investment-focused approach to ESG
(not exclusions-based); engagement with portfolio companies; climate scenario analysis.
(7) Governance: Total Fund Management (TFM) team; Investment Planning Committee;
Board oversight; performance attribution vs. reference portfolio.
Format: TPA Framework with Risk Factor Model, Private Market Integration, Currency
Strategy, Reference Portfolio Construction, ESG Approach, and Governance.
Inputs: [FUND SIZE | CURRENT ASSET MIX | REFERENCE PORTFOLIO | RISK BUDGET |
PRIVATE MARKET ALLOCATION | CURRENCY POLICY | PRIMARY INVESTMENT OBJECTIVE]

title: The Bain Capital Public Equity: Deep Value Stock Analysis
prompt_text:
PROMPT 299 — The Bain Capital Public Equity: Deep Value Stock Analysis
Act as PM at Bain Capital Public Equity. Apply deep value analysis to
identify a materially undervalued public company.
Deliver: (1) Bain's deep value approach: bottom-up, fundamental value investing; buy
businesses trading significantly below intrinsic value with a catalyst for re-rating;
long-term hold (3-7 years); concentrated (15-25 positions).
(2) Sum-of-parts (SOTP) analysis: for conglomerates or complex businesses — value
each business unit separately at appropriate multiple; compare to consolidated
market cap; quantify the conglomerate discount.
(3) Hidden asset analysis: undervalued real estate on balance sheet (below market book
value); IP not reflected in earnings; minority stakes not properly valued by market;
NOL carryforwards with option value.
(4) Normalized earnings power: strip out non-recurring items; adjust for cyclicality
(mid-cycle earnings vs. current-trough earnings); calculate owner earnings.
(5) Catalyst identification: management change; activist involvement; strategic review;
spin-off; asset sale; buyback acceleration; credit rating improvement.
(6) Downside protection: asset coverage (book value, liquidation value); FCF yield;
dividend as a floor; share buybacks providing floor to valuation.
(7) Position sizing: conviction-based sizing; maximum single position 8-10%; how to
build a position without moving the stock (block trading, dark pool).
Format: Deep Value Analysis with SOTP, Hidden Assets, Normalized Earnings, Catalyst
Timeline, Downside Protection, and Position Building Strategy.
Inputs: [COMPANY | TICKER | CURRENT MARKET CAP | BUSINESS SEGMENTS | NORMALIZED
EARNINGS | HIDDEN ASSETS | PRIMARY CATALYST | INTRINSIC VALUE ESTIMATE]

title: The McKinsey Future of Finance: CFO 2030 Roadmap
prompt_text:
PROMPT 300 — The McKinsey Future of Finance: CFO 2030 Roadmap
Act as Senior Partner at McKinsey. Build a CFO 2030 strategic agenda covering
the transformation of the finance function over the next 5 years.
Deliver: (1) CFO role evolution: from scorekeeper → business partner → value architect;
CFO increasingly owns digital transformation, data strategy, and ESG reporting.
(2) AI and automation roadmap: by 2030, 50-70% of transactional finance tasks automated;
Gen AI for narrative generation, anomaly detection, predictive analytics; identify
finance roles that will be eliminated, transformed, and created.
(3) Real-time finance: from periodic close (monthly/quarterly) to continuous close
and real-time P&L; what technology and process changes enable continuous close.
(4) ESG finance leadership: CFO ownership of ESG reporting (ISSB, CSRD, SEC climate
rules); integrating ESG KPIs into management reporting; sustainability-linked financing.
(5) Finance talent 2030: T-shaped finance professionals (deep technical + broad business);
data scientist integration into FP&A; decline of traditional accountants;
finance as a talent destination for tech-savvy graduates.
(6) Technology stack 2030: cloud ERP (SAP S/4 HANA, Oracle Fusion); AI-native FP&A
(Anaplan, Pigment, Cube); embedded analytics; natural language interfaces for financial data.
(7) Risk and resilience: CFO's expanding risk mandate (cyber, climate, geopolitical,
operational resilience); treasury risk management evolution; real-time risk dashboards.
Format: CFO 2030 Roadmap with Role Evolution, AI Automation Plan, Real-Time Finance,
ESG Leadership, Talent Strategy, Technology Stack, and Risk Framework.
Inputs: [COMPANY REVENUE | INDUSTRY | CURRENT FINANCE MATURITY | CFO TENURE |
DIGITAL INVESTMENT BUDGET | PRIMARY TRANSFORMATION PRIORITY | BOARD EXPECTATIONS]

title: The Blackstone BX Credit: Asset-Based Finance Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 301 — The Blackstone BX Credit: Asset-Based Finance Strategy
Act as MD at Blackstone Credit's Asset-Based Finance team. Build an investment
strategy for asset-backed private credit opportunities.
Deliver: (1) Asset-based finance universe: aviation finance, royalty monetization,
equipment leasing, litigation finance, insurance-linked assets, consumer ABS,
residential mortgage credit, and trade receivables.
(2) Aviation finance: aircraft as collateral (liquid secondary market, global demand);
operating lease vs. finance lease; aircraft type (narrowbody vs. widebody) liquidity;
airline credit vs. asset-only financing.
(3) Royalty monetization: pharmaceutical royalties (patent-protected cash flows),
music royalties (catalog acquisitions), technology royalties; valuation using
DCF on contracted cash flows; risk of early payment or patent challenge.
(4) Litigation finance: provide capital to law firms or plaintiffs in exchange for
a share of settlement/judgment; investment-grade-like risk profile if diversified;
duration and outcome uncertainty as key risks.
(5) Residential mortgage credit: non-QM (Non-Qualified Mortgage) loans; DSCR loans
for investors; bridge loans; securitization pathway for portfolio liquidity.
(6) Structural protections across ABF: overcollateralization; first lien on specific
assets; cash flow waterfall; servicer replacement provisions.
(7) Return targets: ABF gross yield 8-14%; lower correlation to corporate credit;
illiquidity premium for complex structures.
Format: Asset-Based Finance Strategy with Sub-Asset Class Map, Aviation/Royalty
Deep-Dives, Structural Protections, Return Analysis, and Portfolio Construction.
Inputs: [FOCUS AREA | DEAL SIZE | COLLATERAL TYPE | TENOR | YIELD TARGET |
STRUCTURAL PREFERENCES | PRIMARY RISK CONCERN | LEVERAGE]

title: The PIMCO Emerging Market Debt Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 302 — The PIMCO Emerging Market Debt Strategy
Act as MD at PIMCO's Emerging Markets portfolio management team.
Build a comprehensive EM debt investment strategy.
Deliver: (1) EM debt universe: EM hard currency sovereign (EMBI Global), EM hard currency
corporate (CEMBI), EM local currency sovereign (GBI-EM), EM frontier.
(2) Hard currency sovereign analysis: external debt sustainability (DSA); political
risk premium; reserves adequacy (import coverage, debt service coverage);
primary fiscal balance requirement for debt stabilization.
(3) EM corporate credit: key issuer countries (China, Brazil, Mexico, India, UAE);
sector concentration (energy, financials, real estate in China); EM corporate
fundamentals vs. EM sovereign risk — which risk dominates?
(4) Local currency investing: real yield attractiveness; inflation-adjusted carry;
FX carry-to-vol ratio; which EM central banks are most credible?
(5) Country selection framework: score 20+ EM countries on growth, inflation, fiscal
(primary balance), external (current account), political risk, and central bank
credibility.
(6) Duration management: EM local duration positioning; how to construct a duration-
neutral EM local bond portfolio to isolate carry/spread.
(7) Tail risk in EM: sudden stop in capital flows (1997 Asian crisis, 2013 taper
tantrum); contagion from DM stress; IMF program sequencing.
Format: EM Debt Strategy with Market Overview, Country Selection Scorecard, Hard vs.
Local Currency Analysis, Duration Framework, Tail Risk Management, and Portfolio.
Inputs: [BENCHMARK | HARD VS. LOCAL PREFERENCE | DURATION BUDGET | FX HEDGE POLICY |
COUNTRY LIMITS | CREDIT QUALITY FLOOR | PRIMARY EM MACRO VIEW]

title: The Ernst & Young IPO Readiness Assessment
prompt_text:
PROMPT 303 — The Ernst & Young IPO Readiness Assessment
Act as Partner at EY's Transaction Advisory Services. Design a comprehensive
IPO readiness program for a pre-IPO company.
Deliver: (1) IPO readiness dimensions: financial reporting (audited financials, GAAP
conversion), governance (board independence, audit committee), systems (ERP, close
cycle), management (CFO capability, IR function), legal (subsidiary clean-up, IP
ownership), and narrative (investment thesis, growth story).
(2) Financial reporting requirements: 2-3 years of audited financials (PCAOB standards
for NYSE/Nasdaq); quarterly reporting cadence post-IPO; segment disclosure;
non-GAAP reconciliation policy.
(3) SOX readiness: 404(b) external audit of controls in Year 1 for large accelerated
filers; internal control framework; material weakness identification and remediation.
(4) Governance build: independent director recruitment (minimum 3 independents;
audit committee financial expert); Compensation and Nomination committees;
board charter and committee charters.
(5) Investor relations preparation: equity story development (why invest, what drives
growth, how sustainable); management roadshow training; analyst day design;
financial model for sell-side analysts.
(6) S-1 / Prospectus preparation: business description; risk factors; MD&A; financial
statements; use of proceeds; lock-up agreements.
(7) Pre-IPO timeline: 12-18 month readiness program; audit firm selection and
onboarding; underwriter selection; PCAOB registration.
Format: IPO Readiness Framework with Readiness Assessment, Financial Reporting Plan,
SOX Program, Governance Build, IR Preparation, and Pre-IPO Timeline.
Inputs: [COMPANY | INDUSTRY | REVENUE | EBITDA | TARGET IPO DATE | CURRENT AUDIT
STATUS | SOX READINESS | PRIMARY READINESS GAP | TARGET LISTING VENUE]

title: The Two Sigma Investments: Machine Learning in Finance
prompt_text:
PROMPT 304 — The Two Sigma Investments: Machine Learning in Finance
Act as Head of Research at Two Sigma. Build a machine learning research
framework for financial signal generation and portfolio management.
Deliver: (1) ML research process: hypothesis generation → data sourcing → feature
engineering → model training → backtesting → live trading → monitoring.
(2) Feature engineering for finance: raw price/volume data → alpha signals; alternative
data processing (NLP on news, earnings calls, filings); technical indicator construction;
cross-sectional normalization and winsorization.
(3) Model selection: gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM) for tabular financial data;
LSTM/Transformer for time series; NLP models (FinBERT, GPT fine-tuned) for text;
ensemble methods to combine signal sources.
(4) Avoiding overfitting: walk-forward validation (not random cross-validation);
multiple testing correction (Bonferroni, BHY); minimum backtest length;
out-of-sample holdout period.
(5) Signal decay analysis: alpha signals decay over time (market learns); measure
IC (Information Coefficient) decay; optimal holding period for each signal.
(6) Portfolio optimization with ML: combine ML signals with covariance matrix;
regularized optimization (ridge, LASSO); transaction cost-aware optimization.
(7) Production deployment: model monitoring (signal degradation detection);
A/B testing for new models vs. incumbent; circuit breaker for model failure.
Format: ML Finance Framework with Research Process, Feature Engineering, Model
Selection, Overfitting Prevention, Signal Decay, Portfolio Optimization, and Production.
Inputs: [UNIVERSE | PREDICTION TARGET (RETURN/RISK/SIGNAL) | HOLDING PERIOD |
DATA SOURCES | COMPUTE BUDGET | TRANSACTION COST ASSUMPTION | RISK CONTROLS]

title: The Carlyle Aviation Finance & Aircraft Leasing
prompt_text:
PROMPT 305 — The Carlyle Aviation Finance & Aircraft Leasing
Act as MD at Carlyle Aviation Partners. Build an aircraft leasing investment
strategy covering fleet management and airline credit.
Deliver: (1) Aviation finance fundamentals: aircraft as collateral — liquid global
secondary market (JOLCO, ABS, sale-leaseback); aircraft type value retention
(narrowbody A320neo/737MAX > widebody in current market).
(2) Lessor business model: acquire aircraft → lease to airlines → earn lease rentals;
remarketing aircraft at lease end; residual value risk management.
(3) Airline credit assessment: airline financial health (EBITDA/revenue, leverage);
geographic diversification of lessee portfolio; FSC (Full Service Carrier) vs.
LCC (Low Cost Carrier) credit differentiation; COVID recovery read-through.
(4) Lease structure: operating lease (12 months-12 years); finance lease;
maintenance reserves (airframe, engine, landing gear events); security deposits;
redelivery conditions.
(5) Aircraft valuation: CMV (Current Market Value) vs. BV (Base Value) — AVAC,
AVITAS, Collateral Verifications appraisers; lease rate factor (monthly rental /
aircraft value); discount to CMV for distressed remarketing.
(6) ABS/EETC financing: Enhanced Equipment Trust Certificates (EETC — airline
bonds secured by aircraft); ABS structures for aircraft portfolios; rating
analysis for aircraft-backed securities.
(7) ESG in aviation: carbon offsetting; SAF (Sustainable Aviation Fuel) adoption;
aging fleet retirement risk (older high-emission aircraft stranded early).
Format: Aviation Finance Strategy with Lessor Model, Airline Credit Framework, Lease
Structure, Aircraft Valuation, ABS/EETC, and ESG.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | AIRCRAFT TYPES | AIRLINE MIX | AVERAGE LEASE TERM |
RESIDUAL VALUE ASSUMPTION | FINANCING STRUCTURE | TARGET YIELD | PRIMARY RISK]

title: The Apax Digital Health & Life Sciences Growth Equity
prompt_text:
PROMPT 306 — The Apax Digital Health & Life Sciences Growth Equity
Act as MD at Apax Partners' Digital Health team. Build an investment thesis
for digital health and life sciences tools companies.
Deliver: (1) Digital health market: $600B+ addressable market; technology-driven

(telehealth, remote monitoring, AI diagnostics).
(2) Sub-sector map: telemedicine platforms (Teladoc model, specialty telehealth),
AI diagnostics (radiology AI, pathology AI), population health management,
behavioral health digital, pharmacy tech, remote patient monitoring.
(3) Business model quality: SaaS-based (subscription per patient or per provider);
outcomes-based contracts (paid for improving clinical outcomes);
FFS (Fee-for-Service) tech-enabled (lower quality, more variable revenue).
(4) Regulatory: FDA 510(k)/De Novo/PMA for SaMD (Software as a Medical Device);
HIPAA compliance; CPT code and reimbursement for telehealth services;
state-by-state telemedicine regulation.
(5) Provider adoption: clinical workflow integration (EHR integration depth);
physician champion development; IT procurement process in hospitals.
(6) Exit: strategic buyers (UnitedHealth Optum, CVS Aetna, Amazon Health);
specialty healthtech acquirers; PE buyout at scale; IPO.
(7) Life sciences tools: genomics (WGS cost declining, clinical adoption expanding);
laboratory automation; spatial biology; CRISPR screening tools.
Format: Digital Health Investment Framework with Sub-Sector Map, Business Model
Quality, Regulatory Landscape, Provider Adoption, Exit Options, and Life Sciences Tools.
Inputs: [COMPANY | PRODUCT/SERVICE | CUSTOMER (PROVIDER/PAYER/PATIENT) | ARR |
REGULATORY STATUS | EHR INTEGRATION | GROWTH RATE | ENTRY VALUATION]

title: The Deutsche Bank Risk-Weighted Asset (RWA) Optimization
prompt_text:
PROMPT 307 — The Deutsche Bank Risk-Weighted Asset (RWA) Optimization
Act as Head of Capital Efficiency at Deutsche Bank. Build an RWA optimization
strategy to improve return on regulatory capital.
Deliver: (1) RWA composition: credit RWA (largest — corporate lending, mortgages,
derivatives exposure); market risk RWA (trading book — FRTB); operational risk RWA.
(2) Credit RWA reduction: (a) Portfolio mix shift — reduce high-RWA assets (unsecured
corporate, sub-investment grade); (b) Credit risk mitigation — eligible collateral
(cash, sovereign bonds, HQLA) to reduce exposure; guarantees from eligible guarantors;
(c) Securitization — synthetic securitization using CLN (Credit-Linked Note) to
transfer credit risk while retaining economic interest.
(3) Internal ratings-based (IRB) optimization: model recalibration within IRB rules;
floor impact of Basel IV output floor; transition from standardized to IRB for
eligible portfolios.
(4) Market risk RWA (FRTB): IMA (Internal Models Approach) desk-level approval;
reduce sensitivity to P&L attribution test failure; SA-TB for desks that fail IMA.
(5) Capital relief trades (CRT): significant risk transfer (SRT) — sell mezzanine
risk via CLN or financial guarantee; ECB and PRA SRT recognition criteria.
(6) Portfolio pruning: identify relationship loans with RoRWA (Return on RWA) below
hurdle; exit or reprice these relationships; impact on revenue and client franchise.
(7) CET1 target management: CET1 ratio vs. MDA (Maximum Distributable Amount) buffer;
dividend and buyback capacity linked to CET1 ratio.
Format: RWA Optimization Strategy with RWA Decomposition, Credit RWA Reduction,
FRTB Optimization, CRT Design, Portfolio Pruning, and Capital Management.
Inputs: [BANK TYPE | CET1 RATIO | RWA BREAKDOWN | TARGET RoRWA | LEVERAGE CONSTRAINT |
SECURITIZATION APPETITE | PRIMARY CAPITAL EFFICIENCY CHALLENGE]

title: The Advent Healthcare Services: Home-Based Care Investment
prompt_text:
PROMPT 308 — The Advent Healthcare Services: Home-Based Care Investment
Act as MD at Advent International. Build a PE investment thesis for
home-based healthcare services.
Deliver: (1) Home-based care thesis: aging population (65+ demographic driving demand);
hospital-at-home trend (50% cheaper than inpatient care); payor preference for
home-based care (lower cost, better outcomes for chronic disease management).
(2) Sub-sector map: home health agencies (Medicare-certified skilled nursing visits);
hospice (Medicare benefit, high-margin terminal care); home infusion therapy;
personal care services (HCBS — Medicaid-funded ADL assistance); hospital-at-home.
(3) Reimbursement: Medicare fee schedule for home health (PDGM — Patient-Driven
Groupings Model); hospice Medicare daily rate by level of care; Medicaid HCBS rates
by state — huge state-by-state variation creates regulatory risk.
(4) Staffing model: home health aide, CNA, LPN, RN, therapist — labor cost 60-70%
of revenue; agency vs. W-2 model; clinical staffing technology.
(5) Buy-and-build: fragmented market (10,000+ home health agencies, mostly small
operators); acquire and consolidate; platform at 8-10× EBITDA vs. add-on at 4-6×.
(6) CMS regulatory risk: home health face-to-face requirement; prior authorization
in some states; fraud and abuse risk (False Claims Act exposure in Medicare billing).
(7) Technology enablement: remote patient monitoring (RPM) to improve outcomes and
reduce hospitalizations; predictive analytics for high-risk patient identification.
Format: Home-Based Care Investment Thesis with Sub-Sector Map, Reimbursement Analysis,
Buy-and-Build Strategy, Regulatory Risk, Technology Enablement, and LBO Returns.
Inputs: [SUB-SECTOR | GEOGRAPHY | COMPANY SIZE | PAYOR MIX | EBITDA MARGIN |
STAFFING MODEL | ACQUISITION TARGETS | ENTRY MULTIPLE | REGULATORY RISK CONCERN]

title: The Morgan Stanley Sustainable Finance: Green Bond Structuring
prompt_text:
PROMPT 309 — The Morgan Stanley Sustainable Finance: Green Bond Structuring
Act as Head of Sustainable Finance at Morgan Stanley. Structure a green bond
framework and inaugural issuance for a corporate issuer.
Deliver: (1) Green Bond Framework development: GBP (ICMA Green Bond Principles) alignment;
Use of Proceeds (eligible green project categories per ICMA taxonomy); project
evaluation and selection process; management of proceeds (ring-fencing mechanism);
reporting (allocation report + impact report).
(2) Eligible categories for this issuer: renewable energy, energy efficiency, clean
transport, green buildings, sustainable water management — map to company's capex plan.
(3) Second Party Opinion (SPO): select SPO provider (Sustainalytics, S&P, Vigeo Eiris,
ISS); SPO process timeline (4-6 weeks); opinion quality signals.
(4) Bond structuring: tenor (5-10 years for IG green bonds); size ($500M typical benchmark);
use-of-proceeds ring-fencing mechanism.
(5) Greenium analysis: Morgan Stanley's research on greenium — tighter pricing by
5-20bps vs. conventional bonds for IG issuers; factors driving greenium size
(ESG investor demand, issuer ESG credentials).
(6) Investor targeting: dedicated ESG funds, Article 8/9 SFDR funds, sovereign green
bonds buyers (pension funds, SWFs with ESG mandates), retail ESG investors.
(7) Reporting obligations: annual allocation report (how proceeds deployed); annual
impact report (renewable energy MWh financed, CO2e avoided, buildings certified).
Format: Green Bond Advisory with Framework Design, Eligible Categories, SPO Process,
Greenium Analysis, Investor Targeting, and Reporting Template.
Inputs: [COMPANY | INDUSTRY | GREEN CAPEX PIPELINE | CREDIT RATING | ISSUANCE SIZE |
EXISTING ESG CREDENTIALS | TARGET INVESTOR BASE | REPORTING CAPACITY]

title: The Citigroup Investment Banking: Defense & Government Services
prompt_text:
PROMPT 310 — The Citigroup Investment Banking: Defense & Government Services
Act as MD at Citi's Aerospace, Defense & Government Services group. Build
an investment banking advisory framework for the defense sector.
Deliver: (1) Defense sector dynamics: DoD budget trajectory (base + supplemental);
NATO 2% GDP spending commitment driving European defense; defense industrial base
modernization (NGAD, hypersonic weapons, autonomous systems, cyber).
(2) Defense company valuation: EV/EBITDA, P/E, and EV/FCF — defense companies trade
at premiums for backlog visibility; P/E premium for companies growing above GDP
(program ramp-ups); EV/Backlog as an alternative metric.
(3) Defense M&A: horizontal consolidation (prime contractors acquiring Tier 1 subs);
ITAR and CFIUS as structural barriers to foreign acquisition of US defense companies;
DoD/NATSEC review process timeline.
(4) Government services (SAIC, Leidos, Booz Allen): time-and-materials vs. cost-plus
vs. fixed-price contracts — risk profile and margin differences; contract re-compete
risk; clearance workforce as competitive moat.
(5) Space defense: commercial space (SpaceX, Blue Origin) disruptive to legacy defense
space primes; DoD space architecture modernization; SDA (Space Development Agency)
creating new competition.
(6) Capital structure: defense companies have stable FCF supporting 2-3× leverage;
share buyback programs as primary capital return; dividend consistency.
(7) European defense: consolidation of European defense industrial base (MBDA, KNDS);
export control regimes (EU EAR equivalent); Rheinmetall/KNDS/BAE growth trajectory.
Format: Defense IB Advisory with Sector Dynamics, Valuation, M&A Landscape, Services
Analysis, Space Defense, Capital Structure, and European Defense.
Inputs: [COMPANY TYPE (PRIME/TIER1/SERVICES/SPACE) | GEOGRAPHY | REVENUE | EBITDA |
BACKLOG | PRIMARY DEFENSE PROGRAM | M&A OBJECTIVE | PRIMARY STRATEGIC CHALLENGE]

title: The GIC Multi-Asset Class Portfolio Risk Management
prompt_text:
PROMPT 311 — The GIC Multi-Asset Class Portfolio Risk Management
Act as Head of Portfolio Risk at GIC. Build a total portfolio risk management
framework for a $700B+ sovereign wealth fund.
Deliver: (1) Total portfolio approach: risk management at the whole-portfolio level
not asset class level; factor-based risk decomposition across public and private assets.
(2) Factor risk model: macro factors (global growth, inflation, rates, credit spreads,
FX); style factors (value, momentum, quality, size); geographic factors; all positions
mapped to underlying factors.
(3) Private asset risk: illiquid assets (PE, infra, real estate) assigned factor exposures
using public market proxies; lagged marking creates stale risk estimates — how to adjust.
(4) Scenario stress testing: GFC 2008 (equity -50%, credit spreads +500bps); COVID
March 2020 (equity -35%, liquidity freeze); EM crisis (EM FX -30%, EM credit +400bps);
geopolitical tail (Taiwan conflict).
(5) Liquidity risk: private asset commitment pacing vs. liquid asset portfolio; modeling
NAV facility drawdowns; stress test for simultaneous 20% portfolio drawdown and large
capital calls from PE commitments.
(6) Concentration risk limits: single country limit (max 25-30% developed, 15% EM);
single sector limit; single manager limit; currency exposure limit.
(7) Risk reporting to Board/IC: quarterly risk dashboard; annual risk budget review;
VaR and CVaR by asset class; active risk vs. reference portfolio.
Format: SWF Risk Framework with Factor Model, Private Asset Risk, Stress Tests,
Liquidity Risk, Concentration Limits, and Board Reporting.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | ASSET MIX | REFERENCE PORTFOLIO | ILLIQUID ALLOCATION |
RISK BUDGET | PRIMARY RISK CONCERN | BOARD REPORTING FREQUENCY]

title: The Apollo Natural Resources & Energy Credit
prompt_text:
PROMPT 312 — The Apollo Natural Resources & Energy Credit
Act as Senior Credit Analyst at Apollo's Natural Resources credit team.
Build a credit investment thesis for an oil & gas or mining company.
Deliver: (1) Natural resources credit framework: commodity price sensitivity is the
dominant credit variable; through-the-cycle credit analysis (what happens to
leverage and coverage at mid-cycle commodity prices, not spot).
(2) Reserve-Based Lending (RBL) analysis: borrowing base = PV10 of proven reserves
at strip pricing; advance rate typically 50-65% of PV10; semi-annual redetermination.
(3) Downside credit scenario: oil at $40/bbl or copper at $2.50/lb — calculate EBITDA,
interest coverage, leverage, and liquidity at distressed commodity prices.
(4) Asset coverage analysis: in a default, what do assets recover? EV at distressed
commodity multiple; comparison to outstanding debt face value.
(5) Hedging analysis: % of production hedged at what price for next 2 years; floor
on cash flows from hedges; hedge counterparty credit risk.
(6) ESG transition risk: carbon price sensitivity; ESG-linked lender covenants;
brown discount in cost of capital; timeline to stranded asset risk.
(7) Recovery analysis: secured creditor recovery in E&P bankruptcy (Apache, Whiting,
Denbury historical precedents); reserve value haircut in restructuring.
Format: Natural Resources Credit Memo with RBL Analysis, Through-Cycle Stress,
Asset Coverage, Hedge Analysis, ESG Transition Risk, and Recovery Scenario.
Inputs: [COMPANY | COMMODITY | PRODUCTION RATE | RESERVE LIFE | HEDGING % |
CURRENT LEVERAGE | DEBT STRUCTURE | COMMODITY PRICE ASSUMPTION | TARGET ENTRY YIELD]

title: The Kirkland & Ellis LBO Credit Agreement Negotiation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 313 — The Kirkland & Ellis LBO Credit Agreement Negotiation
Act as Partner at Kirkland & Ellis advising a PE sponsor on leveraged
finance credit agreement negotiation.
Deliver: (1) Credit agreement architecture: term loan B (TLB) + revolving credit facility
(RCF) + optional second lien or senior notes; intercreditor agreement between tranches.
(2) EBITDA definition — the most important negotiation: what adds back to EBITDA?
Pro-forma run-rate synergies (6-12 month lookback); non-recurring items; cost
savings with 18-month sunset; equity compensation (add back GAAP expense);
management projection add-backs — each $10M of EBITDA = $50-60M of debt at 5-6×.
(3) Negative covenants (incurrence-based in cov-lite TLBs): restricted payment baskets
(cash, builder basket, ratio basket); permitted debt baskets (ratio debt, ratio debt plus
unlimited incremental, cap-based); permitted investment baskets; asset sale proceeds.
(4) Incremental facility (accordion): ability to add debt in the future without
lender consent; ratio-based (leverage ratio test) vs. MFN-based (pricing spread
must match or exceed existing lenders by 50bps for 12 months).
(5) Portability: can debt be transferred to a new owner of the business without
triggering a Change of Control (CoC) put/repricing? Key for future M&A.
(6) Restricted vs. unrestricted subsidiaries: ability to designate subsidiaries as
"unrestricted" (outside the covenant basket) — asset-stripping risk for lenders.
(7) Remedies: cure period for covenant violations; equity cure right; cross-default
triggers to other debt.
Format: Credit Agreement Negotiation Guide with EBITDA Definition, Key Baskets,
Incremental Facility, Portability, Restricted Subsidiaries, and Remedies.
Inputs: [DEAL SIZE | SPONSOR | INDUSTRY | LEVERAGE | PROPOSED BASKETS |
KEY EBITDA ADD-BACKS | INCREMENTAL NEED | PRIMARY NEGOTIATION PRIORITY]

title: The Citi Research: European Banks Equity Analysis
prompt_text:
PROMPT 314 — The Citi Research: European Banks Equity Analysis
Act as Head of European Banks Research at Citi. Build a comprehensive
equity research framework for European universal banks.
Deliver: (1) European bank metrics: NIM (Net Interest Margin) — the primary revenue
driver; CET1 ratio (capital adequacy); RoTE (Return on Tangible Equity) vs. CoE
(Cost of Equity); NPL ratio and provision coverage; cost-to-income ratio.
(2) Rate sensitivity: NIM expansion in rising rate environment (asset repricing faster
than liability); deposit beta (how much of rate increase passed to depositors);
impact of deposit outflows/competition on NIM sustainability.
(3) Capital return capacity: CET1 buffer above regulatory minimum → excess capital
available for buybacks and dividends; DPS (Dividends Per Share) growth.
(4) Asset quality: NPL formation rate; sector concentration risk (CRE, leveraged loans);
provision coverage; through-the-cycle normalized credit cost.
(5) Country-specific risks: Italian BTP/bank correlation; Spanish consumer credit
growth; German corporate credit (Mittelstand exposure); UK mortgage repricing.
(6) Fintech/digital competition: neobank competitive pressure on current accounts;
digital mortgage brokers on margin; how incumbents are responding.
(7) Valuation: P/TBV vs. RoTE (the "magic line" — P/TBV = 1× when RoTE = CoE);
dividend yield vs. bond yield; M&A premium for cross-border consolidation.
Format: European Banks Research Framework with Key Metrics, Rate Sensitivity, Capital
Return, Asset Quality, Country Risks, Digital Competition, and Valuation.
Inputs: [BANK NAME | COUNTRY | CET1 | NIM | RoTE | CoE ESTIMATE |
NPL RATIO | DPS YIELD | PRIMARY INVESTMENT THESIS OR CONCERN]

title: The Brookfield Business Partners: Industrial & Services PE
prompt_text:
PROMPT 315 — The Brookfield Business Partners: Industrial & Services PE
Act as MD at Brookfield Business Partners. Build a PE investment thesis for
an industrial or business services company.
Deliver: (1) Brookfield Business Partners philosophy: value-oriented, contrarian;
invest in large, complex businesses that are out-of-favor; leverage operational
expertise and Brookfield's global scale.
(2) Target characteristics: asset-heavy businesses with underlying value; large
enterprise value (typically $1B+); operations in multiple geographies; complex
carve-outs or operational restructurings.
(3) Operational value creation: Brookfield's operating partners embedded in
businesses; lean operations program; procurement leverage across Brookfield portfolio;
capital recycling (sell non-core assets, reinvest in core).
(4) Contrarian investing: industrial businesses out-of-favor with PE because
of capital intensity; Brookfield's patience with longer hold periods (5-10 years)
and comfort with leverage in asset-heavy businesses.
(5) Services businesses: business process outsourcing (BPO); facility management;
construction services; technology services — asset-light versions of industrials
with predictable contracts.
(6) Financing: blend of infrastructure-style debt (for asset-heavy parts) and
corporate leveraged finance (for services parts); mixed capital structures.
(7) Exit: IPO of stabilized business; strategic sale; separation of asset-heavy
and asset-light components for different buyer audiences.
Format: Industrial PE Investment Thesis with Target Characteristics, Value Creation,
Contrarian Thesis, Services Analysis, Financing, and Exit Strategy.
Inputs: [COMPANY | INDUSTRY | REVENUE | EBITDA | ASSET BASE | COMPLEXITY TYPE |
ENTRY PRICE | PRIMARY VALUE CREATION | HOLD PERIOD | EXIT THESIS]

title: The Banco Bradesco Brazil Corporate Banking & Capital Markets
prompt_text:
PROMPT 316 — The Banco Bradesco Brazil Corporate Banking & Capital Markets
Act as Head of Investment Banking at Banco Bradesco. Build a corporate banking
and capital markets strategy for Brazil's financial sector.
Deliver: (1) Brazil financial market overview: Selic rate trajectory and impact on
credit markets; B3 equity market structure; DCM market (debentures, CRI, CRA);
FX and derivatives market (B3 USD futures, NDF market).
(2) Brazilian capital markets products: debentures (infrastructure debentures with
IR incentives); CRI/CRA (receivables-backed securities); FIDCs (credit receivables
funds); BDRs (Brazilian depositary receipts for global companies listing in Brazil).
(3) Corporate lending: loan pricing in Brazil (CDI spread basis); BNDES
(development bank) credit access and on-lending; working capital revolving credit.
(4) FX and hedging: Brazilian Real volatility; cross-currency swap (PRÉ × PRÉ);
NDF for USD hedge; cupom cambial (offshore BRL interest rate) vs. domestic CDI.
(5) Infrastructure finance: infrastructure debentures (Law 12,431); BNDES FINEM
financing; PPP structures; concession valuations for airports, ports, roads.
(6) M&A advisory: Brazilian M&A market dynamics; CVM regulation; foreign acquisition
CADE (antitrust) approval; family business transitions in Brazilian mid-market.
(7) ESG and sustainability: CVM resolution on climate disclosure; sustainable
debentures; Brazil's role in carbon credit markets (REDD+ credits).
Format: Brazil Corporate Banking Strategy with Market Overview, Product Suite,
Infrastructure Finance, M&A Advisory, FX/Hedging, and ESG Finance.
Inputs: [CLIENT TYPE | INDUSTRY | REVENUE (BRL) | FINANCING NEED | SELIC SENSITIVITY |
USD EXPOSURE | M&A OBJECTIVE | ESG TARGETS]

title: The Citi Treasury: Corporate Balance Sheet & Capital Optimization
prompt_text:
PROMPT 317 — The Citi Treasury: Corporate Balance Sheet & Capital Optimization
Act as Senior Treasurer at a Fortune 500 company. Build a comprehensive
treasury strategy covering cash management, FX risk, and capital structure.
Deliver: (1) Cash and liquidity management: cash pooling structure; minimum operating
cash by entity; excess cash investment policy (MMF, repo, T-bills — yield vs. safety
vs. liquidity trade-off); trapped cash identification and repatriation strategy.
(2) FX risk management: net exposure by currency; natural hedging (match revenues
and costs in same currency); hedging program for residual exposure (forward contracts,
options); hedge accounting designation (IFRS 9 fair value or cash flow hedges).
(3) Interest rate risk: floating vs. fixed debt mix; interest rate swap overlay to
achieve target fixed/floating ratio; sensitivity to +100bps rate shock on P&L.
(4) Debt capital structure: target leverage ratio and rationale; debt maturity ladder
(avoid maturity concentration); pre-funding strategy; revolving credit facility sizing.
(5) Rating agency management: target credit rating and financial policy framework;
key financial metrics monitored by Moody's/S&P (leverage, coverage, FCF);
communication of financial policy to rating agencies.
(6) Capital allocation: return of capital framework (dividends vs. buybacks vs. M&A
allocation); minimum dividend; buyback opportunism vs. commitment.
(7) Financial risk dashboard: real-time KPI monitoring (cash position, FX exposure,
debt maturity, covenant headroom, credit rating triggers).
Format: Treasury Strategy with Cash Management, FX Hedging Program, Interest Rate
Risk, Debt Structure, Rating Agency Policy, Capital Allocation, and Risk Dashboard.
Inputs: [COMPANY | REVENUE | EBITDA | CURRENT DEBT | CASH BALANCE | FX EXPOSURE |
CREDIT RATING | PRIMARY TREASURY CHALLENGE | CAPITAL RETURN POLICY]

title: The Bain & Company Corporate Transformation & Turnaround
prompt_text:
PROMPT 318 — The Bain & Company Corporate Transformation & Turnaround
Act as Senior Partner at Bain & Company's Results Delivery practice.
Design a corporate turnaround strategy for a performing-but-declining company.
Deliver: (1) Turnaround urgency triage: distinguish "burning platform" (immediate
cash crisis) from "strategic decline" (gradual competitive erosion) from
"underperformance" (operational inefficiency); different urgency and approach.
(2) Rapid diagnostic: in 4 weeks — identify the top 3-5 root causes of underperformance;
quantify the EBITDA gap vs. peers; prioritize by impact and speed.
(3) "Results Delivery" program: Bain's proprietary methodology — clear accountability
for each initiative (owner, co-owner, escalation path); weekly tracking of leading
indicators (not just financial outcomes); behavioral change as critical success factor.
(4) Cost transformation: zero-based cost review for indirect spend (SG&A, IT, marketing);
procurement savings program; footprint rationalization (facility closures, offshoring).
(5) Revenue recovery: identify revenue leakage (pricing below market, customer segments
underserved, channels underinvested); commercial excellence program to recover.
(6) Balance sheet repair: working capital release (DSO, DPO, inventory); asset disposal
(non-core real estate, equipment); dividend suspension to preserve cash.
(7) Organizational: senior leadership team changes (where needed); culture shift
from entitlement to accountability; performance management redesign.
Format: Corporate Turnaround Strategy with Diagnostic Methodology, Results Delivery
Framework, Cost Transformation, Revenue Recovery, Balance Sheet Repair, and Org Plan.
Inputs: [COMPANY | INDUSTRY | REVENUE | EBITDA VS. PEER BENCHMARK | PRIMARY DECLINE
DRIVER | CASH POSITION | URGENCY LEVEL | STAKEHOLDER ALIGNMENT]

title: The JPMorgan Private Bank: Alternatives Access & Co-Investment
prompt_text:
PROMPT 319 — The JPMorgan Private Bank: Alternatives Access & Co-Investment
Act as MD at JPMorgan Private Bank's Alternatives Investments group.
Design an alternatives access program for UHNW private banking clients.
Deliver: (1) UHNW alternatives landscape: private equity, private credit, real assets,
hedge funds — why alternatives should form 20-40% of a UHNW portfolio.
(2) Access platform: feeder funds into top-tier PE (KKR, Blackstone, Carlyle);
minimum commitments ($1-5M typical); vintage year diversification program.
(3) Co-investment program: direct co-investments alongside GP investments;
deal-by-deal selection vs. blind pool co-investment vehicle; fee economics
(typically no fee/carry on co-investment).
(4) Private credit access: direct lending funds; NAV loans against PE portfolio;
infrastructure debt; real estate debt — yield-focused alternatives for income-
oriented clients.
(5) Hedge fund allocation: fund of funds vs. direct access; JPMPB's preferred
manager list; managed account negotiation for $25M+ clients; liquidity terms.
(6) Real assets: infrastructure funds; farmland; private real estate funds; royalties —
inflation-hedging component of alternatives portfolio.
(7) Portfolio construction for UHNW: annual commitment pacing model; J-curve management
(feeder fund drawdown schedule vs. distribution timeline); liquidity planning.
Format: UHNW Alternatives Program with Access Platform, Co-Investment, Private Credit,
Hedge Funds, Real Assets, and Portfolio Construction/Liquidity Planning.
Inputs: [CLIENT NET WORTH | LIQUIDITY NEEDS | ALTERNATIVES BUDGET | PREFERRED
STRATEGY | CO-INVESTMENT APPETITE | RISK TOLERANCE | REPORTING REQUIREMENTS]

title: The Boston Consulting Group Platform Business Model Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 320 — The Boston Consulting Group Platform Business Model Strategy
Act as Senior Partner at BCG's Digital Ventures practice. Design a platform
business model strategy for a corporation seeking to build or transition to a platform.
Deliver: (1) Platform fundamentals: two-sided or multi-sided market; network effects
(direct and indirect); winner-take-most dynamics; chicken-and-egg problem at launch.
(2) Platform strategy options: (a) Build greenfield platform; (b) Transform existing
pipeline business into platform; (c) Acquire established platform; (d) Partner/white-label.
(3) Network effect measurement: cross-side network effect (more buyers → more sellers
more valuable to buyers); same-side network effects (social platforms); quantify
the NPS improvement per 10% increase in marketplace liquidity.
(4) Monetization design: take rate (% of transaction value); subscription fee; data
monetization; freemium with premium tiers; advertising. When to monetize and when
to subsidize for network growth.
(5) Trust and governance: platform rules and standards (who can participate, quality standards);
curation vs. open marketplace; dispute resolution; safety and compliance.
(6) Competitive moat: once network effects kick in, switching costs rise; how to defend
against "multi-homing" (buyers/sellers using multiple platforms simultaneously).
(7) Regulatory risk: EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) — gatekeeper designation; antitrust
scrutiny of platform acquisitions; data portability requirements.
Format: Platform Strategy with Network Effect Analysis, Monetization Design, Trust
Governance, Competitive Moat, Regulatory Risk, and Financial Model.
Inputs: [COMPANY | INDUSTRY | EXISTING ASSETS (DATA/CUSTOMERS/DISTRIBUTION) |
PLATFORM TYPE | TARGET PARTICIPANTS | MONETIZATION MODEL | NETWORK EFFECT STRENGTH]

title: The Ares Management Credit Opportunities Fund
prompt_text:
PROMPT 321 — The Ares Management Credit Opportunities Fund
Act as MD at Ares Management's Credit Opportunities team. Build a credit
opportunities strategy targeting liquid and illiquid credit dislocations.
Deliver: (1) Credit opportunities universe: leveraged loans (secondary), HY bonds
(stressed/distressed), private credit (direct lending rescue financing), CLO equity,
structured credit (CMBS, CLO tranches), and trade claims.
(2) Liquid credit opportunities: stressed HY bonds (70-90 cents, yield-to-worst
12-18%); leveraged loans at discount (par minus 5-15 points); CLO equity at wide
NAV discounts; CMBS subordinate bonds on distressed properties.
(3) Illiquid credit opportunities: rescue financing (first lien DIP or priming
financing for stressed companies); preferred equity with PIK option; NAV lending
against PE portfolios.
(4) Credit cycle positioning: identify current phase of cycle; which opportunities
are most attractive — late-cycle (distressed corporate), mid-crisis (rescue),
recovery (loan-to-own, new issue participation).
(5) Portfolio construction: target 40-50% liquid credit, 50-60% illiquid; single-name
concentration max 5% NAV; sector diversification; vintage diversification.
(6) Return targets: gross yield 12-16%; after leverage (1.0-1.5× fund level) 15-20%;
net return target 12-15% after fees.
(7) Liquidity management: quarterly redemption for liquid sleeve; 2-3 year lock-up
for illiquid sleeve; hybrid fund structure with separate liquidity terms.
Format: Credit Opportunities Strategy with Universe Map, Liquid/Illiquid Analysis,
Portfolio Construction, Return Targets, and Liquidity Structure.
Inputs: [FUND SIZE | LIQUID VS. ILLIQUID SPLIT | TARGET RETURN | LEVERAGE | CREDIT
QUALITY RANGE | PRIMARY OPPORTUNITY IN CURRENT CYCLE | INVESTOR TYPE]

title: The McKinsey Banking Revenue Growth & Cross-Sell Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 322 — The McKinsey Banking Revenue Growth & Cross-Sell Strategy
Act as Senior Partner at McKinsey's Banking practice. Design a revenue growth
strategy for a retail/commercial bank through cross-sell and product deepening.
Deliver: (1) Customer revenue diagnostic: revenue per customer by segment (mass,
affluent, HNW, SME, mid-market corporate); benchmark vs. best-in-class banks;
identify the revenue gap by product category.
(2) Primary bank relationship: identify customers who consider the bank their primary
banking relationship vs. a secondary provider; primary bank status drives 3-5×
more revenue per customer; strategy to win primary relationship.
(3) Cross-sell sequences: proven cross-sell pathways by customer lifecycle (checking
→ savings → auto loan → mortgage → investments → insurance); AI-powered next-best-
product recommendation engine.
(4) SME banking deepening: SME cross-sell from business current account to merchant
services, business credit card, commercial lending, insurance, and FX;
relationship manager productivity metrics.
(5) Affluent/HNW deepening: investment product penetration (% of affluent customers
with investment products < 20% at most banks); digital wealth platform; managed
account penetration.
(6) Pricing optimization: relationship pricing (bundle discount for multi-product
customers); dynamic pricing for credit products; fee income recovery.
(7) Sales force effectiveness: branch transformation (from transactional to advisory);
digital sales funnel optimization; lead generation from data analytics.
Format: Revenue Growth Strategy with Customer Diagnostic, Cross-Sell Map, SME Strategy,
Affluent Deepening, Pricing Optimization, and Sales Force Effectiveness.
Inputs: [BANK SIZE | GEOGRAPHY | CUSTOMER SEGMENTS | CURRENT PRODUCTS PER CUSTOMER |
PRIMARY REVENUE GAP | DIGITAL CAPABILITY | SALES FORCE MODEL]

title: The Coller Capital PE Secondaries Deep Dive
prompt_text:
PROMPT 323 — The Coller Capital PE Secondaries Deep Dive
Act as Managing Director at Coller Capital. Build a secondaries investment
analysis for a complex LP portfolio acquisition.
Deliver: (1) LP portfolio secondary analysis: due diligence on a portfolio of 15-25 PE
fund interests being sold by an LP; NAV verification; performance projection.
(2) NAV verification methodology: public company comparable analysis for each
portfolio company; DCF where financial data available; exit timing assumption.
(3) Discount to NAV analysis: what discount is appropriate given: (a) fund vintage
and remaining life; (b) underlying asset quality; (c) J-curve position; (d) GP quality;
(e) liquidity premium required by secondary buyer.
(4) Portfolio construction analysis: does the portfolio add diversification to Coller's
existing portfolio? Vintage overlap; sector overlap; GP concentration.
(5) LP motivation: why is the LP selling? (Liquidity need, portfolio rebalancing,
regulatory capital relief, LP relationship exit) — seller motivation affects
negotiating leverage and price discipline.
(6) Transaction structure: single closing vs. staged closing (for uncertain NAV);
price adjustment mechanism; tail-end assets (difficult to value, held as stub interest).
(7) Return analysis: IRR and MOIC on the secondary purchase; distribution model
from existing fund positions; sensitivity to exit timing and exit multiple.
Format: Secondaries Analysis with NAV Verification, Discount Framework, Portfolio
Construction, Seller Motivation, Transaction Structure, and Return Analysis.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE (# FUNDS AND $ NAV) | GP COMPOSITION | VINTAGE DISTRIBUTION |
SELLER TYPE | ASKING PRICE (% OF NAV) | TARGET DISCOUNT | HOLD PERIOD]

title: The Oliver Wyman Insurance M&A: Life Insurance Block Transactions
prompt_text:
PROMPT 324 — The Oliver Wyman Insurance M&A: Life Insurance Block Transactions
Act as Partner at Oliver Wyman advising on a life insurance block transaction
(reinsurance or portfolio acquisition).
Deliver: (1) Life insurance block transaction overview: acquirer (PE-backed reinsurer,
specialist life insurer) buys a block of life insurance/annuity liabilities from
a carrier seeking capital relief or strategic simplification.
(2) Liability types: term life (mortality risk), whole life (mortality + investment),
annuities (longevity risk), long-term care (multi-risk, most complex).
(3) Actuarial valuation: embedded value (EV) of the block — PV of future distributable
earnings from in-force policies; risk discount rate; assumption setting (mortality,
lapse, expenses, investment returns).
(4) Asset-liability management: matching assets to liabilities; duration gap; convexity
management; investment strategy for acquired liabilities (target asset yield vs.
liability crediting rate = spread).
(5) Reinsurance structures: coinsurance (full transfer of risk and assets), modified
coinsurance (risk transfer but assets stay with ceding company), coinsurance with
funds withheld (risk transfer, ceding company retains assets, credits investment return).
(6) Regulatory approval: state insurance department approval for assumption reinsurance;
policyholder notification requirements; surplus lines treatment.
(7) Pricing: acquisition cost = EV − synergies + strategic premium; IRR on the capital
deployed; return on embedded value (RoEV).
Format: Life Insurance Block Transaction Advisory with Actuarial Valuation, Reinsurance
Structures, ALM Strategy, Regulatory Process, and Transaction Pricing.
Inputs: [BLOCK TYPE (TERM/WHOLE LIFE/ANNUITY/LTC) | FACE VALUE | RESERVE SIZE |
ASSET PORTFOLIO | ACQUIRER TYPE | IRR TARGET | REGULATORY JURISDICTION]

title: The Bernstein Research: Consumer Staples Sector Deep-Dive
prompt_text:
PROMPT 325 — The Bernstein Research: Consumer Staples Sector Deep-Dive
Act as Head of Consumer Staples Research at AllianceBernstein. Build a
comprehensive consumer staples investment framework.
Deliver: (1) Consumer staples investment case: defensive characteristics (inelastic
demand, pricing power, dividend yield); underperforms in risk-on markets; outperforms
in recessions; bond-proxy characteristics in low-rate environments.
(2) Volume vs. price growth analysis: staples companies chose price over volume
post-COVID; price elasticity is now biting back (volume declines despite lower
inflation); earnings quality concern when price growth drives all organic growth.
(3) Premiumization vs. private label threat: premium brands commanding 30-50%
price premium vs. private label; when private label wins market share; brand
equity resilience measurement.
(4) Emerging market growth: EM consumer penetration thesis — under-indexed staples
consumption in EM; Colgate India, Unilever EM — growth rates vs. volume metrics.
(5) Valuation: P/E premium vs. market (typically 15-20% premium); EV/EBITDA;
FCF yield; dividend yield vs. historical and vs. bond yields.
(6) M&A: categories attracting consolidation (pet food, premium beverages, snacking);
strategic rationality of recent acquisitions (synergy delivery track record).
(7) ESG: packaging sustainability; Scope 3 emissions (in value chain); ingredient
sourcing (palm oil, cocoa, coffee deforestation); regulatory pressure timeline.
Format: Consumer Staples Framework with Volume/Price Analysis, Premiumization,
EM Growth, Valuation, M&A, and ESG Assessment.
Inputs: [COMPANY | CATEGORY | GEOGRAPHY | ORGANIC GROWTH COMPONENTS | PRIVATE LABEL
RISK | CURRENT VALUATION | PRIMARY INVESTMENT DEBATE | RATING INTENT]

title: The Rothschild M&A: Corporate Divestiture & Carve-Out
prompt_text:
PROMPT 326 — The Rothschild M&A: Corporate Divestiture & Carve-Out
Act as Senior Partner at Rothschild advising a corporation on a major
business divestiture or carve-out transaction.
Deliver: (1) Divestiture rationale assessment: strategic (portfolio simplification,
focus), financial (capital release, debt reduction), regulatory (antitrust remedy),
or ESG (divest carbon-intensive or controversial business); how rationale shapes
process design. (2) Carve-out preparation: standalone P&L construction (allocate
corporate costs, quantify stranded costs); historical and pro-forma financial statements;
management team assessment (is there a team or must we build one?).
(3) Tax structuring: asset sale vs. entity sale; Section 338(h)(10) election for tax
basis step-up; spin-off vs. split-off tax-free reorganization requirements;
capital gains impact for seller.
(4) Process design: full auction (maximize competition and price) vs. targeted sale
(faster, confidentiality) vs. spin-off (tax-free, returns value to shareholders);
which buyer universe is realistic (strategic, PE, infrastructure fund, SPAC).
(5) Separation planning: transition service agreements (TSAs) — what services does
carve-out need from parent and for how long; IT separation (typically 18-24 months
for full separation); brand licensing arrangements.
(6) Stranded cost analysis: corporate overhead that remains after divestiture but
loses the allocated revenue base; how to quantify and plan to eliminate.
(7) Proceeds allocation: debt paydown vs. buybacks vs. bolt-on M&A; shareholder
return commitment post-divestiture.
Format: Divestiture Advisory with Carve-Out Preparation, Tax Structuring, Process
Design, Separation Planning, Stranded Cost Analysis, and Proceeds Allocation.
Inputs: [PARENT COMPANY | BUSINESS TO DIVEST | REVENUE | EBITDA | STRATEGIC RATIONALE |
TAX STRUCTURE | PREFERRED BUYER TYPE | TIMELINE | PRIMARY CHALLENGE]

title: The HSBC Global Liquidity & Cash Management Advisory
prompt_text:
PROMPT 327 — The HSBC Global Liquidity & Cash Management Advisory
Act as MD at HSBC's Global Liquidity and Cash Management (GLCM). Design
an optimal global treasury and liquidity management structure for a
large multinational corporation.
Deliver: (1) Global cash visibility: real-time balance reporting via SWIFT MT940/MT950
or API; multi-bank reporting aggregation; cash forecasting accuracy improvement
(rolling 13-week forecast; variance analysis vs. actuals).
(2) Cash pooling architecture: physical zero-balance sweeping (ZBA) for same-currency
domestic pools; notional pooling for cross-currency (Euro-zone compatible);
top account (master account) in optimal tax jurisdiction.
(3) In-house bank (IHB): centralize all group treasury functions within an IHB structure;
intercompany lending (replace external bank debt with internal funding); FX netting center
(gross to net exposure reduction 40-60%); payment factory (all group payments processed centrally).
(4) Liquidity investment: surplus cash investment policy — tiered liquidity ladder:
Tier 1 (overnight — MMFs, overnight repo), Tier 2 (1 week-3 months — T-bills, bank deposits),
Tier 3 (3-12 months — short duration bond funds); yield vs. safety vs. liquidity matrix.
(5) Payment infrastructure: SWIFT gpi for cross-border payments; real-time payment rails
by market; virtual accounts for receivables matching and reconciliation automation.
(6) Working capital: DSO reduction program (e-invoicing, early payment incentives);
DPO extension through supply chain finance (reverse factoring with HSBC);
inventory financing solutions.
(7) Technology: ERP integration (SAP, Oracle) for real-time cash position; TMS
(Treasury Management System — Kyriba, GTreasury); bank connectivity platform.
Format: Global Treasury Advisory with Cash Pooling Architecture, IHB Design, Liquidity
Investment Policy, Payment Infrastructure, Working Capital, and Technology Stack.
Inputs: [COMPANY REVENUE | COUNTRIES | ANNUAL PAYMENT VOLUME | CURRENT BANKING RELATIONSHIPS |
PRIMARY TREASURY CHALLENGE | ERP SYSTEM | CASH BALANCE | FX EXPOSURE]

title: The AllianceBernstein Fixed Income: Multi-Sector Bond Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 328 — The AllianceBernstein Fixed Income: Multi-Sector Bond Strategy
Act as Head of Multi-Sector Fixed Income at AllianceBernstein. Build a
diversified multi-sector bond portfolio strategy.
Deliver: (1) Multi-sector opportunity set: US Treasuries, TIPS, Agency MBS, Non-Agency MBS,
IG corporate, HY corporate, EM hard currency, EM local currency, CLO tranches, ABS —
full opportunity set with yield and risk characteristics.
(2) Sector rotation framework: identify which sectors offer best risk-adjusted return
at each point in the credit cycle; early cycle vs. late cycle sector preferences.
(3) Credit spread analysis: current OAS vs. historical median for each sector;
z-score of current spreads; identify sectors that are cheap vs. expensive.
(4) Duration and rate positioning: aggregate portfolio duration target; curve
positioning (barbell vs. bullet vs. ladder); TIPS vs. nominal trade-off at current
breakeven inflation levels.
(5) MBS positioning: TBA vs. specified pools; prepayment risk in rising/falling rates;
non-agency RMBS for spread pick-up vs. IG corporate alternative.
(6) EM positioning: EMBI vs. GBI — hard vs. local currency trade-off at current FX levels;
country selection within EM for highest risk-adjusted yield.
(7) Liquidity management: portfolio liquidity ladder; position sizing in less liquid
sectors (CLOs, non-agency MBS); reserve liquidity for opportunistic purchases.
Format: Multi-Sector Bond Strategy with Sector Allocation, Spread Analysis, Duration
Positioning, MBS Framework, EM Strategy, and Liquidity Management.
Inputs: [BENCHMARK | DURATION BUDGET | CREDIT QUALITY FLOOR | SECTOR LIMITS | YIELD
TARGET | LIQUIDITY REQUIREMENTS | PRIMARY RATE AND CREDIT VIEW]

title: The Lazard Financial Advisory: SPAC Advisory & De-SPAC
prompt_text:
PROMPT 329 — The Lazard Financial Advisory: SPAC Advisory & De-SPAC
Act as MD at Lazard. Advise a SPAC sponsor or target company through
a SPAC merger (business combination) transaction.
Deliver: (1) SPAC structure: IPO proceeds in trust; blank check company; 18-24 month
timeline to complete a business combination; redemption right for public shareholders.
(2) SPAC vs. traditional IPO: speed (6-9 months vs. 12-18 months); certainty of pricing
(negotiated vs. market); PIPE requirement; founder shares (20% promote); ongoing
dilution from warrants.
(3) Target selection criteria: private company seeking public market access without
traditional IPO uncertainty; growth equity story; benefit from sponsor expertise/network.
(4) PIPE structuring: concurrent private placement to institutional investors to fund
the deal and provide certainty of proceeds; PIPE sizing; PIPE investor terms
(registration rights, lockup, pricing relative to SPAC trust).
(5) De-SPAC valuation: how to value the target — typically forward revenue or EBITDA
multiples vs. projected financials; the challenge of "hockey stick" projections;
SEC scrutiny of de-SPAC financial projections.
(6) Redemption management: as the deal approaches, shareholders can redeem (get trust
value back); high redemption = less cash to target; strategies to minimize redemption
(sweeten terms, PIPE backstop, extension votes).
(7) Post-merger performance: de-SPAC companies have significantly underperformed
traditional IPOs — reasons (promote dilution, optimistic projections, less institutional
scrutiny); how to improve success rates.
Format: SPAC Advisory with Structure Overview, Target Selection, PIPE Structuring,
Valuation Approach, Redemption Management, and Post-Merger Performance Analysis.
Inputs: [ROLE (SPONSOR/TARGET) | COMPANY OR SPAC NAME | TRUST SIZE | TARGET SECTOR |
DEAL VALUATION | PIPE SIZE | REDEMPTION RISK | PRIMARY CHALLENGE]

title: The Goldman Sachs Commodities: Energy Trading Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 330 — The Goldman Sachs Commodities: Energy Trading Strategy
Act as Head of Energy Trading at Goldman Sachs Commodities. Build a
comprehensive energy commodity trading strategy.
Deliver: (1) Energy commodity universe: crude oil (WTI, Brent), natural gas (Henry Hub,
TTF), LNG, refined products (gasoline, diesel, jet fuel), power (regional markets),
carbon (ETS, VCR, RGGI).
(2) Crude oil fundamentals: OPEC+ production discipline; US shale production growth;
global demand by region; inventory levels (EIA, IEA data); geopolitical supply risk
premium (Hormuz, Russian oil caps).
(3) Natural gas and LNG: European gas market (TTF pricing); US Henry Hub vs. export
netback; LNG cargo arbitrage (US export to Europe vs. Asia); storage levels and
seasonal dynamics.
(4) Oil complex spread trades: (a) Crack spread (refinery margin: crude → gasoline + diesel);
(b) Timespread (Dec vs. Jan WTI — calendar spread reflecting storage economics);
(c) WTI/Brent differential (quality and geography basis).
(5) Power market trading: load forecasting and price prediction; renewable generation
intermittency trading (wind/solar price impact); peak vs. off-peak spreads;
ancillary services markets.
(6) Carbon trading: EU ETS Phase 4 (cap tightening through 2030); California cap-and-trade;
REDD+ voluntary credits; carbon as a commodity futures market.
(7) Risk management: VaR for energy books; stress test for oil price -40%; gas price spike
(winter 2022 European crisis replay); physical vs. financial position management.
Format: Energy Trading Strategy with Fundamental Analysis, Spread Trade Ideas,
Power Market Trading, Carbon Strategy, and Risk Management.
Inputs: [COMMODITY FOCUS | PHYSICAL VS. FINANCIAL | RISK CAPITAL | LEVERAGE LIMIT |
PRIMARY ENERGY VIEW | KEY SPREAD TRADES | CARBON EXPOSURE]

title: The Perella Weinberg Partners: Financial Institutions M&A
prompt_text:
PROMPT 331 — The Perella Weinberg Partners: Financial Institutions M&A
Act as Senior Partner at Perella Weinberg Partners advising on a financial
institution merger (bank, insurance, or asset manager).
Deliver: (1) FI M&A landscape: bank consolidation drivers (cost synergies, technology scale,
regulatory burden sharing); insurance M&A (liability management, distribution scale);
asset manager consolidation (fee compression, distribution leverage).
(2) Bank merger analysis: cost synergy potential (20-30% of target's non-interest expense);
revenue synergies (cross-sell, geographic expansion, product gaps filled); EPS accretion
model (including purchase accounting amortization and capital impact).
(3) Capital adequacy in bank M&A: combined CET1 ratio post-merger (day-1 impact from
purchase accounting and goodwill); tangible book value dilution (TBVPS) and earn-back
period; Federal Reserve approval requirements.
(4) Insurance M&A: embedded value (EV) as primary valuation metric; synergies in
distribution and underwriting; AM Best rating implications; state insurance department
approval in each domicile state.
(5) Asset manager M&A: EV/AUM and EV/EBITDA multiples; revenue synergy from distribution
cross-sell; investment team retention risk (key person clauses); fee compression trends.
(6) Regulatory approval: OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC for bank mergers; CRA performance
considerations; antitrust review (HERFINDAHL in banking markets); CFIUS for cross-border.
(7) Cultural integration: FI cultural mergers are uniquely difficult (risk cultures,
compensation philosophies, loan underwriting standards differ).
Format: FI M&A Advisory with Transaction Mechanics, Bank Merger Analysis, Capital Impact,
Insurance/AM Specifics, Regulatory Approval, and Cultural Integration.
Inputs: [ACQUIRER TYPE | TARGET TYPE | DEAL SIZE | STRATEGIC RATIONALE | CET1 IMPACT |
COST SYNERGY ESTIMATE | REGULATORY COMPLEXITY | PRIMARY INTEGRATION CHALLENGE]

title: The Oaktree Real Estate Debt & Distressed Property
prompt_text:
PROMPT 332 — The Oaktree Real Estate Debt & Distressed Property
Act as MD at Oaktree Capital's Real Estate Debt team. Build an investment
thesis for distressed commercial real estate debt opportunities.
Deliver: (1) CRE debt opportunity identification: CMBS delinquency monitoring by property
type; maturity wall analysis (CRE loans maturing 2024-2026 at higher rates with
lower valuations — refinancing gap); special servicer transfer acceleration.
(2) CRE stress assessment by property type: office (structural vacancy, sublease
overhang, conversion viability); regional mall (anchor departure cascades); hotels
(RevPAR recovery analysis); multifamily (supply pressure in Sun Belt markets).
(3) Loan acquisition strategy: buying performing but underwater loans at 70-80 cents
on dollar (loan balance > property value at current cap rates); recovery analysis
under orderly sale vs. foreclosure scenarios.
(4) CMBS B-piece investing: subordinate CMBS tranches at 10-15% yield target;
influence on loan underwriting at issuance; servicer relationship importance.
(5) Rescue preferred equity: provide capital to overleveraged sponsors who need
preferred equity ahead of existing equity to avoid foreclosure; 12-15% preferred
return with property-level security.
(6) Mezzanine debt: second-position debt behind senior CMBS or whole loan; 10-13%
target return; cure rights on senior default; intercreditor agreement analysis.
(7) Exit strategies: note sale after stabilization; foreclosure and property management/
repositioning; discounted payoff (DPO) with borrower.
Format: Distressed CRE Debt Strategy with Opportunity Identification, Property Type
Analysis, Loan Acquisition, CMBS B-Piece, Rescue Preferred, Mezz, and Exits.
Inputs: [PROPERTY TYPE | GEOGRAPHY | LOAN FACE VALUE | PURCHASE PRICE (% PAR) |
CURRENT NOI | LTV AT PURCHASE | WORKOUT TIMELINE | TARGET YIELD]

title: The GIC Total Portfolio Sustainability & Climate Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 333 — The GIC Total Portfolio Sustainability & Climate Strategy
Act as Head of Sustainability at GIC. Build a climate and sustainability
integration strategy for a sovereign wealth fund.
Deliver: (1) GIC sustainability framework: investment-led approach (integrate material
ESG factors into investment process) vs. exclusion-based; long-term wealth preservation
justification for sustainability integration.
(2) Climate risk integration: TCFD-aligned assessment; physical risk mapping across
real asset portfolio; transition risk assessment for carbon-intensive equity holdings;
1.5°C and 2°C scenario analysis on portfolio returns.
(3) Net-zero portfolio pathway: science-based targets for portfolio carbon intensity;
Paris alignment assessment using PACTA (Paris Agreement Capital Transition Assessment);
engagement vs. divestment decision framework for high-emission companies.
(4) Green investment themes: energy transition infrastructure (renewable power, grid,
BESS); green real estate (LEED/BREEAM certified, energy efficiency upgrades);
climate tech venture (carbon capture, green hydrogen, sustainable agriculture).
(5) ESG integration in private markets: GP ESG due diligence questionnaire;
ESG monitoring for PE portfolio companies; infrastructure ESG covenants.
(6) Engagement and stewardship: proxy voting policy aligned with climate goals;
collaborative engagement (CA100+, IIGCC); escalation policy for laggard companies.
(7) Reporting: TCFD disclosure; PRI annual reporting; SFDR compliance for EU-distributed
products; carbon footprint disclosure methodology (Scope 1, 2, 3 of portfolio companies).
Format: SWF Climate Strategy with Risk Integration, Net-Zero Pathway, Green Themes,
ESG in Private Markets, Stewardship, and Reporting Framework.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | ASSET MIX | CURRENT CARBON INTENSITY | NET-ZERO TARGET |
ENGAGEMENT RESOURCES | REPORTING REQUIREMENTS | PRIMARY CLIMATE CONCERN]

title: The Blackstone Real Estate: Hotel & Hospitality Investment
The Lazard Sovereign Wealth Fund Advisory
prompt_text:
PROMPT 335 — The Lazard Sovereign Wealth Fund Advisory
Act as Senior Advisor at Lazard's Sovereign Advisory group. Advise a
sovereign wealth fund on institutional design, governance, and investment strategy.
Deliver: (1) SWF typology: stabilization fund (buffer against commodity price volatility);
