savings/wealth fund (inter-generational savings — Norway GPFG model); development fund
(invest in domestic economy — Saudi PIF model); pension reserve fund (pre-fund future
pension obligations).
(2) Governance design: legal structure (statutory fund vs. trust vs. corporate);
ownership and governance chain (Finance Ministry → Governing Board → Management);
independence from political interference — the Santiago Principles (IFSWF standards).
(3) Investment mandate design: strategic asset allocation for the fund type; currency
considerations (domestic vs. international); illiquidity budget; ESG integration requirements.
(4) Asset manager selection: active vs. passive; internal vs. external management;
which asset classes to manage internally (scale required for cost efficiency);
GP selection and due diligence framework for PE/infra/hedge funds.
(5) Transparency and accountability: disclosure standards (GAPP — Generally Accepted
Principles and Practices); annual report requirements; political accountability.
(6) Domestic investment allocation: development mandates vs. pure financial return;
conflict of interest management when investing domestically.
(7) Case study application: Norway GPFG (pure financial return, full transparency);
Saudi PIF (Vision 2030, domestic development + financial return); Singapore GIC/Temasek
(financial return + strategic national interest).
Format: SWF Advisory with Fund Typology, Governance Framework, Investment Mandate,
Manager Selection, Transparency Standards, and International Comparisons.
Inputs: [COUNTRY | FUND TYPE | AUM OR TARGET SIZE | MANDATE | DOMESTIC INVESTMENT
REQUIREMENT | TRANSPARENCY APPETITE | PRIMARY GOVERNANCE CHALLENGE]

title: The Deutsche Bank Corporate Derivatives: FX Hedging Solutions
prompt_text:
PROMPT 336 — The Deutsche Bank Corporate Derivatives: FX Hedging Solutions
Act as MD at Deutsche Bank's Corporate Solutions group. Design FX risk
management solutions for a multinational corporate client.
Deliver: (1) FX exposure identification: transaction exposure (committed contracts
in foreign currency); translation exposure (subsidiary financials consolidated at spot);
economic exposure (competitive position affected by FX — harder to hedge).
(2) Hedging policy design: hedge ratio by exposure type and tenor (typically 50-75%
of forecasted FX for 12 months, less beyond); hedging instruments approved;
speculation prohibition; governance (treasury committee approval for non-standard trades).
(3) Forward contracts: booking a forward to lock in a known exchange rate; forward
points (interest rate differential); impact on P&L if spot moves vs. forward.
(4) Options strategies: vanilla options (higher premium, asymmetric protection);
risk reversals (zero cost but cap on upside); participating forwards (partial hedge,
some upside participation); seagull (even more participation at cost of wider downside band).
(5) Cross-currency swaps: for longer-dated FX risk (2-10 years) matching foreign
currency debt issuance; basis swap dynamics; accounting treatment (IFRS 9 net
investment hedge).
(6) Natural hedging: identify opportunities to denominate contracts in functional
currency; match revenues and costs; intercompany netting.
(7) Hedge accounting: IFRS 9 cash flow hedge (P&L volatility reduction); fair value
hedge; net investment hedge; effectiveness testing; hedge documentation.
Format: FX Hedging Advisory with Exposure Analysis, Policy Design, Instrument Menu,
Options Strategies, Cross-Currency Swaps, Natural Hedging, and Hedge Accounting.
Inputs: [COMPANY | REVENUE | FX EXPOSURE BY CURRENCY | HEDGE RATIO POLICY | TENOR |
INSTRUMENTS APPROVED | ACCOUNTING TREATMENT | PRIMARY FX RISK]

title: The KPMG Valuations: PPA and Goodwill Impairment Testing
prompt_text:
PROMPT 337 — The KPMG Valuations: PPA and Goodwill Impairment Testing
Act as Partner at KPMG's Valuations practice. Conduct a Purchase Price
Allocation (PPA) and annual goodwill impairment test.
Deliver: (1) PPA process under ASC 805 / IFRS 3: allocate total purchase price to
identifiable assets (tangible and intangible) and liabilities; residual = goodwill.
(2) Fair value of tangible assets: property, plant, and equipment at replacement cost
new (RCN) less depreciation; inventory at net realizable value; real estate at
market value (appraisal).
(3) Identifiable intangible assets: relief-from-royalty (RFR) for trademarks and
patents; multi-period excess earnings method (MPEEM) for customer relationships;
cost method for assembled workforce; with-and-without method for non-compete.
(4) Goodwill allocation to reporting units: how purchase price goodwill is allocated
to CGUs (IFRS) or reporting units (US GAAP) for impairment testing purposes.
(5) Annual goodwill impairment test: ASC 350 / IAS 36 — compare carrying value of
reporting unit (including goodwill) to fair value; qualitative assessment option
(Step 0); quantitative one-step test (current ASC 350 post-2016 simplification).
(6) DCF inputs for goodwill impairment: management's projections; terminal growth rate;
discount rate (WACC for the reporting unit, which may differ from entity WACC);
sensitivity to key assumptions.
(7) Impairment triggers: declining business performance; loss of key customer;
technology disruption; macroeconomic deterioration; stock price below book value.
Format: PPA & Goodwill Impairment Framework with Tangible Asset Valuation, Intangible
Methodology, Goodwill Allocation, Annual Test, DCF Inputs, and Impairment Triggers.
Inputs: [ACQUISITION DETAILS | PURCHASE PRICE | INDUSTRY | KEY INTANGIBLES | REPORTING
UNITS | WACC ASSUMPTION | CURRENT BUSINESS PERFORMANCE | IMPAIRMENT RISK LEVEL]

title: The BlackRock Real Assets: Infrastructure & Impact Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 338 — The BlackRock Real Assets: Infrastructure & Impact Strategy
Act as MD at BlackRock Real Assets. Build a renewable infrastructure
and impact investing strategy targeting institutional investors.
Deliver: (1) Renewable infrastructure investment case: contracted, long-duration cash
flows (15-25 year PPAs); inflation-linked revenues; uncorrelated to public markets;
ESG alignment; IRA (US) and EU Green Deal tailwinds.
(2) Core vs. core-plus vs. value-add infra: Core (operational, fully contracted, BBB+,
6-8% yield); Core-Plus (partially contracted, some development risk, 8-11%);
Value-Add (greenfield, merchant exposure, 12-15%+).
(3) Impact measurement: additionality (would the impact occur without the investment?);
IRIS+ metrics (MW capacity installed, MWh generated, tCO2e avoided, jobs created);
SDG alignment (SDG 7 clean energy, SDG 13 climate action, SDG 8 decent work).
(4) Impact vs. financial returns: does pursuing impact reduce financial returns?
Evidence from BlkRk and peers; "impact premium" debate; alignment of impact and returns
in renewable infrastructure (same investment that generates returns also creates impact).
(5) Green bond financing: issue green infrastructure bonds against the portfolio;
GBP compliance; impact reporting obligations; green premium (greenium) at portfolio level.
(6) Just transition: ensure energy transition doesn't create losers (displaced fossil
fuel workers, energy-poor communities); community benefit agreements; local content
requirements in renewable contracts.
(7) Fund structure: closed-end infrastructure fund; LTAF (Long-Term Asset Fund) for UK
DC pension access; ELTIF for EU retail access; open-end core infrastructure.
Format: Infrastructure Impact Strategy with Core/Core-Plus/Value-Add, Impact Metrics,
Financial Returns, Green Bond Financing, Just Transition, and Fund Structures.
Inputs: [TECHNOLOGY MIX | GEOGRAPHY | CONTRACTED VS. MERCHANT | IMPACT OBJECTIVES |
RETURN TARGET | INVESTOR TYPE | REPORTING STANDARD | FUND STRUCTURE PREFERENCE]

title: The Advent International Industrial Technology & Automation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 339 — The Advent International Industrial Technology & Automation
Act as MD at Advent International's Industrial Technology team. Build an
investment thesis for industrial automation and manufacturing technology.
Deliver: (1) Industrial automation investment thesis: labor cost escalation + labor
scarcity driving automation ROI; reshoring trends requiring higher-productivity
domestic manufacturing; Industry 4.0 and smart factory adoption accelerating.
(2) Sub-sector map: industrial robotics (KUKA, ABB, Fanuc — and their software
integrators), collaborative robots (cobots — Universal Robots model), computer
vision and AI quality inspection, MES (Manufacturing Execution Systems), industrial
IoT platforms, digital twins for factory optimization.
(3) Business model quality: OEM equipment vs. software/SaaS model; service and
maintenance revenue as recurring post-installation; how embedded the solution
is in the customer's production process (switching cost = production disruption).
(4) Customer economics: automation ROI for the manufacturer (payback period typically
18-24 months for cobot installation); what % of manual tasks can be automated?
How does this vary by manufacturing sub-sector?
(5) Fragmentation and consolidation: industrial software is highly fragmented (point
solutions for each step of manufacturing); platform consolidation opportunity;
industrial conglomerates (Siemens, Honeywell, Rockwell) as potential acquirers.
(6) AI integration: LLMs applied to manufacturing (predictive maintenance, process
optimization, quality control); Nvidia's Omniverse for industrial simulation.
(7) LBO vs. growth equity: for profitable software/services with recurring revenue —
LBO potential; for high-growth platform business — growth equity.
Format: Industrial Technology Investment Framework with Sub-Sector Map, Business Model
Analysis, Customer Economics, Consolidation Opportunity, AI Integration, and Structure.
Inputs: [SUB-SECTOR | COMPANY | REVENUE | ARR (IF SOFTWARE) | EBITDA | CUSTOMER SEGMENTS |
AUTOMATION ROI FOR CUSTOMERS | ENTRY VALUATION | PRIMARY VALUE CREATION THESIS]

title: The Oliver Wyman Financial Crime & AML Transformation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 340 — The Oliver Wyman Financial Crime & AML Transformation
Act as Partner at Oliver Wyman's Financial Crime practice. Design a
comprehensive AML/Financial Crime transformation for a global bank.
Deliver: (1) Financial crime risk landscape: money laundering (layering, placement,
integration); sanctions evasion (OFAC, EU, UN); fraud (synthetic identity, account
takeover, payment fraud); corruption and bribery; proliferation financing.
(2) Risk-based approach: customer risk scoring model (CDD/EDD criteria); entity
resolution and beneficial ownership; transaction monitoring rule optimization
(reduce false positive rate from 95% to 80% while maintaining detection rate).
(3) Transaction monitoring transformation: rules-based TM → ML-based anomaly detection;
network analytics for interconnected entity detection; typology library maintenance.
(4) KYC program: digital onboarding with eKYC (biometric verification, PEP/sanctions
screening, adverse media); periodic review cadence by risk tier;
perpetual KYC (event-driven re-screening rather than calendar review).
(5) SAR (Suspicious Activity Report) quality: quality over quantity; SAR filing
rate vs. SAR quality (law enforcement feedback); automated SAR drafting using Gen AI.
(6) Sanctions screening: real-time payments screening; list management (OFAC SDN,
EU, HMT); false positive management; nested correspondent banking risk.
(7) Governance: MLRO (Money Laundering Reporting Officer) authority; independent
testing by compliance; regulatory exam readiness; culture of compliance.
Format: AML Transformation Framework with Risk Assessment, TM Transformation, KYC
Program, SAR Quality, Sanctions Screening, and Governance Structure.
Inputs: [BANK TYPE | GEOGRAPHY | ANNUAL SAR FILINGS | FALSE POSITIVE RATE |
CURRENT TM SYSTEM | PRIMARY REGULATORY CONCERN | BUDGET FOR TRANSFORMATION]

title: The Warburg Pincus Healthcare: Outsourced Pharma Services
prompt_text:
PROMPT 341 — The Warburg Pincus Healthcare: Outsourced Pharma Services
Act as MD at Warburg Pincus Healthcare. Build a PE investment thesis for
a pharmaceutical outsourced services company (CDMO or CRO).
Deliver: (1) Outsourced pharma services rationale: big pharma increasingly outsourcing
R&D and manufacturing; CDMO/CRO market $300B+ globally; long-term secular growth.
(2) CDMO (Contract Development and Manufacturing): drug substance (API synthesis);
drug product (formulation, fill-finish); biologics (cell culture, fermentation);
cell & gene therapy (viral vector, plasmid DNA manufacturing).
(3) CRO (Contract Research): clinical trial management (Phase I-III); data management
and biostatistics; regulatory affairs outsourcing; lab services.
(4) Customer concentration risk: top 3 customers often 40-60% of revenue;
long-term supply agreements (multi-year MSAs) provide visibility;
technology transfer risk at contract end.
(5) Capacity and capital intensity: CDMO is capital-intensive (bioreactor suites $200M+);
utilisation rate the key metric; greenfield vs. brownfield expansion trade-off.
(6) Regulatory quality: FDA 483 observations; Warning Letter history; cGMP compliance
as competitive moat; CDMO quality system as barrier to entry.
(7) M&A: CDMO/CRO platform build (Thermo Fisher, Catalent, Lonza as large comps);
add capabilities (biologics, ADC manufacturing) through acquisition.
Format: Outsourced Pharma Services Investment Thesis with CDMO/CRO Analysis, Customer
Concentration, Capacity, Regulatory Quality, and M&A Strategy.
Inputs: [SERVICE TYPE (CDMO/CRO) | MODALITY (SMALL MOLECULE/BIOLOGICS/CGT) | REVENUE |
EBITDA | UTILISATION RATE | CUSTOMER CONCENTRATION | ENTRY MULTIPLE | VALUE CREATION]

title: The Citi Global Markets: Equity Derivatives Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 342 — The Citi Global Markets: Equity Derivatives Strategy
Act as Head of Equity Derivatives Strategy at Citi. Build a client-facing
equity derivatives strategy framework.
Deliver: (1) Equity derivatives universe: vanilla options (calls/puts), structured products
(autocallables, capital-protected notes), dispersion trades, volatility surface trading,
dividend derivatives, variance swaps.
(2) Volatility surface analysis: implied vol by strike (skew — puts more expensive
than calls) and tenor (term structure); VIX as market fear gauge; VVIX (vol of vol).
(3) Autocallable structuring: most popular structured product globally ($500B+/year);
contingent coupon paid if underlying above barrier; autocall if above strike on
observation date; knock-in put if below barrier at maturity.
(4) Risk reversal as directional view: buy call, sell put (or vice versa) at zero cost;
FX and equity risk reversals as client hedging and speculation tool.
(5) Dispersion trading: buy index variance, sell single-stock variance; profit if
single stocks have higher realised vol than index (correlation decreases).
(6) Dividend derivatives: dividend futures (Eurostoxx 50 DEC dividend futures);
pricing dividend risk; corporate action risk in options.
(7) Tail risk hedging: put spread collars for equity portfolio protection;
optimal hedge ratio; cost-efficient tail protection using spreads vs. outright puts.
Format: Equity Derivatives Framework with Volatility Analysis, Autocallable Structuring,
Risk Reversals, Dispersion, Dividend Derivatives, and Tail Risk Hedging.
Inputs: [CLIENT TYPE | PORTFOLIO SIZE | UNDERLYING | DIRECTIONAL VIEW | VOLATILITY VIEW |
HEDGE OBJECTIVE | NOTIONAL | PRIMARY RISK CONCERN]

title: The Goldman Sachs Asset Management: Absolute Return Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 343 — The Goldman Sachs Asset Management: Absolute Return Strategy
Act as PM at GSAM's Absolute Return team. Build a market-neutral
absolute return strategy targeting positive returns in all market conditions.
Deliver: (1) Absolute return philosophy: generate positive alpha independent of market
direction; low correlation to equities and bonds; target Sharpe >1.0 with low drawdown.
(2) Strategy mix: equity market neutral (long/short with zero beta); global macro overlay;
statistical arbitrage; merger arbitrage; relative value fixed income.
(3) Equity market neutral: long undervalued/short overvalued within same sector;
systematic (factor-based) vs. fundamental selection; beta hedging; sector neutrality.
(4) Risk budgeting: allocate VaR budget across strategy sleeves; no single strategy
consumes more than 40% of risk budget; dynamic reallocation to best opportunities.
(5) Correlation management: ensure strategies are genuinely uncorrelated (not all
short vol in different forms); crisis correlation testing (March 2020 stress test).
(6) Leverage: 2-3× gross leverage typical; financing through prime broker;
margin call risk management.
(7) Capacity management: absolute return strategies have capacity constraints (large
AUM degrades alpha); target fund size $3-8B; soft close when capacity reached.
Format: Absolute Return Strategy with Strategy Mix, Market Neutral Construction,
Risk Budgeting, Correlation Management, Leverage, and Capacity.
Inputs: [AUM | RETURN TARGET | VOL TARGET | MAX DRAWDOWN | STRATEGY WEIGHTS |
LEVERAGE LIMIT | BENCHMARK | PRIMARY ALPHA SOURCE]

title: The McKinsey Global Institute: Future of Work & Automation Economics
prompt_text:
PROMPT 344 — The McKinsey Global Institute: Future of Work & Automation Economics
Act as Senior Fellow at McKinsey Global Institute. Build an economic
analysis of automation's impact on labour markets and productivity.
Deliver: (1) Automation potential by occupation: % of tasks automatable using current AI/ML
(McKinsey's 5 categories: physical, data collection, data processing, interaction,
managing others); which occupations are most/least automatable.
(2) Job displacement vs. job creation: history of automation (industrial revolution,
computerisation) shows net job creation; new jobs created by AI (AI trainers,
prompt engineers, data annotators) vs. jobs displaced.
(3) Productivity dividend: McKinsey estimates 0.8-1.4% annual productivity growth
from AI automation; which sectors capture most productivity gain (healthcare,
manufacturing, professional services).
(4) Wage polarisation: automation hollows out middle-skill routine jobs; benefits
accrue to high-skill (complement AI) and some low-skill (non-automatable tasks);
middle-income squeeze.
(5) Transition costs: retraining and reskilling costs; geographic concentration of
job losses (manufacturing communities); policy response (UBI, job guarantee,
wage insurance, education reform).
(6) Country-level impact: automation exposure varies by country (higher manufacturing
share → higher displacement risk); China, Germany most exposed; UK, US less so
(more services-oriented).
(7) Investment implications: automation beneficiaries (productivity tools, robotics,
AI software); displaced sectors (back-office BPO, routine data processing, basic legal).
Format: Future of Work Analysis with Automation Potential, Displacement vs. Creation,
Productivity, Wage Polarisation, Policy Response, Country Analysis, and Investment.
Inputs: [SECTOR FOCUS | COUNTRY | AUTOMATION HORIZON | POLICY CONTEXT |
WORKFORCE COMPOSITION | PRIMARY ECONOMIC CONCERN]

title: The Lazard Asset Management: Global Thematic Equity
prompt_text:
PROMPT 345 — The Lazard Asset Management: Global Thematic Equity
Act as Head of Thematic Equity at Lazard Asset Management. Build a
global thematic equity portfolio around 3-5 long-term structural themes.
Deliver: (1) Theme selection framework: large TAM ($1T+ addressable); multi-decade
duration (not cyclical); underappreciated by market today; investable universe
(50+ quality companies globally).
(2) Theme 1 — Ageing Population: demand for healthcare (novel therapeutics, diagnostics),
wealth management, senior living, silver economy consumer brands; Japan as leading
indicator.
(3) Theme 2 — Energy Transition: renewable energy equipment, grid modernisation,
EV supply chain, green hydrogen, carbon capture; bifurcated by region (IRA, EU
Green Deal, Asia catch-up).
(4) Theme 3 — Digital Infrastructure: data centres, semiconductor equipment, cloud
hyperscalers, AI chips, edge computing, fibre networks; AI accelerating demand.
(5) Theme 4 — Water Scarcity: water treatment, water efficiency technology, water
utilities, desalination; global water stress as underappreciated long-term risk.
(6) Portfolio construction: 50-80 stocks across 3-5 themes; avoid pure thematic ETF
(overlap, low quality); quality screen within theme (ROIC, FCF, balance sheet).
(7) Valuation discipline: thematic stocks can become expensive; price discipline
using DCF/EV per unit of theme exposure (EV/installed capacity, EV/subscriber).
Format: Global Thematic Equity with Theme Selection, Deep-Dives on 4 Themes,
Portfolio Construction, Quality Screen, and Valuation Discipline.
Inputs: [FUND SIZE | THEME MIX | QUALITY CRITERIA | GEOGRAPHIC LIMITS |
VALUATION CEILING | BENCHMARK | TIME HORIZON | PRIMARY THEMATIC VIEW]

title: The Permira Growth: European Technology Scale-Up
prompt_text:
PROMPT 346 — The Permira Growth: European Technology Scale-Up
Act as MD at Permira Growth Equity. Build an investment thesis for a
European technology scale-up at Series C/D or growth stage.
Deliver: (1) European tech landscape: London (fintech, AI), Berlin (SaaS, marketplace),
Stockholm (gaming, fintech), Paris (deep tech, AI), Amsterdam (payments, software);
European tech closing the gap with US but still at 40% valuation discount.
(2) Target profile: €20-100M ARR; 40-80% growth; Series C or D stage;
B2B SaaS or marketplace; pan-European or global ambition.
(3) European SaaS benchmarks: NRR >115%; gross margin >75%; CAC payback <18 months;
Rule of 40 >50 at growth stage; what separates best-in-class from median.
(4) US expansion: €/$ parity in SaaS pricing; product-market fit replication;
GTM in US (hire US CRO, open NY/SF office); when to expand vs. consolidate in Europe.
(5) UK regulatory post-Brexit: GDPR vs. UK GDPR; financial services regulation
(FCA vs. EU passporting lost); talent visa changes for non-UK EU workers.
(6) Dual-class and founder alignment: European founders increasingly seeking dual-class
structures (Wise, Deliveroo precedents); governance at growth stage.
(7) Exit: US strategic acquirers (largest buyer universe for European tech);
US IPO (Nasdaq for largest European tech); UK/EU IPO for €2B+ companies.
Format: European Tech Growth Investment with Market Overview, Target Profile, US
Expansion, Regulatory, Founder Alignment, and Exit Strategy.
Inputs: [COMPANY | COUNTRY | ARR | GROWTH RATE | NRR | US TRACTION |
ENTRY VALUATION | FUND STAGE | PRIMARY GROWTH CHALLENGE]

title: The Citigroup Global Markets: FX Macro Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 347 — The Citigroup Global Markets: FX Macro Strategy
Act as Head of FX Macro Strategy at Citi. Build a comprehensive G10 and
EM FX investment strategy.
Deliver: (1) G10 FX framework: current account (trade surplus/deficit), interest rate
differentials (carry), growth differentials, central bank policy divergence,
terms of trade, reserve currency status.
(2) USD framework: DXY (Dollar Index); US exceptionalism thesis (growth + rate premium);
twin deficits risk (fiscal + current account); USD smile (USD strong in risk-off AND
in US outperformance; weak in global growth acceleration).
(3) EUR/USD: ECB vs. Fed cycle divergence; European energy shock absorption;
EUR undervaluation on purchasing power parity; political risk (Italy, fiscal rules).
(4) JPY: BoJ yield curve control (YCC) normalisation; JPY carry unwind risk (largest
carry trade in G10); JPY as safe haven in risk-off scenarios.
(5) GBP: post-Brexit structural current account deficit; BoE policy; UK growth.
(6) EM FX carry trade: identify high-yielding EM currencies with stable macro
fundamentals; carry-to-vol ratio screen; BRL, INR, MXN as examples.
(7) Positioning and sentiment: CFTC COT (Commitment of Traders) report; speculative
positioning as contrarian indicator; consensus positioning risk.
Format: FX Strategy with G10 Framework, USD Analysis, EUR/USD, JPY, GBP, EM Carry,
and Positioning Analysis.
Inputs: [G10 OR EM FOCUS | DIRECTIONAL VIEW | CARRY SCREEN | POSITIONING DATA |
RISK EVENTS | HEDGE RATIO | PRIMARY FX THESIS]

title: The KPMG Tax: OECD Pillar Two Global Minimum Tax Implementation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 348 — The KPMG Tax: OECD Pillar Two Global Minimum Tax Implementation
Act as Partner at KPMG's International Tax practice. Guide a multinational
through OECD Pillar Two (15% Global Minimum Tax) implementation.
Deliver: (1) Pillar Two framework: Income Inclusion Rule (IIR) — parent entity tops up
tax if subsidiary ETR <15%; Undertaxed Profits Rule (UTPR) — backstop if IIR not applied;
Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-Up Tax (QDMTT) — local jurisdiction tops up first.
(2) GloBE (Global Anti-Base Erosion) computation: GloBE Income = financial accounting
income adjusted for Pillar Two adjustments; Covered Taxes = income taxes paid;
ETR = Covered Taxes / GloBE Income by jurisdiction.
(3) Substance-Based Income Exclusion (SBIE): carve-out for genuine economic substance
(5% payroll cost + 5% book value of tangible assets = excluded from top-up base).
(4) Impact assessment: identify jurisdictions with ETR <15%; quantify top-up tax;
jurisdictions most affected (Ireland 12.5% → 15%, Switzerland, Singapore, UAE, Cayman).
(5) Data requirements: new data collection from each entity (financial accounts →
GloBE adjustments → covered taxes); ERP system changes for GloBE data.
(6) Tax planning response: is it worth restructuring to avoid top-up? SBIE optimisation;
QDMTT election (pay locally rather than to parent jurisdiction); deferred tax positions.
(7) Compliance and reporting: GloBE Information Return (GIR) — new filing requirement;
timing (first filing 2026 for CY2024 MNEs); safe harbours (UTPR safe harbour, transitional
CBCR safe harbour).
Format: Pillar Two Implementation with GloBE Computation, Impact Assessment, SBIE,
Data Requirements, Tax Planning, and Compliance Reporting.
Inputs: [COMPANY | JURISDICTIONS | CURRENT ETR BY JURISDICTION | PAYROLL/TANGIBLE ASSETS |
ESTIMATED TOP-UP EXPOSURE | DATA READINESS | PRIMARY PLANNING CONCERN]

title: The Apax Partners: Tech-Enabled B2B Software Buyout
prompt_text:
PROMPT 349 — The Apax Partners: Tech-Enabled B2B Software Buyout
Act as MD at Apax Partners' Tech & Telco team. Build a buyout investment
thesis for a tech-enabled B2B software company.
Deliver: (1) Apax software buyout philosophy: acquire mission-critical B2B software
companies with high switching costs; leverage Apax Digital team to accelerate
product and go-to-market transformation.
(2) Target profile: $50-300M ARR; EBITDA positive (or near breakeven); category
leader in vertical market; sticky enterprise customer base (NRR >105%).
(3) Value creation playbook: (a) Go-to-market intensification (add enterprise sales,
land-and-expand motion, international expansion); (b) Product extension (add modules
to expand ARPU); (c) M&A to add adjacent capabilities; (d) Operational efficiency.
(4) Multiple expansion: buy at 5-7× revenue with 25% growth → sell at 7-10×
revenue with 35% growth (growth re-rating + multiple expansion + ARR growth = IRR).
(5) AI integration as value creation: embedding AI into software product (pricing
premium, reduced churn, competitive moat); Gen AI accelerating product development.
(6) Management team: software buyout requires specialist management — CRO with SaaS
experience, CPO with AI background; Apax portfolio company network for talent.
(7) Leverage: 4-6× EBITDA leverage for software businesses with high recurring revenue;
covenant package; refinancing risk if EBITDA path deviates from plan.
Format: Tech-Enabled Software Buyout with Target Profile, Value Creation Playbook,
Multiple Expansion, AI Integration, Management Team, and Leverage.
Inputs: [COMPANY | ARR | NRR | GROSS MARGIN | RULE OF 40 | LEVERAGE | ENTRY MULTIPLE |
VALUE CREATION PRIORITY | HOLD PERIOD | EXIT TARGET]

title: The Blackstone Real Estate: Net Lease & Sale-Leaseback
prompt_text:
PROMPT 350 — The Blackstone Real Estate: Net Lease & Sale-Leaseback
Act as MD at Blackstone Real Estate. Build an investment thesis for
net lease and sale-leaseback real estate transactions.
Deliver: (1) Net lease fundamentals: tenant pays rent + operating expenses (NNN lease);
landlord receives predictable rent with minimal management burden; WALT (Weighted
Average Lease Term) as primary credit quality indicator.
(2) Sale-leaseback rationale for corporates: unlock capital from owned real estate;
retain operational use of the asset; off-balance-sheet treatment (IFRS 16 limits this);
proceeds used for M&A, capex, debt reduction.
(3) Credit analysis of tenant: investment-grade (risk-free) vs. sub-investment-grade
(higher yield, higher risk); cap rate premium for non-IG tenants (100-200bps);
business model durability.
(4) Property types: industrial (Amazon, FedEx logistics — most sought after); retail
(drug stores, QSR, dollar stores — traffic resilient); office (avoided); medical outpatient.
(5) Lease structure: rent escalations (1.5-2% fixed annual or CPI-linked); renewal
options (tenant's option to renew at market); termination provisions.
(6) Portfolio diversification: across tenants, industries, geographies; single-tenant
concentration risk; dark store risk (tenant vacates but still obligated on lease).
(7) Cap rate environment: NNN cap rates 5-6.5% for IG tenants; spread vs. long Treasury;
duration risk (long lease = long bond-like duration).
Format: Net Lease Strategy with Tenant Credit Analysis, Property Types, Lease Structure,
Portfolio Construction, Cap Rate Framework, and Sale-Leaseback Advisory.
Inputs: [TENANT | INDUSTRY | PROPERTY TYPE | LEASE TERM | RENT ESCALATION |
CAP RATE | TENANT CREDIT RATING | GEOGRAPHY | ACQUISITION PRICE]

title: The Evercore: Contested M&A and Activism Defense
prompt_text:
PROMPT 351 — The Evercore: Contested M&A and Activism Defense
Act as Senior Partner at Evercore's Shareholder Advisory group. Design a
defense strategy for a company facing activist pressure or a hostile bid.
Deliver: (1) Activist landscape: hedge fund activists (Elliott, Carl Icahn, Starboard,
ValueAct); activist demands (board seats, spin-offs, buybacks, CEO replacement,
operational improvement); activist holding period and exit strategy.
(2) Vulnerability assessment: low valuation (discount to peers); operational
underperformance; complex portfolio (sum-of-parts discount); excess cash or
under-leveraged balance sheet; weak governance (staggered board, classified stock).
(3) Pre-activism defense: proactive shareholder engagement; stock buyback programme;
portfolio simplification; governance improvements; investor day to communicate strategy.
(4) Responding to an activist: analyse demands objectively (are they value-creating?);
engage privately before public statement; consider settlement (board seat, agreed
operational changes) vs. proxy fight.
(5) Proxy fight: white solicitation firm (Innisfree, MacKenzie Partners); letter
campaign to shareholders; ISS and Glass Lewis engagement; director slate preparation.
(6) Hostile bid defense: poison pill (Rights Plan) adoption; staggered board delays
control; white knight search; standalone plan articulation with credible financial plan.
(7) Settlement mechanics: board seat agreement; standstill agreement (activist agrees
not to buy more stock or make additional demands for agreed period).
Format: Activism Defense with Vulnerability Assessment, Pre-Activism Defense, Response
Strategy, Proxy Fight Toolkit, Hostile Bid Defense, and Settlement Mechanics.
Inputs: [COMPANY | ACTIVIST OR BIDDER | DEMANDS | PRIMARY VULNERABILITY |
GOVERNANCE PROFILE | SHAREHOLDER COMPOSITION | PREFERRED RESPONSE | TIMELINE]

title: The PIMCO Mortgage & Structured Finance
prompt_text:
PROMPT 352 — The PIMCO Mortgage & Structured Finance
Act as Head of Mortgage Strategy at PIMCO. Build a comprehensive
mortgage and structured finance investment strategy.
Deliver: (1) Agency MBS market: $9T+ market; Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Ginnie Mae
guarantees; prepayment risk (refinancing → faster repayment in falling rates);
negative convexity (duration extends when rates rise, shortens when rates fall).
(2) TBA (To-Be-Announced) market: forward market for agency MBS; dollar roll
financing; specified pool premium; TBA vs. specified pool strategy.
(3) Prepayment modelling: PSA (Public Securities Association) prepayment speed;
CPR (Conditional Prepayment Rate); S-curve (incentive to refinance based on
rate differential); burnout effect.
(4) Non-agency RMBS: credit risk (no government guarantee); Prime Jumbo (high-quality
borrowers), Alt-A, Subprime (legacy crisis securities trading at discount);
CRT (Credit Risk Transfer — Fannie Mae CAS, Freddie Mac STACR) as synthetic.
(5) CMBS: commercial mortgage-backed securities; conduit vs. SASB; IO (interest-only)
strip risk; stress by property type.
(6) ABS: credit card ABS, auto loan ABS, student loan ABS, equipment ABS;
revolving vs. amortising structures; credit enhancement.
(7) Duration management: agency MBS negative convexity requires dynamic duration
hedging (Treasury futures, swaptions); option-adjusted duration.
Format: Mortgage & Structured Finance Strategy with Agency MBS, Prepayment Modelling,
Non-Agency, CMBS, ABS, and Duration Management.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO TYPE | DURATION TARGET | AGENCY VS. NON-AGENCY MIX | CREDIT QUALITY |
PREPAYMENT VIEW | LEVERAGE | PRIMARY RISK | BENCHMARK]

title: The Blackstone Hedge Fund Solutions: Portfolio Construction
prompt_text:
PROMPT 353 — The Blackstone Hedge Fund Solutions: Portfolio Construction
Act as Head of Portfolio Construction at Blackstone's Hedge Fund Solutions group.
Build an optimal hedge fund portfolio for institutional investors.
Deliver: (1) Hedge fund portfolio rationale: diversification (low correlation to
stocks/bonds); alpha generation; tail risk reduction; absolute return in bear markets.
(2) Strategy allocation: equity L/S (25%), global macro (20%), credit (20%),
relative value/arb (20%), multi-strategy (15%) — rationale for each allocation.
(3) Manager selection: quantitative screening (Sharpe, Sortino, drawdown, correlation);
qualitative assessment (edge, process, team, culture, infrastructure).
(4) Portfolio-level risk management: aggregate factor exposures (net equity beta,
duration, credit spread DV01, FX); ensure no unintended concentrations.
(5) Liquidity management: monthly liquidity (40%), quarterly (40%), annual (20%);
liquidity ladder matches institutional redemption requirements.
(6) Fees: average all-in cost of HF portfolio (weighted average management fee
+ performance fee); net return to investor; fee negotiation leverage.
(7) Performance attribution: alpha from each strategy; HF portfolio vs. 60/40
benchmark; Sharpe ratio and max drawdown comparison.
Format: HF Portfolio Construction with Strategy Allocation, Manager Selection, Risk
Management, Liquidity, Fees, and Performance Attribution.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO SIZE | INVESTOR TYPE | RETURN TARGET | VOL BUDGET | STRATEGY
PREFERENCES | LIQUIDITY REQUIREMENTS | FEE BUDGET | BENCHMARK]

title: The Nomura: Japan Government Bond (JGB) Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 354 — The Nomura: Japan Government Bond (JGB) Strategy
Act as Head of JGB Strategy at Nomura Securities. Build a comprehensive
Japan rates investment framework.
Deliver: (1) BoJ policy framework: yield curve control (YCC) history and evolution;
negative interest rate policy (NIRP) exit; BoJ's inflation mandate (2% target);
when does BoJ normalise rates fully?
(2) JGB supply and demand: MoF (Ministry of Finance) JGB issuance; BoJ as dominant
buyer (holding >50% of outstanding JGBs); life insurers and pension funds as natural
JGB buyers; foreign investor role.
(3) Duration risk in JGBs: 10yr JGB yield 0.5-1.0% — any normalisation creates
significant capital losses; duration of JGB index (7-9 years); convexity.
(4) Inflation and real yields: Japan breaking out of deflation (2022-2024);
real JGB yields deeply negative; TIPS equivalent (JGBi) market.
(5) JPY and JGB linkage: JPY weakness → imported inflation → BoJ forced to hike;
yen carry trade unwind risk (global implications — 2024 August episode).
(6) Cross-market: JGB vs. US Treasury spread (JPY-hedged US Treasuries vs. JGBs);
Japanese investor demand for foreign bonds when hedge costs are low.
(7) Steepening trade: front end anchored by BoJ; long end could sell off as BoJ
reduces QE; 2s10s steepener as primary JGB trade idea.
Format: JGB Strategy with BoJ Policy, Supply/Demand, Duration Risk, Inflation, JPY
Linkage, Cross-Market, and Steepener Trade Recommendation.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO TYPE | DURATION BUDGET | JGB ALLOCATION | YEN HEDGE RATIO |
CROSS-MARKET ALLOCATION | BOJ VIEW | PRIMARY JGB TRADE]

title: The Boston Consulting Group: Mergers Integration Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 355 — The Boston Consulting Group: Mergers Integration Strategy
Act as Senior Partner at BCG's Transaction Centre. Design a comprehensive
post-merger integration strategy for a large-scale corporate merger.
Deliver: (1) Integration strategy design: integration ambition (full integration vs. holding
company vs. federation model); how much of each company's operating model is preserved
vs. replaced by the combined company's design.
(2) Day 1 readiness: legal Day 1 (entity creation, regulatory notifications); operational
Day 1 (systems access, employee communication, customer communication, financial reporting);
100-day plan milestones.
(3) Operating model design: combined org structure (which company's model wins?);
reporting lines; spans and layers optimisation; leadership selection process.
(4) Synergy programme: cost synergies (headcount, procurement, real estate, IT rationalisation);
revenue synergies (cross-sell, new products, geographic expansion); dis-synergies (customer
churn, employee attrition, management distraction); synergy governance.
(5) Cultural integration: cultural assessment (both companies); where cultural differences
are an integration risk; pulse surveys during integration.
(6) Technology and data integration: ERP consolidation (most complex, longest lead time);
data migration; cyber security during transition.
(7) Stakeholder management: employee retention (retention bonuses for key talent);
customer communication (no disruption to service); regulatory commitments monitoring.
Format: PMI Strategy with Integration Model, Day 1 Readiness, Operating Design, Synergy
Programme, Culture, Technology, and Stakeholder Management.
Inputs: [ACQUIRER | TARGET | DEAL RATIONALE | INTEGRATION AMBITION | SYNERGY TARGET |
CULTURAL GAP | ERP PLATFORMS | KEY STAKEHOLDER CONCERNS | TIMELINE]

title: The Citi Research: Global Shipping & Logistics Sector
prompt_text:
PROMPT 356 — The Citi Research: Global Shipping & Logistics Sector
Act as Head of Shipping & Logistics Research at Citi. Build an investment
framework for the global shipping and logistics industry.
Deliver: (1) Shipping market structure: container shipping (Maersk, MSC, CMA CGM),
dry bulk (Capesize, Panamax), tankers (VLCC, Suezmax, Aframax), LNG carriers;
cyclical commodity business driven by supply-demand balance.
(2) Container shipping cycle analysis: SCFI (Shanghai Containerized Freight Index);
fleet capacity growth vs. demand growth; scrapping and ordering cycle; congestion
(ports, canals — Suez, Panama) as temporary demand amplifier.
(3) Dry bulk analysis: Baltic Dry Index (BDI); commodity demand (iron ore, coal,
grain) drives demand; fleet age profile; ordering activity.
(4) Tanker market: VLCC rates; geopolitical impact (Russia shadow fleet, Iran oil,
Red Sea diversions adding tonne-miles); IMO 2030 sulphur compliance fleet.
(5) Logistics: 3PL (Third-Party Logistics) market growth; e-commerce fulfillment
driving last-mile demand; freight forwarding digitalisation; Maersk/DB Schenker
vertical integration strategy.
(6) ESG — decarbonisation: IMO 2050 net-zero target; methanol and ammonia as
alternative fuels; LNG as transition fuel; carbon levy on international shipping.
(7) Valuation: NAV (Net Asset Value) approach for asset-heavy shipping companies;
P/NAV premium or discount; EV/EBITDA for logistics companies.
Format: Shipping & Logistics Framework with Container Cycle, Dry Bulk, Tankers,
Logistics, ESG Decarbonisation, and Valuation.
Inputs: [SECTOR (CONTAINER/BULK/TANKER/LOGISTICS) | COMPANY | KEY METRICS |
RATE ENVIRONMENT | FLEET PROFILE | FUEL STRATEGY | VALUATION | PRIMARY INVESTMENT THESIS]

title: The Kohlberg Kravis Roberts: Infrastructure Technology & Digital
prompt_text:
PROMPT 357 — The Kohlberg Kravis Roberts: Infrastructure Technology & Digital
Act as MD at KKR's Infrastructure team. Build an investment thesis for
digital and technology-enabled infrastructure assets.
Deliver: (1) Digital infrastructure categories: data centres (hyperscale, colocation),
fibre networks (dark fibre, FTTP), wireless towers (macro, small cell), subsea cables,
satellite networks, smart grid technology.
(2) Data centre investment thesis: AI-driven power demand creating unprecedented
demand for compute infrastructure; hyperscaler pre-leasing creates high revenue
visibility; power availability as primary constraint.
(3) Fibre network economics: cost per home passed (£500-1,200 in UK); take rate
(25-35% after 3 years in UK FTTP); ARPU (£25-35/month); payback period (8-12 years).
(4) Tower infrastructure: mature, well-understood asset class; tenancy ratio (1.8-2.5×);
CPI-linked rent escalations; 5G densification driving small cell growth.
(5) Subsea cables: 99% of international internet traffic travels via subsea cables;
hyperscaler-owned (Google, Meta, Amazon) vs. consortium cables;
route diversification premium.
(6) Risk profile: digital infrastructure has contract risk (hyperscaler tenants are
also potential competitors building own infrastructure); technology obsolescence risk
(data centre cooling technology, fibre vs. wireless).
(7) Financing: project finance for fibre (long-term, predictable take-rate ramp);
corporate financing for tower companies (rated entities); green financing for energy-
efficient data centres.
Format: Digital Infrastructure Strategy with Data Centres, Fibre Economics, Towers,
Subsea Cables, Risk Profile, and Financing.
Inputs: [ASSET TYPE | GEOGRAPHY | TENANT TYPE | REVENUE VISIBILITY | POWER SOURCE |
RETURN TARGET | FINANCING STRUCTURE | PRIMARY RISK CONCERN]

title: The Oliver Wyman Private Banking: Wealth Management Product Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 358 — The Oliver Wyman Private Banking: Wealth Management Product Strategy
Act as Partner at Oliver Wyman's Private Banking practice. Design a
product strategy for a private bank serving HNW and UHNW clients.
Deliver: (1) Private banking product architecture: deposits and cash management; lending
(lombard, mortgage, aircraft/yacht finance); investments (discretionary portfolio
management, advisory, execution-only); structured products; alternatives.
(2) Lombard lending: collateralised lending against investment portfolio (typically
50-70% LTV); yield spread between lending rate and portfolio return;
margin call procedures; risk-adjusted revenue contribution.
(3) Discretionary Portfolio Management (DPM): client delegates investment decisions
to bank; fee 0.5-1.0% of AUM; model portfolio approach; CIO strategy cascaded
to client portfolios; DPM penetration as key profitability metric.
(4) Structured products: capital protection notes, yield enhancement (autocallables),
leverage products; private bank distributes bank-structured products;
suitability (MiFID II) and disclosure requirements.
(5) Alternative investments: private equity, hedge funds, real estate, private credit
for qualified investors; minimum €250K investment; feeder fund access;
illiquidity communication to clients.
(6) Family office services: consolidated reporting (across all assets, banks, custodians);
estate planning; philanthropy advisory; next-generation education programmes.
(7) Digital: digital onboarding; portfolio viewing app; automated rebalancing;
AI-assisted investment proposal generation; robo-advisory for smaller HNW segment.
Format: Private Bank Product Strategy with Lombard Lending, DPM, Structured Products,
Alternatives, Family Office Services, and Digital Capabilities.
Inputs: [BANK TYPE | CLIENT SEGMENTS | AUM | DPM PENETRATION | LENDING BOOK |
ALTERNATIVES CAPABILITY | DIGITAL MATURITY | PRIMARY PRODUCT GAP]

title: The Macquarie Global Infrastructure: Airport Operations & Value
prompt_text:
PROMPT 359 — The Macquarie Global Infrastructure: Airport Operations & Value
Act as MD at Macquarie Infrastructure and Real Assets. Build an operational
value creation strategy for an airport infrastructure investment.
Deliver: (1) Airport value creation levers: (a) Traffic growth (route development,
airline relationship management, capacity expansion); (b) Non-aeronautical revenue
growth (retail, F&B, car parking, real estate development, hotel);
(c) Cost efficiency (procurement, energy, headcount); (d) Capital recycling.
(2) Route development: airline incentive programmes (marketing support, rebates for
new routes); connectivity analysis (underserved O&D pairs); LCC attraction strategy.
(3) Retail and concession optimisation: retail $/pax benchmark vs. comparable airports;
specialty retail mix vs. F&B mix; dwell time extension strategies;
digital pre-order and click-and-collect.
(4) Car parking revenue: PRM (Parking Revenue Management); dynamic pricing for
car parks; valet, meet-and-greet premium services; EV charging as new revenue.
(5) Real estate and aerotropolis: airport city concept; landside commercial development
(hotels, logistics parks, offices); ground lease income; planning and entitlement.
(6) Energy and sustainability: airport carbon accreditation (ACI Airport Carbon
Accreditation); renewable energy on-site (solar canopies, wind); sustainable
aviation fuel (SAF) infrastructure.
(7) Capex programme management: terminal expansion; airfield capacity; technology
(biometrics, automated security, self-service baggage); capital efficiency.
Format: Airport Value Creation Strategy with Traffic Growth, Non-Aero Revenue,
Retail Optimisation, Car Parking, Real Estate, Sustainability, and Capex.
Inputs: [AIRPORT | ANNUAL PASSENGERS | AERONAUTICAL REVENUE | NON-AERO REVENUE |
RETAIL $/PAX | CAR PARK CAPACITY | EXPANSION PLAN | PRIMARY VALUE CREATION LEVER]

title: The Advent International: Logistics & Supply Chain Technology
prompt_text:
PROMPT 360 — The Advent International: Logistics & Supply Chain Technology
Act as MD at Advent International's Services and Technology team. Build a
PE investment thesis for a logistics or supply chain technology company.
Deliver: (1) Logistics technology landscape: TMS (Transportation Management Systems),
WMS (Warehouse Management Systems), freight marketplaces, last-mile delivery tech,
supply chain visibility platforms, autonomous warehouse robotics.
(2) TMS investment thesis: shippers moving from spreadsheet to SaaS TMS; carrier
management, rate management, load optimisation; high switching costs once integrated
with ERP; 3-5 year contracts.
(3) Freight marketplace: digital freight matching (Convoy, Flexport model); spot
market digitisation; take rate (2-5% of freight value); liquidity challenge (chicken
and egg problem).
(4) Last-mile technology: route optimisation software; delivery management platforms;
proof of delivery; network-as-a-service (multi-carrier intelligent routing).
(5) Supply chain visibility: end-to-end shipment tracking; predictive ETAs;
exception management; supply chain risk monitoring; customer expectations for visibility.
(6) Autonomous warehouse: AMR (Autonomous Mobile Robot) software; goods-to-person
fulfillment; pick rate improvement (2-3× vs. manual); ROI for 3PL and retail customers.
(7) Exit: strategic (Oracle, SAP, Salesforce acquiring supply chain SaaS); large
logistics operator; PE secondary; IPO for $1B+ ARR companies.
Format: Logistics Tech Investment Framework with TMS, Freight Marketplace, Last-Mile,
Visibility, Autonomous Warehouse, and Exit Strategy.
Inputs: [SUB-SECTOR | COMPANY | ARR | NRR | GROSS MARGIN | CUSTOMER TYPE |
COMPETITIVE POSITION | ENTRY VALUATION | VALUE CREATION THESIS]

title: The Apollo Global Management: Insurance & Annuity Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 361 — The Apollo Global Management: Insurance & Annuity Strategy
Act as MD at Apollo's Insurance & Annuity business (Athene). Build an
asset-liability management strategy for an annuity-focused insurer.
Deliver: (1) Athene/Apollo model: raise low-cost annuity liabilities (fixed-rate
annuities, funding agreements), invest in higher-yielding illiquid credit assets
(direct loans, CLOs, ABS) → earn spread; PE sponsor provides proprietary deal flow.
(2) Liability management: fixed annuity pricing (crediting rate vs. treasury yield);
surrender charge structure; MYGA (Multi-Year Guaranteed Annuity) competition; liability
duration (typically 5-8 years for fixed annuities).
(3) Asset allocation for annuity liabilities: investment-grade bias (NAIC 1-2 rated);
target asset yield 100-150bps above comparable public market yield; illiquid credit
allocation (private credit, CLOs, ABS) generating the spread pickup.
(4) Regulatory capital: RBC ratio management; NAIC-2 vs. NAIC-3 capital charges;
state domicile selection for capital efficiency (Bermuda vs. Iowa vs. Texas);
reserve funding strategies.
(5) Interest rate risk: asset/liability duration mismatch management; impact of rising
rates on fixed annuity demand (positive — more attractive vs. bank deposits);
interest rate swap overlay for residual duration gap.
(6) Reinsurance: Bermuda reinsurance (Athene Re) for offshore reserve financing;
Treaty structure; NYDFS/state regulatory scrutiny of offshore reinsurance.
(7) Growth: FIA (Fixed Index Annuity) market share competition; bank channel
distribution (key for fixed annuity distribution); pension risk transfer (PRT).
Format: Insurance ALM Strategy with Liability Analysis, Asset Allocation, Capital
Management, Interest Rate Risk, Bermuda Reinsurance, and Growth Strategy.
Inputs: [INSURER SIZE | LIABILITY TYPE | CREDITING RATE | ASSET YIELD TARGET |
RBC RATIO | DURATION GAP | DOMICILE | PRIMARY ALM CHALLENGE]

title: The Berkshire Hathaway Energy: Regulated Utility Transformation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 362 — The Berkshire Hathaway Energy: Regulated Utility Transformation
Act as Chief Strategy Officer at Berkshire Hathaway Energy. Build a
strategic transformation plan for a regulated utility group.
Deliver: (1) BHE portfolio: PacifiCorp, MidAmerican Energy, NV Energy, UK grid assets,
BHE Renewables — diversified multi-state, multi-fuel regulated utility.
(2) Renewable energy capital allocation: $29B+ investment in wind/solar across the
portfolio; rate base growth from clean energy capex driving regulated EPS growth.
(3) Rate base growth as earnings engine: regulated utilities earn allowed ROE on rate
base; each $1B of capex adds ~$90-100M of annual regulated earnings (at 9-10% ROE);
how to sustain 5-7% EPS growth through capital deployment.
(4) Wildfire liability risk: PacifiCorp's Oregon wildfire litigation exposure; how
catastrophic wildfire liability is managed; inverse condemnation doctrine; insurance
adequacy; rate recovery of wildfire mitigation costs.
(5) Transmission investment: FERC-regulated transmission earns higher ROE incentives;
transmission as growth platform for renewable energy interconnection.
(6) Nuclear: BHE's interest in nuclear power (consistent with Warren Buffett's recent
nuclear advocacy); small modular reactors (SMR) investment thesis; existing nuclear
fleet extension economics.
(7) Financing: investment-grade utility bonds (A/BBB range); green bond issuance
for clean energy capex; BHE corporate structure and parent support.
Format: Regulated Utility Strategy with Portfolio Overview, Rate Base Growth Model,
Renewable Capital Allocation, Wildfire Risk, Transmission, Nuclear, and Financing.
Inputs: [UTILITY NAME | RATE BASE | ALLOWED ROE | CAPEX PLAN | RENEWABLE % |
WILDFIRE EXPOSURE | NUCLEAR ASSETS | PRIMARY REGULATORY JURISDICTION]

title: The KPMG Global Transfer Pricing Controversy & MAP
prompt_text:
PROMPT 363 — The KPMG Global Transfer Pricing Controversy & MAP
Act as Partner at KPMG's Transfer Pricing Controversy practice. Guide a
multinational through a transfer pricing audit and MAP resolution.
Deliver: (1) Transfer pricing audit triggers: CbCR flag (low-tax profits, high royalty
payments to IP holding cos); customs vs. TP price inconsistency; whistleblower;
industry focus (pharma IP, tech intangibles, financial services).
(2) Audit defense strategy: contemporaneous documentation quality; economic analysis
robustness; comparability analysis support; advance documentation review.
(3) Unilateral Advance Pricing Agreement (APA): bilateral APA vs. unilateral; timeline
(2-4 years for bilateral); tax authority relationships; APA rollback.
(4) Mutual Agreement Procedure (MAP): treaty-based dispute resolution between two
countries; Article 25 OECD Model Tax Convention; timeline (2-3 years average);
mandatory binding arbitration under MLI (BEPS Action 14).
(5) BEPS impact on TP: OECD BEPS Actions 8-10 (hard-to-value intangibles, DEMPE
functions, risk allocation); Action 13 (CbCR, local file, master file);
how audits are increasingly using CbCR data.
(6) Penalty mitigation: reasonable cause defense; contemporaneous documentation
penalty protection (reasonable penalty protection under IRC §6662); disclosure
strategies.
(7) Dispute resolution trends: tax authorities increasingly coordinating TP audits
across jurisdictions; joint audits; Pillar Two impact on TP dispute economics.
Format: TP Controversy Framework with Audit Defense, APA Process, MAP Procedure,
BEPS Impact, Penalty Mitigation, and Dispute Resolution Trends.
Inputs: [COMPANY | INDUSTRY | JURISDICTIONS UNDER AUDIT | TP ISSUE TYPE |
PROPOSED ADJUSTMENT | DOCUMENTATION STATUS | MAP APPETITE | PILLAR TWO EXPOSURE]

title: The Warburg Pincus India Growth Equity Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 364 — The Warburg Pincus India Growth Equity Strategy
Act as MD at Warburg Pincus India. Build a comprehensive India-focused
growth equity investment strategy.
Deliver: (1) India macro investment thesis: largest democracy, 1.4B population, 6-7% GDP
growth, digital infrastructure (UPI, Aadhaar, ONDC), demographic dividend (median age 28),
rising middle class (500M by 2030), and manufacturing ambition (PLI schemes).
(2) Target sectors: financial services (insurance, AMC, NBFC, fintech — large
underbanked population), healthcare (hospital chains, diagnostics, pharma CDMOs),
consumer (premiumization, rural penetration), technology (SaaS, IT services, data centers),
renewable energy (India's 500GW target by 2030).
(3) Growth equity vs. buyout in India: majority buyouts are rare (promoter resistance
to loss of control); minority growth equity with governance protections is the
dominant model; typical stake 15-40%.
(4) Governance protections in Indian deals: shareholders' agreement (SHA) protections
(tag-along, drag-along, anti-dilution, information rights, board representation);
SEBI regulations on minority shareholder rights; exit mechanisms (IPO put, strategic sale put).
(5) IPO as primary exit: BSE/NSE are deep markets; Indian IPO market has been active;
pre-IPO investment → IPO exit typically within 3-5 years.
(6) Currency: INR has depreciated ~3-4% annually vs. USD long-term; hedging cost
is expensive; INR returns need to be 15-20% to achieve 12-15% USD returns.
(7) Regulatory environment: FDI limits by sector (insurance 74%, defense 74%);
FEMA compliance; SEBI PE/VC regulations; tax treaty benefits (Mauritius/Singapore route).
Format: India Growth Equity Framework with Macro Thesis, Sector Priorities, Deal
Structure, Governance Protections, IPO Exit, Currency, and Regulatory Framework.
Inputs: [SECTOR | COMPANY STAGE | REVENUE | GROWTH RATE | STAKE SIZE | SHA PROTECTIONS |

title: The Evercore ISI: US Equity Strategy & Asset Allocation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 365 — The Evercore ISI: US Equity Strategy & Asset Allocation
Act as Chief US Equity Strategist at Evercore ISI. Build a comprehensive
US equity market outlook and sector allocation strategy.
Deliver: (1) S&P 500 earnings outlook: consensus EPS estimate for next 12 months;
top-down earnings model (GDP growth × operating leverage × margin assumptions);
where does Evercore's forecast differ from consensus and why?
(2) Valuation framework: current P/E vs. historical average; Shiller CAPE; earnings
yield vs. risk-free rate (Fed model); P/E justified by earnings growth vs. rates.
(3) Interest rate sensitivity: equity duration concept; how much does the S&P 500
decline for every 100bps rise in 10yr yield? Growth vs. value divergence in rate moves.
(4) Sector allocation: overweight/underweight each S&P 500 sector with rationale;
identify sectors with: (a) earnings revisions momentum, (b) valuation support,
(c) macro tailwind alignment.
(5) Style: growth vs. value; large vs. small cap (relative valuation, interest rate
sensitivity, economic sensitivity); quality factor as defensive overlay.
(6) Market structure: buyback programs (S&P 500 buyback yield ~3%); passive vs.
active flows; options market gamma positioning and its impact on daily volatility.
(7) Top 5 stock ideas: high conviction long ideas with specific investment thesis,
catalyst, target price, and risk factors.
Format: US Equity Strategy with Earnings Outlook, Valuation, Rate Sensitivity, Sector
Allocation, Style Framework, Market Structure, and Top 5 Stock Ideas.
Inputs: [TIME HORIZON | CURRENT S&P LEVEL | EARNINGS ESTIMATE | PRIMARY MACRO VIEW |
INTEREST RATE ASSUMPTION | BIGGEST RISK | PORTFOLIO POSITIONING]

title: The Invest AB Nordic Industrial Conglomerate M&A
prompt_text:
PROMPT 366 — The Invest AB Nordic Industrial Conglomerate M&A
Act as Head of M&A at Investor AB (Sweden). Build an M&A strategy for

(2) Portfolio management: listed core holdings (Investor's model — major stakes in

NAV discount management.
(3) M&A philosophy: buy market-leading industrial companies at fair prices; long-term
hold (permanent capital); operational improvement vs. financial engineering.
(4) Target identification: DACH and Nordic Mittelstand companies (industrial technology,
B2B services); global market leaders in niche industrial segments.
(5) Deal process for industrial M&A: proprietary deal flow (relationship with founding
families, trusted advisor relationships); NBIO (non-binding indication of interest)
to SPA timeline for private transactions.

ESG standards; industrial transformation to low-carbon production.
(7) Governance post-acquisition: active board membership; financial targets (ROIC,

Format: Nordic Industrial M&A Framework with Conglomerate Model, Portfolio Management,

STRATEGIC RATIONALE | GOVERNANCE PLAN | HOLD PERIOD]

title: The Jefferies Technology M&A: SaaS Transaction Advisory
prompt_text:
PROMPT 367 — The Jefferies Technology M&A: SaaS Transaction Advisory
Act as MD at Jefferies' Technology group. Advise on a SaaS company M&A

Deliver: (1) SaaS M&A market: strategic buyer universe (Microsoft, Salesforce, ServiceNow,

who pays highest multiples and why.
(2) SaaS valuation in M&A: EV/NTM Revenue multiple as primary metric; what drives

precedent transactions by EV/Revenue vs. NTM revenue growth rate scatter plot.
(3) Process design for SaaS sale: targeted vs. broad process; how to run a competitive
process that creates auction tension; management presentation design.
(4) Strategic vs. financial buyer dynamics: strategic pays synergy premium (revenue
synergies through distribution, technology integration) vs. PE pays standalone value
+ operational improvement (Rule of 40 improvement, ARR growth acceleration).
(5) Due diligence for SaaS M&A: technical DD (code quality, technical debt, security);
commercial DD (customer concentration, churn interviews, competitive win/loss analysis);
financial DD (ARR bridge reconciliation, deferred revenue analysis).
(6) Deal structure: all-cash preferred; earnouts (revenue-based earnout for founder
sellers wanting upside participation); equity rollover for management in PE deals.
(7) Integration planning: for strategic acquirers — product roadmap decisions (integrate
vs. maintain standalone); for PE — 100-day plan for ARR growth acceleration.
Format: SaaS M&A Advisory with Valuation Framework, Process Design, Buyer Dynamics,
Due Diligence, Deal Structure, and Integration Planning.
Inputs: [COMPANY NAME | ARR | NRR | GROSS MARGIN | RULE OF 40 | ROLE (BUY/SELL SIDE) |
BUYER PREFERENCE | TIMING | PRIMARY TRANSACTION OBJECTIVE]

title: The Société Générale Structured Finance: NAV Financing
prompt_text:
PROMPT 368 — The Société Générale Structured Finance: NAV Financing
Act as MD at Société Générale's Private Assets Finance group. Design
a NAV (Net Asset Value) financing solution for a PE fund.
Deliver: (1) NAV financing rationale: PE funds borrow against their portfolio NAV
(rather than single asset) to: (a) fund distributions to LPs without selling assets;
(b) fund new bolt-on acquisitions; (c) provide liquidity to GPs for management fees;
(d) manage LP liquidity requests.
(2) NAV loan structure: revolving credit facility secured by LP interests in the PE fund
(not by underlying portfolio companies directly); lender has rights over distributions
from the fund; typically 15-25% of NAV at close.
(3) Borrowing base: portfolio company valuations (audited NAV) × advance rate (10-20%
for diversified buyout portfolio); concentration limits (single asset cap); quality
tests (remove distressed companies from borrowing base).
(4) Pricing: SOFR/EURIBOR + 300-450bps for senior NAV facilities; reflects illiquidity
and complexity; higher pricing than fund subscription lines.
(5) Covenant package: NAV maintenance covenant (facility must remain below 20% of NAV);
diversification test (no single portfolio company > X%); GP Key Man provisions.
(6) Risks: LTV creep if portfolio companies decline in value; subordination to portfolio
company debt; GP incentive misalignment (over-leveraging mature portfolio).
(7) LP concerns about NAV financing: dilution of LP returns from interest cost; opacity
of NAV loans in fund reporting; potential for GP to use NAV financing to mask performance.
Format: NAV Financing Advisory with Structure, Borrowing Base, Pricing, Covenants,
Risks, and LP Communication Strategy.
Inputs: [FUND SIZE | NAV AT CLOSE | PORTFOLIO COMPANY COUNT | SECTOR MIX | FACILITY
PURPOSE | TARGET SIZE | ADVANCE RATE | PRICING EXPECTATION | LP SENSITIVITY]

title: The Brookfield Oaktree: Distressed Real Assets Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 369 — The Brookfield Oaktree: Distressed Real Assets Strategy
Act as MD at Brookfield's Special Situations group. Build a distressed
real assets investment strategy spanning energy, real estate, and infrastructure.
Deliver: (1) Distressed real assets universe: distressed oil & gas producing assets,
stranded midstream infrastructure, non-performing commercial real estate loans,
distressed infrastructure concessions, mining assets in financial distress.
(2) Oil & gas distressed investing: acquire producing assets out of bankruptcy at
distressed multiples; reserve-based valuation at current strip prices; production
decline curves; operating cost structure improvement post-acquisition.
(3) Distressed midstream: gathering and processing systems stranded by E&P bankruptcies;
acquire at discount to replacement cost; recontract at market rates; sell to
infrastructure buyer at stabilized value.
(4) Hotel and hospitality distress: acquire REO (Real Estate Owned) hotels from
CMBS special servicers; repositioning costs; flag change economics; RevPAR recovery model.
(5) Infrastructure concession distress: PPP concessions in financial distress due to
lower-than-forecast traffic; debt restructuring; renegotiation of concession terms;
government support mechanisms.
(6) Distressed mining: acquire producing mines at below book value from miners needing
liquidity; operating efficiency improvements; commodity price recovery upside.
(7) Returns: distressed real assets target gross IRR 20-25%; driven by distressed entry
price, operational recovery, and exit at normalized multiples.
Format: Distressed Real Assets Strategy with Universe Map, O&G Distressed Analysis,
Midstream/Hotel/Infrastructure Deep-Dives, Mining Strategy, and Returns Analysis.
Inputs: [ASSET TYPE | GEOGRAPHY | DISTRESS CAUSE | ACQUISITION PRICE | RECOVERY PLAN |
TIMELINE | TARGET IRR | PRIMARY OPERATIONAL CHALLENGE]

title: The BlackRock ETF: Fixed Income ETF Market Making & Liquidity
prompt_text:
PROMPT 370 — The BlackRock ETF: Fixed Income ETF Market Making & Liquidity
Act as Head of Fixed Income ETF Capital Markets at BlackRock iShares. Build
a framework for fixed income ETF liquidity management and market making.
Deliver: (1) Fixed income ETF liquidity paradox: ETF is more liquid than its underlying
bonds (daily trading vs. OTC bond market); how ETF liquidity decouples from bond
liquidity in stress events (March 2020 — HYG traded at discount to NAV).
(2) ETF creation/redemption mechanism: authorized participant (AP) delivers a basket
of bonds to ETF in exchange for new ETF shares (creation); reverse for redemption;
AP arbitrage keeps ETF price close to NAV.
(3) Primary market (creations/redemptions): cash vs. in-kind creations; ETF spread
in primary market (AP's cost to assemble bond basket); cash creation for illiquid
bonds.
(4) Secondary market liquidity: iShares ETF market makers (Jane Street, Virtu,
Citadel Securities); bid-ask spread in secondary market; relationship to bond
market depth; ETF size as liquidity indicator.
(5) March 2020 stress analysis: HYG traded at 5-7% discount to NAV; ETF was price-
discovering the true value of the underlying illiquid HY bonds (not broken);
Federal Reserve SMCCF purchasing ETFs as precedent.
(6) ETF arbitrage: NAV discount > AP's cost to redeem → AP creates arbitrage profit
by buying ETF cheap, redeeming for bonds, selling bonds at NAV; keeps ETF near NAV.
(7) Institutional use cases: cash equitization; duration overlay; portfolio completion;
tactical asset allocation.
Format: FI ETF Framework with Liquidity Paradox, Creation/Redemption Mechanics,
Primary/Secondary Market, March 2020 Analysis, Arbitrage, and Institutional Uses.
Inputs: [ETF TICKER | UNDERLYING ASSET CLASS | AUM | TYPICAL BID-ASK | PRIMARY
LIQUIDITY CONCERN | INSTITUTIONAL USE CASE | STRESS SCENARIO TO ANALYZE]

title: The Advent International: Payments & Financial Technology
prompt_text:
PROMPT 371 — The Advent International: Payments & Financial Technology
Act as MD at Advent International's Payments & Fintech team. Build an
investment thesis for a payments technology company.
Deliver: (1) Payments industry structure: issuer (bank) → network (Visa/MC/Amex) →
acquirer (Stripe, Square, Fiserv) → merchant; where value is captured in the stack;
take rate compression trends.
(2) Target segments: merchant acquiring (payment acceptance for SME/enterprise),
B2B payments (accounts payable automation, cross-border B2B), embedded payments
(vertical SaaS platforms adding payments), and payment infrastructure (processing APIs).
(3) Business model quality: payments volume (TPV) vs. revenue take rate; net revenue
retention (NRR) as TPV grows; gross margin (payments is a high-volume, moderate-
margin business); Rule of 40 adaptation for payments (TPV growth + margin).
(4) Competitive positioning: Stripe's developer-first model; Square's SME ecosystem;
PayFac (Payment Facilitator) model economics; ISO vs. PayFac margin comparison.
(5) Real-time payments: FedNow and RTP impact on ACH volumes; cross-border real-time
payments (Swift GPI competitors: Wise, Currencycloud, Nium).
(6) Embedded payments value: vertical SaaS companies adding payments for retention,
margin expansion, and data intelligence; Shopify Payments, Toast, Mindbody as models.
(7) Regulatory: PCI-DSS compliance requirements; money transmitter licenses;
CFPB open banking rules (1033 data portability) impact on payments.
Format: Payments Investment Framework with Industry Structure, Target Segments,
Business Model Quality, Competitive Dynamics, RTP Impact, Embedded Payments, and Regulatory.
Inputs: [COMPANY | PAYMENTS SUB-SEGMENT | TPV | TAKE RATE | NRR | GROSS MARGIN |
COMPETITIVE POSITION | ENTRY VALUATION | VALUE CREATION THESIS]

title: The Goldman Sachs Global Credit Research: Credit Cycle Analysis
prompt_text:
PROMPT 372 — The Goldman Sachs Global Credit Research: Credit Cycle Analysis
Act as Head of Global Credit Research at Goldman Sachs. Build a credit cycle
analysis and portfolio positioning framework.
Deliver: (1) Credit cycle framework: identify the current phase (expansion, late-cycle,
contraction, recovery); key indicators for each phase (default rate, credit creation,
lending standards, leverage ratio trends).
(2) Default rate forecasting: Moody's and S&P historical default rate data; ML model
using lagged leverage, interest coverage, and macro variables to forecast 12-month
default rates; current forecast vs. consensus.
(3) Spread vs. fundamentals: current IG and HY OAS vs. implied default probability;
identify whether spreads are tight (priced for perfection) or wide (fear excessive).
(4) Sector stress analysis: which sectors are most vulnerable in late-cycle?
(Highly leveraged, near-term maturities, rate-sensitive revenues); CMBS and CRE credit
stress; private credit vintage analysis.
(5) Recovery rate outlook: recovery rates are cyclically depressed in severe downturns;
cov-lite documentation impact on recovery rates vs. historical (lower recovery);
asset coverage in an inflationary vs. deflationary environment.
(6) Portfolio positioning recommendations: rotate toward quality within HY (BB over B/CCC);
reduce single-B to reduce default risk; extend duration in IG as rates peak.
(7) Liquidity premium: credit liquidity is cyclical — tight in bull markets, wide in
stress; how to measure and capture the liquidity risk premium.
Format: Credit Cycle Analysis with Cycle Phase Assessment, Default Forecast, Spread
Analysis, Sector Stress, Recovery Rates, Portfolio Positioning, and Liquidity Premium.
Inputs: [BENCHMARK | CREDIT QUALITY MIX | DURATION | SECTOR ALLOCATION | PRIMARY
CREDIT VIEW | FORECAST HORIZON | BIGGEST CREDIT RISK CONCERN]

title: The Bain Capital Ventures: Enterprise Software Series B/C
prompt_text:
PROMPT 373 — The Bain Capital Ventures: Enterprise Software Series B/C
Act as General Partner at Bain Capital Ventures. Evaluate a Series B/C
investment in an enterprise software company.
Deliver: (1) BCV investment thesis for enterprise software: partner with category creators
($5-50M ARR with path to category leadership); focus on vertical SaaS, workflow
automation, AI-native enterprise software.
(2) Category creation assessment: is the company creating a new software category
or competing in an existing one? Category creators earn 70-80% of category market cap.
(3) GTM motion quality: product-led growth (PLG) vs. top-down enterprise sales;
SDR/AE efficiency (CAC payback < 18 months); expansion ARR contribution (should
exceed new ARR contribution by Series C).
(4) Series B/C metrics: $10-50M ARR; NRR >120% (net retention must show expansion
offsetting churn); gross margin >75% (software); growth rate >50% at Series B,
>40% at Series C; Rule of 40 improving.
(5) Product moat: how defensible is the product? Workflow integration depth;
data flywheel; API integrations creating switching costs; time-to-value for customers.
(6) Enterprise sales motion: land-and-expand (start with 1 department, expand to
enterprise); CLTV/CAC by segment; enterprise renewal rate.
(7) Investment terms: Series B typical: $20-50M round, pre-money $100-300M;
board composition; pro-rata rights; full-ratchet anti-dilution vs. weighted average.
Format: Enterprise Software Investment Memo with Category Analysis, GTM Quality,
Series B/C Metrics, Product Moat, Enterprise Sales, and Investment Terms.
Inputs: [COMPANY | ARR | NRR | GROSS MARGIN | CAC PAYBACK | GROWTH RATE |
CATEGORY SIZE | PROPOSED VALUATION | ROUND SIZE | PRIMARY INVESTMENT THESIS]

title: The HSBC Emerging Markets Corporate Finance Advisory
prompt_text:
PROMPT 374 — The HSBC Emerging Markets Corporate Finance Advisory
Act as MD at HSBC's Emerging Markets Corporate Finance. Build a financing
and strategic advisory framework for a large EM conglomerate.
Deliver: (1) EM conglomerate analysis: family-owned diversified groups (Tata Group India,
CP Group Thailand, Grupo Carso Mexico, Naspers Africa); valuation discount (holding
company discount); governance challenges; capital allocation across businesses.
(2) Holding company discount: HoldCo discount = sum of parts value − market cap;
typical discount 20-40% for complex conglomerates; strategies to close the gap
(spin-offs, asset sales, buybacks, governance improvements).
(3) Capital markets access: equity capital markets (rights issues, secondary offerings);
debt capital markets (USD bonds, local currency bonds); hybrid securities; EMTN
(Euro Medium Term Note) program for flexible debt issuance.
(4) Currency and cross-border financing: parent guarantee vs. subsidiary standalone debt;
cross-currency optimization (which entity issues in which currency); USD vs. local
currency debt mix; repatriation and dividend upstream structures.
(5) M&A advisory in EM: family business succession as M&A catalyst; intra-group
reorganization; cross-border acquisitions by EM conglomerates (outbound M&A trends).
(6) Debt capital structure optimization: net leverage across conglomerate; holding
company debt vs. subsidiary debt; structural subordination management.
(7) ESG and governance: EM conglomerate governance (dual-class shares, family board
control, related party transactions); ESG disclosure improving access to international
capital; UNGC, GRI, ISSB adoption.
Format: EM Conglomerate Advisory with Holding Company Discount, Capital Markets Access,
Currency Optimization, M&A, Debt Structure, and ESG Governance.
Inputs: [CONGLOMERATE | COUNTRY | SECTORS | NAV VS. MARKET CAP | CURRENCY MIX |
FAMILY GOVERNANCE | PRIMARY FINANCING NEED | ESG DISCLOSURE LEVEL]

title: The Institutional Shareholder Services (ISS) Proxy Advisory
prompt_text:
PROMPT 375 — The Institutional Shareholder Services (ISS) Proxy Advisory
Act as Senior Analyst at ISS (Institutional Shareholder Services).
Build a comprehensive proxy voting analysis and recommendation.
