independent directors, independent lead director if CEO is chairman); board
diversity (gender, racial/ethnic representation); overboarding (max 4-6 boards).
(3) Executive compensation Say-on-Pay analysis: pay-for-performance alignment
(CEO pay vs. TSR relative to peers); problematic pay practices checklist
(excise tax gross-ups, single-trigger CoC, outsized severance multiples);
CEO pay ratio disclosure.
(4) Director election analysis: independence determination; attendance record;
committee membership appropriateness; audit committee financial expertise.
(5) Shareholder proposals: ESG-related proposals (climate disclosure, political
spending, workforce diversity reporting); how ISS evaluates shareholder proposals
vs. management opposition.
(6) M&A vote analysis: fairness of consideration (investment banker opinions);
deal protections (termination fees, match rights, force-the-vote provisions);
go-shop assessment.
(7) Corporate governance evolution: universal proxy (September 2022 SEC rule enabling
proxy contest without full slate); advance notice bylaws as defense; forum selection.
Format: Proxy Advisory Framework with Board Assessment, Compensation Analysis, Director
Election, Shareholder Proposals, M&A Votes, and Governance Evolution.
Inputs: [COMPANY | MEETING TYPE (ANNUAL/SPECIAL) | KEY PROPOSALS | EXECUTIVE PAY
STRUCTURE | BOARD COMPOSITION | TSR VS. PEERS | PRIMARY GOVERNANCE CONCERN]

title: The Brookfield Infrastructure: Data Centre & AI Power Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 376 — The Brookfield Infrastructure: Data Centre & AI Power Strategy
Act as MD at Brookfield Infrastructure Partners. Build an investment thesis
for data centre infrastructure focused on AI compute demand.
Deliver: (1) AI-driven data centre demand: hyperscaler capex (Microsoft, Google, Amazon,
Meta spending $200B+ annually on data centres and AI infrastructure); GPU cluster
density requirements (100kW+ per rack vs. 5-10kW traditional).
(2) Power infrastructure bottleneck: data centre growth is constrained by power
availability; grid connection queues of 4-7 years in most US markets; how
Brookfield's infrastructure expertise provides advantage in navigating grid connection.
(3) Power purchase strategy: long-term PPAs with utilities for data centre power;
behind-the-meter renewable generation; nuclear power agreements (Microsoft/Constellation
deal); gas peaker backup for reliability.
(4) Data centre asset types: hyperscale campuses (100MW+, built-to-suit for single
tenant); colocation (multi-tenant, Equinix model); edge data centres.
(5) Leasing structure: pre-leased vs. speculative development; 10-20 year NNN leases;
power purchase agreement linked to lease; rent escalation (2-4% annually).
(6) Capital recycling: develop data centres → lease to hyperscalers → sell to
pension/insurance capital at 5-6% cap rate → redeploy into development;
Brookfield's capital recycling advantage.
(7) Geography: US (primary — Virginia, Dallas, Phoenix); Europe (Ireland, Amsterdam,
Frankfurt, London); APAC (Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo — demand growing with AI).
Format: Data Centre Strategy with AI Demand Analysis, Power Bottleneck, PPA Strategy,
Asset Types, Leasing, Capital Recycling, and Geographic Map.
Inputs: [GEOGRAPHY | ASSET TYPE | POWER CAPACITY | TENANT TYPE | LEASE STRUCTURE |
TARGET YIELD | CAPITAL RECYCLING PLAN | PRIMARY RISK CONCERN]

title: The PwC Corporate M&A Integration: IT Systems Separation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 377 — The PwC Corporate M&A Integration: IT Systems Separation
Act as Partner at PwC's Deals Technology practice. Design an IT systems
separation plan for a major corporate divestiture.
Deliver: (1) IT separation scope: application landscape map (identify which applications
serve only the divested entity, only the parent, or both); data separation requirements;
infrastructure separation (servers, networks, data centres).
(2) Transition Service Agreements (TSAs): interim IT services provided by parent to
divestiture entity post-close; service catalogue (ERP, email, network, HR systems,
security); pricing (cost-plus 10-15%); TSA exit timeline (12-24 months typical).
(3) Carve-out IT budget: one-time separation costs (licence carve-outs, new infrastructure,
data migration, testing); run-rate IT cost of the standalone entity; shadow IT budget
hidden in allocated overhead.
(4) ERP strategy for standalone: does the entity need a new ERP instance? Oracle/SAP
carve-out options (template-based lift vs. reimplementation); timeline (18-24 months
for major ERP carve-out); cost ($50-500M+ for large ERP implementations).
(5) Data separation: customer data, financial data, IP data — legal ownership
determination; GDPR-compliant data transfer; data cleaning and deduplication.
(6) Cybersecurity separation: network segmentation day-1; identity and access
management (new AD/Azure AD for the entity); security monitoring independence.
(7) Day-1 IT readiness: minimum viable IT capabilities required for Day-1 (transaction
processing, payroll, email, basic connectivity); cutover testing and rehearsal.
Format: IT Separation Plan with Application Landscape, TSA Design, ERP Strategy,
Data Separation, Cybersecurity, and Day-1 Readiness.
Inputs: [PARENT COMPANY | DIVESTED ENTITY | INDUSTRY | REVENUE | SHARED SYSTEMS |
ERP PLATFORM | TSA EXPECTED DURATION | IT SEPARATION BUDGET | CLOSE DATE]

title: The Cerberus Capital: Distressed Financial Institution Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 378 — The Cerberus Capital: Distressed Financial Institution Strategy
Act as MD at Cerberus Capital Management evaluating a distressed bank or
financial institution investment.
Deliver: (1) Distressed bank opportunity identification: bank trading below TBV (tangible
book value); elevated NPL ratio; regulatory consent order; capital adequacy concern.
(2) Bank valuation: P/TBV for distressed banks (0.3-0.7× TBV in distress); normalized
earnings power (what can the bank earn on cleaned-up balance sheet?); franchise value.
(3) Asset quality deep-dive: non-performing loan analysis by portfolio (CRE, C&I, consumer);
ALLL (Allowance for Loan and Lease Losses) adequacy; stress test of loss rates in
various scenarios; net charge-off projections.
(4) Capital injection analysis: how much capital is needed to recapitalize to CET1
target? What price per share for new capital? Dilution to existing shareholders.
(5) Regulatory engagement: OCC/FDIC/Federal Reserve approval for change of control;
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) commitments; consent order resolution timeline.
(6) Operational turnaround: new management team; expense reduction (branch closures,
headcount); technology modernization; core deposit franchise restoration.
(7) Exit: once turnaround complete, sell to larger bank at 1.0-1.5× TBV; IPO;
PE secondary.
Format: Distressed Bank Investment Framework with Opportunity Identification, Valuation,
Asset Quality, Capital Injection, Regulatory Strategy, Turnaround Plan, and Exit.
Inputs: [BANK NAME | ASSETS | CET1 RATIO | NPL RATIO | CURRENT P/TBV | CONSENT ORDER
STATUS | REQUIRED CAPITAL | TURNAROUND TIMELINE | TARGET RETURN]

title: The Macquarie Green Energy Transition Infrastructure
prompt_text:
PROMPT 379 — The Macquarie Green Energy Transition Infrastructure
Act as MD at Macquarie Asset Management's Green Investment Group (GIG).
Build a comprehensive energy transition infrastructure investment strategy.
Deliver: (1) Energy transition investment spectrum: generation (wind, solar, hydro),
storage (BESS, pumped hydro, hydrogen), transmission (HVDC, grid upgrades),
enabling infrastructure (EV charging, green hydrogen, carbon capture), and
demand-side (heat pumps, industrial decarbonisation).
(2) Offshore wind economics: capex per MW (£2-4M/MW offshore vs. £0.8-1.2M onshore);
P50 capacity factor (35-50% offshore vs. 25-35% onshore); CfD (Contract for
Difference) mechanism in UK; PPA/auction revenue visibility.
(3) BESS (Battery Energy Storage) investment: 4-hour duration systems; revenue stacking
(frequency response, wholesale arbitrage, capacity market, renewable firming);
degradation and augmentation costs; merchant vs. contracted revenue mix.
(4) Green hydrogen: electrolysis economics (capex + power cost = hydrogen cost of
production); cost curve decline (2030 target <$2/kg); offtake structures; transport
and storage infrastructure.
(5) EV charging infrastructure: charging network economics (utilisation rate <15% in
early years creates J-curve); revenue per charger; grid connection costs.
(6) Carbon markets integration: high-quality carbon offsets from natural climate
solutions (reforestation, mangrove restoration); REDD+ project development;
carbon credit monetisation alongside infrastructure returns.
(7) Blended finance structures: combining concessional DFI capital with commercial
capital to de-risk early-stage energy transition projects in EM.
Format: Energy Transition Strategy with Technology Economics, Offshore Wind, BESS,
Green Hydrogen, EV Charging, Carbon Markets, and Blended Finance.
Inputs: [TECHNOLOGY FOCUS | GEOGRAPHY | STAGE (DEVELOPMENT/OPERATING) | CONTRACTED
VS. MERCHANT | TARGET IRR | CARBON MARKET INTEGRATION | DFI PARTNERSHIP]

title: The Bain & Company Financial Services: Wealth Management Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 380 — The Bain & Company Financial Services: Wealth Management Strategy
Act as Senior Partner at Bain & Company's Financial Services practice.
Design a strategic transformation for a wealth management business.
Deliver: (1) Wealth management market segmentation: mass market (< $250K), mass affluent
($250K-$1M), affluent ($1-5M), HNW ($5-25M), UHNW ($25M+) — profitability by segment,
competitive intensity, digital vs. human advice ratio.
(2) Robo-advisory vs. human advice: hybrid model as the winning approach; which
client segments benefit from digital-only vs. need human relationships; AI in wealth
management (portfolio construction, tax optimisation, financial planning).
(3) Advisor productivity: AUM per advisor (industry benchmark $100-150M; elite $250M+);
client-to-advisor ratio; technology tools that improve advisor productivity; high-value
activity vs. administrative time allocation.
(4) Product architecture: open architecture (best-in-class external products) vs.
captive products (proprietary funds — higher margin, lower client outcomes in some cases);
alternative product access for affluent and HNW clients.
(5) Client acquisition: organic referral-based (traditional) vs. digital marketing (HNW
clients increasingly research digitally before engaging); affinity channels (CPA, attorney
referral networks).
(6) Fee compression response: AUM-based fee erosion (1% → 0.75% → 0.5% for large
accounts); value-based fee justification (financial planning, tax optimisation, estate
planning); fee-for-service model for specific services.
(7) M&A in wealth management: RIA consolidation (Mercer, Captrust, Wealth Enhancement
Group roll-up model); valuation (2-3% of AUM or 7-10× EBITDA); integration of
advisor teams post-acquisition.
Format: Wealth Management Strategy with Market Segmentation, Hybrid Model, Advisor
Productivity, Product Architecture, Client Acquisition, Fee Response, and M&A.
Inputs: [FIRM TYPE | AUM | ADVISOR COUNT | CLIENT SEGMENTS | FEE STRUCTURE |
DIGITAL CAPABILITY | PRIMARY STRATEGIC CHALLENGE | GROWTH TARGET]

title: The Alvarez & Marsal: Distressed M&A and 363 Sale Advisory
prompt_text:
PROMPT 381 — The Alvarez & Marsal: Distressed M&A and 363 Sale Advisory
Act as Managing Director at Alvarez & Marsal's Restructuring group. Build
an advisory framework for distressed M&A and 363 sale processes.
Deliver: (1) Distressed M&A vs. traditional M&A: compressed timeline (30-60 days);
limited reps & warranties; as-is/where-is sale; carve-out of liabilities;
buyer takes operating and technology risk.
(2) Section 363 sale mechanics: free and clear of liens and claims (most valuable
aspect — bankruptcy court extinguishes successor liability); stalking horse selection
and protections; bidding procedure approval; auction dynamics.
(3) Stalking horse process: identifying and selecting the stalking horse bid;
break-up fee (2-3% of deal value); expense reimbursement; match right vs. topping
right; how to market a 363 process while maintaining stalking horse exclusivity.
(4) Buyer due diligence in compressed timeline: what can be completed in 30 days?
Priority focus: customer contracts (assignable?), key employee retention, IP ownership,
environmental liabilities, union contracts; red flag vs. full DD approach.
(5) Credit bid: secured lender bids using debt as currency (credit bid); valued at
face value of secured debt; how cash bidders defeat a credit bid (must exceed face value).
(6) Successor liability: claims that can attach to buyer despite 363 sale (product
liability, CERCLA environmental, COBRA health, pension funding — exceptions to
free and clear order).
(7) Post-363 integration: accelerated 100-day plan; cash management on Day 1;
IT transition (domain, systems, data); employee communication.
Format: Distressed M&A Advisory with 363 Mechanics, Stalking Horse, Compressed DD,
Credit Bid, Successor Liability, and Post-Close Integration.
Inputs: [COMPANY | INDUSTRY | DEBT STRUCTURE | ASSETS BEING SOLD | STALKING HORSE
IDENTIFIED | BUYER TYPE | TIMELINE | PRIMARY SUCCESSOR LIABILITY CONCERN]

title: The Deutsche Bank Research: US Housing Market Analysis
prompt_text:
PROMPT 382 — The Deutsche Bank Research: US Housing Market Analysis
Act as Head of US Housing Research at Deutsche Bank. Build a comprehensive
US housing market investment framework.
Deliver: (1) Housing market fundamentals: supply (housing starts, existing home inventory,
months of supply); demand (household formation, demographic drivers — Millennials
peaking in prime home-buying years); affordability (mortgage payment as % of median income).
(2) Affordability crisis: 30yr mortgage rate × median home price → monthly payment;
benchmark affordability index; impact on first-time buyer market.
(3) New construction analysis: single-family starts vs. permits; builder confidence
(NAHB index); land, labour, lumber cost trends; homebuilder margin compression.
(4) Existing home market: "lock-in effect" (homeowners with 3% mortgages reluctant
to sell and buy at 7%); inventory constraint; why new construction is filling the gap.
(5) Geographic divergence: Sun Belt (affordability migration from expensive metros
but now facing supply glut); Coastal (affordability extreme but constrained supply);
Midwest (most affordable, steady appreciation).
(6) Housing as investment: REIT exposure (AvalonBay, Invitation Homes, American Homes
4 Rent); homebuilder equities (DR Horton, Lennar, NVR — land-light model);
mortgage REITs (interest rate sensitivity).
(7) Recession scenario: historical housing recessions (2008 was credit/construction
bubble; 2022-23 correction was affordability — not credit); current cycle comparison.
Format: US Housing Analysis with Supply/Demand, Affordability, New Construction,
Existing Home Market, Geography, Investment Vehicles, and Recession Scenario.
Inputs: [GEOGRAPHIC FOCUS | INVESTMENT VEHICLE (REIT/BUILDER/MREIT) | RATE ASSUMPTION |
HOME PRICE FORECAST | AFFORDABILITY VIEW | INVENTORY OUTLOOK | PRIMARY HOUSING THESIS]

title: The Brookfield Asset Management: Real Estate Secondaries
prompt_text:
PROMPT 383 — The Brookfield Asset Management: Real Estate Secondaries
Act as MD at Brookfield's Real Estate Secondaries group. Build an investment
strategy for real estate fund secondary transactions.
Deliver: (1) Real estate secondaries market: $20-30B annual volume; LP portfolio sales,
GP-led secondaries (continuation vehicles), preferred equity, NAV lending.
(2) LP portfolio secondary: buy a portfolio of LP interests in private real estate
funds; discount to NAV reflects illiquidity, fund vintage, property type.
(3) GP-led secondary (continuation vehicle): GP moves trophy assets from expiring
fund into a new continuation vehicle; new and rollover investors; pricing at fair value;
LPAC approval required.
(4) NAV verification: independent appraisal of underlying real estate; desk review
vs. full appraisal; adjustment for unreported capex; roll-forward of recent
appraisals for older valuations.
(5) Discount framework: fund vintage (near end of life → smaller discount);
property type quality (industrial/multifamily → smaller discount, office → larger);
GP quality; fund size (large funds more liquid → smaller discount).
(6) Preferred equity: provide capital at preferred return (10-13%) to real estate
sponsor in exchange for priority return; used to recapitalise overleveraged properties.
(7) Deal sourcing: banking relationships; institutional LP portfolio monitoring;
GP relationship for continuation vehicles; secondary advisor community.
Format: Real Estate Secondaries Strategy with Market Overview, LP Portfolio,
GP-Led Vehicles, NAV Verification, Discount Framework, Preferred Equity, and Sourcing.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO TYPE | PROPERTY SECTORS | NAV SIZE | DISCOUNT TARGET | FUND VINTAGE |
PREFERRED EQUITY APPETITE | DEAL SIZE | RETURN TARGET]

title: The Goldman Sachs Private Wealth Management: Tax Planning
prompt_text:
PROMPT 384 — The Goldman Sachs Private Wealth Management: Tax Planning
Act as Senior Tax Advisor at Goldman Sachs Private Wealth Management.
Build a comprehensive tax planning strategy for a UHNW client.
Deliver: (1) UHNW tax landscape: federal income tax (37% top rate); NIIT (3.8% on net
investment income); LTCG (20% + NIIT = 23.8% federal); estate tax (40% above $13.6M
exemption per person); state income tax (CA 13.3%, NY 10.9%).
(2) Capital gains management: tax-loss harvesting programme; asset location (place
high-income assets in tax-deferred accounts); opportunity zone investment (defer and
reduce capital gains); qualified small business stock (QSBS — $10M or 10× gain exclusion).
(3) Estate planning: annual exclusion gifts ($18K/person); 529 superfunding (5-year
election); irrevocable trusts: GRAT (Grantor Retained Annuity Trust — transfer
appreciation above IRS hurdle rate); SLATs (Spousal Lifetime Access Trust).
(4) Charitable giving: donor-advised fund (DAF — immediate deduction, invest, distribute
later); charitable remainder trust (CRT — income stream + deduction + remainder to charity);
qualified charitable distribution (QCD) from IRA.
(5) Business sale planning: instalment sale; charitable remainder trust funded with
pre-sale; QSBS planning for founders; S-corp to C-corp conversion for QSBS eligibility.
(6) International considerations: PFIC rules for foreign funds; FBAR/FATCA disclosure;
foreign tax credits; foreign trusts; pre-immigration planning.
(7) 2025 sunset: TCJA sunset (2025 — exemption halves to ~$7M per person);
urgency to use exemption before sunset; estate freeze strategies.
Format: UHNW Tax Planning with Capital Gains, Estate Planning, Charitable Giving,
Business Sale, International, and 2025 TCJA Sunset Strategy.
Inputs: [CLIENT NET WORTH | INCOME TYPE | ESTATE SIZE | CHARITABLE INTENT |
BUSINESS INTERESTS | INTERNATIONAL EXPOSURE | PRIMARY TAX CONCERN | TIMELINE]

title: The Advent International: Business Process Outsourcing
prompt_text:
PROMPT 385 — The Advent International: Business Process Outsourcing
Act as MD at Advent International's Services team. Build a PE investment
thesis for a Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) company.
Deliver: (1) BPO market: $280B+ globally; outsourcing of non-core business processes
(F&A, HR, customer service, procurement, IT helpdesk); offshore delivery (India,
Philippines, Eastern Europe) driving 30-50% cost savings.
(2) Sub-segment selection: F&A BPO (finance and accounting — AP, AR, RTR);
HR BPO (payroll, benefits administration, HRIS); customer care/CX BPO;
knowledge process outsourcing (KPO — higher-value analytics, legal, research).
(3) Business model: multi-year contract (3-5 year MSA); FTE-based or outcome-based
pricing; seat-based billing; annual price escalation clauses; minimum revenue
commitments.
(4) Offshore leverage: India delivery (50-60% of FTEs offshore); Philippines for
English-language CX; Poland/Romania for European clients; blended labour cost.
(5) AI disruption and opportunity: Gen AI automating 30-50% of transactional BPO
tasks (AP processing, basic customer queries); offset by AI augmentation of
higher-value KPO tasks; how BPO companies are adapting.
(6) Value creation: margin expansion (offshore ratio improvement, automation);
revenue growth (new logo wins, scope expansion with existing clients);
M&A to add capabilities.
(7) Multiple dynamics: BPO companies trade at 8-12× EBITDA; AI disruption discount
or premium? Winner-take-most for companies that adopt AI first.
Format: BPO Investment Thesis with Sub-Segment, Business Model, Offshore Leverage,
AI Disruption, Value Creation, and Valuation.
Inputs: [SUB-SEGMENT | COMPANY | REVENUE | EBITDA | OFFSHORE RATIO | CONTRACT LENGTH |
AI DISRUPTION RISK | ENTRY MULTIPLE | VALUE CREATION PLAN]

title: The Morgan Stanley: Equity Capital Markets — Convertible Bond Issuance
prompt_text:
PROMPT 386 — The Morgan Stanley: Equity Capital Markets — Convertible Bond Issuance
Act as Head of Convertible Bonds at Morgan Stanley ECM. Structure and
execute a convertible bond issuance for a corporate issuer.
Deliver: (1) Convertible bond rationale for issuers: lower cash coupon vs. straight bond
(investors pay for the equity option); dilution deferred until conversion; accounting
treatment (ASC 470-20 — bifurcation into debt and equity components).
(2) CB structure: face value; conversion premium (20-35%); coupon; maturity (3-5 years);
call option for issuer (contingent call after 3 years at 130% of par); put option
for investor (change of control put at par + accrued).
(3) Investor base: CB-dedicated funds (convert arb — buy CB, short stock); long-only
equity investors (CB as lower-risk equity exposure); credit investors (bond floor appeal).
(4) Pricing: theoretical value using binomial tree (stock price, vol, rate, credit spread);
implied vol of the CB vs. listed options vol; new issue concession (NIC) to listed options.
(5) Execution: overnight marketed deal (announcement → price → close in 1 day);
use of equity forward (share lending by existing shareholders to facilitate delta hedging);
bookbuild in US and Europe simultaneously.
(6) Hedge accounting treatment: IFRS 9 convertible as compound instrument (equity +
liability component); day-1 bifurcation; subsequent measurement.
(7) Post-issuance dynamics: CB arb trading dynamics; delta hedging impact on stock price
on pricing day; parity tracking over bond life.
Format: Convertible Bond Advisory with Structure, Investor Base, Pricing, Execution,
Accounting Treatment, and Post-Issuance Dynamics.
Inputs: [COMPANY | SECTOR | CREDIT RATING | MARKET CAP | PROPOSED SIZE |
CONVERSION PREMIUM | TENOR | COUPON | PRIMARY OBJECTIVE (FINANCING/DILUTION DEFERRAL)]

title: The CDPQ Equity Markets: Smart Beta & Factor Investing
prompt_text:
PROMPT 387 — The CDPQ Equity Markets: Smart Beta & Factor Investing
Act as Head of Equity Factor Investing at CDPQ. Build a smart beta and
factor investing strategy for a large pension fund.
Deliver: (1) Factor investing rationale: systematic exposure to documented risk premia
(value, quality, momentum, low volatility, size) at lower cost than active management.
(2) Factor definitions: value (P/B, P/E, EV/EBITDA); quality (ROE, low leverage,
earnings stability); momentum (12-month price return, earnings revision momentum);
low volatility (historical beta, realised vol); size (small cap premium — diminished).
(3) Factor cycle management: factors go through periods of underperformance ("factor
drought"); how to manage through a factor drawdown (stay the course vs. rotate);
2020 value factor crash and subsequent recovery.
(4) Multi-factor combination: combining factors reduces drawdowns (value + momentum
are negatively correlated); optimise combination weights.
(5) Implementation: physical replication vs. synthetic (futures overlay on benchmark);
turnover management (factor indices rebalance 2-4 times/year); transaction costs;
tax efficiency.
(6) ESG integration: ESG-adjusted factor indices (exclude governance laggards from
quality factor); sustainable factor investing (low-carbon factor tilt).
(7) Capacity: factor investing at scale ($5B+) requires implementation sophistication;
market impact; securities lending revenue to offset costs.
Format: Factor Investing Strategy with Factor Definitions, Cycle Management, Multi-Factor
Combination, Implementation, ESG Integration, and Capacity Analysis.
Inputs: [AUM | BENCHMARK | FACTOR FOCUS | TRACKING ERROR BUDGET | ESG REQUIREMENTS |
REBALANCE FREQUENCY | IMPLEMENTATION VEHICLE | PRIMARY FACTOR VIEW]

title: The Barclays Investment Banking: UK Domestic M&A Advisory
prompt_text:
PROMPT 388 — The Barclays Investment Banking: UK Domestic M&A Advisory
Act as MD at Barclays' UK Corporate Advisory group. Advise a UK FTSE 250
company on M&A strategy and execution.
Deliver: (1) UK M&A market: FTSE 100/250 M&A landscape; overseas acquirers of UK assets
(sterling weakness; regulatory environment); UK companies acquiring internationally.
(2) Takeover Code (City Code): Panel on Takeovers and Mergers; 28-day PUSU (Put Up
or Shut Up); mandatory bid rule (30% threshold); offer timetable (D+60 to close);
Rule 9 cash offer requirement.
(3) UK Merger Control: CMA (Competition and Markets Authority); share of supply test
(25%); Phase 1 (40 days) and Phase 2 (24 weeks) review; remedies (behavioural vs.
structural); CMA's increasingly assertive approach (2023-2024).
(4) NSIA (National Security and Investment Act): mandatory notification for defined
sensitive sectors (AI, semiconductors, critical infrastructure, defence);
call-in power for other sectors; remedy options.
(5) UK pension considerations: Pension Regulator in UK deals; deficit funding
requirements; clearance process for deals affecting defined benefit pension schemes.
(6) UK listed company valuation: DCF, comparable company, transaction precedents;
NAV for property and natural resource companies; sum-of-parts for conglomerates.
(7) Shareholder approval: Class 1 transaction (≥25% size test → shareholder vote);
related party transactions (independent shareholder vote); scheme vs. offer for
recommended deals.
Format: UK M&A Advisory with Takeover Code, CMA, NSIA, Pension, Valuation, and
Shareholder Approval Mechanics.
Inputs: [COMPANY | DEAL TYPE (ACQUIRE/DEFEND/DIVEST) | DEAL SIZE | SECTOR |
CMA RISK ASSESSMENT | NSIA SENSITIVITY | PENSION DEFICIT | PRIMARY CHALLENGE]

title: The Citigroup: Leveraged Finance New Issue Underwriting
prompt_text:
PROMPT 389 — The Citigroup: Leveraged Finance New Issue Underwriting
Act as Head of Leveraged Finance Origination at Citi. Underwrite and
syndicate a leveraged loan and high yield bond package.
Deliver: (1) LevFin package structure: senior secured Term Loan B (TLB) + senior secured
revolving credit facility (RCF) + senior unsecured HY bonds;
TLB and RCF are bank-syndicated; HY bonds are publicly registered or 144A.
(2) TLB pricing: SOFR + spread (350-500bps for BB/B credits); OID (1-2%);
call protection (101 soft call for 6 months); floor (0% SOFR floor standard).
(3) HY bond pricing: fixed coupon; spread-to-Treasury; non-call (NC) period (4-year
NC for 8-year bond); make-whole call (Treasuries + 50bps); equity clawback
(35% clawback for 3 years using equity proceeds).
(4) Rating agency process: Moody's/S&P leveraged finance rating; B2/B rating typical;
leverage ratios; coverage; recovery rates by tranche; rating triggers for covenant.
(5) Syndication: building the book (CLO demand for TLB; HY mutual funds, insurance
for bonds); flex mechanism (price adjusts to clear the market);
anchor investors (CLO managers, large HY funds).
(6) Covenant package: TLB incurrence covenants (baskets — see Prompt 313);
HY bond indenture (negative pledge, restricted payments, change of control);
RCF maintenance covenant (springing leverage test at 35% utilisation).
(7) Risk management: underwriting risk (Citi on hook before syndication closes);
hung deal risk (2022 Twitter/Elon Musk precedent); flex protection.
Format: LevFin Underwriting with Package Structure, TLB/HY Pricing, Rating Agency,
Syndication, Covenant Package, and Underwriting Risk Management.
Inputs: [DEAL SIZE | ISSUER | INDUSTRY | LEVERAGE | PROPOSED STRUCTURE | RATING |
MARKET CONDITIONS | SYNDICATION STRATEGY | PRIMARY UNDERWRITING RISK]

title: The Lazard Asset Management: Emerging Market Equities
prompt_text:
PROMPT 390 — The Lazard Asset Management: Emerging Market Equities
Act as Head of Emerging Market Equities at Lazard Asset Management.
Build a quality-focused EM equity investment framework.
Deliver: (1) EM equity investment case: higher long-term growth than DM; demographic
dividend; rising middle class; structural reform potential; valuation discount to DM.
(2) Country allocation framework: score markets on macro stability (current account,
inflation, reserves), governance (WGI political stability, rule of law), corporate
governance, and valuation (CAPE, dividend yield).
(3) China investment: regulatory uncertainty (tech, property); strategic competition
with US; AI and EV leadership; VIE structure risk; weighting reduction in EM indices.
(4) India investment: rule of law; demographic dividend; manufacturing PLI; digital
infrastructure (UPI, Aadhaar); premium valuation (30× P/E).
(5) Southeast Asia: Indonesia (domestic consumption, commodities, digital); Vietnam
(manufacturing hub, Apple supply chain); Philippines (BPO, remittances).
(6) Quality screen in EM: ROIC above cost of capital; avoid SOEs (state-owned enterprises
— low efficiency, political interference); corporate governance scoring.
(7) Currency management: unhedged for long-term (long-term EM FX should appreciate
vs. USD in productivity catch-up thesis); tactical hedging for short-term positions.
Format: EM Equity Framework with Country Allocation, China/India Deep-Dives, SEA,
Quality Screen, Currency Management, and Portfolio Construction.
Inputs: [BENCHMARK | COUNTRY LIMITS | QUALITY CRITERIA | CHINA WEIGHT |
CURRENCY APPROACH | TRACKING ERROR | PRIMARY EM VIEW | PRIMARY RISK CONCERN]

title: The EY Transaction Advisory: Commercial Due Diligence
prompt_text:
PROMPT 391 — The EY Transaction Advisory: Commercial Due Diligence
Act as Partner at EY's Transaction Advisory Services. Build a commercial
due diligence framework for a PE buy-side transaction.
Deliver: (1) CDD purpose: validate the investment thesis; size the market; assess
competitive position; test management's forecast assumptions; identify risks.
(2) Market sizing: total addressable market (TAM); served addressable market (SAM);
growth rate assumptions; market share trajectory.
(3) Competitive analysis: Porter's Five Forces; market share by competitor; competitive
moat assessment (pricing power, switching costs, network effects, brand); 
win/loss analysis.
(4) Customer diligence: reference calls (structured questionnaire); NPS; churn reasons;
budget trajectory; willingness to pay more; competitive alternatives considered.
(5) Revenue quality assessment: recurring vs. one-time; customer concentration; channel
mix; geographic mix; contract length and renewal rates.
(6) Management plan challenge: what assumptions are most at risk? Revenue growth
(market vs. share gain); margin expansion (operational leverage vs. investment needs);
capex intensity.
(7) Red flags: customer concentration >20% in top customer; product lifecycle risk
(end-of-life approaching); key person dependency; regulatory change risk.
Format: Commercial DD Framework with Market Sizing, Competitive Analysis, Customer
Diligence, Revenue Quality, Management Plan Challenge, and Red Flags.
Inputs: [COMPANY | INDUSTRY | REVENUE | GROWTH RATE | CUSTOMER CONCENTRATION |
COMPETITIVE INTENSITY | MANAGEMENT FORECAST | PRIMARY CDD CONCERN]

title: The HSBC Fixed Income: Asian Credit Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 392 — The HSBC Fixed Income: Asian Credit Strategy
Act as Head of Asian Credit at HSBC Global Asset Management. Build a
comprehensive Asian fixed income and credit investment strategy.
Deliver: (1) Asian credit market: $5T+ USD-denominated Asian credit (JACI — JP Morgan
Asia Credit Index); sovereign (China, Indonesia, Philippines, India), quasi-sovereign,
investment-grade corporate, high yield (China real estate historically dominant).
(2) China credit: China real estate sector post-Evergrande (2021) — understanding
legacy vs. new policy framework; onshore (CNY) vs. offshore (USD) debt; China sovereign
(AA/A2 — geopolitical discount); Chinese banks (AT1 complexity).
(3) Southeast Asian investment-grade: Singapore (AAA quasi-sovereign Temasek, GIC bonds);
Indonesia sovereign (BBB); Philippines (BBB); Thailand corporate.
(4) India credit: Indian sovereign USD bond market; Indian corporate Reg S bonds;
infrastructure bonds (NHAI, IRFC); NBFC credit.
(5) Asian HY: ex-China HY opportunities (Indonesia mining, India property, Vietnam);
where is valuation most attractive?
(6) FX in Asian credit: most Asian credit is USD-denominated (no FX risk for USD
investors); local currency Asian bond strategy (GBI-EMGD Asian portion).
(7) Duration and rate sensitivity: Asian IG duration 5-7 years; how does Asian credit
perform in a US rate rise? Spread widening vs. carry income trade-off.
Format: Asian Credit Strategy with Market Overview, China Deep-Dive, SEA/India IG,
Asian HY, FX Considerations, and Duration Management.
Inputs: [BENCHMARK | QUALITY TIER | COUNTRY LIMITS | CHINA EXPOSURE | DURATION TARGET |
FX APPROACH | PRIMARY CREDIT VIEW | RISK BUDGET]

title: The Citi Research: Global Consumer Discretionary
prompt_text:
PROMPT 393 — The Citi Research: Global Consumer Discretionary
Act as Head of Global Consumer Discretionary Research at Citi. Build
a comprehensive investment framework for the consumer discretionary sector.
Deliver: (1) Consumer discretionary drivers: consumer confidence, employment, wage growth,
household savings rate, credit availability; cyclical sector (underperforms in recessions).
(2) Sub-sector map: luxury goods (LVMH, Richemont, Hermès — China exposure, pricing
power); automotive (EV transition, traditional OEMs); specialty retail (omnichannel);
restaurants (QSR vs. casual dining); hotels and travel; gaming.
(3) Luxury deep-dive: China luxury spending (50% of global luxury demand); aspirational
vs. ultra-luxury resilience; logo fatigue and quiet luxury trend; pricing power discipline.
(4) Automotive sector: EV adoption trajectory; OEM margin pressure (legacy ICE cash
flow declining before EV profitable at scale); supplier disruption (EV has 40% fewer
parts than ICE).
(5) E-commerce and omnichannel: department store secular decline; specialty retailers
defending with experience and service; direct-to-consumer (DTC) margin advantage.
(6) Restaurant sector: franchise model (asset-light, royalty income — McDonald's model);
QSR defensive characteristics vs. casual dining vulnerability in recession.
(7) Valuation: consumer discretionary is highly cyclical — P/E at trough earnings vs.
peak earnings leads to wrong conclusions; normalised earnings approach.
Format: Consumer Discretionary Framework with Sector Drivers, Sub-Sector Map, Luxury
Deep-Dive, Automotive, E-Commerce, Restaurants, and Valuation.
Inputs: [SUB-SECTOR | COMPANY | KEY METRICS | CHINA EXPOSURE | CYCLE POSITIONING |
VALUATION | PRIMARY INVESTMENT DEBATE]

title: The Kirkland & Ellis: High Yield Bond Indenture Negotiation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 394 — The Kirkland & Ellis: High Yield Bond Indenture Negotiation
Act as Partner at Kirkland & Ellis advising an HY bond issuer on indenture
negotiation with bondholders.
Deliver: (1) HY indenture architecture: restricted vs. unrestricted subsidiary framework;
covenant suite (restricted payments, limitations on debt, liens, mergers, asset sales,
transactions with affiliates); events of default; trustee and paying agent.
(2) Restricted payment covenant: dividend and distribution limitations; permitted
payment baskets (fixed basket, builder basket — grows with NI, ratio basket);
restricted payment conditions (leverage test + no default + solvency).
(3) Debt incurrence covenant: permitted debt exceptions (credit facility cap, general
debt basket, ratio debt); ratio test (EBITDA-based coverage ratio for ratio debt);
refinancing debt definition.
(4) Asset sale covenant: proceeds waterfall (offer to repurchase at par with excess
proceeds); carve-outs for permitted asset sales; definition of "Net Cash Proceeds".
(5) Change of control put: 101% put on change of control; definition of change of
control (>50% ownership change most common); carve-outs (internal restructurings).
(6) Unrestricted subsidiary designation: carve assets out of restricted group;
investment capacity required to designate; prohibited if would cause default.
(7) Fallen angel protection: cross-default to revolving credit; cross-acceleration;
what triggers a default under the indenture.
Format: HY Indenture Negotiation Guide with Covenant Framework, Restricted Payments,
Debt Incurrence, Asset Sales, Change of Control, Unrestricted Subsidiaries, and Defaults.
Inputs: [ISSUER | INDUSTRY | DEAL SIZE | RATING | LEVERAGE | PROPOSED BASKETS |
UNRESTRICTED SUBSIDIARY PLAN | KEY NEGOTIATION PRIORITY | MARKET CONDITIONS]

title: The Lazard Restructuring: Prepackaged Bankruptcy Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 395 — The Lazard Restructuring: Prepackaged Bankruptcy Strategy
Act as MD at Lazard's Restructuring group. Design a prepackaged bankruptcy
strategy for a highly leveraged company.
Deliver: (1) Pre-pack rationale: negotiate restructuring with key creditors before filing;
Chapter 11 used only to implement agreed plan; in/out in 45-60 days vs. 12-18 months.
(2) Pre-pack vs. pre-arranged vs. free-fall: pre-pack (plan votes solicited before filing);
pre-arranged (deal agreed before filing, votes solicited in-court);
free-fall (no pre-negotiation — highest cost, longest duration).
(3) Solicitation requirements: Disclosure Statement must be approved; meets requirements
of Section 1125 (adequate information); can use out-of-court disclosure statement
to pre-solicit if met SEC exemption.
(4) Impaired class voting: each impaired class must vote; confirmation requires 2/3
in amount AND >1/2 in number for each accepting class; cramdown if one class rejects.
(5) Plan design: new equity to fulcrum creditors; new money (DIP or exit financing);
management incentive plan; treatment of trade creditors (generally paid in full).
(6) RSA (Restructuring Support Agreement): lock up key creditors before filing;
fiduciary out clause; termination events; PSA (Plan Support Agreement).
(7) Out-of-court alternative: out-of-court restructuring (exchange offer) if high
creditor cooperation — avoids Chapter 11 costs and stigma; when pre-pack better
than out-of-court.
Format: Pre-Pack Strategy with Process Comparison, Solicitation, Voting, Plan Design,
RSA Structure, and Out-of-Court Alternative.
Inputs: [COMPANY | DEBT STRUCTURE | KEY CREDITOR GROUPS | FULCRUM ANALYSIS |
PLAN CONCEPT | RSA STATUS | TIMELINE | PRIMARY RISK TO PRE-PACK]

title: The PwC Corporate Finance: Valuation for Financial Reporting
prompt_text:
PROMPT 396 — The PwC Corporate Finance: Valuation for Financial Reporting
Act as Partner at PwC's Valuation practice. Build a financial reporting
valuation framework for Level 3 assets and liabilities.
Deliver: (1) Fair value hierarchy: Level 1 (quoted prices in active markets — mark-to-market);
Level 2 (observable inputs other than Level 1); Level 3 (unobservable inputs —
mark-to-model); ASC 820 / IFRS 13 framework.
(2) Level 3 valuation techniques: income approach (DCF — most common for Level 3);
market approach (comparable companies and transactions with adjustments);
cost approach (replacement cost for tangibles).
(3) Key DCF assumptions: discount rate (WACC selection using comparable public
companies' cost of capital); terminal growth rate; risk-adjusted cash flows;
probability of success for pre-revenue assets.
(4) Portfolio company valuation for PE firms (ASC 820): calibrate to recent transaction;
assess whether portfolio is tracking transaction assumptions; update for market
conditions; enterprise value bridge to equity value.
(5) PE co-investment accounting: if investor has significant influence → equity method;
consolidated if control; cost method if no significant influence.
(6) Warrants, options, and contingent consideration valuation: Black-Scholes for
simple options; binomial tree for American options with early exercise features;
Monte Carlo for path-dependent payoffs.
(7) Audit considerations: auditor challenges to Level 3 fair values; independent
specialist involvement; sensitivity analysis disclosure (ASC 820 required disclosures).
Format: Financial Reporting Valuation with Level 3 Framework, DCF Best Practices, PE
Portfolio Valuation, Contingent Consideration, and Audit Considerations.
Inputs: [ASSET TYPE | INDUSTRY | VALUATION PURPOSE | KEY ASSUMPTIONS | COMPARABLE
COMPANIES | AUDIT SCRUTINY LEVEL | PRIMARY VALUATION CHALLENGE]

title: The Macquarie Equities: Australian Resources Sector
prompt_text:
PROMPT 397 — The Macquarie Equities: Australian Resources Sector
Act as Head of Australian Resources Research at Macquarie. Build an
investment framework for Australian mining and energy companies.
Deliver: (1) Australian resources sector: world's largest exporter of iron ore (Pilbara —
BHP, Rio Tinto, Fortescue), LNG (Gorgon, Wheatstone, Ichthys), coal (thermal and
met), lithium (Pilgangoora, Mt Cattlin), gold (Newcrest, Northern Star), copper.
(2) Iron ore market: seaborne iron ore demand (China ~70%); major price drivers;
60-65% Fe premium; China steel production and property sector health; Australian
vs. Brazilian supply (Vale cost curve).
(3) LNG sector: Australian LNG competitive position (proximity to Japan/Korea/China
customers); Take-or-Pay contracts (20-year LTAs); LNG project construction risk.
(4) Lithium cycle: spodumene concentrate vs. lithium carbonate; EV demand driver;
cost curve (Australian hard rock vs. Chilean brine); 2023-24 price crash analysis.
(5) Gold: AUD-denominated gold price (hedge currency risk); AISC (All-In Sustaining
Cost) analysis; M&A consolidation (Newmont/Newcrest); streaming and royalty companies.
(6) ESG and mine closure: tailings management; Scope 1+2+3 emissions for resources
companies; mine closure liability; Indigenous community engagement.
(7) Valuation: NAV model (EV = NPV of mine life cash flows at commodity price deck);
EV/EBITDA for near-term; P/NPV multiple by commodity.
Format: Australian Resources Framework with Iron Ore, LNG, Lithium, Gold, ESG,
and NAV Valuation Methodology.
Inputs: [COMPANY | COMMODITY | PRODUCTION | RESERVE LIFE | COST QUARTILE |
COMMODITY PRICE DECK | CAPEX PIPELINE | ESG RISKS | RATING INTENT]

title: The BlackRock Solutions: Aladdin Risk Platform Advisory
prompt_text:
PROMPT 398 — The BlackRock Solutions: Aladdin Risk Platform Advisory
Act as Head of Client Advisory at BlackRock Solutions. Build a risk analytics
advisory framework using the Aladdin platform for an institutional investor.
Deliver: (1) Aladdin platform overview: enterprise risk operating system; used by 200+
institutions managing $20T+ in assets; analytics for fixed income, equities,
alternatives, derivatives.
(2) Fixed income analytics: OAS (Option-Adjusted Spread); duration; convexity;
key rate duration; scenario analysis; prepayment modelling for MBS.
(3) Portfolio risk analytics: factor model (systematic vs. idiosyncratic risk);
VaR (Value at Risk) by confidence level; CVaR (Conditional VaR); contribution to risk.
(4) Liquidity analytics: liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) simulation; time-to-liquidate
by asset; portfolio liquidity stress test (can you liquidate 20% in 5 days?).
(5) Climate risk analytics: TCFD scenario analysis embedded in Aladdin Climate;
physical and transition risk scores by asset; portfolio carbon footprint.
(6) Private asset integration: mark-to-model for illiquid assets; stale pricing
adjustment; factor exposure for private equity and infrastructure.
(7) Reporting: client reporting dashboards; regulatory reporting (PRIIPS, MiFID II,
SFDR); automated report generation.
Format: Aladdin Advisory with Fixed Income Analytics, Portfolio Risk, Liquidity,

REQUIREMENT | CURRENT RISK SYSTEM | CLIMATE REPORTING OBLIGATION]

title: The Oliver Wyman: P&C Insurance Underwriting Transformation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 399 — The Oliver Wyman: P&C Insurance Underwriting Transformation
Act as Partner at Oliver Wyman's Insurance practice. Design an underwriting
transformation for a Property & Casualty (P&C) insurer.
Deliver: (1) P&C underwriting transformation drivers: rising loss costs (social inflation,
climate-driven CAT losses, reinsurance cost escalation); technology disruption
(telematics, AI pricing); competitive pressure from InsurTech.
(2) Technical pricing transformation: from relativities-based GLM (Generalized Linear
Model) to gradient boosting/XGBoost pricing; feature engineering from alternative data;
price optimisation and elasticity.
(3) Data strategy: telematics data (UBI — driving behaviour for auto); IoT (smart home
sensors for property); third-party data enrichment (credit score, geospatial, satellite
imagery); data governance for pricing data.
(4) CAT model management: PML (Probable Maximum Loss) at 1-in-100 and 1-in-250 year;
RMS/AIR/Verisk CAT models; secondary peril risk (wildfire, flood, hail increasingly
dominant); climate model uncertainty.
(5) Reinsurance optimisation: XL reinsurance attachment point and limit optimisation;
quota share vs. excess of loss trade-off; ILS (Insurance Linked Securities) as
reinsurance alternative; parametric reinsurance triggers.
(6) Underwriter workflow: AI-assisted triage (automate standard risks, escalate complex);
digital submission processing (OCR + NLP); real-time pricing indication; automated
declination.
(7) Performance metrics: combined ratio target by line; loss ratio monitoring
(prior accident year development); expense ratio reduction from automation.
Format: P&C Underwriting Transformation with Technical Pricing, Data Strategy, CAT
Management, Reinsurance Optimisation, Workflow Automation, and Performance Metrics.
Inputs: [INSURER SIZE | LINES OF BUSINESS | CURRENT COMBINED RATIO | PRICING MODEL |
CAT EXPOSURE | REINSURANCE STRUCTURE | TECH INVESTMENT | PRIMARY CHALLENGE]

title: The Morgan Stanley: Global Economic Outlook and Investment Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 400 — The Morgan Stanley: Global Economic Outlook and Investment Strategy
Act as Chief Global Economist at Morgan Stanley. Build a comprehensive
global economic outlook and cross-asset investment strategy.
Deliver: (1) Global growth outlook: GDP growth forecast for US, Eurozone, UK, Japan, China,
India, EM; where is Morgan Stanley's view differentiated from consensus; leading indicators.
(2) Inflation and central bank policy: inflation trajectory by region; Fed, ECB, BoE, BoJ
policy path; terminal rate forecast; rate cut timing and magnitude.
(3) US outlook: recession probability; labour market (JOLTS, claims, NFP); consumer
(savings rate, credit card delinquency); housing; corporate sector health.
(4) China outlook: property sector resolution; consumer recovery; export competition;
deflationary pressure; policy stimulus; geopolitical growth drag.
(5) EM outlook: EM divergence (commodity exporters vs. importers; EM with high USD
debt vs. local currency funded); India structural outperformance.
(6) Cross-asset allocation: equities (US vs. international; growth vs. value);
fixed income (duration, credit quality); FX (USD direction); commodities.
(7) Key risks: geopolitical (Taiwan, Russia-Ukraine escalation, Middle East);
financial stability (bank credit cycles, CRE stress); AI upside surprise;
policy error (hike too long or cut too early).
Format: Global Economic Outlook with Regional GDP Forecasts, Central Bank Analysis,
US/China/EM Deep-Dives, Cross-Asset Allocation, and Key Risks.
Inputs: [INVESTOR TYPE | PORTFOLIO MANDATE | GEOGRAPHIC FOCUS | RATE SENSITIVITY |
RISK APPETITE | PRIMARY ECONOMIC CONCERN | TIME HORIZON]

title: The Sequoia Capital Growth: Late-Stage Private Investment
prompt_text:
PROMPT 401 — The Sequoia Capital Growth: Late-Stage Private Investment
Act as Partner at Sequoia Capital's Growth fund. Evaluate a late-stage
private investment ($100M-$500M round) in a high-growth technology company.
Deliver: (1) Late-stage investment criteria: $200M+ ARR, 40%+ growth, clear path
to profitability within 18-24 months, category leadership position.
(2) Public market comparables: identify 5-8 public company comparables; NTM EV/Revenue
multiples; growth-adjusted multiples (EV/Revenue ÷ NTM growth rate); private market
premium or discount to public comparables.
(3) Pre-IPO positioning: probability of IPO within 24 months; IPO readiness gaps
(governance, financials, SOX); public market reception analysis.
(4) Downside scenario: if IPO is delayed or market conditions deteriorate, what is
the secondary market valuation floor? Secondary market liquidity for large positions.
(5) Deal terms: preferred stock terms (participating vs. non-participating); liquidation
preference (1×, 1.5×, 2×); anti-dilution (weighted average vs. full ratchet);
information rights and board observer.
(6) Lock-up and liquidity: post-IPO lock-up (180 days); secondary liquidity options
pre-IPO (tender offers, secondary transactions); fund return impact of lock-up.
(7) Portfolio signaling: Sequoia's ability to signal quality to other investors and
IPO underwriters; lead vs. follow dynamics at late stage.
Format: Late-Stage Investment Memo with Comp Analysis, Pre-IPO Assessment, Downside
Scenario, Terms Negotiation, Liquidity Analysis, and Portfolio Signaling.
Inputs: [COMPANY | ARR | ARR GROWTH | NRR | GROSS MARGIN | PROPOSED VALUATION |
ROUND SIZE | IPO TIMELINE | PRIMARY INVESTMENT THESIS | BIGGEST RISK]

title: The Goldman Sachs Investment Management: Multi-Strategy HF
prompt_text:
PROMPT 402 — The Goldman Sachs Investment Management: Multi-Strategy HF
Act as CIO at a Goldman Sachs-affiliated multi-strategy hedge fund.
Build a multi-strategy portfolio combining 5+ hedge fund strategies.
Deliver: (1) Multi-strategy rationale: diversify across uncorrelated strategies
within a single fund structure; risk allocation across strategies based on
Sharpe ratio, capacity, and correlation; central risk management overlay.
(2) Strategy allocation: equity L/S (30%), global macro (20%), fixed income relative
value (20%), merger arb (10%), quantitative (10%), credit (10%) — rationale.
(3) Risk allocation: risk budget by strategy (VaR or vol budget); dynamically
reallocate to strategies with best current risk-adjusted opportunity.
(4) Central risk management: aggregate portfolio factor exposures across all strategies;
netting of offsetting positions; tail risk overlay (VIX calls, CDS index).
(5) PM accountability: each strategy PM is a profit centre; base salary + P&L
share (typically 15-25% of strategy P&L after cost allocation); risk limits.
(6) Capital allocation: seed PM-level AUM with firm capital; scale successful PMs;
redeem from underperforming PMs without full fund redemption (key advantage over FoF).
(7) Investor terms: 1.5%/15-20% fees; quarterly liquidity with 45-day notice;
quarterly transparency reports; side pockets for illiquid positions.
Format: Multi-Strategy HF Framework with Strategy Allocation, Risk Budgeting, Central
Risk Management, PM Accountability, Capital Allocation, and Investor Terms.
Inputs: [AUM | STRATEGY MIX | RISK BUDGET | PM COUNT | FEE STRUCTURE |
INVESTOR TYPE | PRIMARY STRATEGY FOCUS | GROSS/NET EXPOSURE LIMITS]

title: The Citi M&A: Spin-Off and Corporate Separation Advisory
prompt_text:
PROMPT 403 — The Citi M&A: Spin-Off and Corporate Separation Advisory
Act as MD at Citi's M&A group. Design a corporate separation strategy
for a conglomerate divesting a non-core business through a spin-off.
Deliver: (1) Spin-off vs. alternatives: spin-off (tax-free, shareholders receive shares
in new company), split-off (exchange offer — shareholders tender parent shares for spinco),
carve-out IPO (sell minority stake first, complete separation later), direct sale.
(2) Tax-free spin-off requirements: Section 355 of IRC; business purpose test;
device test (not merely distributing earnings); active business requirement (5-year rule);
distribution of 80%+ of spinco stock; IRS PLR (Private Letter Ruling) process.
(3) Capital structure design for SpinCo: target credit rating for SpinCo debt;
leverage ratio appropriate for SpinCo's business risk; distribute debt proceeds
to parent (special dividend before spin); SpinCo pro-forma financials.
(4) Governance: SpinCo board composition (independent directors, CEO); executive
retention (equity awards stranded at parent vs. SpinCo replacement awards);
management team completeness.
(5) Separation planning: shared services agreement; transition service agreements
(TSAs); supply agreements; real estate sublease; IP license arrangements.
(6) Financial statement preparation: two-year pro-forma financials for SpinCo (Rule 10B-5
standard); management discussion and analysis; segment reclassification.
(7) Shareholder reception: investor day for SpinCo before distribution; research
analyst coverage initiation; index inclusion (Russell, S&P) timeline.
Format: Spin-Off Advisory with Structure Options, Tax-Free Requirements, SpinCo Capital
Structure, Governance, Separation Planning, Financials, and Market Reception.
Inputs: [PARENT COMPANY | SPINCO BUSINESS | REVENUE | EBITDA | TAX BASIS |
STRATEGIC RATIONALE | IRS PLR APPETITE | TIMELINE | PRIMARY CONCERN]

title: The Lazard Restructuring: Out-of-Court Liability Management
prompt_text:
PROMPT 404 — The Lazard Restructuring: Out-of-Court Liability Management
Act as MD at Lazard's Restructuring group. Design an out-of-court liability
management transaction for a stressed company.
Deliver: (1) LMT (Liability Management Transaction) spectrum: amend-and-extend (A&E),
exchange offer (old bonds → new bonds at different terms), tender offer (buy back
debt at discount), consent solicitation (amend existing covenants), new money raise
with uptier (new priming debt in exchange for existing holder participation).
(2) Amend-and-extend: extend maturity of approaching debt; lenders require fee
(50-100bps) and higher spread; requires >50% holder consent for amendment.
(3) Exchange offer: offer new bonds (longer maturity, potentially different terms)
in exchange for tendering existing bonds; minimum tender condition; use to extend
maturity and potentially reduce principal.
(4) Uptier exchange (controversial): existing debt holders who participate get new
senior secured debt; non-participating holders are primed (left with subordinated
claim); requires careful reading of "open market purchase" and "majority lender"
definitions in credit agreement; Serta/Envision precedents.
(5) Restricted payment exception: using restricted payment baskets to move assets
out of restricted group to unrestricted subsidiaries (asset stripping defense).
(6) Company assessment: liquidity runway with and without LMT; EBITDA trajectory;
creditor composition (hedge funds vs. CLOs — different negotiating dynamics).
(7) Intercreditor dynamics: cooperation agreement among lenders; ad hoc group
formation; majority lender amendment thresholds.
Format: LMT Advisory with Transaction Spectrum, A&E Mechanics, Exchange Offer,
Uptier Design, Asset Stripping Analysis, Company Assessment, and Creditor Dynamics.
Inputs: [COMPANY | DEBT STRUCTURE | MATURITIES | EBITDA | LIQUIDITY | PRIMARY
CREDITOR TYPES | TARGET OUTCOME | TIMELINE | LITIGATION RISK TOLERANCE]

title: The Fidelity Equity Research: Technology Sector Deep-Dive
prompt_text:
PROMPT 405 — The Fidelity Equity Research: Technology Sector Deep-Dive
Act as Senior Technology Analyst at Fidelity Investments. Build a
comprehensive technology sector research framework.
Deliver: (1) Technology sector landscape: semiconductor, hardware, software (SaaS,
enterprise, consumer), internet (search, social, e-commerce, streaming), IT services,
fintech, cybersecurity — where in the tech cycle does each sub-sector sit?
(2) Semiconductor cycle analysis: DRAM and NAND pricing cycles; wafer starts and
lead times as cycle indicators; AI demand as secular overlay on cyclical business.
(3) Software fundamentals: CAC payback, NRR, gross margin, FCF margin — which
metrics matter most at which stage? Public SaaS trading metrics vs. private market.
(4) Internet platform moats: network effects measurement; search moat (Google default
payment to Apple); social media engagement and attention economy; e-commerce flywheel.
(5) AI investment framework: pick and shovels (Nvidia, TSMC — infrastructure) vs.
enablers (cloud providers — Azure, AWS, GCP) vs. application layer (vertical AI apps);
who captures most AI value long-term?
(6) Cybersecurity: TAM ($500B by 2030); consolidation from point solutions to platforms
(Microsoft, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto); identity security, cloud security, OT security growth.
(7) Valuation discipline: how to value high-growth tech (EV/NTM Revenue vs. Rule of 40;
DCF using terminal FCF margin assumptions); when to use EV/EBITDA for mature tech.
Format: Technology Research Framework with Sub-Sector Cycle Analysis, Software Metrics,
Internet Moats, AI Framework, Cybersecurity, and Valuation Discipline.
Inputs: [SUB-SECTOR FOCUS | COMPANY | CURRENT VALUATION | KEY FINANCIAL METRICS |
COMPETITIVE POSITION | PRIMARY INVESTMENT DEBATE | ANALYST RATING INTENT]

title: The CDPQ Infrastructure: Long-Duration Asset Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 406 — The CDPQ Infrastructure: Long-Duration Asset Strategy
Act as Senior PM at CDPQ Infrastructure. Build a long-duration infrastructure
investment strategy for a Canadian pension fund.
Deliver: (1) CDPQ Infrastructure mandate: generate long-duration, stable cash flows
matching pension liabilities; target 7-9% net return; global diversification.
(2) Asset class fit for pension liabilities: infrastructure cash flows are long duration
(20-40 years), inflation-linked, and uncorrelated to public markets — ideal for
pension ALM.
(3) Core infrastructure categories: regulated utilities (electricity, gas, water);
transport (airports, toll roads, ports); social infrastructure (hospitals, schools
under availability PPP); digital infrastructure (towers, fiber, data centres).
(4) Global portfolio construction: target geographic diversification (Americas 40%,
Europe 35%, APAC 25%); currency matching (CAD liabilities → prefer CAD or hedged assets);
sector diversification across infrastructure categories.
(5) Greenfield vs. brownfield: CDPQ's increasing greenfield allocation (higher return,
higher risk, development capability required); brownfield (lower risk, competitive).
(6) ESG integration: Net-Zero 2050 commitment for infrastructure portfolio; exclusion
of thermal coal infrastructure; climate physical risk in asset selection.
(7) Co-investment and consortium: CDPQ co-invests with other pension funds in large
infrastructure deals (saving on fund management fees); direct deal capability.
Format: Long-Duration Infrastructure Strategy with Asset Class Fit, Portfolio Construction,
Geographic Allocation, Greenfield vs. Brownfield, ESG, and Co-Investment Model.
Inputs: [PENSION FUND SIZE | INFRASTRUCTURE ALLOCATION | RETURN TARGET | LIABILITY
DURATION | GEOGRAPHIC FOCUS | GREENFIELD APPETITE | ESG COMMITMENT]

title: The Citi Research: Global Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT) Analysis
prompt_text:
PROMPT 407 — The Citi Research: Global Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT) Analysis
Act as Head of REIT Research at Citi. Build a comprehensive REIT
investment framework across property sectors.
Deliver: (1) REIT fundamentals: REIT structure (distribute 90% of taxable income); FFO
(Funds From Operations = Net Income + D&A − Gains on Sales) as primary earnings metric;
AFFO (Adjusted FFO) deducting maintenance capex; dividend yield as valuation anchor.
(2) REIT valuation: P/FFO (price-to-FFO multiple); NAV analysis (property values minus
debt = equity NAV); premium or discount to NAV; WACC for REIT cap rate analysis.
(3) Sector allocation — winners and losers:
(a) Industrial/Logistics (Prologis — structural tailwind from e-commerce, near-shoring);
(b) Data Centres (Equinix, Digital Realty — AI demand surge);
(c) Multifamily (AvalonBay, EQR — rental demand strength but supply risk in Sun Belt);
(d) Healthcare (Welltower, Ventas — senior housing occupancy recovery);
(e) Office (structural headwind — hybrid work, sublease overhang).
(4) Interest rate sensitivity: REITs are rate-sensitive (bond proxy); rising rates compress
REIT multiples and increase cost of capital; floating rate debt risk.
(5) Cap rate analysis: implied cap rate for each REIT subsector; cap rate vs. Treasury
spread (risk premium); compression/expansion scenarios.
(6) Capital structure: conservative leverage (35-45% debt-to-total assets); unencumbered
asset pool; ATM equity issuance for accretive acquisitions.
(7) ESG in REITs: GRESB (Global Real Estate Sustainability Benchmark) scores; energy
efficiency certifications; tenant ESG demands.
Format: REIT Research Framework with Valuation Methodology, Sector Allocation, Rate
Sensitivity, Cap Rate Analysis, Capital Structure, and ESG Assessment.
Inputs: [REIT NAME | SECTOR | FFO/SHARE | DIVIDEND YIELD | LEVERAGE | NAV ESTIMATE |
RATE SENSITIVITY | PRIMARY INVESTMENT THESIS | RATING INTENT]

title: The Blackstone Tactical Opportunities Fund
prompt_text:
PROMPT 408 — The Blackstone Tactical Opportunities Fund
Act as MD at Blackstone's Tactical Opportunities (Tac Opps) group. Build
an opportunistic cross-asset investment thesis for a complex situation.
Deliver: (1) Tac Opps mandate: invest in complex, often mispriced opportunities across
asset classes and geographies that don't fit neatly into traditional PE, credit, or
real estate buckets; target gross IRR 20%+.
(2) Opportunity identification: forced sellers (regulatory-driven asset sales, COVID-
distressed, emerging market currency crises); complexity discount (intercreditor disputes,
regulatory uncertainty); illiquidity premium (assets that aren't broadly auctioned).
(3) Tac Opps asset types: distressed sovereign debt, structured equity (warrants +
debt in restructuring), royalty streams, financial regulatory capital trades,
insurance portfolio acquisitions, structured credit in stressed markets.
(4) Due diligence for complex situations: rapid diligence framework (limited time to act);
key assumptions checklist; independent expert sourcing.
(5) Structuring: tailored transaction structure to capture maximum upside while
protecting downside; equity kickers on debt; warrants; convertible instruments.
(6) Risk management: position sizing for high-conviction complex trades; portfolio
diversification across uncorrelated Tac Opps themes; scenario analysis.
(7) Exit flexibility: structure investments with multiple exit pathways (IPO, secondary,
strategic sale, loan repayment, maturity); avoid single-path dependency.
Format: Tac Opps Framework with Opportunity Identification, Asset Types, Due Diligence,
Structuring, Risk Management, and Exit Flexibility.
Inputs: [OPPORTUNITY TYPE | GEOGRAPHY | COMPLEXITY DRIVER | INVESTMENT SIZE |
PROPOSED STRUCTURE | TARGET IRR | PRIMARY UPSIDE CATALYST | DOWNSIDE PROTECTION]

title: The Oliver Wyman Climate Stress Testing for Banks
prompt_text:
PROMPT 409 — The Oliver Wyman Climate Stress Testing for Banks
Act as Partner at Oliver Wyman's Climate Risk practice. Design a
climate stress testing framework for a major commercial bank.
Deliver: (1) Climate stress testing framework: TCFD-aligned scenario analysis; physical
risk vs. transition risk; NGFS (Network for Greening the Financial System) scenarios
(Net Zero 2050, Delayed Transition, Current Policies, Hot House World).
(2) Transition risk modeling: loan portfolio carbon intensity by sector; sector-level
PD (Probability of Default) uplift under carbon pricing scenarios; most vulnerable
sectors (oil & gas, coal, steel, cement, auto, aviation).
(3) Physical risk modeling: property-level flood, wildfire, and storm surge exposure
in real estate and mortgage portfolios; damage cost estimation; LTV deterioration
under physical climate scenarios.
(4) Stress test scenarios: (a) Orderly transition (carbon price reaches $250/tonne
by 2050 gradually); (b) Disorderly transition (abrupt policy change, stranded assets);
(c) Hot House World (no policy action, severe physical damage by 2080).
(5) Credit loss quantification: climate-adjusted PD and LGD for each sector;
additional credit losses vs. baseline scenario; capital adequacy under climate stress.
(6) Regulatory compliance: ECB Guide on climate risks; Bank of England CBES (Climate
Biennial Exploratory Scenario); Fed pilot climate scenario analysis (2023).
(7) Data challenges: scope 3 data gaps; PCAF (Partnership for Carbon Accounting
Financials) methodology for financed emissions; third-party data quality.
Format: Climate Stress Testing Framework with Scenario Library, Transition/Physical Risk
Modeling, Credit Loss Quantification, Regulatory Compliance, and Data Management.
Inputs: [BANK TYPE | PORTFOLIO COMPOSITION | KEY SECTORS | CLIMATE SCENARIO PREFERENCE |
REGULATORY REQUIREMENT | DATA AVAILABILITY | PRIMARY CLIMATE RISK CONCERN]

title: The KKR Global Macro: Inflation and Interest Rate Strategy
prompt_text:
PROMPT 410 — The KKR Global Macro: Inflation and Interest Rate Strategy
Act as Chief Global Economist at KKR. Build a comprehensive inflation and
interest rate investment framework for the current macroeconomic environment.
Deliver: (1) Inflation regime analysis: structural drivers of higher inflation (fiscal
expansion, deglobalisation, energy transition costs, labour market tightening);
cyclical vs. structural inflation debate; K&M (KKR's McVey) New Regime thesis.
(2) Central bank credibility: inflation expectations anchoring vs. unanchoring risk;
Fed terminal rate assessment; real rate trajectory (nominal minus inflation expectations).
(3) Asset class implications of persistent inflation: (a) Fixed income (negative for
long bonds — duration risk); (b) Equities (inflation benefits pricing-power companies,
hurts interest-rate-sensitive, growth stocks); (c) Real assets (inflation hedge —
infrastructure, real estate, commodities); (d) Private credit (floating rate — positive).
(4) Sector rotation for inflation: overweight energy, materials, financials, and
real assets; underweight long-duration growth stocks and REITs with fixed rents.
(5) Term premium: historically suppressed term premium re-pricing (QT + fiscal supply);
impact on 10yr Treasury yield; duration shortening strategy.
(6) Credit quality preference: in inflationary environment with rising rates, avoid
highly leveraged lower-quality credit (debt service burden increases); prefer
floating-rate senior secured and high-quality IG.
(7) Portfolio construction for inflation: target 20-30% real assets; floating rate
credit overweight; equity tilted toward pricing power quality; short duration bias.
Format: Inflation/Rate Strategy with Regime Analysis, Central Bank Assessment,
Asset Class Implications, Sector Rotation, Term Premium, Credit Quality, and Portfolio.
Inputs: [PORTFOLIO TYPE | CURRENT INFLATION RATE | RATE ASSUMPTION | DURATION TARGET |
REAL ASSET ALLOCATION | CREDIT QUALITY | GEOGRAPHIC FOCUS | PRIMARY MACRO VIEW]

title: The Deloitte Valuation: Business Combination Accounting
prompt_text:
PROMPT 411 — The Deloitte Valuation: Business Combination Accounting
Act as Partner at Deloitte's Valuation and Business Modeling practice.
Design a business combination accounting and financial reporting framework.
Deliver: (1) ASC 805 / IFRS 3 overview: identify the acquirer; determine the acquisition
date; measure and recognize identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value;
calculate and record goodwill.
(2) Acquisition method mechanics: purchase price (consideration transferred +
contingent consideration at fair value + equity awards held by target employees);
NCI (Non-Controlling Interest) measurement (full goodwill vs. partial goodwill method).
(3) Intangible asset recognition: must recognize all identifiable intangibles meeting
separability or contractual-legal criterion; common intangibles (customer relationships,
trade names, technology, order backlog, non-competes, favorable leases).
(4) Fair value measurement for PPA: level 1 (quoted prices) — rare in M&A; level 2
(observable inputs); level 3 (unobservable — most PPA intangibles); income approach
(DCF for customer relationships), market approach, cost approach.
(5) Contingent consideration: earnouts at fair value on acquisition date; subsequent
fair value changes recognized in P&L (not goodwill); financial instrument vs.
equity classification of earnout.
(6) Measurement period: up to 12 months after acquisition date to finalize PPA;
measurement period adjustments affect goodwill retrospectively.
(7) Disclosure requirements: ASC 805/IFRS 3 footnote disclosures; pro-forma revenue
and earnings; goodwill by segment; intangible assets by class; contingent consideration.
Format: Business Combination Accounting Framework with Acquisition Method, Intangible
Recognition, FV Measurement, Contingent Consideration, Measurement Period, and Disclosures.
Inputs: [ACQUIRER | TARGET | DEAL CONSIDERATION | INDUSTRY | KEY INTANGIBLES |
CONTINGENT CONSIDERATION | NCI MEASUREMENT METHOD | PRIMARY ACCOUNTING CHALLENGE]

title: The JPMAM Long-Duration Fixed Income for Pension Funds
prompt_text:
PROMPT 412 — The JPMAM Long-Duration Fixed Income for Pension Funds
Act as Head of Long-Duration Fixed Income at JPMorgan Asset Management.
Build a long-duration bond portfolio for pension liability matching.
Deliver: (1) Pension LDI context: liability discount rate (corporate AA bond rate);
liability duration (typically 12-16 years for mature closed plans); match asset
duration to liability duration to minimize funded status volatility.
(2) Long-duration instruments: long US Treasury (30yr), long IG corporate (20-30yr),
STRIPS (zero coupon — maximum duration per dollar), long-duration TIPS for
inflation-linked liabilities.
(3) Credit allocation within LDI: long IG corporate bonds offer 100-150bps OAS premium
over Treasuries; spread risk vs. credit enhancement of funded status; sector
allocation (utilities, financials, industrials) within long duration.
(4) Physical vs. overlay: physical long bonds (full allocation); swap overlay (use
interest rate swaps to add duration without full cash outlay — allows more return-
seeking in the growth portfolio); combination approach.
(5) Liability benchmark construction: custom liability-matching benchmark using BAML
LGFUT or Bloomberg Long Gov/Credit; duration matching precision.
(6) Glide path integration: as funded status improves (above 100%), increase LDI
hedge ratio (from 50% to 75% to 100% hedge); coordinate LDI trades with
de-risking triggers.
(7) Credit risk management: credit deterioration tracking (fallen angels in LDI portfolio);
sector and issuer concentration limits; turnover minimization for tax efficiency.
Format: LDI Portfolio with Duration Framework, Instrument Selection, Physical vs.
Overlay, Liability Benchmark, Glide Path Integration, and Credit Risk Management.
Inputs: [PLAN SIZE | LIABILITY DURATION | FUNDED RATIO | CURRENT HEDGE RATIO |
CREDIT QUALITY LIMITS | PHYSICAL VS. OVERLAY PREFERENCE | GLIDE PATH TRIGGERS]

title: The McKinsey Corporate Strategy: Portfolio Choices and Capital Allocation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 413 — The McKinsey Corporate Strategy: Portfolio Choices and Capital Allocation
Act as Senior Partner at McKinsey's Strategy practice. Build a corporate
portfolio strategy and capital allocation framework for a diversified corporation.
Deliver: (1) Portfolio strategy framework: GE-McKinsey 9-box matrix (industry attractiveness
× competitive position); which businesses to invest, hold, or divest.
(2) Capital allocation principles: allocate capital to businesses earning above their
cost of capital; reduce allocation to value-destroying businesses regardless of size;
zero-based capital allocation (not incremental to prior year).
(3) Business unit performance assessment: ROIC vs. WACC by business unit (create vs.
destroy value); organic growth rate vs. market growth rate; competitive position trend.
(4) Divestiture case: when to divest — structural underperformance, strategic misfit,
better owner for the asset (private equity or strategic), capital redeployment opportunity.
(5) M&A allocation: which business units have the most value-accretive inorganic growth
opportunities? M&A capability by unit (integration track record, deal pipeline).
(6) Capital return: when excess cash exceeds investment needs, return to shareholders;
dividend policy (stable vs. progressive vs. special dividends); buyback program mechanics.
(7) Corporate centre costs: justify corporate overhead by services provided to business
units; zero-based approach to corporate costs; shared services economics.
Format: Portfolio Strategy with 9-Box Matrix, Capital Allocation Framework, Business
Unit Assessment, Divestiture Case, M&A Allocation, Capital Return, and Corporate Costs.
Inputs: [COMPANY | REVENUE | BUSINESS UNITS | ROIC BY UNIT | WACC | M&A BUDGET |
CURRENT CAPITAL ALLOCATION | PRIMARY PORTFOLIO CHALLENGE | BOARD PRIORITIES]

title: The Morgan Stanley Investment Banking: Cross-Border M&A Execution
prompt_text:
PROMPT 414 — The Morgan Stanley Investment Banking: Cross-Border M&A Execution
Act as MD at Morgan Stanley's International M&A team. Manage the execution
of a complex cross-border M&A transaction.
Deliver: (1) Cross-border M&A complexity: regulatory approvals in multiple jurisdictions;
currency and financing coordination; cultural integration across different management
styles; differing legal frameworks (contract law, employment law, IP law).
(2) Multi-jurisdictional regulatory timeline: identify all required regulatory approvals
(antitrust: DOJ/FTC/EU Commission/China SAMR; foreign investment: CFIUS/NSIA/FIRB;
sector-specific: banking, telecom, defense); longest-path analysis (which jurisdiction
governs closing timeline?).
(3) CFIUS process: mandatory filing vs. voluntary filing; covered business determination;
national security risk assessment; mitigation agreements (NSPAS — National Security
Agreements); timing (30-day review + 45-day investigation).
(4) Financing: multi-currency acquisition financing (bridge in USD, EUR); bank
commitment letter in multiple currencies; post-close refinancing strategy.
(5) MAC (Material Adverse Change): definition must capture target-specific risks vs.
industry-wide risks; COVID-era precedents (Bed Bath & Beyond, Akorn); seller
resistance to broad MAC definitions.
(6) Employee matters cross-border: European Works Council consultation requirement
(must begin before signing in some jurisdictions); TUPE/ARD in EU; retention plans
for key employees in each market.
(7) Post-close integration planning: Day-1 country-by-country operational readiness;
brand and customer communication in each market; ERP harmonisation across geographies.
Format: Cross-Border M&A Execution Guide with Regulatory Timeline, CFIUS Analysis,
Multi-Currency Financing, MAC Definition, Employee Matters, and Integration Planning.
Inputs: [ACQUIRER COUNTRY | TARGET COUNTRY | INDUSTRY | DEAL SIZE | REGULATORY
CONCERNS | FINANCING STRUCTURE | TIMELINE | PRIMARY EXECUTION CHALLENGE]

title: The Fitch Ratings: Project Finance Credit Rating
prompt_text:
PROMPT 415 — The Fitch Ratings: Project Finance Credit Rating
Act as Director at Fitch Ratings' Infrastructure & Project Finance group.
Apply Fitch's rating methodology to a project finance transaction.
Deliver: (1) Fitch project finance criteria: Midpoint Rating approach (evaluate project
performance across multiple scenarios); construction risk, operating risk, revenue
risk, counterparty risk, and structural risk.
(2) Revenue risk assessment: volume risk (user demand forecasts — traffic, power output);
price risk (regulated tariff vs. PPA vs. merchant); revenue certainty score.
(3) Operating risk: O&M (Operations & Maintenance) cost forecasting; independent
engineer assessment; technology risk (proven vs. emerging); performance bonuses/penalties.
(4) Debt service coverage: base case DSCR (must exceed 1.0× in all scenarios);
minimum average DSCR across project life; LLCR (Loan Life Cover Ratio); PLCR.
(5) Scenario analysis: low case (revenue -15%, opex +10%, construction delay 6 months);
high case (revenue +10%, opex on budget); minimum DSCR in low case determines rating.
(6) Counterparty analysis: offtaker credit (if offtaker is rated <BBB-, project rating
is capped at offtaker); EPC contractor credit for construction completion guarantee.
(7) Structural features: DSRA (6 months of debt service); distribution lock-up
(DSCR must exceed 1.10× to distribute to equity); step-in rights for lenders.
Format: Project Finance Rating Analysis with Revenue Risk, DSCR Model, Scenario
Analysis, Counterparty Assessment, Structural Features, and Rating Rationale.
Inputs: [PROJECT TYPE | COUNTRY | REVENUE STRUCTURE | BASE CASE DSCR | LOW CASE DSCR |
TENOR | OFFTAKER | TARGET RATING | PRIMARY CREDIT CONCERN]

title: The Accenture Finance Shared Services Transformation
prompt_text:
PROMPT 416 — The Accenture Finance Shared Services Transformation
Act as Managing Director at Accenture's Finance Transformation practice.
Design a Global Business Services (GBS) and Shared Services transformation.
Deliver: (1) GBS model: consolidate finance transactional activities into centralized
GBS centres; reduce cost (30-50% savings typical) and improve quality and control.
(2) Scope definition: which processes move to GBS (accounts payable, accounts receivable,
general ledger, payroll, expense management, reporting) vs. remain local (tax, treasury,
FP&A, business partnering).
(3) Location strategy: nearshore (India, Philippines, Poland, Mexico) vs. offshore vs.
hybrid; cost-quality-timezone trade-offs; talent availability by process type.
(4) Process standardisation: before moving to GBS, standardise processes (one
global chart of accounts, one expense policy, one AP process); non-standard processes
increase GBS cost, not reduce.
(5) Technology enablement: RPA for invoice processing; AI for expense report auditing;
OCR for invoice data extraction; ServiceNow for GBS service management.
(6) Governance model: GBS as a cost centre vs. service company vs. profit centre;
SLA (Service Level Agreement) framework; chargeback methodology to business units.
(7) Change management: business unit resistance to losing local finance teams;
country HR implications (redundancies, TUPE); communication strategy.
Format: GBS Transformation with Scope Definition, Location Strategy, Process
Standardisation, Technology, Governance Model, and Change Management.
Inputs: [COMPANY REVENUE | CURRENT FINANCE HEADCOUNT | COUNTRIES | PRIMARY PROCESSES |
TARGET SAVINGS | LOCATION PREFERENCE | ERP PLATFORM | TIMELINE]

title: The Pemberton Asset Management: European Private Credit
prompt_text:
PROMPT 417 — The Pemberton Asset Management: European Private Credit
Act as MD at Pemberton Asset Management. Build a European private credit
strategy targeting senior secured direct lending.
Deliver: (1) European direct lending differentiation: bank retrenchment (Basel IV
increasing bank capital cost for leveraged lending); PE sponsor demand for certainty;
covenant-lite evolution in European direct lending.
(2) Pemberton's focus: senior secured unitranche lending (€10-100M EBITDA companies);
pan-European coverage; sector diversification across defensive sectors.
